summary.scope: All unique canonicalDifficulty=hard questions, regardless of instructionalRole; automated indicators are screening candidates, not final editorial findings.

items.stem: A hurricane permanently destroys part of an economy's productive capital, and real GDP falls below its old potential level. Why would it be wrong to assume ordinary recessionary-gap self-correction must restore the old level of output?
options: Destroyed capital can shift LRAS left and lower potential output.
Any fall in real GDP forces aggregate demand to shift permanently left.
Nominal wages cannot adjust after a supply-side disturbance.
SRAS always shifts right enough to restore the pre-shock LRAS position.
items.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

items.stem: Comparing the original long-run equilibrium C with the new long-run equilibrium B, what is true?
options: GDP returns to 100; prices rise from 125 to 175.
GDP rises to 125; prices remain fixed at 125 throughout.
GDP falls to 75; prices remain fixed at 150 throughout.
GDP stays at 100; prices fall from 125 back to 100.
items.feedback: LRAS stays at 100, so long-run real GDP returns to 100. The long-run price level is higher at B than at C.

items.stem: A student attributes the move from A to B to higher aggregate demand because real GDP rises. Which correction best fits the graph?
options: AD shifts right while SRAS and LRAS both stay fixed.
SRAS shifts left while AD0 and LRAS both stay fixed.
LRAS shifts left while SRAS and AD0 both stay fixed.
SRAS and LRAS shift right while AD0 stays fixed.
items.feedback: The graph holds AD constant and shows the supply side improving. That raises potential output and lowers the price level.

items.stem: Real GDP is below its old potential level after a permanent decline in labor-force participation. Which diagnostic prevents a mistaken forecast that ordinary self-correction must restore the old output level?
options: Check whether lower productive capacity shifted LRAS left.
Assume every output decline is caused by aggregate demand.
Hold LRAS fixed because productive capacity cannot change.
Assume falling wages always restore the pre-shock quantity of labor and output.
items.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

items.stem: Consumer confidence rises while firms become more pessimistic about future sales. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: Consumption and investment both tend to rise; both changes shift AD right
Consumption and investment both tend to fall; both changes shift AD left
Consumption tends to rise and investment to fall; the two changes cancel because they oppose
Consumption tends to rise and investment to fall; relative changes determine the net shift
items.feedback: Confidence raises consumption, while pessimism lowers investment; magnitudes determine the net shift.

items.stem: The price level falls, but taxes rise at the same time. Which statement is most precise?
options: Price level: movement along AD; taxes: movement along AD.
Price level: AD shifts right; taxes: AD shifts left.
Price level: movement along AD; taxes: AD shifts left.
Price level: AD shifts left; taxes: AD shifts left.
items.feedback: The price level is on the graph’s vertical axis; taxes are an external shifter.

items.stem: Foreign income falls sharply while domestic firms increase investment. The effect on domestic aggregate demand is:
options: A certain rightward shift
A certain leftward shift
Ambiguous because net exports fall while investment rises.
A movement upward along AD
items.feedback: Lower foreign income reduces exports, while higher investment raises AD.

items.stem: A higher price level increases money demand, which raises interest rates and reduces investment. This sequence explains:
options: A rightward shift of LRAS
A rightward shift of AD
A leftward shift of SRAS
A movement upward and leftward along the existing AD curve.
items.feedback: The interest-rate effect is one reason quantity of real GDP demanded falls as the price level rises.

items.stem: The price level rises at the same time that the government cuts taxes. Which graph description is correct?
options: The price rise shifts AD left; the tax cut moves downward along that curve
The price rise moves upward along AD; the tax cut shifts AD right
The price rise moves downward along AD; the tax cut shifts AD right
The price rise moves upward along AD; the tax cut shifts AD left
items.feedback: The price-level change causes movement along AD; the tax cut shifts the curve.

items.stem: A student calls the change from AD0 to AD1 an increase in aggregate supply because more output is shown. At a price level of 50, which response fits the diagram?
options: Quantity demanded falls by about 55 units; this is a demand contraction, not a reduction in productive capacity.
Output capacity rises by about 55 units; the horizontal distance measures the shift in long-run supply.
Quantity demanded rises by about 55 units; this is a demand shift, not evidence of increased productive capacity.
Quantity demanded rises by about 155 units; the new quantity is also the size of the demand shift.
items.feedback: At price 50 the two demand curves show roughly 100 and 155 units. Their difference is about 55. Comparing quantities at a common price identifies an AD shift; it does not measure productive capacity.

items.stem: If policymakers wanted to offset the AD shift shown, which short-run pattern are they responding to?
options: Lower output with downward pressure on the price level
Higher output with upward pressure on the price level
Higher output with downward pressure on the price level
Lower output with upward pressure on the price level
items.feedback: A decrease in AD lowers both real GDP and the price level in the short run.

items.stem: A country’s currency appreciates and foreign economies enter recession while domestic consumer confidence rises. The net AD effect is:
options: Left: consumption and net exports both fall
Right: consumption and net exports both rise
Ambiguous: consumption rises while net exports fall
Unchanged: higher consumption exactly offsets lower net exports
items.feedback: Confidence raises C, while appreciation and lower foreign income reduce NX.

items.stem: In the liquidity-preference model, a lower price level reduces transaction money demand. At the same time the central bank independently reduces nominal money supply. The relative sizes of the changes are not given, and other investment determinants are fixed. Which interest-rate and investment conclusion is warranted?
options: Lower money demand lowers the rate; lower supply also lowers it; investment must rise
Lower money demand raises the rate; lower supply also raises it; investment must fall
Lower money demand raises the rate; lower supply lowers it; the changes must cancel
Lower money demand lowers the rate; lower supply raises it; investment’s net change is undetermined
items.feedback: Lower money demand tends to reduce the equilibrium rate; a lower money supply tends to increase it. Without relative magnitudes, the net rate and therefore interest-sensitive investment cannot be signed. The usual price-level channel is not a guarantee about the outcome when policy also changes.

items.stem: The price level falls while firms cut investment. What occurs?
options: Only movement upward along AD
Only a rightward AD shift
Movement downward along AD plus a leftward AD shift.
A rightward SRAS shift only
items.feedback: The lower price level changes quantity demanded; lower investment shifts AD left.

items.stem: Consumer confidence rises and the currency appreciates. The net AD direction is:
options: No change because the effects are equal
Ambiguous; the two effects oppose each other.
Certainly rightward
Certainly leftward
items.feedback: The two components move in opposite directions, and magnitudes matter.

items.stem: A country initially sells $80 of exports. Foreign income rises while domestic business confidence falls. No magnitudes are given. What can be concluded about aggregate demand when both changes occur?
options: Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; the net AD direction is uncertain
Exports and investment both tend to rise; AD shifts right
Exports and investment both tend to fall; AD shifts left
Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; opposite signs establish exactly unchanged AD
items.feedback: Foreign demand supports exports while weaker confidence reduces investment. Competing components require relative magnitudes before assigning a net AD shift.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank makes a loan by crediting the borrower's checking account. The borrower then pays a supplier at another bank, so reserves are transferred between the banks. How does making the loan change the first bank's balance sheet, and how does the later payment change it?
options: Making the loan adds a loan asset and a deposit liability; the later payment reduces the first bank's reserves and the borrower's deposit.
Making the loan reduces reserves; the later payment creates the loan and increases bank capital.
Making the loan adds reserves and a deposit; the later payment leaves both banks' reserves unchanged.
Making the loan reduces deposits; the later payment cancels the first bank's loan asset.
items.feedback: Crediting the account initially adds a loan asset and a deposit liability. The later outgoing payment reduces reserves and the deposit liability; the loan remains an asset.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a 10 percent reserve requirement, and $95,000 in reserves. If deposits increase by $100,000 and reserves rise by $20,000, the bank’s new excess reserves are:
items.feedback: New deposits are $900,000, required reserves are $90,000, and actual reserves are $115,000.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has $25 million in assets and $1.5 million in capital. An 8 percent asset loss occurs. What is the new capital position?
options: $0.5 million.
-$0.5 million.
-$2.0 million.
$1.5 million.
items.feedback: An 8 percent asset loss is $2 million, reducing $1.5 million of capital to -$0.5 million.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A banking system has a 10 percent reserve requirement, but banks hold an additional 5 percent of deposits as excess reserves and the public holds no currency. A simple effective deposit multiplier is closest to:
items.feedback: If 15 percent of deposits is retained, the simple effective multiplier is about 1/0.15 = 6.67.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: Assume the bank cannot obtain extra reserves, sell assets, or retain any new loan proceeds as deposits; every new loan payment would leave the bank. A bank has $900,000 in deposits, a 15 percent reserve requirement, and $135,000 in actual reserves. What can the bank do immediately?
options: It cannot lend more because actual reserves equal required reserves.
It can lend $135,000 because all reserves are excess reserves.
It can lend $765,000 because deposits minus reserves are lendable.
It must borrow $15,000 from the Fed.
items.feedback: Required reserves are 0.15 x $900,000 = $135,000. Actual reserves equal required reserves, so there are no excess reserves to lend.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has $1,200,000 in deposits, $210,000 in reserves, and a 12.5 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, how much can it lend?
items.feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $1,200,000 = $150,000. Excess reserves are $210,000 - $150,000 = $60,000.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has $1 million in deposits and $90,000 in reserves. The reserve requirement is 10 percent. What is the bank's reserve problem?
options: It is short $10,000 in required reserves.
It has $90,000 in excess reserves.
It can lend $10,000 immediately.
It has exactly enough reserves.
items.feedback: Required reserves are $100,000. The bank has $90,000, so it is short $10,000.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: If excess reserves are $25,000, actual reserves are $85,000, and the reserve ratio is 12 percent, what are deposits?
items.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $85,000 - $25,000 = $60,000. Deposits = $60,000 / 0.12 = $500,000.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has $50 million in assets, $46 million in liabilities, and then suffers a 9 percent asset loss. What is the new capital position?
options: Capital falls from $4 million to negative $500,000.
Capital falls from $4 million to $3.64 million.
Capital rises from $4 million to $8.5 million.
Capital is unchanged because liabilities absorb asset losses first.
items.feedback: Initial capital is $4 million. A 9 percent asset loss on $50 million is $4.5 million, so capital becomes negative $500,000.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has actual reserves of $96,000, excess reserves of $24,000, and a reserve requirement of 12 percent. What are deposits?
items.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $96,000 - $24,000 = $72,000. Deposits are $72,000 / 0.12 = $600,000.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank’s assets fall by 4 percent while its liabilities remain unchanged. Before the loss, capital was 5 percent of assets. What percentage of the initial capital is lost?
options: 80 percent
4 percent
20 percent
100 percent
items.feedback: Taking initial assets as 100, initial capital is 5. The asset loss is 4, so 4/5 = 80 percent of the initial capital is lost.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a required reserve ratio of 12.5 percent, and actual reserves of $140,000. How much can it lend before hitting its required reserve level?
items.feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $800,000 = $100,000. Excess reserves are $140,000 - $100,000 = $40,000.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: Use a reserve-constrained banking model, with no other changes. A bank has $300,000 in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It currently holds $45,000 in reserves. If it lends all excess reserves, what will its reserves and loans change by? Assume the borrower immediately pays someone at another bank and the entire payment settles in reserves.
options: Reserves fall by $15,000 and loans rise by $15,000.
Reserves fall by $30,000 and loans rise by $30,000.
Reserves fall by $45,000 and loans rise by $45,000.
Reserves rise by $15,000 and loans fall by $15,000.
items.feedback: Required reserves are $30,000, so excess reserves are $15,000. Lending those lowers reserves by $15,000 and raises loans by $15,000.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has $2 million in assets and $100,000 in capital. If asset values fall by 5 percent, what happens to capital?
options: It falls to zero.
It falls by $5,000.
It rises to $200,000.
It stays at $100,000.
items.feedback: Five percent of $2 million is $100,000. That wipes out the bank's $100,000 in capital.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has reserves of $320 and deposits of $1600; the simplified required reserve ratio is 10%. Management says it can lend all $320 without acquiring reserves. Which correction is justified before considering capital and credit risk?
options: Only $160 is initially excess reserves; the $160 required portion must remain against existing deposits
All $320 is excess because required reserves are calculated only after lending
No reserves are excess because every reserve dollar is bank capital
It can lend $3200 immediately from its own reserves because the system multiplier applies to one bank's first loan
items.feedback: Required reserves are .10×1600 = 160; excess is 320−160 = 160. A single bank's immediate capacity is distinct from a system-wide redepositing maximum.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has deposits of $1800, reserves of $360, and a required reserve ratio of 10% in a simplified model. A depositor withdraws $180 in currency. Assume no other balance-sheet change. How does the withdrawal affect required and excess reserves?
options: Reserves stay $360, required reserves become $162, and excess reserves $198
Reserves become $180, required reserves become $198, and there is a $18 shortfall
Reserves become $180, required reserves $162, and excess reserves $18
Reserves become $180, required reserves remain $180, and excess reserves are zero
items.feedback: The cash withdrawal reduces deposits and reserves by 180. Required reserves are 10% of 1620 = 162; actual reserves 180 leave 18 excess. Both sides of the reserve calculation must reflect the withdrawal.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank has assets of $2400, deposit liabilities of $2000 and capital of $400. Loan losses reduce assets by $600; liabilities do not fall. Which remedy addresses the resulting problem?
options: Capital: +$400; loan losses affect liquidity rather than the owners' residual claim.
Capital: +$1000; writing off loans reduces deposit liabilities rather than bank assets.
Capital: $0 after borrowing $200; the loan raises assets without matching liabilities.
Capital: −$200; new equity addresses insolvency, a liquidity loan alone does not.
items.feedback: After losses, assets are 1800 and liabilities 2000; capital is −200. Borrowed liquidity raises assets and liabilities equally, leaving net worth unchanged.

items.topic: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
items.stem: A bank grants a $220 loan by crediting the borrower's checking account; no cash leaves initially. Which entries and subsequent constraint are correct?
options: Deposit liabilities fall $220 while loan assets rise; the bank's net worth rises immediately
The bank must first reduce another customer's deposit by $220; total deposits cannot increase
Loan assets and deposit liabilities each rise $220; later payments may require reserve settlement
Reserve assets and capital each rise $220; no deposit liability is created
items.feedback: Loan origination creates a bank asset and a matching deposit liability, not instant bank equity. If the deposit is spent to another bank, settlement can create a reserve need.

items.stem: A price ceiling is set above equilibrium. Why does it usually have no effect?
options: The market price remains below the legal maximum
Because all price ceilings create shortages
Because sellers are forced to charge the maximum
Because quantity supplied must equal zero
items.feedback: A nonbinding ceiling is above equilibrium, so the market can still reach equilibrium below the legal maximum.

items.stem: A rent ceiling lowers the money rent but causes long search times, side payments, and poorer maintenance. What is the best interpretation?
options: Lower legal rent can be offset by nonmoney costs.
The ceiling eliminated scarcity
The ceiling created a surplus of apartments
The price ceiling shifted demand left
items.feedback: A binding ceiling can lower the legal price but create search costs, rationing, and quality decline.

items.stem: Refer to the price-control graph. Officials lower a price ceiling from $50 to $40 and predict that the market price will fall by $10. With demand and supply unchanged, which assessment is correct?
options: Price falls from $50 to $40 because the ceiling sets the transaction price.
Price stays $30 because both legal maxima permit the equilibrium price.
Price rises from $30 to $40 because sellers charge the highest legal price.
Price falls from $30 to $20 because the legal maximum fell by $10.
items.feedback: The intersection is $30 and 200 units. Both ceilings are above $30, so both are nonbinding. Lowering a nonbinding ceiling while it remains above equilibrium changes the legal limit, not the competitive market outcome.

items.stem: Refer to the price-control graph. A policy holds the price at $20. What is the full market result?
options: A binding price ceiling with a shortage of 100 units
A nonbinding price ceiling with no effect
A binding price floor with a surplus of 100 units
A nonbinding price floor with no effect
items.feedback: $20 is below the $30 equilibrium, so it is a binding ceiling. At $20, Qd is 250 and Qs is 150, so the shortage is 100.

items.stem: Refer to the price-control graph. At $10, what are quantity demanded and quantity supplied?
options: Quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100
Quantity demanded is 100 and quantity supplied is 300
Quantity demanded is 150 and quantity supplied is 250
Quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150
items.feedback: At a low price of $10, buyers demand 300 units while sellers supply 100 units.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Relative to the competitive equilibrium, how do quantity demanded and quantity supplied change at the $1,000 ceiling?
options: Quantity demanded -100; quantity supplied +100.
Quantity demanded +200; quantity supplied unchanged.
Quantity demanded unchanged; quantity supplied -200.
Quantity demanded +100; quantity supplied -100.
items.feedback: At equilibrium both quantities are 150. At $1,000, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 50. Demand therefore rises by 100 while supply falls by 100, opening a 200-unit shortage.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What effect does the $2,000 rent ceiling have on the market?
options: Nonbinding; the market clears at 1,500 dollars
Binding; it creates a 200-thousand shortage
Binding; it forces rent to exactly 2,000 dollars
Nonbinding; it creates a 200-thousand surplus
items.feedback: The $2,000 ceiling is above the $1,500 equilibrium rent, so it is nonbinding and the market remains at equilibrium.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What price and quantity result when the rent ceiling is set at $2,000?
options: $2,000 and 100 thousand apartments
$1,500 and 200 thousand apartments
$2,000 and 300 thousand apartments
$1,000 and 200 thousand apartments.
items.feedback: A nonbinding ceiling leaves equilibrium unchanged.

items.stem: A $50 price ceiling is imposed with demand and supply unchanged. Which statement correctly classifies the policy using the equilibrium shown?
options: Nonbinding: the legal price is above the $30 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
Nonbinding: the legal price is above the $40 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
Binding: the legal price is above the $30 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $50.
Binding: the legal price is above the $40 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $50.
items.feedback: The graph’s competitive equilibrium price is $30. A $50 maximum is above that price, so the ceiling does not prevent the equilibrium trade. It is nonbinding, and the market remains at $30 and 200 units.

items.stem: An enforced $20 price ceiling is imposed. What additional consequence, beyond the lower posted price, follows from the quantities shown in the graph?
options: A shortage of 100 units makes waiting, search, or another form of nonprice rationing necessary.
A shortage of 50 units makes waiting, search, or another form of nonprice rationing necessary.
A surplus of 100 units leaves sellers competing to dispose of unsold goods.
A surplus of 50 units leaves sellers competing to dispose of unsold goods.
items.feedback: At the $20 ceiling, buyers demand 250 units and sellers supply 150, leaving a shortage of 100. Because the legal price cannot rise to clear the market, waiting, search, or another nonprice allocation method must ration the available units.

items.stem: A city caps rent below equilibrium. The advertised rent falls, but apartment searches become longer, maintenance falls, and landlords screen tenants harder. What is the best economic diagnosis?
options: The ceiling lowers the posted price but creates shortage and nonmoney rationing
The ceiling lowers the posted price and therefore eliminates scarcity
The ceiling raises quantity supplied and creates seller competition
The ceiling is nonbinding because landlords still choose tenant quality
items.feedback: The posted money price is only part of the cost. Binding ceilings create shortage and hidden rationing costs.

items.stem: A legal maximum price is set above equilibrium. A student predicts a shortage. What is wrong?
options: A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a shortage
Any price ceiling always creates a shortage
A ceiling above equilibrium creates a surplus
A ceiling above equilibrium is actually a price floor
items.feedback: A price ceiling binds only when it is below equilibrium.

items.stem: A binding price ceiling on gasoline leads stations to sell out early. Some stations favor regular customers. What is the best interpretation?
options: The shortage creates nonprice rationing
The market clears because the legal price is low
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling increases supply
items.feedback: When price cannot ration the good, other methods like waiting, favoritism, and side payments can take over.

items.stem: A rent ceiling causes landlords to convert apartments into short-term rentals outside the regulated market. What does this show?
options: The ceiling reduced regulated rental supply by changing landlord incentives.
A ceiling always increases quantity supplied
A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes
items.feedback: A binding ceiling lowers returns in the regulated market and can push suppliers to adjust around the policy.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At the binding $1,000 rent ceiling, what is the maximum number of apartments that can actually be rented?
options: 200 thousand apartments
300 thousand apartments
400 thousand apartments
100 thousand apartments
items.feedback: Transactions are limited by the short side, quantity supplied.

items.stem: A price ceiling is set at $18 when equilibrium price is $25. At $18, Qd = 900 and Qs = 600. Which statement is correct?
options: The ceiling is binding and creates a shortage of 300
The ceiling is nonbinding and creates no shortage
The ceiling is binding and creates a surplus of 300
The ceiling is a price floor because it is below equilibrium
items.feedback: A ceiling below equilibrium is binding. Shortage is 900 - 600 = 300.

items.stem: Refer to the price-control graph. If a price ceiling is set at $10, what shortage results?
options: 200 units
100 units
300 units
400 units
items.feedback: At $10, quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100. The shortage is 300 - 100 = 200 units.

items.stem: A city sets a price ceiling below equilibrium to make apartments affordable. The legal rent falls, but renters wait longer, landlords reduce maintenance, and some units are rented off-book. What is the strongest economic conclusion?
options: The posted price falls, but shortage shifts part of the cost into waiting, quality loss, and rationing
The posted price falls, so the policy removes the main cost renters face in the market
The posted price falls, but the shortage means sellers now compete harder for renters
The posted price falls, so the market clears through a lower equilibrium rent
items.feedback: A binding ceiling can lower the posted price while creating shortage, search costs, lower quality, rationing, and misallocation.

items.stem: Refer to the price-control graph and treat the plotted curves as straight lines. An enforced ceiling rises from $20 to $25. All units sellers offer are purchased, and there are no side payments or other changes. What happens to the shortage and quantity actually traded?
options: Shortage falls by 25 units; quantity traded rises by 50 units.
Shortage rises by 50 units; quantity traded falls by 25 units.
Shortage falls by 50 units; quantity traded falls by 25 units.
Shortage falls by 50 units; quantity traded rises by 25 units.
items.feedback: At $20, Qd=250 and Qs=150: shortage is 100 and trades are 150. Halfway to the $30 equilibrium, at $25, Qd=225 and Qs=175: shortage is 50 and trades are 175. The smaller gap reflects both lower quantity demanded and higher quantity supplied; trades are limited by the latter.

items.stem: Initially Qd=140-2P and Qs=2P, with a price ceiling of $40. Later demand becomes Qd=200-2P while supply stays fixed. What happens to the ceiling’s effect?
options: Initially nonbinding at equilibrium $35; later binding at $40, with Qd=120, Qs=80 and a shortage of 40.
Initially binding at $40 with a shortage of 20; later nonbinding because demand growth raises equilibrium above the ceiling.
Initially nonbinding at $35; later nonbinding at $50 because a ceiling never changes when only demand shifts.
Initially nonbinding at $35; later binding at $40, with a surplus of 40 because sellers supply more than buyers demand.
items.feedback: Initially 140-2P=2P gives P=35. Later 200-2P=2P gives P=50, above the ceiling. At P=40, demand is 120 and supply 80, so the previously nonbinding maximum becomes binding and creates a 40-unit shortage.

items.stem: A binding price ceiling reduces the legal price from $100 to $70. At $70, buyers want 500 units and sellers offer 300 units. Which outcome is most likely?
options: A shortage of 200 units and rationing by waiting, favoritism, or side payments
A surplus of 200 units and falling inventories
No shortage because the legal price is lower
A demand decrease because buyers dislike lower prices
items.feedback: At the ceiling, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by 200 units. Because price cannot rise, the good must be rationed some other way.

items.stem: A policy lowers the legal price, creates a shortage, reduces product quality, and causes buyers to spend time searching. Which policy best matches this pattern?
options: A binding price ceiling
A binding price floor
A nonbinding price floor
A seller tax with perfectly elastic demand
items.feedback: Lower legal price plus shortage and search costs points to a binding price ceiling.

items.stem: A binding rent ceiling creates a 200-unit shortage. The city allocates apartments to whoever waits in line longest. Which conclusion best completes the analysis?
options: Lower rent can bring longer waits and inefficient allocation.
The lower money price eliminates the economic cost of housing
Waiting lines prove that quantity supplied now exceeds quantity demanded
The allocation is efficient because every renter faces the same legal price
items.feedback: A binding ceiling lowers the posted price but can replace money costs with waiting, search, quality loss, and inefficient rationing.

items.stem: A price floor is set below equilibrium. Why does it usually have no effect?
options: The market price remains above the legal minimum
Because all price floors create surpluses
Because buyers must pay the legal minimum even if equilibrium is higher
Because quantity demanded must equal zero
items.feedback: A nonbinding floor is below equilibrium, so the market can still reach equilibrium above the legal minimum.

items.stem: Refer to the price-control graph. If a price floor is set at $20, what happens?
options: It is nonbinding because it is below equilibrium
It creates a shortage of 100 units
It creates a surplus of 100 units
It forces price up to $40
items.feedback: Equilibrium is $30. A floor at $20 is below equilibrium, so it does not prevent the market from reaching $30.

items.stem: Refer to the price-control graph. A policy holds the price at $40. What is the full market result if the policy is a legal minimum?
options: A binding price floor with a surplus of 100 units
A nonbinding price floor with no effect
A binding price ceiling with a shortage of 100 units
A nonbinding price ceiling with no effect
items.feedback: $40 is above the $30 equilibrium, so a legal minimum at $40 is a binding floor. Qs is 250 and Qd is 150, so the surplus is 100.

items.stem: Refer to the price-control graph. At $50, what are quantity demanded and quantity supplied?
options: Quantity demanded is 100 and quantity supplied is 300
Quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100
Quantity demanded is 150 and quantity supplied is 250
Quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150
items.feedback: At a high price of $50, buyers demand 100 units while sellers supply 300 units.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Compared with competitive equilibrium, how do the quantities of labor supplied and demanded change at the $10 minimum wage?
options: Quantity of labor supplied decreases by 75 thousand; quantity demanded increases by 75 thousand.
Quantity of labor supplied increases by 75 thousand; quantity demanded decreases by 75 thousand.
Quantity of labor supplied increases by 150 thousand; quantity demanded is unchanged.
Quantity of labor supplied is unchanged; quantity demanded decreases by 150 thousand.
items.feedback: At equilibrium, both labor supplied and demanded equal 175 thousand. At $10, labor supplied is 250 thousand and labor demanded is 100 thousand, so the two 75-thousand movements create the 150-thousand surplus.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What effect does the $6 minimum wage have on the labor market?
options: Binding; it creates a 200-thousand labor surplus
Binding; it forces the wage to exactly 6 dollars
Nonbinding; the market clears at 12 dollars
Nonbinding; it creates a 200-thousand labor shortage
items.feedback: The $6 minimum wage is below the $12 equilibrium wage, so it is nonbinding and the market remains at equilibrium.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What wage and employment level result when a $6 minimum wage is imposed?
options: $6 and 100 thousand workers
$6 and 300 thousand workers
$18 and 200 thousand workers
$12 and 200 thousand workers.
items.feedback: A nonbinding floor leaves equilibrium unchanged.

items.stem: A $10 price floor is imposed with demand and supply unchanged. Which statement correctly classifies the policy using the equilibrium shown?
options: Nonbinding: the legal price is below the $30 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
Nonbinding: the legal price is below the $40 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
Binding: the legal price is below the $30 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $10.
Binding: the legal price is below the $40 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $10.
items.feedback: The graph’s competitive equilibrium price is $30. A $10 minimum is below that price, so the floor does not prevent the equilibrium trade. It is nonbinding, and the market remains at $30 and 200 units.

items.stem: A minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage. Some workers receive higher pay, firms hire fewer workers, and more workers seek jobs. What is the cleanest interpretation?
options: The floor helps some employed workers but creates a labor surplus
The floor helps all workers because everyone now earns the legal wage
The floor raises labor demand because the wage is higher
The floor is nonbinding because firms still hire some workers
items.feedback: A binding wage floor creates winners among some employed workers and losers among workers unable to find jobs.

items.stem: A legal minimum price is set below equilibrium. A student predicts a surplus. What is wrong?
options: A floor below equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a surplus
Any price floor always creates a surplus
A floor below equilibrium creates a shortage
A floor below equilibrium is actually a price ceiling
items.feedback: A price floor binds only when it is above equilibrium.

items.stem: A student says the minimum wage shown will create a surplus of workers. What wage and employment will actually result? How would the outcome differ if the same legal wage were a maximum rather than a minimum?
options: $12 and 200 thousand workers remain the equilibrium; the floor is nonbinding, while a ceiling at $6 would sustain a 200-thousand-worker shortage.
$10 and 150 thousand workers remain the equilibrium; the floor is nonbinding, while a ceiling at $6 would sustain a 100-thousand-worker shortage.
$12 and 200 thousand workers remain the equilibrium; the floor is nonbinding, while a ceiling at $6 would sustain a 200-thousand-worker surplus.
$10 and 150 thousand workers remain the equilibrium; the floor is nonbinding, while a ceiling at $6 would sustain a 100-thousand-worker surplus.
items.feedback: The graph’s equilibrium is $12 and 200 thousand workers, above the $6 minimum. At $6, Qd = 300 thousand and Qs = 100 thousand: a shortage of 200 thousand. A ceiling could hold wages there, but a floor permits the equilibrium wage.

items.stem: A minimum wage is set at $16 when equilibrium wage is $12. At $16, labor supplied is 95,000 and labor demanded is 72,000. What is the labor surplus?
options: 23,000 workers
72,000 workers
95,000 workers
167,000 workers
items.feedback: The labor surplus is labor supplied minus labor demanded: 95,000 - 72,000 = 23,000.

items.stem: Refer to the price-control graph. If a price floor is set at $50, what surplus results?
options: 200 units
100 units
300 units
400 units
items.feedback: At $50, quantity supplied is 300 and quantity demanded is 100. The surplus is 300 - 100 = 200 units.

items.stem: A minimum wage is set at $16 when the equilibrium wage is $12. At $16, firms demand 70,000 workers and 110,000 workers want jobs. What is the best diagnosis?
options: The floor is binding and creates a labor surplus of 40,000 workers
The floor is binding and creates a labor shortage of 40,000 workers
The floor is nonbinding because workers prefer higher wages
The floor increases labor demand by 40,000 workers
items.feedback: A price floor above equilibrium is binding. Labor surplus equals quantity supplied minus quantity demanded, so 110,000 - 70,000 = 40,000 workers.

items.stem: A minimum wage raises pay for workers who keep their jobs, but firms hire fewer workers and more workers seek jobs. Which statement gives the best economic interpretation?
options: The policy helps some employed workers, but it also creates a labor surplus among workers seeking jobs
The policy helps workers as a group because the higher wage applies to anyone willing to work
The policy helps firms attract more workers, so labor demand rises with the legal wage
The policy leaves employment unchanged because only the legal wage has changed
items.feedback: A binding minimum wage creates winners and losers. Some employed workers earn more, but firms hire fewer workers and a labor surplus appears.

items.stem: A labor market initially has Qd=440-10W and Qs=10W. A minimum wage of $18 is imposed. Later labor demand falls to Qd=280-10W, with supply unchanged. Which account is correct?
options: The floor is initially nonbinding at $22; later it binds at $18, with 100 employed and a labor surplus of 80.
The floor initially binds at $18; later it becomes nonbinding at $14, with 180 employed and no surplus.
The floor is initially nonbinding at $22; later it binds at $18, with 180 employed and a labor shortage of 80.
The floor stays nonbinding because its statutory value is unchanged, so employment remains at the original 220.
items.feedback: Initial equilibrium solves 440-10W=10W, giving W=22. Later equilibrium would be W=14. At the $18 floor, labor demand is 100 and supply 180; employment is demand-limited and excess supply is 80.

items.stem: A binding price floor raises the legal price from $30 to $45. At $45, sellers offer 900 units and buyers want 600 units. Which outcome is most likely?
options: A surplus of 300 units and extra effort by sellers to unload the good
A shortage of 300 units and long lines for buyers
No surplus because sellers prefer the higher price
A demand increase because the higher price signals quality
items.feedback: At the floor, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by 300 units. Sellers compete to find buyers, often through nonprice margins.

items.stem: A policy raises the legal price, creates unsold output, and benefits some sellers while making buyers purchase less. Which policy best matches this pattern?
options: A binding price floor
A binding price ceiling
A nonbinding price ceiling
A buyer tax that leaves quantity unchanged
items.feedback: Higher legal price plus unsold output points to a binding price floor.

items.stem: The government sets a crop price floor above equilibrium and promises to buy any unsold output. Which result is most likely?
options: Farmers produce more than consumers buy, so the government purchases and stores the surplus
Consumers buy more because the legal price is higher
The policy creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
The floor is nonbinding because the government participates in the market
items.feedback: A binding price floor creates excess supply. A purchase guarantee shifts the unsold surplus to the government rather than making it disappear.

items.stem: Revenues rise from $4.9 trillion to $5.2 trillion while outlays rise from $6.0 trillion to $6.1 trillion. How does the budget balance change?
options: It worsens by $0.2 trillion
It improves by $0.3 trillion and becomes a budget surplus
It remains unchanged as both rise
It improves by $0.2 trillion but remains negative
items.feedback: The balance moves from −$1.1 trillion to −$0.9 trillion, an improvement of $0.2 trillion.

items.stem: In a simplified closed-economy account, net taxes are $300 and government purchases $360. A new policy raises both by $60. Which conclusion separates the budget position from the balanced policy change?
options: Public saving becomes zero; any equal tax-and-spending change balances the whole budget
Public saving becomes −$120; count higher purchases but ignore higher net taxes
Public saving becomes +$60; the larger tax total makes the initial deficit irrelevant
Public saving remains −$60; equal changes leave the initial deficit unchanged
items.feedback: Before: T−G=300−360=−60. After: 360−420=−60. Equal changes do not erase the initial imbalance.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: The domestic real interest rate rises, but political risk also rises sharply. What can be concluded about NCO?
options: NCO rises because risk determines flows independently of returns
NCO is unchanged because NX = NCO forces the channels to cancel
The direction is ambiguous because the two forces push NCO oppositely
NCO falls because interest returns determine flows independently of risk
items.feedback: Higher domestic returns tend to lower NCO, while greater domestic risk tends to raise it; relative magnitudes are needed.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: National saving is $520 billion, domestic investment is $610 billion, and domestic residents buy $160 billion of foreign assets. How much do foreigners buy in domestic assets?
options: $250 billion
$70 billion
$160 billion
$770 billion
items.feedback: NCO = S − I = −$90 billion. Since −90 = 160 − foreign purchases, foreign purchases are $250 billion.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: Why does a higher domestic real interest rate lower NCO rather than raise it in the standard model?
options: It makes foreign assets relatively more attractive to domestic savers
It raises outward investment by increasing the return on foreign bonds
It favors domestic assets over foreign assets for both domestic and foreign investors
It attracts foreign funds that enter positively in the definition of NCO
items.feedback: The relative-return change keeps more domestic funds at home and attracts more foreign funds.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: Gross capital outflows rise while NCO falls. Which change can explain both facts?
options: The trade balance becomes unrelated to NCO
Gross capital inflows rise by more than gross outflows
Gross inflows fall by the same amount
Domestic purchases of foreign assets become zero
items.feedback: NCO is a net measure; it can fall despite larger outflows if foreign purchases of domestic assets rise even more.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: NCO moves from −$80 billion to $30 billion while domestic foreign-asset purchases rise $40 billion. How must foreign purchases of domestic assets change?
options: They must rise by $150 billion
They must fall by $70 billion
They must rise by $70 billion
They must fall by $110 billion
items.feedback: NCO rises $110 billion. With domestic foreign purchases up $40 billion, foreign domestic-asset purchases must fall $70 billion to make the net rise $110 billion.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: Political instability raises desired foreign-asset purchases, and the domestic real interest rate rises in response. How should the second effect be interpreted?
options: The higher rate reinforces NCO by making foreign assets more attractive
The rate converts the capital outflow into domestic investment
The rate leaves NCO unchanged because capital flight is permanent
The higher rate partly restrains the initial increase in NCO
items.feedback: Capital flight shifts desired NCO outward, while the higher domestic return produces movement toward domestic assets along the new relationship.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: A country has net capital outflow of −$120 billion, and residents purchase $200 billion of foreign assets. How much do foreigners purchase in domestic assets, and does NX = NCO imply a trade surplus or deficit?
options: Foreign purchases remain $300 billion; NX must be −$100 billion despite the fixed NCO figure
Foreign purchases must be $320 billion; NX is +$120 billion because a capital inflow is an export
Foreign purchases must be $320 billion; NX is −$120 billion, a trade deficit
Foreign purchases must be $80 billion; NX is +$120 billion, a trade surplus
items.feedback: NCO = resident foreign purchases − foreign domestic purchases. Thus −120=200−F implies F=320. With NX=NCO, NX=−120; the inflow finances a trade deficit rather than changing its sign.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: Domestic rates rise while foreign risk also rises. What is the likely combined effect on domestic NCO?
options: The effects necessarily cancel
Both changes tend to reduce it
Both changes tend to increase it
The rate raises it while foreign risk lowers it
items.feedback: Higher domestic returns favor home assets, and riskier foreign assets further discourage purchases abroad.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: Residents reduce net acquisition of foreign assets by selling assets and repatriating funds. Foreign net acquisition of domestic assets is unchanged. What happens to residents’ net outward asset flow and NCO?
options: Both fall
Both rise
The outward asset flow falls while NCO rises
NCO is unchanged because foreign investors did not act
items.feedback: Resident net acquisition of foreign assets enters positively in NCO; a reduction lowers NCO when foreign net acquisition of domestic assets is fixed. This statement concerns period asset flows, not revaluations of existing holdings.

items.topic: Capital Flows and Net Capital Outflow
items.stem: The domestic real interest rate rises and NCO falls. How does this change reach the foreign-exchange market?
options: A lower NCO raises demand for domestic currency
A higher rate makes foreign-exchange supply horizontal
NCO affects only goods markets
A lower NCO reduces the supply of domestic currency
items.feedback: With fewer net foreign-asset purchases, residents exchange less domestic currency for foreign currency, so the supply of domestic currency in the foreign-exchange market shifts left.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: During a panic, a solvent bank cannot obtain short-term funding even though its assets exceed its liabilities. What central-bank response best fits the lender-of-last-resort role?
options: Guarantee every bank loss without conditions.
Finance a permanent tax cut.
Raise reserve requirements solely to remove liquidity.
Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral.
items.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems while safeguards limit losses and moral hazard.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: Which institutional arrangement best combines central-bank independence with democratic accountability?
options: Public officials set the mandate; the central bank chooses instruments and reports transparently.
The central bank chooses national goals and never explains its decisions to the public.
Elected officials directly set policy interest rates before every national election.
The Treasury secretly directs monetary operations without a published mandate.
items.feedback: Instrument independence can coexist with a legislated mandate, transparency, and public accountability.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: When the central bank buys a large quantity of longer-term securities, what happens directly on its balance sheet?
options: Tax revenue rises while currency liabilities disappear from the balance sheet.
Its securities assets and reserve liabilities usually both rise.
Government purchases of goods rise automatically with the securities purchase.
Commercial-bank capital is converted directly into federal tax receipts.
items.feedback: A central-bank asset purchase expands its asset holdings and typically creates reserve liabilities.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: The short-term policy rate is near its effective lower bound. Which action is still a monetary-policy option?
options: Change federal income-tax rates through the banking system.
Authorize a new congressional spending program immediately.
Use forward guidance or buy longer-term securities.
Set private-sector wages and prices by administrative order.
items.feedback: Central banks may use communication and balance-sheet tools when conventional rate cuts are constrained.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: During a panic, a bank has valuable assets but cannot obtain enough short-term funding to meet payments. Later analysis shows another bank’s assets are worth less than its liabilities. Why should a central bank treat the two cases differently?
options: Liquidity can address the first bank’s funding problem, but it cannot erase the second bank’s insolvency
Both banks should receive unlimited central-bank loans because any funding problem proves that losses and insolvency are irrelevant
The insolvent bank needs only a lower reserve requirement, while the solvent bank must be closed immediately
The central bank should finance both banks permanently because recognizing losses is a fiscal-policy function
items.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: A central-bank asset purchase sharply increases reserve balances, yet commercial-bank lending changes little. Which statement best separates the institutions’ roles?
options: The central bank failed to create any reserve balances because commercial banks did not expand loans after the asset purchase
Commercial banks create central-bank reserves whenever they choose not to lend
Reserve balances are identical to bank capital, so unchanged lending proves capital was unchanged
The central bank creates reserves; commercial-bank deposit creation still depends on lending and borrowing
items.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: Emergency lending stops a bank run, but banks now expect rescue whenever they take large risks. What tradeoff does the central bank face?
options: Financial stability today versus greater moral hazard tomorrow.
Lower inflation today versus a permanently lower natural rate.
Higher taxes today versus lower government spending tomorrow.
More exports today versus fewer imports tomorrow.
items.feedback: Liquidity support can stabilize the system, but poorly designed guarantees can encourage excessive risk.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: Inflation is well above target and output is near potential, but elected officials demand easier money before an election. What is the strongest case for central-bank independence?
options: It guarantees that monetary tightening has no short-run output cost.
It allows the central bank to eliminate every federal budget deficit.
It resists election-driven easing and protects price-stability credibility.
It permanently fixes unemployment below the natural rate.
items.feedback: Independence can support credible commitment to price stability even when near-term political incentives favor expansion.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: A crisis program has two parts: the central bank lends temporarily against sound collateral to solvent banks, while the fiscal authority injects taxpayer capital into an insolvent institution. What principle best distinguishes the two actions?
options: Central-bank liquidity support addresses funding; fiscal recapitalization addresses losses and solvency
Both actions are ordinary open-market operations because each changes a financial balance sheet
The central bank is conducting fiscal policy in both cases because all emergency lending uses tax revenue
The fiscal authority is acting as lender of last resort while the central bank is collecting taxes
items.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: The central bank expands its balance sheet and reserve balances surge. Banks, however, become more selective about approving loans and firms postpone borrowing because sales prospects are weak. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The central bank did not actually create reserves because bank lending failed to rise
Weak borrowing proves that commercial banks, not the central bank, issue reserve balances
The simple multiplier guarantees the same deposit expansion regardless of banks or borrowers
Creating reserves does not mechanically force commercial-bank lending or deposit expansion
items.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: A government wants a central bank to finance $160 million of spending to avoid current taxes. The central bank's mandate instead prioritizes its stated stabilization objectives. Which institutional rationale for independence fits?
options: It guarantees that monetary policy never makes an economic forecasting error
It gives the central bank authority to set tax brackets instead of the legislature
It removes the need to explain policy choices because independent agencies have no mandate
It can reduce pressure to trade monetary stability for short-run financing, while retaining legal accountability
items.feedback: Independence can limit short-run political financing pressure and support credible policy. It is not a guarantee of perfect forecasts or a transfer of fiscal lawmaking powers.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: A solvent bank faces $180 million of withdrawals before sound long-term assets mature. A different bank has assets below its liabilities. Which distinction guides central-bank liquidity support?
options: Neither bank can face a liquidity problem because every asset can always be sold instantly at book value
The first bank needs only a fiscal tax cut; the second needs only a new deposit classification
Temporary liquidity can bridge the first bank's timing gap; lending alone does not erase the second bank's capital loss
Both banks become solvent whenever a central bank supplies reserves, regardless of asset values
items.feedback: A sound but illiquid balance sheet can have a cash-timing problem. Insolvency is insufficient asset value relative to liabilities; a loan adds an asset and a liability and does not automatically restore net worth.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: A legislature authorizes $200 million of spending while the central bank adjusts its monetary stance. Which accountability distinction is valid?
options: The Treasury must approve every private bank loan because it authorizes public spending
Fiscal authorities authorize spending; the central bank implements monetary policy under its legal mandate and accountability framework
The central bank writes the spending appropriation whenever monetary policy is independent
Independence means the central bank has no legal mandate or reporting obligation
items.feedback: Institutional separation distinguishes fiscal appropriations from monetary policy. Operational independence is compatible with a legislated mandate and accountability, not an absence of constraints.

items.topic: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
items.stem: A solvent bank faces $260 million of withdrawals before sound long-term assets mature. A different bank has assets below its liabilities. Which distinction guides central-bank liquidity support?
options: Both banks become solvent whenever a central bank supplies reserves, regardless of asset values
Neither bank can face a liquidity problem because every asset can always be sold instantly at book value
The first bank needs only a fiscal tax cut; the second needs only a new deposit classification
Temporary liquidity can bridge the first bank's timing gap; lending alone does not erase the second bank's capital loss
items.feedback: A sound but illiquid balance sheet can have a cash-timing problem. Insolvency is insufficient asset value relative to liabilities; a loan adds an asset and a liability and does not automatically restore net worth.

items.stem: A restaurant market has many sellers, but each offers a differentiated experience. Which statement is best?
options: The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.
The large number of restaurants makes each a price taker despite customers’ preferences for particular experiences.
Differentiation gives each restaurant the pricing freedom of a sole supplier because other dining experiences are distinct.
Competition should be assessed only through price differences, since differences in service quality do not affect buyer choice.
items.feedback: Many restaurants can compete for customers even when differentiated experiences give individual sellers some price discretion. Differentiation means the strict identical-product price-taking benchmark need not hold, but competing restaurants can still constrain each other’s prices.

items.stem: A firm in a competitive market raises price above the market price while rivals do not. The likely result is:
options: Higher sales because price signals quality.
A sharp loss of customers to close substitutes.
No change because buyers cannot switch.
Automatic market-wide inflation.
items.feedback: Buyers can switch to other sellers offering the same or similar product.

items.stem: A licensing rule sharply limits new sellers. What is the most direct competitive effect?
options: The rule guarantees lower prices.
The rule creates perfect information.
Reduced entry can increase the market power of existing sellers.
The rule makes every firm a price taker.
items.feedback: Barriers can weaken competitive pressure and preserve market power.

items.stem: A market has many sellers, but buyers face high search costs and cannot compare prices. Why might price-taking be weakened?
options: Many sellers always eliminate market power.
High search costs strengthen competition by making buyers compare prices more carefully.
Price comparison is unrelated to competition.
Information frictions can give individual sellers some pricing discretion.
items.feedback: Competition also depends on buyer information and ability to switch.

items.stem: A market appears to have many separate sellers, but four firms own most capacity through subsidiaries. What should an analyst examine?
options: Only the number of storefronts.
Whether prices are written in dollars.
Whether consumers enjoy variety.
Which firms control capacity, rather than the number of brands.
items.feedback: Competitive pressure depends on independent control of capacity and decisions.

items.stem: Each participant trades at most one home-repair visit. Buyer values are Ava $42, Ben $33, Cam $25, Dina $14. Seller costs are Alba $8, Brock $17, Cora $29, Dev $38. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 4 trades and $22 of total surplus
2 trades and $75 of total surplus
2 trades and $50 of total surplus
1 trade and $34 of total surplus
items.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 2 trades create $50 total surplus.

items.stem: Each participant trades at most one festival wristband. Buyer values are Eli $38, Fern $31, Gus $23, Hana $17, Ivan $9. Seller costs are Esme $5, Finn $12, Gia $20, Hugo $28, Inez $36. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 5 trades and $17 of total surplus
3 trades and $92 of total surplus
2 trades and $52 of total surplus
3 trades and $55 of total surplus
items.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 3 trades create $55 total surplus.

items.stem: Each participant trades at most one meal-kit box. Buyer values are Jules $34, Kai $26, Lena $19, Mia $10. Seller costs are Jae $7, Kira $15, Leo $22, Mara $30. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 2 trades and $38 of total surplus
4 trades and $15 of total surplus
2 trades and $60 of total surplus
1 trade and $27 of total surplus
items.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 2 trades create $38 total surplus.

items.stem: Each participant trades at most one parking space. Buyer values are Noah $45, Omar $37, Pia $28, Quinn $18, Rae $11. Seller costs are Nico $6, Opal $14, Pax $24, Rina $33, Sol $41. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 5 trades and $21 of total surplus
3 trades and $66 of total surplus
3 trades and $110 of total surplus
2 trades and $62 of total surplus
items.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 3 trades create $66 total surplus.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Which expression correctly calculates producer surplus?
items.feedback: Producer surplus is the triangle below the $14 equilibrium price and above supply through Q = 8.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Output is limited to 6 units. What is true about units 7 and 8?
options: Their cost exceeds value, so omitting them raises surplus
Omitting them loses $4 of total surplus.
They transfer $4 from producers to consumers
No loss can be measured
items.feedback: Between Q=6 and Q=8, demand lies above supply; the missing triangle is $4.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Output is pushed to 10 units. What is true about units 9 and 10?
options: Their value exceeds cost, so they add $4
They transfer $4 from consumers to producers
Producing them destroys $4 of total surplus.
More output is always efficient
items.feedback: Between Q=8 and Q=10, supply lies above demand; the excess-cost triangle is $4.

items.stem: A price change raises producer surplus by $30 and lowers consumer surplus by $30, with no quantity change. Total surplus:
options: Rises by $30
Falls by $30
Falls by $60
Is unchanged
items.feedback: The equal gain and loss are a transfer.

items.stem: A restriction raises producer surplus by $24 and lowers consumer surplus by $39. The change in total surplus is:
options: A decrease of $15
An increase of $24
A decrease of $39
No change
items.feedback: Add +$24 and -$39.

items.stem: A price rise causes one low-value buyer to leave and one high-cost seller to enter. Why can total surplus change?
options: Any price rise raises total surplus
Surplus stops existing
The price change alters which trades occur.
The outcome becomes equitable
items.feedback: Participation changes can create or destroy gains.

items.stem: Why does the area between demand and supply through the efficient quantity measure total surplus?
options: Each gap is the market price
The area is seller revenue
Each vertical gap is the gain from one marginal unit
The area is buyer expenditure
items.feedback: Demand is marginal value and supply is marginal cost.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Demand shifts from D1 to D2. Which statement is correct?
options: Consumer surplus rises to $50; producer surplus falls to $0; total surplus falls to $50.
Consumer surplus stays $32; producer surplus stays $32; total surplus stays $64.
Consumer surplus falls to $25; producer surplus falls to $25; total surplus falls to $50.
Consumer surplus rises to $50; producer surplus rises to $50; total surplus rises to $100.
items.feedback: Initially, consumer surplus is (18 − 10) × 8 / 2 = $32 and producer surplus is (10 − 2) × 8 / 2 = $32. After the shift, consumer surplus is (22 − 12) × 10 / 2 = $50 and producer surplus is (12 − 2) × 10 / 2 = $50. Total surplus rises from $64 to $100.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Supply shifts from S1 to S2. Which statement is correct?
options: Consumer and producer surplus both fall; total surplus falls to $36.
Consumer surplus rises because price rises
Producer surplus rises because price rises
Total surplus stays $64
items.feedback: Higher marginal cost reduces quantity and both surplus areas.

items.stem: Refer to the step-demand graph. At a price of $10, how many buyers purchase and what is total consumer surplus?
options: 2 buyers and $13
3 buyers and $15
4 buyers and $20
5 buyers and $10
items.feedback: The $18, $15, and $12 buyers receive $8, $5, and $2.

items.stem: Refer to the step-supply graph. At price $10, how many sellers participate and what is total producer surplus?
options: 2 sellers and $11
4 sellers and $14
3 sellers and $12
5 sellers and $10
items.feedback: The $3, $6, and $9 sellers receive $7, $4, and $1.

items.stem: A buyer values a good at $35, pays $20, and seller cost is $11. How is total surplus divided?
options: $20 to the buyer and $4 to the seller
$9 to the buyer and $15 to the seller
$35 to the buyer and $11 to the seller
$15 to the buyer and $9 to the seller
items.feedback: CS is $15 and PS is $9.

items.stem: A buyer values a good at $35 and the seller's cost is $11. If the market price rises from $20 to $26, what changes?
options: Consumer surplus falls $6, producer surplus rises $6, and total surplus stays $24
Consumer and total surplus both fall $6
Producer and total surplus both rise $6
Both sides gain $6
items.feedback: Price redistributes the fixed value-cost gain.

items.stem: Which claim is strongest about an efficient market outcome?
options: It guarantees equal surplus
Maximum total surplus does not guarantee the fairest distribution.
It proves willingness to pay measures need perfectly
It eliminates every market failure
items.feedback: Under the stated market assumptions, efficiency maximizes measured total surplus. It does not guarantee equal surplus or resolve judgments about the fairness of its distribution.

items.stem: A low-income buyer can pay $12 for a vital item while a wealthy buyer will pay $40 for convenience. What limitation appears?
options: Consumer surplus cannot use dollars
Producer surplus is always negative
Willingness to pay can reflect ability to pay, not only need
Demand measures seller cost
items.feedback: Income can constrain measured willingness to pay.

items.stem: Before a restriction, consumer surplus is $45 and producer surplus is $35. The restriction prevents exchanges with combined gains of $12 and has no other effects. What is total surplus afterward?
items.feedback: Initial total surplus is $45 + $35 = $80. The prevented beneficial exchanges remove $12, leaving $68. The question specifies that the reported CS and PS precede the restriction.

items.stem: A price ceiling transfers $18 from producers to consumers and prevents $7 of gains. Total surplus:
options: Rises by $18
Falls by $7
Falls by $25
Is unchanged
items.feedback: The transfer cancels; the lost gains remain.

items.stem: A tax sends $40 to government revenue and eliminates $9 of gains. Ignoring administration, total surplus:
options: Falls by $49
Rises by $40
Falls by $9
Is unchanged
items.feedback: Revenue is a transfer; eliminated gains are a loss.

items.stem: A scarce good is allocated to the buyers with the highest willingness to pay. Which limitation of surplus analysis should be kept in mind?
options: Surplus analysis cannot compare alternative allocations.
Market prices eliminate all distributional concerns.
Willingness to pay measures need independently of income.
Willingness to pay reflects purchasing power as well as preferences.
items.feedback: Willingness to pay is measured in dollars and can be constrained by purchasing power. A surplus-maximizing allocation can therefore be efficient without resolving questions of need or fairness.

items.stem: Market A has consumer surplus of $80 and producer surplus of $70, but production creates $40 of external damage. Market B has consumer surplus of $75 and producer surplus of $65 with no external damage. Which statement is strongest?

External damage should be ignored because it is outside buyer and seller surplus
Private surplus favors A, but including the stated external damage gives B higher social surplus
A is necessarily socially efficient because its private surplus is larger
items.feedback: A has $150 private surplus but $110 after the external cost; B has $140 and no stated external cost.

items.stem: Two allocations produce the same total surplus. Allocation X gives almost all gains to one household; Allocation Y distributes gains across many households. Which conclusion is economically defensible from surplus data alone?
options: The allocations cannot have equal total surplus if distributions differ
They are tied on measured efficiency, while choosing between distributions requires an equity judgment
X is more efficient because concentrated gains are larger per person
Y is more efficient because more people receive gains
items.feedback: Total surplus measures the size of the pie; distribution of the pie is a separate criterion.

items.stem: Buyer value is $50, seller cost is $20, and price is $47. Which statement is correct?

items.feedback: Total surplus is $50−$20=$30. The buyer receives $50−$47=$3, and the seller receives $47−$20=$27; the two shares add to $30.

items.stem: A buyer values a good at $50 and the seller's cost is $20. At a market price of $23, which statement is correct?

items.stem: A ceiling increases surplus for continuing buyers by $25, but buyers who lose access forfeit $5 of prior surplus. Producer surplus falls by $40. There are no search costs or other effects. What happens to total surplus?

items.stem: A student calls the highest-surplus buyer the marginal buyer. What is wrong?

The lowest-cost seller never sells

items.stem: A buyer values a unit at $42, the seller’s cost is $26, and the price is $34. Which complete statement is correct?

items.stem: Each participant trades at most one fitness class. Buyer values are Mia $29, Noah $23, Omar $14, Pia $7. Seller costs are Mara $3, Nico $12, Opal $19, Pax $26. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 4 trades and $13 of total surplus
2 trades and $37 of total surplus
2 trades and $52 of total surplus
1 trade and $26 of total surplus
items.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 2 trades create $37 total surplus.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What amount represents consumer spending?
items.feedback: Equilibrium expenditure is P × Q = $10 × 8 = $80.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the height of the triangle used to calculate consumer surplus?
items.feedback: The demand intercept is $30 and equilibrium price is $14, giving a height of $16.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is total buyer expenditure at equilibrium?
items.feedback: Equilibrium price is $14 and quantity is 5, so expenditure is $70.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What total revenue do sellers receive at equilibrium?
items.feedback: Equilibrium revenue is P × Q = $10 × 8 = $80.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. How tall is the producer-surplus triangle?
items.feedback: Equilibrium price is $14 and the supply intercept is $6, so the triangle height is $8.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is sellers’ total production cost at equilibrium?
items.feedback: Seller revenue is $70 and producer surplus is $25, so total production cost is $45.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the difference between consumer surplus and producer surplus at equilibrium?
items.feedback: Consumer surplus and producer surplus are both $32, so the difference is zero.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What fraction of total surplus is consumer surplus?
options: Two-thirds
One-third
One-half
Three-fourths
items.feedback: Consumer surplus is $64 out of $96 total surplus, which is two-thirds.

items.stem: What is the difference between consumer surplus and producer surplus in the graph?
items.feedback: Consumer surplus and producer surplus are each $25.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. By how much does consumer surplus rise when price falls from P1 to P2?
items.feedback: Consumer surplus rises from $32 to $72.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. By how much does producer surplus rise when price rises from P1 to P2?
items.feedback: Producer surplus rises from $18 to $50.

items.stem: Buyer values are $30, $24, $18, and $12. Seller costs are $7, $14, $21, and $28. How many units maximize total surplus?
options: 1 unit
2 units
3 units
4 units
items.feedback: The first two units create gains; the third costs more than it is valued.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. A student labels the price-times-quantity rectangle as consumer surplus. What is consumer surplus at E, and what does that rectangle actually measure?
options: Consumer surplus is $64; the rectangle measures expenditure.
Consumer surplus is $48; the rectangle measures expenditure.
Consumer surplus is $64; the rectangle measures the buyers’ net gain.
Consumer surplus is $48; the rectangle measures the buyers’ net gain.
items.feedback: Q = 8, P = $14 and the demand intercept is $30. CS = 0.5 × 8 × (30−14) = $64. The rectangle 8 × 14 = $112 is payment to sellers, not buyers’ net gain.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Output is 6 rather than 8. Total-surplus loss is:
items.feedback: Stopping at Q = 6 leaves $4 of mutually beneficial gains unrealized relative to the efficient quantity Q = 8.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At the overproduction outcome, how much total surplus is lost relative to the efficient quantity?
items.feedback: Producing beyond the efficient quantity creates $4 of deadweight loss because marginal cost exceeds marginal willingness to pay on the extra units.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. After demand shifts from D1 to D2, total surplus is:
items.feedback: After demand shifts to D2, the consumer- and producer-surplus regions sum to $100 of total surplus.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. After supply shifts from S1 to S2, total surplus is:
items.feedback: After supply shifts to S2, the higher marginal costs reduce the efficient quantity and leave $36 of total surplus.

items.stem: Each participant trades at most one home-repair visit. Buyer values are Ava $44, Ben $35, Cam $27, Dina $13. Seller costs are Alba $7, Brock $18, Cora $25, Dev $39. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 4 trades and $30 of total surplus
3 trades and $106 of total surplus
3 trades and $56 of total surplus
2 trades and $54 of total surplus
items.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 3 trades create $56 total surplus.

items.stem: Each participant trades at most one festival wristband. Buyer values are Eli $37, Fern $30, Gus $21, Hana $12. Seller costs are Esme $6, Finn $16, Gia $24, Hugo $33. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 4 trades and $21 of total surplus
2 trades and $67 of total surplus
1 trade and $31 of total surplus
2 trades and $45 of total surplus
items.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 2 trades create $45 total surplus.

items.stem: Consumer surplus falls $48, producer surplus rises $31, and revenue is $12. Total surplus:
options: Falls $5
Falls $17
Rises $43
Falls $29
items.feedback: The net change is -$48 + $31 + $12 = -$5, so total surplus falls by $5.

items.stem: A price ceiling raises consumer surplus by a net $22 before search costs, reduces producer surplus by $34, and creates $3 of real search costs not included in either surplus figure. What is the change in total surplus?
options: Falls $12
Falls $15
Rises $19
Falls $37
items.feedback: Add the net consumer-surplus change to the producer-surplus change and subtract the separately stated real search cost: $22−$34−$3=−$15. A transfer component alone would not measure the full consumer-surplus change.

items.stem: Three feasible units have buyer values $30, $24, $17 and seller costs $10, $18, $21. A rule requires all three to trade. Which policy change increases total surplus, assuming efficient matching and no other costs?
options: Require a fourth unit without any value/cost evidence because more trades always raise total surplus.
Stop all trade because the third unit’s loss proves the first two also lose surplus.
Allow only the first two units: it removes a third-unit loss of $4 while retaining positive gains of $20 and $6.
Keep all three because payments from buyers necessarily cover social opportunity costs.
items.feedback: The three marginal gains are $20, $6 and −$4. Efficiency retains positive-gain trades and rejects the negative one rather than maximizing quantity alone.

items.stem: A competitive market allocates goods to the highest willingness to pay, but some users impose uncompensated disposal harm and low-income households receive few goods. Which assessment separates efficiency assumptions from equity?
options: Competition rules out unpriced harm, while unequal access alone proves that all trades reduce total surplus.
Correcting harm necessarily gives every household an equal share, so no separate equity judgment remains.
The highest willingness-to-pay rule establishes social efficiency regardless of external harm and income differences.
Unpriced harm can invalidate the private surplus benchmark; unequal access raises a distinct equity question even after that harm is corrected.
items.feedback: Private willingness to pay and cost omit the external harm. Internalizing that cost targets efficiency, while deciding whether the resulting distribution is fair is a separate judgment.
