items.stem: A buyer values a unit at $52, seller cost is $18 and price is $45. A proposal lowers price to $25 while the same trade occurs and uses $3 of real administrative resources. Which comparison is correct?
options: Buyer: $7 to $27; seller: $27 to $7; gross total: $34; net total after administration: $31.
Buyer: $7 to $27; seller: $27 to $27; gross total: $54; net total after administration: $51.
Buyer: $7 to $7; seller: $27 to $7; gross total: $14; net total after administration: $11.
Buyer: $7 to $27; seller: $27 to $27; gross total: $54; net total after administration: $54.
items.feedback: Buyer surplus is initially 52 − 45 = $7 and becomes 52 − 25 = $27. Seller surplus is initially 45 − 18 = $27 and becomes 25 − 18 = $7. Gross total remains 52 − 18 = $34; using $3 of real resources leaves $31 net.

items.stem: A buyer values a unit at $52 and seller cost is $18. Price falls from $45 to $25 with the same buyer and seller. A second proposed cut to $15 would leave the seller unwilling to produce and there is no subsidy. Which comparison is right?
options: Both cuts only redistribute surplus because price can never affect whether a trade occurs.
The first cut redistributes a $34 gain; the second prevents the trade and loses that $34 gain.
The first cut creates $20 of new total surplus; the second creates another $10 even without production.
The first cut loses $20 of total surplus; the second restores it by lowering consumer spending.
items.feedback: At $25 the seller still covers the $18 cost, so total gains remain $34. At $15 production is not privately viable without other support; if the trade disappears, its positive gain is lost.

items.stem: A policy lowers producer surplus by $80, raises consumer surplus by $45 and generates $25 of government revenue. It uses no additional administrative resources. What is the social loss, and why is it not $80?
options: $80; producer-surplus losses are always identical to social losses.
$150; add every group’s change without signs.
$10; $70 of the producer loss appears as gains to consumers and government.
$0; any government revenue exactly offsets all private losses.
items.feedback: Total-surplus change is −$80+$45+$25=−$10. Transfers to other groups explain why the loss to one group is not the total social loss.

items.stem: A policy raises consumer surplus by $90 and reduces producer surplus by $65, but requires a $40 government payment. With no other resource effects, which conclusion correctly counts taxpayers?
options: Net total surplus rises $25: ignore the government payment when adding private surplus.
Net total surplus rises $90 because the consumer gain alone measures the benefit.
Net total surplus falls $105 because consumer gains cannot count toward welfare.
Net total surplus falls $15: $90−$65−$40.
items.feedback: Consumers, producers and government must be included consistently. The government payment is a cost to taxpayers: 90−65−40=−15. The net loss remains after internal transfers cancel.

items.stem: A trade creates $24 of total gains. A price rule shifts $7 from seller to buyer without changing the trade, while enforcing the rule consumes $5 of real resources. Which result separates distribution from the resource effect?
options: The $7 changes the split, while net total surplus falls from $24 to $19 because of enforcement.
Net total surplus rises to $26 because the $7 transfer is a benefit and enforcement costs $5.
Net total surplus falls to $12 because both the transfer and enforcement are social losses.
Net total surplus stays $24 because both enforcement and the payment rule are transfers.
items.feedback: The buyer’s $7 gain is the seller’s $7 loss, canceling in the total. Enforcement uses $5 of resources, leaving $19.

items.stem: Four trades have marginal gains $18, $9, $2 and −$4. Policy A allows the efficient trades; Policy B requires all four. Both transfer $10 from sellers to buyers and use $3 of administration. Which net-surplus comparison follows?
options: A yields $36 and B yields $32.
A yields $26 and B yields $22.
Both yield $26.
A yields $16 and B yields $12.
items.feedback: The efficient first three gains sum to $29. A uses $3, leaving $26. B also includes the −$4 trade, leaving $22 after administration. The common $10 transfer changes distribution, not total surplus.

items.stem: Two policies preserve the same trades and total production cost. Policy A leaves $90 of surplus with sellers and $10 with buyers. Policy B leaves $60 with sellers and $40 with buyers. Which conclusion follows from surplus accounting alone?
options: B yields more total surplus because buyers receive a larger share.
A yields more total surplus because sellers receive a larger share.
Both yield $100 of total surplus; choosing between distributions requires an equity criterion beyond the sum.
Neither can be efficient because the two groups do not receive equal shares.
items.feedback: The totals are 90+10=100 and 60+40=100. With production and allocation fixed, the difference is distribution rather than measured total efficiency.

items.stem: A policy keeps the goods and buyer allocation unchanged, saves $12 in production resources, but requires $5 of new search effort. It also transfers $20 from buyers to sellers. What is the total-surplus change?
options: A $27 increase: add the transfer to the net resource saving.
A $13 decrease: subtract the transfer from the net resource saving.
A $12 increase: search effort has no resource value.
A $7 increase: count the $12 saving and $5 search cost, while the $20 transfer cancels.
items.feedback: The unchanged allocation preserves gross buyer value. Net resource use falls $12−$5=$7. The $20 payment affects the split of gains rather than their total.

items.stem: Calculate consumer and producer surplus at E. Does the difference between them show that the market is inefficient?
options: CS = $48 and PS = $24; unequal shares alone do not establish inefficiency.
CS = $64 and PS = $32; unequal shares alone establish inefficiency.
CS = $48 and PS = $24; unequal shares alone establish inefficiency.
CS = $64 and PS = $32; unequal shares alone do not establish inefficiency.
items.feedback: E gives Q = 8 and P = $14. CS = 0.5 × 8 × 16 = $64; PS = 0.5 × 8 × 8 = $32. Marginal value equals marginal cost at E, so unequal shares do not establish an efficiency problem. Redistribution may reflect an equity objective.

items.stem: Calculate consumer and producer surplus at E. Do their equal values show that every efficient market must divide its gains equally?
options: CS and PS are each $25; their equality here does not establish a general efficiency requirement.
CS and PS are each $20; their equality here does not establish a general efficiency requirement.
CS and PS are each $25; their equality here establishes a general efficiency requirement.
CS and PS are each $20; their equality here establishes a general efficiency requirement.
items.feedback: At E, Q = 5 and P = $14, with demand and supply intercepts $24 and $4. Each area is 0.5 × 5 × 10 = $25. Efficiency depends on marginal value equaling marginal cost, not equal surplus shares.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Starting at the marked quantity through A and B, what change in total surplus would expanding output to E cause, and why?
options: A $8 gain: it adds trades whose value exceeds their resource cost.
A $4 gain: it adds trades whose value exceeds their resource cost.
A $4 gain: the change transfers that amount from sellers to buyers.
An $8 gain: the change transfers that amount from sellers to buyers.
items.feedback: The restricted quantity is 6 and E is at 8. At Q = 6, value is $12 and cost $8. The surplus gain is 0.5 × 2 × 4 = $4. A transfer by itself does not change total surplus.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Starting at the marked quantity through A and B, what change in total surplus would reducing output to E cause, and why?
options: A $8 gain: it avoids producing units whose cost exceeds their value.
A $4 gain: the change transfers that amount from sellers to buyers.
A $4 gain: it avoids producing units whose cost exceeds their value.
An $8 gain: the change transfers that amount from sellers to buyers.
items.feedback: The restricted quantity is 10 and E is at 8. At Q = 10, cost is $12 and value $8. The surplus gain is 0.5 × 2 × 4 = $4. A transfer by itself does not change total surplus.

items.stem: Price falls from P1 to P2. How much does consumer surplus increase, and how much of that gain comes from units consumers were already buying?
options: An increase of $32, including $28 on original units and $4 on additional units.
An increase of $40; it consists entirely of the gain on original units.
An increase of $32; it consists entirely of the gain on original units.
An increase of $40, including $32 on original units and $8 on additional units.
items.feedback: Demand intercept $20; (Q, P) changes from (8, 12) to (12, 8). Consumer surplus rises from $32 to $72, an increase of $40. The price change on existing units contributes $32; the additional-unit triangle contributes $8.

items.stem: Price rises from P1 to P2. How much does producer surplus increase, and how much of that gain comes from units sellers were already supplying?
options: An increase of $32, including $24 on original units and $8 on additional units.
An increase of $24, including $20 on original units and $4 on additional units.
An increase of $32; it consists entirely of the gain on original units.
An increase of $24; it consists entirely of the gain on original units.
items.feedback: Supply intercept $2; (Q, P) changes from (6, 8) to (10, 12). Producer surplus rises from $18 to $50, an increase of $32. The price change on existing units contributes $24; the additional-unit triangle contributes $8.

items.stem: A report adds seller revenue to consumer surplus at E to measure gains from trade. What are consumer, producer and total surplus, and should revenue be added?
options: CS = $60, PS = $0, total surplus = $60; adding revenue would double-count a transfer.
CS = $72, PS = $0, total surplus = $72; adding revenue would double-count a transfer.
CS = $72, PS = $0, total surplus = $72; adding revenue would capture an extra resource benefit.
CS = $60, PS = $0, total surplus = $60; adding revenue would capture an extra resource benefit.
items.feedback: Demand intercepts at $18, supply is horizontal at $6 and Q = 12. CS = 0.5 × 12 × (18−6) = $72 and PS = 0. Total surplus is $72; seller revenue is not an additional gain.

items.stem: At X = 10, read the Y quantities on IC1 and IC2. If more of either good is preferred, why would a crossing of these curves contradict consistent preferences?
options: IC1 has Y between 5 and 10 and IC2 between 10 and 15; a crossing would contradict the ranking established by more Y at the same X.
IC1 has Y below 5 and IC2 between 5 and 10; a shared bundle may consistently have two different preference ranks.
IC1 has Y below 5 and IC2 between 5 and 10; a crossing would contradict the ranking established by more Y at the same X.
IC1 has Y between 5 and 10 and IC2 between 10 and 15; a shared bundle may consistently have two different preference ranks.
items.feedback: At X = 10, IC1 is below Y = 5 while IC2 is between Y = 5 and 10, so the IC2 bundle is preferred. A common point would be indifferent to bundles on both curves. Transitivity would equate ranks that more-is-better distinguishes.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Which labeled bundle is the best affordable choice?
options: Bundle A at (5,15)
Bundle C at (10,10)
Bundle B at (15,5)
Any point northeast of the budget line
items.feedback: C reaches the highest attainable indifference curve and is tangent to the budget line.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. What is the consumer's optimal bundle?
options: 20 units of X and 10 units of Y
20 units of each good
40 units of Y and no X
10 units of X and 20 units of Y
items.feedback: The marked tangency A is located at X=10 and Y=20.

items.stem: X initially costs $5 and Y costs $12. X rises to $6 while Y rises to $18. Has X become more or less costly in units of Y?
options: More costly: the ratio rises because X has a higher dollar price.
Unchanged: both prices increased.
Less costly: the ratio falls from 12/5 to 3.
Less costly: the ratio falls from 5/12 to 1/3.
items.feedback: Relative cost depends on Px/Py. It falls from about 0.417 to 0.333 even though the dollar price of X rises.

items.stem: X costs $3 and Y costs $10. A student says that doubling income halves the opportunity cost of X. What is the error?
options: Income changes the price ratio, but the opportunity cost remains 3 Y.
The opportunity cost doubles because purchasing power doubles.
Income changes affordability, but the unchanged price ratio still makes one X cost 0.3 Y.
The student should halve both money prices when income doubles.
items.feedback: Opportunity cost in units of Y is Px/Py = 3/10. An income increase shifts the budget line outward without changing its slope.

items.stem: Bundle A has utility 40 and bundle B has utility 20. Which conclusion is not justified by ordinal utility?
options: A is preferred to B
B has the lower assigned number
The numbers preserve a ranking
A provides exactly twice as much satisfaction as B
items.feedback: Ordinal utility conveys order, not ratios or measurable amounts of satisfaction.

items.stem: A consumer has a unique optimum with smooth, strictly convex, more-is-better preferences. Income and both goods’ prices then triple. A student predicts more consumption because income rose; another predicts less because prices rose. Which conclusion follows?
options: Consumption of both goods must triple because nominal income triples.
The consumer must move toward X because a higher Px changes relative prices.
The same bundle remains optimal; the budget set and preferences are unchanged.
The optimum becomes indeterminate because all three nominal magnitudes changed.
items.feedback: Multiplying the budget inequality by three leaves the same feasible set. Relative prices and preferences are unchanged, so the same unique optimum remains.

items.stem: Initially X costs $6 and Y costs $12. Both prices then double while income stays fixed. Which comparison is correct?
options: The opportunity cost of X doubles; both budget intercepts halve.
The opportunity cost of X stays at 0.5 Y; both budget intercepts stay fixed.
The opportunity cost of X halves; both budget intercepts double.
The opportunity cost of X stays at 0.5 Y; both budget intercepts halve.
items.feedback: Doubling both prices leaves their ratio unchanged, but fixed income buys half as much of either good.

items.stem: A consumer has income $24, Px = $2 and Py = $1. Preferences are smooth, strictly convex and more-is-better. At A = (8, 8), MRS = 3; at B = (10, 10), MRS = 2. A student selects B because MRS equals Px/Py. What is the strongest diagnosis?
options: B is optimal because tangency overrides the budget constraint.
A is optimal because exhausting income is sufficient.
Neither bundle is affordable, so no adjustment from A is possible.
B is unaffordable, and A is affordable but can be improved by shifting spending toward X.
items.feedback: B costs $30, above income. A costs $24, but its MRS of 3 exceeds the price ratio of 2, so a small move toward more X and less Y raises utility.

items.stem: A consumer uses X and Y only in one-to-one pairs and spends $24 on them. Initially each good costs $2. If X rises to $4 while Y stays at $2, how does the number of pairs purchased change?
options: It falls from 6 to 4; only purchases of X fall.
It remains at 6 because Y’s price is unchanged.
It falls from 6 to 4; purchases of both goods fall.
It rises from 6 to 8 because X is more expensive.
items.feedback: The cost of a pair rises from $4 to $6. With fixed income, pairs fall from 24/4 = 6 to 24/6 = 4, reducing demand for both complements.

items.stem: Starting from bundle B in the graph, cereal rises to $10 per box while income and the yogurt price stay fixed. If the consumer keeps B’s yogurt quantity, what is the most cereal the consumer can afford, and how does the budget change?
options: 1.2 boxes; the budget pivots inward.
1.6 boxes; the budget pivots inward.
1.6 boxes; the budget shifts inward in parallel.
1.2 boxes; the budget shifts inward in parallel.
items.feedback: B contains six yogurts. They cost 6 × $4 = $24, leaving $16 of the $40 income for cereal: 16/10 = 1.6 boxes. Only the cereal intercept changes, so the line pivots rather than shifting in parallel.

items.stem: The consumer moves from BC0 to BC1 in the graph; only the cereal price changes. Income then falls to $32. Compared with BC0, what happens to cereal’s opportunity cost and to the affordability of four yogurts plus four cereal boxes?
options: The opportunity cost falls from three yogurts to one; the bundle changes from unaffordable to just affordable.
The opportunity cost falls from two yogurts to one; falling income by itself proves the bundle remains unaffordable.
The opportunity cost falls from three yogurts to one; falling income by itself proves the bundle remains unaffordable.
The opportunity cost falls from two yogurts to one; the bundle changes from unaffordable to just affordable.
items.feedback: BC0 has prices $4 and $8 and income $40. BC1 retains the yogurt intercept of 10 and raises the cereal intercept to 10, implying a cereal price of $4. Cereal’s opportunity cost falls from 8/4 = 2 yogurts to 4/4 = 1. The bundle costs $48 originally and $32 finally; both prices and income matter for feasibility.

items.stem: After the move from BC0 to BC1, income rises to $80 and prices stay at their BC1 levels. How much of each good could the consumer buy if all income were spent on that good? Has the original price ratio been restored?
options: Eight of each good; the original price ratio is not restored.
Ten of each good; the original price ratio is not restored.
Ten of each good; the income increase restores the original price ratio.
Eight of each good; the income increase restores the original price ratio.
items.feedback: BC1 has intercepts 5 and 5 at income $40, implying prices of $8 each. At income $80 both intercepts are 10. BC0’s intercepts were 10 and 5. Income cannot undo the relative-price change.

items.stem: Prices and tastes stay fixed as the budget changes from BC0 to BC1. The chosen bundle changes from four yogurts and three cereal boxes to six yogurts and one cereal box. How much did income change? Over this change, which good behaves as a normal good and which as an inferior good?
options: Income falls $12; yogurt behaves as inferior and cereal as normal over this change.
Income falls $8; yogurt behaves as normal and cereal as inferior over this change.
Income falls $12; yogurt behaves as normal and cereal as inferior over this change.
Income falls $8; yogurt behaves as inferior and cereal as normal over this change.
items.feedback: At the plotted yogurt price of $4, the intercept falls from 10 to 8, so income falls from $40 to $32. Yogurt consumption rises when income falls, the inferior-good pattern. Cereal consumption falls with income, the normal-good pattern. The observed choices, not the budget lines alone, establish these responses.

items.stem: Use the graph. The move from BC0 to BC1 changes only the cereal price. Income then falls to $32. What are the final yogurt and cereal intercepts, and is the final budget a parallel shift of BC0?
options: Six of each good; no, the price ratio differs from BC0.
Eight of each good; no, the price ratio differs from BC0.
Eight of each good; yes, an income change reverses the change in the price ratio.
Six of each good; yes, an income change reverses the change in the price ratio.
items.feedback: BC1’s intercepts are both 10 with income $40, so both prices are $4. Final intercepts are 32/4 = 8. BC0 had intercepts 10 and 5. Income scales a budget without restoring the original relative price.

items.stem: The graph shows BC0 and BC1 with unchanged prices. After the move to BC1, both prices fall 20%. What are the final yogurt and cereal intercepts, and how do the relative prices compare with BC0?
options: 12 and 6; the relative price is unchanged.
10 and 5; the relative price is unchanged.
10 and 5; proportional price cuts change the relative price.
12 and 6; proportional price cuts change the relative price.
items.feedback: BC1’s intercepts are 8 and 4. Dividing by 0.8 gives 10 and 5, exactly BC0’s intercepts, so the original feasible set is restored. The two prices fall by the same proportion, leaving their ratio unchanged.

items.stem: The consumer initially chooses the best affordable bundle shown. An unrestricted cash grant makes IC3 attainable. A cereal-only voucher of equal face value improves on the initial choice but cannot reach IC3. What is the initial optimum, and which grant permits higher utility?
options: The starting optimum is (8, 12); cash permits higher utility than the voucher despite equal face values.
The starting optimum is (10, 10); cash permits higher utility than the voucher despite equal face values.
The starting optimum is (10, 10); equal face values imply equal utility despite the different feasible sets.
The starting optimum is (8, 12); equal face values imply equal utility despite the different feasible sets.
items.feedback: C = (10, 10) is tangent to IC2 and is the starting optimum. Under the stated policy conditions, cash attains IC3 while the voucher cannot. A spending restriction can change feasible choices and attained utility even when nominal benefits match.

items.stem: At the interior optimum shown, the price of X falls while income and the price of Y stay fixed. Find the original price ratio Px/Py. At the old bundle, how does the price cut change marginal utility per dollar and the incentive to buy X? Assume diminishing marginal utility and an interior new optimum.
options: One; MUx/Px rises relative to MUy/Py, favoring more spending on X subject to the new budget.
Two; MUx/Px rises relative to MUy/Py, favoring more spending on X subject to the new budget.
Two; MUx/Px falls relative to MUy/Py, favoring less spending on X subject to the new budget.
One; MUx/Px falls relative to MUy/Py, favoring less spending on X subject to the new budget.
items.feedback: The budget intercepts are 20 for X and 40 for Y, so Px/Py = 40/20 = 2. At the old tangency MUx/Px = MUy/Py. Lower Px raises MUx/Px at the unchanged bundle. Reallocation toward X helps restore equality, while the final bundle must satisfy the new budget.

items.stem: X costs $4 and Y costs $12. A shopper replaces two units of Y with X while keeping spending fixed. How many units of X can be added?
options: 2/3 of a unit
2 units
8 units
6 units
items.feedback: Two Y release $24; dividing by $4 per X gives six X. This applies the relative-price tradeoff to a bundle change.

items.stem: Northstar Bakery pays each worker $120. Worker 3 raises output from 20 to 34. Which pair is correct?
options: MP=34 units and MC=$120
MP=14 units and MC=$24
MP=14 units and MC=$8.57 per unit
AP=14 units and MC=$3.53
items.feedback: MP is the output change; with a constant wage, MC is wage divided by MP.

items.stem: At Ironwood Furniture, Q=41, TFC=$300, and 4 workers each cost $135. Which cost identity is correct?
items.feedback: Divide each total by output and verify ATC=AFC+AVC.

items.stem: Harbor Roasters has output schedule (workers: total units produced) 0:0, 1:10, 2:23, 3:36, 4:47, 5:56, 6:63, 7:68, 8:71. With all else fixed, diminishing marginal product first appears when which worker is added?
options: Worker 4
Worker 3
Worker 6
Only when total output falls
items.feedback: Find the first worker whose marginal product is below the previous worker’s marginal product.

items.stem: Cedar Trail Bikes pays each worker $150. Worker 6 raises output from 54 to 60. Which pair is correct?
options: MP=60 units and MC=$150
MP=6 units and MC=$25 per unit
MP=6 units and MC=$21.67
AP=6 units and MC=$2.50
items.feedback: MP is the output change; with a constant wage, MC is wage divided by MP.

items.stem: At Blue Peak Printing, Q=31, TFC=$210, and 3 workers each cost $110. Which cost identity is correct?
items.feedback: Divide each total by output and verify ATC=AFC+AVC.

items.stem: Riverbend Textiles has output schedule (workers: total units produced) 0:0, 1:11, 2:25, 3:40, 4:53, 5:64, 6:73, 7:80, 8:85. With all else fixed, diminishing marginal product first appears when which worker is added?
options: Worker 3
Worker 6
Only when total output falls
Worker 4
items.feedback: Find the first worker whose marginal product is below the previous worker’s marginal product.

items.stem: Juniper Foods pays each worker $125. Worker 5 raises output from 44 to 54. Which pair is correct?
options: MP=10 units and MC=$12.50 per unit
MP=54 units and MC=$125
MP=10 units and MC=$17.50
AP=10 units and MC=$2.31
items.feedback: MP is the output change; with a constant wage, MC is wage divided by MP.

items.stem: At Summit Glassworks, Q=79, TFC=$480, and 6 workers each cost $160. Which cost identity is correct?
items.feedback: Divide each total by output and verify ATC=AFC+AVC.

items.stem: Maple Street Media has output schedule (workers: total units produced) 0:0, 1:6, 2:15, 3:26, 4:37, 5:47, 6:55, 7:61, 8:65. With all else fixed, diminishing marginal product first appears when which worker is added?
options: Worker 4
Worker 7
Worker 5
Only when total output falls
items.feedback: Find the first worker whose marginal product is below the previous worker’s marginal product.

items.stem: Granite Toolworks pays each worker $145. Worker 4 raises output from 39 to 52. Which pair is correct?
options: MP=52 units and MC=$145
MP=13 units and MC=$21.15
AP=13 units and MC=$2.79
MP=13 units and MC=$11.15 per unit
items.feedback: MP is the output change; with a constant wage, MC is wage divided by MP.

items.stem: At Lakeside Ceramics, Q=58, TFC=$225, and 5 workers each cost $115. Which cost identity is correct?
items.feedback: Divide each total by output and verify ATC=AFC+AVC.

items.stem: Prairie Solar has output schedule (workers: total units produced) 0:0, 1:13, 2:29, 3:46, 4:61, 5:74, 6:85, 7:94, 8:101. With all else fixed, diminishing marginal product first appears when which worker is added?
options: Worker 3
Worker 4
Worker 6
Only when total output falls
items.feedback: Find the first worker whose marginal product is below the previous worker’s marginal product.

items.stem: A firm receives a property-tax increase that does not depend on output. Which immediate short-run curve change is correct?
options: AVC and MC shift upward together
Only MC shifts upward
All curves shift downward
ATC shifts upward while AVC is unchanged
items.feedback: A property tax is fixed with respect to output.

items.stem: The wage paid to every production worker rises. Which curve combination shifts upward?
options: AVC, ATC, and MC
AFC and ATC only
AFC and MC only
TFC and AFC only
items.feedback: The wage changes variable and marginal costs.

items.stem: A process improvement raises output from every labor level. With input prices unchanged, the most defensible cost prediction is:
options: AFC rises and MC is unchanged
MC and ATC shift downward over the affected output range
TFC becomes zero
All costs rise because output rises
items.feedback: More output from the same inputs reduces marginal and average cost.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Where does MC cross AVC and ATC, and what do the marginal-average relationships imply at the crossings?
options: At roughly Q = 25 and Q = 30, respectively; the next units switch from lowering to raising the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
At roughly Q = 32 and Q = 38, respectively; the next units switch from raising to lowering the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
At roughly Q = 32 and Q = 38, respectively; the next units switch from lowering to raising the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
At roughly Q = 25 and Q = 30, respectively; the next units switch from raising to lowering the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
items.feedback: MC crosses AVC and ATC at roughly Q = 32 and Q = 38, respectively. Before each crossing MC is below that average and pulls it down; after the crossing MC is above it and pulls it up. Thus the crossing identifies a minimum, not a maximum.

items.stem: Where LRATC is flat over an output interval, the firm experiences:
options: Diminishing marginal product
Constant returns to scale
Rising AFC
Negative marginal product
items.feedback: A flat LRATC indicates unchanged cost per unit as all inputs and output expand proportionally.

items.stem: The first output at which the flat minimum begins is:
options: The largest feasible scale
Maximum efficient scale
Minimum efficient scale
The first positive marginal product
items.feedback: MES is the smallest output attaining minimum LRATC.

items.stem: The LRATC envelope represents:
options: The average of all SRATC curves
The highest fixed cost at each output
A firm’s demand curve
The lowest attainable ATC among available plant sizes at each output
items.feedback: In the long run the firm can choose the least-cost plant for each output.

items.stem: A bicycle-fitting workshop bills clients $168,000 for the year. It pays $54,000 to employees, $27,000 for supplies and $15,000 for utilities and insurance. The proprietor gives up an outside salary of $46,000 and could rent the workshop she owns for $18,000 a year. What are accounting profit and economic profit?
options: $72,000 accounting profit; $8,000 economic profit
$72,000 accounting profit; $26,000 economic profit
$90,000 accounting profit; $8,000 economic profit
$8,000 accounting profit; $72,000 economic profit
items.feedback: Explicit payments total $96,000, leaving accounting profit of $72,000. Forgone salary and rent total $64,000 in implicit costs, leaving $8,000 economic profit. Owning the workshop does not make its alternative rental use free.

items.stem: A firm has zero economic profit and positive accounting profit. The best interpretation is:
options: The firm cannot pay its bills
Revenue covers explicit costs and the owner’s opportunity costs
The owner receives no return
Implicit costs must be zero
items.feedback: Zero economic profit includes normal compensation for owner resources.

items.stem: A machine lease can be canceled next month without penalty, but the current month’s payment is already made. For a decision next month, the lease is:
options: A sunk cost forever
A variable cost per unit
A fixed but avoidable cost
An implicit cost
items.feedback: Future fixed commitments can be avoidable even when current payments are sunk.

items.stem: Assume input prices are unchanged. A firm doubles every input and output rises by only 70%. This is evidence of:
options: Diminishing marginal product
Economies of scale
Constant returns to scale
Diseconomies of scale
items.feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a smaller percentage, so long-run average cost rises—consistent with diseconomies of scale.

items.stem: Assume input prices are unchanged. A firm doubles every input and output more than doubles. LRATC should generally:
options: Fall
Rise
Remain fixed by definition
Equal marginal product
items.feedback: With unchanged input prices, output rises more than proportionally to total input cost, so long-run average cost falls.

items.stem: Which change can lower MC without changing TFC?
options: A higher building lease
A higher marginal product of labor
A larger sunk advertising payment
A higher annual license fee
items.feedback: Higher MP means fewer variable-input dollars per extra unit.

items.stem: A firm’s MC is below AVC but above ATC. This combination is:
options: Possible whenever AFC is falling
Evidence of economies of scale
Impossible because ATC exceeds AVC
Possible only at zero output
items.feedback: Since ATC=AVC+AFC, ATC is above AVC; MC cannot be below AVC and above ATC simultaneously.

items.stem: A firm chooses the output with the lowest total cost. Why is that rule defective?
options: Total cost excludes fixed cost
Total cost is always constant
Marginal cost is revenue
Different output levels cannot be compared using total cost alone
items.feedback: The level of total cost alone does not identify the best output. An output decision requires comparing the additional revenue and additional cost associated with changing quantity.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Around Q = 35, as output rises slightly, which pattern is consistent with the cost curves?
options: Both AVC and AC fall
Both AVC and AC rise
AVC rises while AC falls
AVC falls while AC rises
items.feedback: Around Q=35, MC lies above AVC but below AC, so it pulls AVC up and AC down.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Just to the right of Q = 50, what happens to both average-cost curves as output increases?
options: Both AC and AVC fall
AC falls while AVC rises
AC rises while AVC falls
Both AC and AVC rise
items.feedback: Beyond Q=50, MC lies above both averages, so both are pulled upward.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. To the left of Q = 25, which movement of the average-cost curves is consistent with the graph?
options: Both AC and AVC are falling
Both AC and AVC are rising together
AC rises while AVC continues falling
AC is flat while AVC continues rising
items.feedback: Before the AVC minimum, MC is below the average curves, pulling them downward.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Around Q = 300, what happens to AVC and AC as output rises?
options: Both averages rise
Both averages fall
AVC rises while AC falls
AVC falls while AC rises
items.feedback: Between the two minima, MC is above AVC but below AC.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At Q = 400, what total fixed cost is implied by the marked values?
items.feedback: AFC is $20−$12=$8; multiplying by 400 units gives TFC=$3,200.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At Q = 120, approximately what is average fixed cost?
options: $2.00 per unit
$6.67 per unit
$3.33 per unit
$10.00 per unit

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Between about 6 and 9 workers, which description of marginal product fits the total-product curve?
options: MP is negative and decreasing
MP is zero
MP is positive but decreasing
MP is positive and increasing throughout
items.feedback: TP still rises, so MP is positive; the flattening slope shows MP is decreasing.

items.stem: At eight workers, estimate marginal and average product. Would a small increase in labor raise or lower total product and average product?
options: MP ≈ 18 and AP ≈ 21; TP rises while AP falls.
MP ≈ 13 and AP ≈ 17; TP falls while AP rises.
MP ≈ 13 and AP ≈ 17; TP rises while AP falls.
MP ≈ 18 and AP ≈ 21; TP falls while AP rises.
items.feedback: At L = 8, MP is about 13 and AP about 17. MP is positive but below AP. More labor adds to TP while pulling average product down.

items.stem: At the MP–AP crossing, MP changes from above AP to below AP. What does this imply about average product?
options: AP reaches zero there
AP begins rising after the crossing
AP equals total product there
AP reaches a local maximum there
items.feedback: An average is maximized where the marginal value crosses it from above.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. If output expands from about 30 toward 60 units, what happens to LRAC?
options: LRAC rises, indicating diseconomies of scale
LRAC falls, indicating economies of scale
LRAC stays constant
LRAC falls, indicating diseconomies of scale
items.feedback: The left side of the U-shaped LRAC slopes downward toward its minimum.

items.stem: Refer to the LRAC graph. If the firm expands all adjustable inputs to raise output from about 60 toward 90 units, what happens to LRAC?
options: LRAC falls, indicating economies of scale
LRAC stays at the minimum of about $12
LRAC rises, indicating diseconomies of scale
LRAC rises, indicating economies of scale
items.feedback: To the right of the minimum, LRAC rises as scale expands.

items.stem: Two otherwise identical businesses each pay $80,000 in recorded expenses. Owner A gives up a $50,000 salary; Owner B gives up a $35,000 salary and $20,000 of investment income. Which has the higher economic cost?
options: Owner B’s business by $5,000
Owner A’s business by $5,000
They have the same economic cost
It cannot be determined without revenue
items.feedback: A has $130,000 of economic cost; B has $135,000 because both forgone salary and forgone investment income count.

items.stem: A repair cooperative receives $144,000 from maintenance contracts and $36,000 from parts sales. It pays $98,000 in wages and parts purchases plus $22,000 in rent and other bills. Its owner forgoes a $48,000 job and $9,000 of investment income. Which profit assessment is correct?
options: $60,000 accounting profit and $12,000 economic profit
$82,000 accounting profit and $25,000 economic profit
$60,000 accounting profit and $3,000 economic profit
$3,000 accounting profit and a $54,000 economic loss
items.feedback: Total revenue is $180,000 and explicit costs are $120,000. Accounting profit is $60,000; subtract the $57,000 return available from the owner’s next-best alternatives to obtain $3,000 economic profit.

items.stem: Firm A earns $70,000 accounting profit and has $20,000 implicit cost. Firm B earns $90,000 accounting profit and has $50,000 implicit cost. Which has the larger economic profit?
options: Firm B by $20,000
Firm A by $10,000
Firm B by $10,000
They are equal
items.feedback: Firm A earns $50,000 economic profit; Firm B earns $40,000.

items.stem: An owner could earn $75,000 elsewhere and could earn $10,000 interest on invested capital. The firm’s accounting profit is $85,000. Which statement is correct?
options: The firm earns zero economic profit
The firm earns $85,000 economic profit
The firm loses $10,000 accounting profit
Normal profit must be zero
items.feedback: The $85,000 accounting profit exactly covers the $85,000 of implicit opportunity costs.

items.stem: A firm’s revenue rises by $20,000 while explicit costs rise by $8,000 and implicit costs rise by $5,000. Compared with before, economic profit changes by:
options: An increase of $12,000
An increase of $15,000
A decrease of $7,000
An increase of $7,000
items.feedback: Economic profit changes by the revenue change minus both cost changes: $20,000 − $8,000 − $5,000.

items.stem: At Q = 40, ATC is $25 and AFC is $5. If TFC is unchanged, what is TVC at this output?
AFC falls from $12 to $8 while TFC remains $240. Output must have changed from:
options: 30 units to 20 units
12 units to 8 units
20 units to 24 units
20 units to 30 units
items.feedback: Q = TFC/AFC, so output rises from 240/12 = 20 to 240/8 = 30.

items.stem: At Q = 50, TC is $1,400 and TFC is $400. Which average-cost values are correct?
options: AFC = $20 and AVC = $8
AFC = $28 and ATC = $8
AVC = $20 and ATC = $28
AVC = $28 and ATC = $20
items.feedback: TVC = $1,000; AVC = $20, AFC = $8, and ATC = $28.

items.stem: A firm’s AVC is $16 at 30 units and its AFC is $6. If output rises and AFC falls to $4 while AVC stays $16, ATC becomes:
items.feedback: ATC = AVC + AFC = $16 + $4.

items.stem: A firm has already paid a nonrefundable $6,000 permit fee. Completing a project requires $14,000 more and will generate $17,000 in additional revenue. What is the correct decision logic?
options: Complete the project because the relevant incremental gain is $3,000
Cancel because total cost is $20,000
Cancel because the permit fee must be recovered
Complete only if revenue exceeds $23,000
items.feedback: The sunk permit is irrelevant; compare $17,000 additional revenue with $14,000 avoidable completion cost.

items.stem: A plant pays $10,000 per month on a contract. If it closes now, $7,000 can be canceled but $3,000 must still be paid. For the close-or-operate choice, how much of the monthly contract is avoidable?
items.feedback: Only the portion that disappears when the plant closes is avoidable.

items.stem: A publisher spent $25,000 editing a book. It can print the book for an additional $12,000 and expects $15,000 in additional sales. Which statement is correct?
options: The editing cost should be allocated to each future copy before deciding
The firm must recover all $25,000 before printing
Printing raises profit by $3,000 relative to not printing.
Printing loses $22,000 because total cost is $37,000
items.feedback: The current decision compares the $15,000 incremental revenue with the $12,000 avoidable printing cost. The $25,000 editing cost is sunk and is incurred whether or not the book is printed.

items.stem: A fixed annual license can be surrendered halfway through the year for a $4,000 refund. For a midyear shutdown decision, which amount is relevant?
options: Only variable labor cost can be relevant
$4,000 because shutting down recovers it
$0 because every fixed cost is sunk
The full original license price regardless of refund
items.feedback: The recoverable amount differs across choices and is therefore avoidable rather than sunk.

items.stem: At Q = 1,000 the lowest ATC among three plants is $22; at Q = 2,000 it is $17; at Q = 3,000 it is $19. Which sequence best describes LRAC over these outputs?
options: It falls and then rises
It rises and then falls
It is constant
It must equal the ATC of the smallest plant
items.feedback: LRAC takes the lowest attainable ATC at each output, producing $22, $17, then $19.

items.stem: A firm increases every input by 50%, while output rises by 80%. Holding input prices constant, what should happen to average cost?
options: Average cost should rise
Average cost must remain unchanged
Average cost becomes fixed cost only
Average cost should fall
items.feedback: Output rises more than proportionally to total input use, spreading cost over a larger proportional output increase.

items.stem: A manager blames rising LRAC at very large scale on “diminishing marginal product of labor.” What is the best correction?
options: Diseconomies require total product to fall
Diminishing marginal product and diseconomies are identical definitions
Diseconomies of scale concern varying all inputs, not adding labor to fixed inputs.
The explanation is correct because the long run always has fixed capital
items.feedback: Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary.

items.stem: LRAC values are $22 at Q=1, $18 at Q=2, $15 at Q=3, $15 at Q=4, and $17 at Q=5. If quantities are thousands of units, which statement is correct?
options: MES is 5 thousand units because LRAC rises there
MES is 2 thousand units because LRAC is already falling
MES is 3 thousand units and constant returns hold from 3 to 4 thousand
MES is 4 thousand units because it is the largest minimum-cost output
items.feedback: The minimum $15 first appears at 3 and remains unchanged through 4.

items.stem: A firm triples every input and output also triples. If input prices are unchanged, what happens to LRAC?
options: It must rise
It remains unchanged
It falls to one-third
It triples
items.feedback: Proportional output and input expansion implies constant returns to scale and unchanged long-run unit cost.

items.stem: A firm can produce 6,000 units at LRAC $20, 8,000 at $16, 10,000 at $16, and 12,000 at $18. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: MES is 8,000 units; 8,000–10,000 is a minimum-cost range
MES is 10,000 units because output is larger
MES is 12,000 units because LRAC turns upward there
There is no MES because two outputs share the minimum
items.feedback: MES is the smallest output attaining the minimum $16 LRAC.

items.stem: Harbor Roasters TFC rises by $120 while Q=47 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
options: AFC and ATC rise $2.55; AVC and MC are unchanged
AVC and MC rise $2.55; AFC is unchanged
AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $2.55
ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
items.feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/47 = $2.55 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

items.stem: Riverbend Textiles TFC rises by $120 while Q=80 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
options: AVC and MC rise $1.50; AFC is unchanged
AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $1.50
ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
AFC and ATC rise $1.50; AVC and MC are unchanged
items.feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/80 = $1.50 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

items.stem: Maple Street Media TFC rises by $120 while Q=37 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
options: AVC and MC rise $3.24; AFC is unchanged
AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $3.24
AFC and ATC rise $3.24; AVC and MC are unchanged
ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
items.feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/37 = $3.24 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

items.stem: Prairie Solar TFC rises by $120 while Q=94 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
options: AVC and MC rise $1.28; AFC is unchanged
AFC and ATC rise $1.28; AVC and MC are unchanged
AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $1.28
ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
items.feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/94 = $1.28 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

items.stem: Harbor Roasters TFC rises by $120 while Q=56 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
options: AFC and ATC rise $2.14; AVC and MC are unchanged
AVC and MC rise $2.14; AFC is unchanged
AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $2.14
ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
items.feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/56 = $2.14 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

items.stem: Riverbend Textiles TFC rises by $120 while Q=85 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
options: AVC and MC rise $1.41; AFC is unchanged
AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $1.41
ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
AFC and ATC rise $1.41; AVC and MC are unchanged
items.feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/85 = $1.41 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

items.stem: A restaurant owner uses a building she owns. Comparable rent is $40,000, and she gives up a $60,000 salaried job. The business earns $120,000 after explicit expenses. Economic profit is:
items.feedback: Economic profit is $120,000 minus $40,000 forgone rent minus $60,000 forgone salary.

items.stem: An entrepreneur can keep a salaried job paying $82,000 or launch a venture expected to earn $105,000 after explicit expenses while using an owned office that could rent for $16,000. Ignoring risk differences, what is expected economic profit?
options: $7,000 after both implicit costs
$23,000 after salary alone
$89,000 after rent alone
$105,000 because explicit expenses are paid
items.feedback: Subtract $82,000 salary and $16,000 rent from $105,000 to obtain $7,000.

items.stem: A self-employed designer earns $95,000 after explicit expenses but gives up a $72,000 salary and could rent the home studio for $18,000. Economic profit is:
items.feedback: Economic profit is $95,000 minus $72,000 minus $18,000.

items.stem: A chef opens a restaurant that earns $130,000 after explicit expenses. The chef gives up a $78,000 salary, uses an owned space that could rent for $32,000, and supplies equipment that could lease for $9,000. What is economic profit?
items.feedback: Implicit costs total $119,000, so economic profit is $130,000 minus $119,000, or $11,000.

items.stem: A business earns $160,000 after explicit expenses. The owner gives up a $90,000 salary and $35,000 in rent. Economic profit is:
items.feedback: Subtract both forgone salary and rent from accounting profit.

items.stem: A firm earns $190,000 after explicit expenses. The owner gives up a $105,000 salary, $45,000 in rental income, and $20,000 from leasing equipment. What is economic profit?
items.feedback: Implicit costs total $170,000, leaving $20,000 in economic profit.

items.stem: An owner uses a shop that could rent for $36,000 and works there instead of earning a $64,000 salary. The shop earns $112,000 after explicit expenses. What is economic profit?
items.feedback: Subtract $64,000 salary and $36,000 rent from $112,000 to obtain $12,000.

items.stem: At Q=50, AFC is $6 and AVC is $24. At Q=60, AFC is $5 and AVC is $23. Which statement is true?
options: ATC falls from $30 to $28
ATC remains $30 at both outputs
ATC falls from $30 to $29
ATC rises from $30 to $33
items.feedback: ATC equals AFC plus AVC. At Q=50 it is $6+$24=$30; at Q=60 it is $5+$23=$28. Both fixed cost per unit and variable cost per unit fall by $1.

items.stem: A firm has standard U-shaped ATC. Initially MC crosses ATC from below at Q=80, where both equal $32. An annual license fee then rises, increasing fixed cost by $720 without changing variable cost. At Q=80, which comparison is correct, and what happens to the output that minimizes ATC?
options: ATC and MC both rise to $41; the ATC-minimizing output stays at 80.
ATC rises to $41 while MC stays $32; the new ATC-minimizing output is less than 80.
ATC rises to $41 while MC stays $32; the new ATC-minimizing output is greater than 80.
ATC stays $32 while MC rises to $41; the new ATC-minimizing output is greater than 80.
items.feedback: At 80 units the added fixed cost raises ATC by $720/80=$9, while MC is unchanged. MC is now below ATC, so expanding output lowers ATC; with the stated U-shaped curves, the minimum occurs at a larger output.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Using the horizontal TFC line at Q = 200, what average fixed cost is implied?
options: $0 per unit
$2 per unit
$4 per unit
$8 per unit

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At the total-product maximum, use the labeled output and labor input to calculate average product.
options: 0 units per worker
15 units per worker
10 units per worker
150 units per worker
items.feedback: AP=TP/L=150/10=15, even though MP is zero at the TP maximum.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Near the TP maximum, what total product is implied by the shown AP and labor values?
options: About 15 units
About 100 units
About 300 units
About 150 units
items.feedback: TP=AP×L≈15×10=150 units.

items.stem: A firm earns $500 in revenue. Its explicit variable costs are $280 and its explicit fixed lease cost is $70. The owner also forgoes $40 of income from another job. What is accounting profit, and why is the forgone income treated that way?
options: $110; accounting profit subtracts explicit costs and the $40 forgone income.
$220; accounting profit excludes both the fixed lease and the $40 forgone income.
$190; accounting profit subtracts the lease but adds the $40 forgone income.
$150; accounting profit subtracts explicit costs, so the $40 forgone income is excluded.
items.feedback: Accounting profit is revenue minus explicit costs: $500−$280−$70=$150. The forgone $40 is an implicit opportunity cost used in economic profit, not an additional explicit cost.

items.stem: How many units do the fifth and sixth workers each add? What does this imply about the rate at which total output is growing?
options: They add 12 and 10 units; TP rises at a decreasing rate.
They add 10 and 8 units; diminishing MP means TP falls.
They add 10 and 8 units; TP rises at a decreasing rate.
They add 12 and 10 units; diminishing MP means TP falls.
items.feedback: TP at four, five and six workers is 46, 56 and 64. The marginal products are 10 and 8. They remain positive but decrease, so TP continues rising more slowly.

items.stem: A manager says positive output per worker proves that hiring more labor raises total output. At 10.5 workers, does the graph support the claim?
options: AP is about 15 while MP is below zero; total output is falling despite positive average output.
AP is about 12 while MP is below zero; total output is falling despite positive average output.
AP is about 15 while MP is below zero; positive AP proves that total output is rising.
AP is about 12 while MP is below zero; positive AP proves that total output is rising.
items.feedback: At 10.5 workers, the AP curve is near 15 while MP is negative. AP measures the positive level TP/L; MP measures the effect of more labor. Positive AP therefore does not refute falling TP.

items.stem: How many units do the fifth and sixth workers each add? What does this imply about the rate at which total output is growing?
options: They add 9 and 7 units; TP rises at a decreasing rate.
They add 11 and 9 units; TP rises at a decreasing rate.
They add 9 and 7 units; diminishing MP means TP falls.
They add 11 and 9 units; diminishing MP means TP falls.
items.feedback: TP at four, five and six workers is 47, 56 and 63. The marginal products are 9 and 7. They remain positive but decrease, so TP continues rising more slowly.

items.stem: At Q = 25, compare marginal cost with AVC and ATC. How would a small increase in output affect AVC and ATC?
options: Both AVC and ATC fall.
AVC rises while ATC falls.
Both AVC and ATC rise.
AVC falls while ATC rises.
items.feedback: At Q = 25, MC is below both AVC and ATC, so an increase in output lowers both averages.

items.stem: At Q = 35, compare marginal cost with AVC and ATC. How would a small increase in output affect AVC and ATC?
options: Both AVC and ATC fall.
Both AVC and ATC rise.
AVC rises and ATC falls.
AVC falls and ATC rises.
items.feedback: MC lies above AVC but below ATC. Additional units raise AVC but lower ATC.

items.stem: At Q = 50, compare marginal cost with AVC and ATC. How would a small increase in output affect AVC and ATC?
options: Both AVC and ATC fall.
AVC rises while ATC falls.
Both AVC and ATC rise.
AVC falls while ATC rises.
items.feedback: MC lies above both AVC and ATC, so additional units raise both averages.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At Q = 40, which ordering holds, and what does it imply about a small increase in output?
options: MC < AVC < AC; the next units cost less than either average, lowering both AVC and AC.
AVC < MC < AC; the next units cost more than AVC but less than AC, lowering AVC and raising AC.
MC < AVC < AC; the next units cost less than either average, raising both AVC and AC.
AVC < MC < AC; the next units cost more than AVC but less than AC, raising AVC and lowering AC.
items.feedback: At Q = 40, MC lies above AVC but below AC. A marginal cost above an average pulls that average up; a marginal cost below an average pulls it down. Thus AVC rises and AC falls.

items.stem: A firm adds one worker beyond the total-product maximum in the graph. Which worker is this, and what can be inferred about marginal and average product?
options: The 13th worker; MP is negative but AP remains positive.
The 11th worker; both MP and AP must be negative.
The 11th worker; MP is negative but AP remains positive.
The 13th worker; both MP and AP must be negative.
items.feedback: TP peaks at 10 workers. The 11th worker lowers TP, giving negative MP, but TP remains positive. AP = TP/L therefore remains positive. Marginal and average product need not have the same sign.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Where does MC cross AVC and ATC, and what do the marginal-average relationships imply at the crossings?
options: At roughly Q = 32 and Q = 36, respectively; the next units switch from lowering to raising the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
At roughly Q = 25 and Q = 30, respectively; the next units switch from lowering to raising the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
At roughly Q = 32 and Q = 36, respectively; the next units switch from raising to lowering the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
At roughly Q = 25 and Q = 30, respectively; the next units switch from raising to lowering the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
items.feedback: MC crosses AVC and ATC at roughly Q = 32 and Q = 36, respectively. Before each crossing MC is below that average and pulls it down; after the crossing MC is above it and pulls it up. Thus the crossing identifies a minimum, not a maximum.

items.stem: A manager says marginal product cannot fall while total output is still rising. Which labor interval shown disproves that claim, and why?
options: From 6 to 8 workers, TP rises with a declining slope; diminishing MP need not be negative MP.
From 2 to 4 workers, TP rises with a declining slope; diminishing MP need not be negative MP.
From 6 to 8 workers, TP rises with a declining slope; diminishing MP means total output is already falling.
From 2 to 4 workers, TP rises with a declining slope; diminishing MP means total output is already falling.
items.feedback: The curve is still rising but flattening between 6 and 8 workers. Additional workers add output, but by smaller amounts. Diminishing marginal product begins before negative marginal product and the decline in TP beyond the peak.

items.stem: Blue Peak Printing has revenue $138,000, explicit cost $83,000, and implicit cost $39,000. What is economic profit?
items.feedback: Subtract all costs from revenue.

items.stem: Riverbend Textiles has revenue $274,000, explicit cost $176,000, and implicit cost $73,000. What is economic profit?
items.feedback: Subtract all costs from revenue.

items.stem: Juniper Foods has revenue $205,000, explicit cost $132,000, and implicit cost $55,000. What is economic profit?
items.feedback: Subtract all costs from revenue.

items.stem: Summit Glassworks has revenue $356,000, explicit cost $229,000, and implicit cost $95,000. What is economic profit?
items.feedback: Subtract all costs from revenue.

items.stem: Northstar Bakery production schedule (workers: total units produced) through worker 3: 0:0, 1:8, 2:20, 3:34. What is the marginal product of worker 3?
options: 14 units
34 units
11.33 units
20 units
items.feedback: MP is the output change.

items.stem: Ironwood Furniture production schedule (workers: total units produced) through worker 4: 0:0, 1:6, 2:16, 3:29, 4:41. What is the marginal product of worker 4?
options: 41 units
12 units
10.25 units
29 units
items.feedback: MP is the output change.

items.stem: Blue Peak Printing produces 18 printers with two workers earning $110 each. Fixed cost is $210, and labor is the only variable input. What is total cost?
Riverbend Textiles has TFC $360, 3 workers at $140, and Q=40. What is total cost?
items.feedback: TC=TFC+TVC.

items.stem: Juniper Foods has TFC $270, 4 workers at $125, and Q=44. What is total cost?
items.feedback: TC=TFC+TVC.

items.stem: Summit Glassworks has TFC $480, 5 workers at $160, and Q=69. What is total cost?
items.feedback: TC=TFC+TVC.

items.stem: Riverbend Textiles TC rises from $640 to $780 as Q rises from 25 to 40. What is marginal cost over this output change?
items.feedback: Divide ΔTC by ΔQ.

items.stem: Granite Toolworks produces 40 units. Average fixed cost is $7.50 and average variable cost is $16.75. What is total cost?
All inputs and total cost double while output rises from 1,000 to 2,400 units. LRAC begins at $30. New LRAC?
items.feedback: Cost becomes $60,000 and output 2,400.

items.stem: Long-run TC is $480,000 at 12,000 units and $675,000 at 15,000 units. Which has lower LRAC, and by how much?
options: 15,000 units, by $5 per unit
12,000 units, by $5 per unit
12,000 units, by $15 per unit
Equal LRAC
items.feedback: LRAC is $40 versus $45.

items.stem: At eight workers, estimate marginal product. Has average product already reached its maximum? Has total product?
options: MP is about 13; AP has passed its maximum, while TP has not.
MP is about 10; AP has passed its maximum, while TP has not.
MP is about 13; TP has passed its maximum, while AP has not.
MP is about 10; TP has passed its maximum, while AP has not.
items.feedback: At L = 8, MP ≈ 13 is positive and below AP ≈ 17. AP is already falling, but positive MP means TP still rises. Their maxima occur at different labor inputs.

items.stem: A $900 annual fee is already paid and cannot be refunded. For today’s output decision it is:
options: A variable cost
Marginal cost
A sunk cost
Avoidable revenue
items.feedback: The payment is unrecoverable.

items.stem: A monthly lease can be canceled next month. For next month’s plant decision it is:
options: Sunk forever
A per-unit variable cost
An implicit cost only
Avoidable even if fixed with respect to output
items.feedback: Fixed does not automatically mean sunk.

items.stem: A wage rises while plant rent stays fixed. Which measures rise?
options: TVC, AVC, ATC, and MC
TFC and AFC only
AFC only
No cost measures
items.feedback: The wage is a variable-input price.

items.stem: A property tax rises while output is unchanged. Which measures rise?
options: TVC, AVC, and MC
TFC, AFC, TC, and ATC
MC only
AP and MP
items.feedback: A fixed-cost increase affects total and average fixed components.

items.stem: Technology raises MP with wages unchanged. Which relationship is expected?
options: MC rises
TFC falls necessarily
MC falls
AFC rises
items.feedback: Higher MP lowers variable input cost per extra unit.

items.stem: Assume input prices are unchanged. All inputs double and output more than doubles. The firm experiences:
options: Diminishing marginal product
Diseconomies of scale
Negative marginal product
Economies of scale
items.feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a larger percentage, so long-run average cost falls—consistent with economies of scale.

items.stem: Assume input prices are unchanged. All inputs and output double. The firm experiences:
options: Constant returns to scale
Economies of scale
Diseconomies of scale
Diminishing marginal product
items.feedback: With unchanged input prices, proportional increases in all inputs and output leave long-run average cost unchanged, consistent with constant returns to scale.

items.stem: Assume input prices are unchanged. All inputs double and output rises 60%. The firm experiences:
options: Economies of scale
Diseconomies of scale
Constant returns to scale
Increasing MP
items.feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a smaller percentage, so long-run average cost rises—consistent with diseconomies of scale.

items.stem: LRATC first reaches its minimum at 25,000 units and remains flat through 40,000. MES is:
options: 40,000 units
32,500 units
25,000 units
The largest possible output
items.feedback: MES is the first minimum-cost output.

items.stem: At a given output, three plants have ATC of $28, $24, and $31. LRATC is:
items.feedback: Choose the least-cost feasible plant.

items.stem: A firm automates production, raising TFC but lowering AVC. Which conclusion is certain?
options: ATC falls at every output
AFC rises at each positive output
MC rises at every output
TFC becomes sunk by definition
items.feedback: Only the fixed-cost component’s direction is certain.

items.stem: Why can a higher fixed cost leave MC unchanged?
options: MC excludes all cost
Fixed cost is revenue
Fixed cost does not change when output changes.
Output is long run
items.feedback: A constant addition to TC cancels in ΔTC.

items.stem: A plant’s output schedule shows falling MP. At constant wages, which cost pattern follows?
options: Falling MC
Constant MC
Falling TFC
Rising MC
items.feedback: Less output per worker raises cost per extra unit.

items.stem: Which long-run force can create diseconomies of scale?
options: Coordination and communication problems
Spreading fixed cost only
Early specialization only
A decline in TFC
items.feedback: Organizational complexity can raise LRATC.

items.stem: Which long-run force can create economies of scale?
options: Negative MP by definition
Specialization and use of indivisible equipment
Higher coordination burden
A rise in every input price
items.feedback: Scale can spread specialized resources and indivisible inputs.

items.stem: The LRATC envelope is below available SRATC curves because:
options: It excludes variable cost
It averages only fixed cost
The firm selects the least-cost plant at each output
Every plant is efficient at every output
items.feedback: Long-run flexibility permits plant choice.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What output represents minimum efficient scale?
options: 30 units
90 units
60 units
120 units
items.feedback: MES is the smallest output attaining minimum LRAC; here that point is Q=60.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Which claim is NOT supported by the LRAC curve?
options: LRAC falls as output approaches 60 from the left side
LRAC rises as output moves above 60 on the right side
The minimum LRAC occurs at approximately Q=60
There is a broad flat interval of constant returns to scale
items.feedback: The graph has a single rounded minimum rather than a visibly flat minimum-cost interval.

items.stem: The base-year basket cost is $640, last year’s CPI was 125, and the basket costs $856 now. Which pair gives the current CPI and inflation since last year?
options: 133.75 and 8.75 percent.
856 and 33.75 percent.
133.75 and 7 percent.
125 and 7 percent.
items.feedback: Current CPI is 100 × 856/640 = 133.75; inflation is (133.75 − 125)/125 = 7 percent.

items.stem: A basket contains 4 units of A and 6 units of B. Base prices are $5 and $10; current prices are $8 and $12. What is the CPI?
items.feedback: Base cost is $80; current cost is $104; CPI = 130.

items.stem: A basket has 10 units of food and 1 unit of electronics. Food prices rise 4 percent and the electronics price rises 40 percent. Which conclusion is justified without more information?
options: ‘Food must dominate because there are more units.’
The CPI change depends on each item’s expenditure weight.
‘The CPI must rise 40 percent.’
‘The two percentage changes should be averaged equally.’
items.feedback: The contribution of each item depends on quantity times price in the basket.

items.stem: A CPI basket contains 5 bus tickets and 2 meals. Base-year prices are $2 per bus ticket and $10 per meal. Current prices are $3 per bus ticket and $14 per meal. What is the CPI?
A basket costs $750 when the CPI is 125. One year later the same basket costs $810. Which new index and claim about inflation are correct?
options: CPI 135; inflation is 8%, although the index rose 10 points
CPI 108; inflation is 8%, because the old index resets each year
CPI 135; inflation is 10%, matching the index-point increase
CPI 162; inflation is 35%, measured from the base year
items.feedback: The unchanged base-basket cost is 750/1.25 = 600. The new index is 810/600 × 100 = 135. The 10-point increase is 10/125 = 8%, not 10%.

items.stem: A basket cost $1,200 in the base year. CPI is now 150. Last year CPI was 125. What is the basket cost now and the inflation rate since last year?
items.feedback: Current basket cost = 1,200 x 1.5 = 1,800. Inflation = (150 - 125)/125 = 20%.

items.stem: A fixed basket has two meals at a base price of $4 each and one fare at $12. Meal prices rise 10%; the fare is unchanged. What CPI results, with the base set to 100?
options: 106.7; meals were two-thirds of the units
110; use the price change of the only item that rose
140; the meal expenditure weight is the inflation rate
104; meals had 40% of base basket spending
items.feedback: Base cost is 2 × 4 + 12 = 20. Current cost is 2 × 4.40 + 12 = 20.80, giving CPI 104. The relevant weight is the 8/20 spending share, not the two-of-three item count.

items.stem: A fixed-basket index is 125 in the initial period and 130 in the next. A $150 nominal payment rises 3%. Does its purchasing power keep pace?
options: No; real purchasing power falls exactly 5% because the index rises five points
No; prices rise 4%, and real purchasing power falls about 1.0%
Yes; prices rise only 3.8%, which is below the payment rise
Yes; a rising nominal payment guarantees more purchasing power
items.feedback: Inflation is (130−125)/125 = 4%. The real payment factor is 1.03/1.04, a decline of about 0.96%.

items.stem: A basket cost is $240 before prices change. Its index rises from 160 to 168. A clerk multiplies the old cost by 1.08. Which corrected cost and reason are right?
options: $259.2; index points are automatically percentages
$403.2; apply the new index as though the old index were 100
$228; the higher index implies a lower basket cost
$252; the relevant price factor is 168/160
items.feedback: The price factor is new index/old index = 168/160 = 1.05. An eight-point rise from 160 is 5%, not 8%.

items.stem: A worker earns $250 before a 6% nominal raise. The relevant CPI rises 8%. By what percentages do nominal pay and real pay change?
options: Nominal and real pay both rise 6%; prices do not enter.
Nominal pay rises 6%; real pay rises 14% after adding inflation.
Nominal pay rises 6%; real pay falls about 1.9%.
Nominal pay rises 6%; real pay falls 8% after ignoring the raise.
items.feedback: Purchasing power changes by 1.06/1.08−1 ≈ −1.85%. A positive nominal raise can accompany a real loss.

items.stem: The CPI rises from 120 to 132. The statistical agency then makes the first of these years the base year, using the same fixed basket. What are the rebased indexes and the inflation rate, and does rebasing change measured inflation?
options: 100 and 112; inflation rises to 12%.
100 and 110; inflation remains 10%.
100 and 132; inflation rises to 32%.
120 and 132; inflation remains 12%.
items.feedback: Multiply both indexes by 100/120. They become 100 and 110. Inflation is 132/120 − 1 = 110/100 − 1 = 10%; choosing a new index base does not change the price change.

items.stem: A fixed basket costs $100 in the base year, $120 this year and $132 next year. What are next year's CPI and inflation rate?
options: The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 32%
The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 10%
The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 12%
The next CPI is 120; next inflation is 10%
items.feedback: CPI levels are 120 and 132. Inflation is (132−120)/120×100 = 10%, not the 12-point change or the 32% cumulative rise.

items.stem: Which scenario combines two CPI biases at once?
options: A new streaming service draws consumers from expensive cable
A worker becomes unemployed during a recession
Exports rise faster than imports
Government purchases increase
items.feedback: New goods and substitution both complicate CPI measurement.

items.stem: A streaming service did not exist in the base year and later gives consumers a cheaper alternative to cable. Which CPI problems are most directly involved?
options: Introduction of new goods and substitution bias
Only GDP deflator bias
Only cyclical unemployment
Only nominal interest error
items.feedback: New goods improve choice, and substitution toward them can reduce actual cost-of-living increases.

items.stem: A replacement device costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other quality change. Separately, a new service gives households a cheaper way to meet a need, but the price index will not include it for several years. Which measurement treatment addresses both problems?
options: Record 20% device inflation without adjustment, and wait to count the new service until its price has risen.
Compare the device’s price per unit of service, which rises 20%, and treat the new service as a change in the old basket’s quantities.
Record a 50% device-price decline from the quality change alone, and assume the new service cannot affect the cost of living.
Compare the device’s price per unit of service, which falls 40%, and account for the new service’s benefit from expanded choice.
items.feedback: The quality-adjusted relative price is 1.20/2=0.60, a 40% fall per unit of service. Delaying the new service can also miss a lower cost of achieving a given utility through expanded choice. Quality change and new-goods bias are distinct measurement problems.

items.stem: A product originally costs $230. Its replacement costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality changes. How should the price change be interpreted after allowing for the improved service?
options: The comparable price rises 20%; improved service should have no role in measuring a like-for-like price.
The comparable price is unchanged; a new version is always treated as having the old price.
The price per unit of service falls; counting the entire sticker-price increase as inflation ignores the quality improvement.
The price per unit of service doubles; the quality gain should be added to rather than allowed for in the comparison.
items.feedback: The replacement's price per service unit is 1.20/2 = 0.60 of the old level. A like-for-like comparison must adjust for quality rather than automatically calling the full 20% higher price inflation.

items.stem: A new product expands choice while the price index still records spending of $240 on older products. How does the delayed inclusion of the new product limit what the CPI tells us?
options: Delayed inclusion proves CPI understates every household's inflation by the same fixed amount
Delayed inclusion can miss gains in purchasing opportunities; that limitation does not make every observed CPI change meaningless
Delayed inclusion means CPI is a complete cost-of-living measure because consumers previously did not buy the new product
Delayed inclusion means actual prices cannot change until the product enters the official basket
items.feedback: New goods can improve purchasing opportunities before an index incorporates them. The limitation is specific; it does not invalidate all price evidence or establish one universal bias size.

items.stem: A $250 payment is indexed to measured CPI. A careful study estimates measured inflation at 5% but the cost of maintaining the recipient's utility at 3%, owing to substitution and new choices. How does indexation affect the payment's purchasing power under these estimates?
options: Real value falls about 2%; measured inflation exceeds estimated cost growth.
Real value rises about 8%; add measured and estimated inflation rates.
Real value is unchanged; official indexation exactly preserves the recipient's utility.
Real value rises about 1.9%; indexation exceeds estimated cost growth.
items.feedback: The relevant factor is 1.05/1.03, about a 1.94% gain relative to the estimated utility-maintaining cost. The conclusion is conditional on the supplied estimates, not an assertion that every index overstates inflation by two points.

items.stem: A benefit of $1,000 rises with a fixed-basket index that increases 8%. For these recipients, the minimum cost of maintaining last year’s utility rises 5% after substitution. How does the indexed benefit compare with that cost, and what follows if the adjustment instead uses 5%?
options: It pays $30 more than the $1,050 needed; a 5% adjustment would preserve the stated utility at the new prices.
It pays $30 less than the $1,080 needed; a 5% adjustment would create an even larger shortfall.
It pays exactly the $1,080 needed; any smaller adjustment must reduce the stated utility.
It pays $80 more than the $1,000 needed; substitution means prices have no effect on the required benefit.
items.feedback: Indexation pays 1,000×1.08=1,080, while the stated cost is 1,000×1.05=1,050. The excess is $30. A 5% adjustment matches this recipients’ constant-utility cost increase; the conclusion uses their stated costs, not a claim about every household.

items.stem: A product originally costs $110. Its replacement costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality changes. How should the price change be interpreted after allowing for the improved service?
options: The comparable price rises 20%; improved service should have no role in measuring a like-for-like price.
The comparable price is unchanged; a new version is always treated as having the old price.
The price per unit of service doubles; the quality gain should be added to rather than allowed for in the comparison.
The price per unit of service falls; counting the entire sticker-price increase as inflation ignores the quality improvement.
items.feedback: The replacement's price per service unit is 1.20/2 = 0.60 of the old level. A like-for-like comparison must adjust for quality rather than automatically calling the full 20% higher price inflation.

items.stem: A product originally costs $150. Its replacement costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality changes. How should the price change be interpreted after allowing for the improved service?
options: The comparable price rises 20%; improved service should have no role in measuring a like-for-like price.
The price per unit of service falls; counting the entire sticker-price increase as inflation ignores the quality improvement.
The comparable price is unchanged; a new version is always treated as having the old price.
The price per unit of service doubles; the quality gain should be added to rather than allowed for in the comparison.
items.feedback: The replacement's price per service unit is 1.20/2 = 0.60 of the old level. A like-for-like comparison must adjust for quality rather than automatically calling the full 20% higher price inflation.

items.stem: After apple prices rise, a household’s old basket costs $8 instead of $4. By switching toward pears, it can maintain the same satisfaction for $6. How much does the fixed basket overstate the increase needed to maintain satisfaction?
items.feedback: The fixed basket suggests a $4 increase, but the adjusted basket requires only $2 more than before. The overstatement is $2.

items.stem: Prices of domestically produced aircraft exports rise while imported smartphones bought by households become cheaper. Which combination is plausible?
options: The GDP deflator rises while the CPI falls
The CPI rises while the GDP deflator falls
Both indexes must rise because one price increased
Both indexes must fall because consumers buy smartphones
items.feedback: The aircraft exports are domestic production and enter the GDP deflator, so their higher prices push it up. Imported smartphones enter the CPI but not the GDP deflator; their lower price can pull CPI inflation down.

items.stem: Between two years, individual prices do not change, but domestic production shifts toward goods whose current prices are higher relative to their base-year prices. Why can a fixed-base GDP deflator rise?
options: The deflator must be unchanged whenever current-year prices are unchanged
The deflator begins including imported consumer goods as domestic output
A shift toward goods with higher dollar prices raises every index regardless of base prices
Current quantities put more weight on goods with larger price increases since the base year
items.feedback: The deflator compares current-price and base-price values of current quantities. Changing the output mix toward larger current-to-base price relatives can raise the ratio even with no new individual price changes. High dollar prices alone do not establish that result.

items.stem: A country imports most consumer goods but produces mostly capital equipment. Imported consumer prices rise while domestic capital prices fall. Which statement is most accurate?
