options: CPI and GDP deflator can move in opposite directions
CPI and GDP deflator must move together
GDP deflator must include imported consumer goods
CPI must include capital equipment bought by firms
items.feedback: Different baskets mean the CPI and GDP deflator can diverge sharply.

items.stem: Imported home solar panels become cheaper while domestically produced industrial turbines become more expensive. Why can CPI and the GDP deflator move in opposite directions?
options: The indexes cover different goods and use different weighting frameworks
Both indexes measure only domestic consumer purchases
The CPI excludes imports while the deflator includes them
The GDP deflator fixes a household basket while CPI tracks current output
items.feedback: CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.

items.stem: An economy with nominal output $170 reports a higher GDP deflator but unchanged CPI. Which proposed explanation could reconcile the reports without concluding either index is wrong?
options: Prices of imported household goods rose while every domestic output price stayed fixed
Every household and domestic output price rose in exactly the same proportion
Only current quantities changed while all current and base-year prices stayed identical
Prices of domestic investment goods rose while household-consumption prices stayed fixed
items.feedback: Investment goods are domestic final output but not household consumption. Their prices can raise the deflator while CPI remains unchanged; different scopes can explain the divergence.

items.stem: A domestic economy buys $180 of imported household fuel and produces machinery only for export. Fuel prices rise while machinery prices are unchanged. Holding quantities fixed, what happens to the CPI and GDP deflator?
options: Both rise equally; household fuel belongs in both indexes at equal weight.
CPI is unchanged; the GDP deflator rises through the import-price component.
CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
Both are unchanged; imported consumption is excluded from either price index.
items.feedback: CPI covers household consumption including imports. The GDP deflator covers domestically produced final output, including exports; unchanged domestic output prices need not reflect imported fuel inflation.

items.stem: A household benefit of $190 must track consumption costs, while nominal domestic GDP must be converted into real output. Imported food becomes dearer and domestic investment equipment becomes cheaper. Which index should be used for each purpose, and must the two indexes move together?
options: CPI for both uses; consumer prices also measure domestic capital-goods prices.
CPI for benefits, deflator for GDP; different coverage permits different movements.
Deflator for both uses; domestic output prices measure imported household costs.
Deflator for benefits, CPI for GDP; imported food belongs to domestic output.
items.feedback: The purpose determines index choice. CPI tracks consumption costs; the deflator matches domestic final output. Imports and investment equipment enter these measures differently, so divergent movements are possible.

items.stem: A domestic economy buys $220 of imported household fuel and produces machinery only for export. Fuel prices rise while machinery prices are unchanged. Holding quantities fixed, what happens to the CPI and GDP deflator?
options: Both rise equally; household fuel belongs in both indexes at equal weight.
CPI is unchanged; the GDP deflator rises through the import-price component.
CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
Both are unchanged; imported consumption is excluded from either price index.
items.feedback: CPI covers household consumption including imports. The GDP deflator covers domestically produced final output, including exports; unchanged domestic output prices need not reflect imported fuel inflation.

items.stem: A household benefit of $230 must track consumption costs, while nominal domestic GDP must be converted into real output. Imported food becomes dearer and domestic investment equipment becomes cheaper. Which index should be used for each purpose, and must the two indexes move together?
options: CPI for both uses; consumer prices also measure domestic capital-goods prices.
CPI for benefits, deflator for GDP; different coverage permits different movements.
Deflator for both uses; domestic output prices measure imported household costs.
Deflator for benefits, CPI for GDP; imported food belongs to domestic output.
items.feedback: The purpose determines index choice. CPI tracks consumption costs; the deflator matches domestic final output. Imports and investment equipment enter these measures differently, so divergent movements are possible.

items.stem: A domestic economy buys $100 of imported household fuel and produces machinery only for export. Fuel prices rise while machinery prices are unchanged. Holding quantities fixed, what happens to the CPI and GDP deflator?
options: Both rise equally; household fuel belongs in both indexes at equal weight.
CPI is unchanged; the GDP deflator rises through the import-price component.
Both are unchanged; imported consumption is excluded from either price index.
CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
items.feedback: CPI covers household consumption including imports. The GDP deflator covers domestically produced final output, including exports; unchanged domestic output prices need not reflect imported fuel inflation.

items.stem: A household benefit of $110 must track consumption costs, while nominal domestic GDP must be converted into real output. Imported food becomes dearer and domestic investment equipment becomes cheaper. Which index should be used for each purpose, and must the two indexes move together?
options: CPI for both uses; consumer prices also measure domestic capital-goods prices.
Deflator for both uses; domestic output prices measure imported household costs.
CPI for benefits, deflator for GDP; different coverage permits different movements.
Deflator for benefits, CPI for GDP; imported food belongs to domestic output.
items.feedback: The purpose determines index choice. CPI tracks consumption costs; the deflator matches domestic final output. Imports and investment equipment enter these measures differently, so divergent movements are possible.

items.stem: A country produces only $120 of export machinery and households consume only imported food. Machinery prices fall 4% while food prices rise 6%, with quantities fixed. Which pair is consistent?
options: Both indexes fall 4% because domestic output determines every index
CPI rises 6%; the GDP deflator falls 4%
CPI falls 4%; the GDP deflator rises 6%
Both indexes rise 6% because households pay that inflation
items.feedback: Under the deliberately distinct baskets, CPI follows imported household food and the deflator follows domestic machinery, even though all machinery is exported.

items.stem: A government deficit increases by $30 billion while planned private saving rises by $10 billion at each real interest rate. With investment demand unchanged, how does the net saving change affect the loanable-funds market?
options: National saving rises $40 billion, shifting supply right; a lower rate raises investment.
National saving falls $20 billion, shifting investment demand left and lowering the rate.
National saving is unchanged because an increase in private saving fully offsets any deficit.
National saving falls $20 billion, shifting supply left; a higher rate crowds out investment.
items.feedback: Public saving falls $30 billion while private saving rises $10 billion, reducing national saving by $20 billion at a given rate. Supply shifts left; the real rate rises and investment falls along unchanged demand.

items.stem: A larger deficit causes the shift shown in the supply of loanable funds. How should the resulting change in firms' investment from A to B be interpreted?
options: Investment falls 80 units as firms move along D0 in response to the higher real rate.
Investment falls 40 units because the higher real rate shifts the entire investment-demand curve left.
Investment falls 40 units as firms move along D0 in response to the higher real rate.
Investment falls 40 units because the deficit directly reduces project profitability at every real rate.
items.feedback: A is at 100 and B at 60, so equilibrium investment falls 40 units. D0 remains fixed: the saving contraction raises the real rate from 6% to 8%, making fewer projects worthwhile along the existing demand schedule.

items.stem: Planned private saving rises by $30 billion and public saving falls by $10 billion at each real rate. What happens to investment in the loanable-funds model if investment demand is unchanged?
options: Lower national saving raises the real rate and reduces investment along the existing demand curve.
Higher national saving lowers the real rate and raises investment along the existing demand curve.
The $20 billion net saving increase shifts investment demand right and raises the real rate.
Investment is unchanged because opposing saving changes must cancel completely.
items.feedback: The net national-saving increase is $20 billion at a given rate. Supply shifts right, lowering the real rate and encouraging investment along its unchanged demand curve.

items.stem: A deficit increases by $30 billion while private saving rises by $10 billion. In the loanable-funds model, how does this affect the real interest rate and private investment?
options: Aggregate demand must fall by exactly $20 billion after every multiplier effect
Investment demand shifts right by $30 billion because deficits directly raise project profitability
Supply shifts left, raising the rate and crowding out investment
National saving rises $40 billion, so the real rate falls and private investment expands
items.feedback: The relevant chain is public saving down, only partly offset by private saving, then national saving and loanable-funds supply down. The task does not calculate short-run aggregate-demand multipliers.

items.stem: Crowding out reduces new machinery purchases, while depreciation and all other growth determinants are unchanged. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: The existing capital stock falls immediately by the full amount of forgone investment
Future output must decline by exactly the reduction in machinery spending
The capital stock is unchanged because investment affects only financial claims
The future capital stock is lower than otherwise, but may still grow
items.feedback: Less gross investment means less addition to the capital stock than in the counterfactual. The stock can still grow if remaining investment exceeds depreciation, so an absolute decline is not implied.

items.stem: A budget improvement raises planned public saving by $25 billion while private saving falls by $10 billion at each real rate. An analyst says this directly raises firms' investment demand. How should that claim be corrected?
options: National saving rises $15 billion; investment demand shifts right because all additional saving is a new project.
National saving falls $35 billion; supply shifts left and investment falls.
National saving is unchanged; any change in public saving is canceled by private saving.
National saving rises $15 billion; supply shifts right, and the lower rate induces investment along unchanged demand.
items.feedback: National saving rises by $15 billion at each rate, shifting supply right. The lower equilibrium real rate then increases investment along unchanged demand. A saving increase does not itself raise project profitability at every rate.

items.stem: National saving rises and lowers the real interest rate, but many funded projects have low returns and depreciation is unusually high. What is the careful long-run conclusion?
options: The higher saving rate guarantees an equal permanent increase in productive capacity
More financing can support capital formation, but does not guarantee it
Every financed project becomes physical capital, so project quality and depreciation are irrelevant
Greater saving must reduce investment because the closed-economy identity fixes the capital stock
items.feedback: Greater saving can lower financing costs and enable more investment. Actual capital accumulation and future output still depend on project quality, depreciation, technology, and other conditions.

items.topic: Debt Measures, Debt Burden, and Fiscal Data
items.stem: A Treasury observation reports total public debt outstanding, while a CBO projection reports debt held by the public as a percentage of GDP. What must be aligned before comparing them?
options: Only the agency names
Only whether both reported fiscal values have positive signs
Definition, date, status, and units
Nothing, because all federal debt measures and dates are interchangeable
items.feedback: A sound comparison requires the same measure, date/status, and units.

items.topic: Debt Measures, Debt Burden, and Fiscal Data
items.stem: A projection has public debt of $400 and GDP $800. An alternative has debt $480 and GDP $1200. Which ranking respects both nominal levels and the debt ratio?
options: The alternative has less nominal debt because its debt ratio is lower
The alternative has a higher ratio because its nominal debt is higher
The two ratios are equal because both debt and GDP changed
The alternative has more nominal debt but a lower ratio: 40% rather than 50%
items.feedback: Use the same measure in each numerator and its matching GDP denominator: 10/20=50%, 12/30=40%. A ratio and its numerator can rank differently.

items.topic: Debt Measures, Debt Burden, and Fiscal Data
items.stem: Federal debt held by the public is $600; intragovernmental holdings are $120. A report adds foreign-held debt, already inside public holdings, again. Which correction avoids double counting?
options: Gross debt requires adding foreign holdings again because residence changes the liability's identity
Gross federal debt is $720; foreign holdings are a subset of public debt, not a third component
Gross debt is $600; intragovernmental holdings are never part of gross federal debt
Gross debt is $120; only accounts within government create debt
items.feedback: Gross debt = public 600+intragovernmental 120=720. A residence breakdown of public holders does not create another liability.

items.stem: A government raises purchases with net taxes unchanged. Private-saving behavior is unchanged. Which sequence describes the fiscal consequence?
options: Private saving falls but public saving is unchanged, because government purchases are household consumption
Public saving rises and the budget moves toward surplus, reducing the need to issue government debt
Public saving falls and the budget moves toward deficit, increasing borrowing needs if the shortfall is debt-financed
Public saving falls but issuing debt counts as revenue, so borrowing restores the budget balance
items.feedback: With net taxes unchanged, higher government purchases reduce public saving T − G and move the budget toward deficit. Borrowing can finance the shortfall, but debt issuance does not count as revenue or reverse the decline in public saving.

items.stem: The deficit becomes smaller, nominal debt rises, and debt-to-GDP falls. Which combination can explain all three facts?
options: A surplus raises debt
Debt falls faster than GDP while the annual deficit becomes larger
Debt rises, but nominal GDP grows faster
A balanced budget erases existing debt while nominal GDP remains unchanged
items.feedback: The deficit can still add to nominal debt, while faster GDP growth lowers the debt ratio.

items.stem: Public debt starts at $200 and ends two years later at $260. The first-year budget deficit is $20. Assume deficits are financed entirely by borrowing and there are no other debt adjustments. What is the second-year deficit, and how is it calculated?
options: $60; the entire two-year increase is the second-year deficit
$40; subtract initial debt and the first deficit from the ending stock
$260; an ending debt stock is the deficit for its final year
$240; subtract only the first-year deficit from ending debt
items.feedback: The two-year debt increase is 260−200=60. Subtract the known first-year deficit 20 to infer the missing second-year deficit 40. The ending stock includes earlier borrowing; it is not a one-year flow.

items.stem: The overall deficit is $40, including interest outlays of $80. Define the primary balance as revenues minus noninterest outlays. What is the primary balance?
options: The primary balance is a $40 surplus even though the overall budget is in deficit
The primary balance is a $120 deficit because interest is added a second time
The primary balance is zero because all deficits consist entirely of interest
The primary balance equals the outstanding debt stock of $40
items.feedback: Overall deficit = primary deficit + interest. Primary deficit = 40−80=−40, so there is a primary surplus of 40. Flow definitions matter.

items.stem: The price of peanut butter rises. If jelly is a complement, what happens in the jelly market?
options: Demand for jelly decreases
Demand for jelly increases
Supply of jelly decreases
Quantity demanded of jelly increases
items.feedback: Peanut butter and jelly are complements. If peanut butter gets more expensive, demand for jelly falls.

items.stem: The price of bus rides rises. If subway rides are substitutes, what happens in the subway market?
options: Demand for subway rides increases
Demand for subway rides decreases
Supply of subway rides decreases
Quantity supplied of bus rides increases
items.feedback: When the price of a substitute rises, demand for the other good increases.

items.stem: Consumers expect the price of coffee to fall next month. What happens to current demand for coffee, other things equal?
options: Current demand decreases
Current demand increases
Current quantity supplied increases
Supply shifts left
items.feedback: If buyers expect a lower future price, they delay purchases, reducing current demand.

items.stem: The market initially clears at D1/S1. A substitute becomes more expensive, while supply conditions remain unchanged. Which explanation and equilibrium movement fit the graph?
options: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P1, Q2) to (P2, Q3).
Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P1, Q2) to (P2, Q3).
items.feedback: A higher substitute price increases demand for this good, shifting demand right from D1 to D2. With supply fixed at S1, the graph moves from (P2,Q1) to (P3,Q2). Both equilibrium price and quantity rise.

items.stem: The market initially clears at D2/S2. A close substitute becomes cheaper, while supply conditions remain unchanged. Which explanation and equilibrium movement fit the graph?
options: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q3) to (P1, Q2).
Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P3, Q2) to (P2, Q1).
Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q3) to (P1, Q2).
Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P3, Q2) to (P2, Q1).
items.feedback: A cheaper substitute reduces demand for this good, shifting demand left from D2 to D1. On unchanged S2, equilibrium moves from (P2,Q3) to (P1,Q2). Both equilibrium price and quantity fall.

items.stem: Use the graph. From A to B, what is the quantity response per $1 price decrease, and what economic change does it represent?
options: Quantity demanded rises by 25 thousand donuts per dollar through movement along the existing demand curve.
Quantity demanded rises by 20 thousand donuts per dollar through movement along the existing demand curve.
Demand increases by 25 thousand donuts per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
Demand increases by 20 thousand donuts per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
items.feedback: A is at $10 and 100 thousand donuts; B is at $5 and 225 thousand. Quantity demanded rises by 125/5 = 25 thousand per $1 price decrease. This is movement along the unchanged demand curve, not a price-induced increase in demand.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At $6, compare D0 with D1. If this is a normal good, which change could explain the difference, and how large is it?
options: A fall in the good’s own price; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
Higher consumer income; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
Higher consumer income; 100 thousand more units demanded at that price.
A cheaper substitute; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
items.feedback: At $6, D0 shows 150 thousand and D1 shows 225 thousand: a 75-thousand increase at the same price. Higher income shifts demand right for a normal good; an own-price fall moves along a curve, and a cheaper substitute shifts demand left.

items.stem: Refer to the tea graph. What can be concluded from the horizontal distance between D0 and D1 at the same prices?
options: Demand decreases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a leftward curve shift
Quantity demanded decreases by 100 thousand solely because tea's own price rises
Demand increases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a rightward curve shift
Supply decreases by 100 thousand units, causing movement from D0 to D1
items.feedback: At both $4 and $6, D1 lies 100 thousand units left of D0. A repeated horizontal difference at fixed prices identifies a decrease in demand rather than movement along one curve.

items.stem: Streaming subscriptions are substitutes for theater visits. With production conditions unchanged, the movie-ticket market moves from A to B. Which explanation and equilibrium changes match the graph?
options: Streaming becomes more expensive; ticket price rises $2 and sales rise 50 thousand
Streaming becomes more expensive; ticket price rises $4 and sales rise 50 thousand
Streaming becomes cheaper; ticket price falls $2 and sales fall 50 thousand
Streaming becomes cheaper; ticket price falls $4 and sales fall 50 thousand
items.feedback: A is ($10,200 thousand) and B is ($12,250 thousand). A higher streaming price increases demand for theater tickets, consistent with the $2 price increase and 50-thousand increase in ticket sales.

items.stem: A product gets cheaper because supply increases. Students say demand increased because quantity sold rose. What is the error?
options: They confused an increase in quantity demanded with an increase in demand
They correctly identified a demand shift
They confused a price floor with a price ceiling
They ignored that supply can never change price
items.feedback: If price falls because supply increases, buyers move along the demand curve. Quantity demanded rises, but demand itself does not shift.

items.stem: A product becomes cheaper and sales rise. A follow-up survey finds that buyers now want more at EVERY unchanged price after a favorable health report. A student attributes all extra purchases to movement along the old demand curve. Which correction uses the survey evidence?
options: Demand is unchanged; every increase in sales is a movement along demand.
Demand shifts left; lower prices mean buyers want less at each fixed price.
Supply must shift left; buyer surveys establish producers’ costs.
Demand shifts right; the price change alone cannot explain greater planned purchases at a fixed price.
items.feedback: Unlike a supply-driven price fall alone, the survey reports greater demand at fixed prices after new health information. That identifies a demand shift, although the survey alone does not determine the separate supply change or how much of observed sales growth each cause explains.

items.stem: The only change in the donut market is the good’s own price, taking the market from A to B. Which conclusion fits the graph?
options: Quantity demanded rises by 125 thousand along the existing curve; demand is unchanged.
Quantity demanded rises by 75 thousand along the existing curve; demand is unchanged.
Demand increases by 125 thousand because the lower price shifts the demand curve right.
Demand increases by 75 thousand because the lower price shifts the demand curve right.
items.feedback: A shows 100 thousand donuts and B shows 225 thousand, an increase of 125 thousand. The only change is the good’s own price, so this is an increase in quantity demanded along the existing curve. Demand itself does not shift.

items.stem: The price of a substitute for coffee rises. What happens in the coffee market, holding other factors constant?
options: Demand for coffee increases, raising equilibrium price and quantity
Quantity demanded of coffee decreases along the same curve
Supply of coffee increases because coffee is now profitable
Demand for coffee decreases because substitutes are now expensive
items.feedback: When a substitute becomes more expensive, demand for the original good rises.

items.stem: The price of peanut butter falls. What happens to the demand for jelly, assuming they are complements?
options: Demand for jelly increases
Quantity demanded of jelly falls along the same curve
Supply of jelly decreases
Demand for jelly decreases because peanut butter is cheaper
items.feedback: A lower price for a complement increases demand for the related good.

items.stem: Electric scooters are normal goods. Household incomes rise, but a close substitute becomes cheaper. At an unchanged scooter price, can we predict the direction of scooter purchases without knowing the strength of each effect?
options: Yes, purchases rise; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand right.
Yes, purchases fall; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand left.
No; higher income pushes demand right while the cheaper substitute pushes it left.
No change occurs; an unchanged scooter price prevents any change in quantity purchased.
items.feedback: Income growth increases normal-good demand, while a cheaper substitute reduces scooter demand. Their unknown relative strengths make the net fixed-price quantity effect ambiguous.

items.stem: Movie tickets are a normal good. Income rises, but the price of streaming subscriptions, a substitute, falls. What is the strongest conclusion about movie-ticket demand?
options: Demand rises because higher income and a cheaper substitute both increase demand for movie tickets.
Demand falls because the cheaper substitute lowers ticket demand while income does not shift demand for a normal good.
Quantity demanded changes along one curve because both events change the ticket price
The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other
items.feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good, while a cheaper substitute reduces demand for movie tickets. The effects oppose each other and their relative sizes are not supplied, so the net shift cannot be determined. These are demand shifters, not changes caused by the ticket’s own price.

items.stem: Concert attendance falls after ticket prices rise. A fan claims demand decreased. Surveys show fans’ planned purchases at each fixed price are unchanged, but later a popular performer joins the tour. Which sequence is supported?
options: The first decline is movement along demand; the later performer change can shift demand right.
The first decline is a leftward demand shift; the later performer change is movement down that curve.
Both events are movements along demand because each changes the number of tickets sold.
Both events shift demand left because ticket price and performer popularity are market conditions.
items.feedback: Unchanged fixed-price plans imply the first attendance decline is due to movement along demand. Greater performer appeal changes a nonprice determinant and can shift the demand schedule right.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. The economy begins at AD1-AS1. Higher planned spending moves demand to AD2 while lower production costs move short-run supply to AS2. Compared with the starting equilibrium, what happens to output and the price level?
options: Output rises from Y3 to Y2 while the price level stays at P2.
Output stays at Y1 while the price level rises from P1 to P3.
Output falls from Y2 to Y3 while the price level stays at P2.
Output rises from Y3 to Y1 while the price level falls from P2 to P1.
items.feedback: The starting AD1-AS1 intersection is Y3/P2 and the ending AD2-AS2 intersection is Y2/P2. The two rightward shifts reinforce output and offset in the price level in this particular drawing.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS1, which change gets the economy to Y2 and P2?
options: AD rises and SRAS rises
AD falls and SRAS rises
AD rises and SRAS falls
AD falls and SRAS falls
items.feedback: Starting from AD1-AS1 at Y3-P2, moving to AD2-AS2 requires AD to rise and SRAS to rise.

items.stem: A tax increase reduces consumption and aggregate demand. Productive capacity is unchanged, and equilibrium output falls below potential. What kind of gap has opened, and through which curve did the tax increase create it?
options: A recessionary gap caused by a leftward AD shift.
An inflationary gap caused by a rightward AD shift.
A recessionary gap caused by a leftward LRAS shift.
An inflationary gap caused by a movement up an unchanged AD curve.
items.feedback: Lower consumption shifts AD left. With potential output unchanged, the resulting output shortfall is a recessionary gap.

items.stem: An economy faces higher oil prices and falling output. Why is aggressive AD stimulus risky?
options: It may restore output but add inflation pressure
It must lower prices and raise unemployment
It shifts SRAS right without cost
It removes the natural rate
items.feedback: Stimulating AD can support output but may worsen inflation after an adverse supply shock.

items.stem: The economy begins in long-run equilibrium on AD0, SRAS0 and LRAS0. Aggregate demand rises to AD1. Which sequence traces the short-run response and the long-run adjustment as wages and expectations catch up?
options: C to A to D
A to C to B
D to C to A
C to D to B
items.feedback: The economy begins at C, moves to D in the short run when AD increases, and returns to long-run output at B after SRAS shifts left.

items.stem: If aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 at the same time aggregate supply decreases from AS0 to AS1, which point shows the resulting equilibrium?
options: Point A
Point C
Point B
Point D
items.feedback: The simultaneous changes place the economy at the intersection of AD1 and AS1, which is point C.

items.stem: A student attributes the move from A to B to increased aggregate supply. What do the direction of the changes and the fixed curve imply?
options: Supply increased: output rises and the price level falls along unchanged AD0.
Demand increased: output and the price level rise along unchanged AS0.
Supply increased: output and the price level rise because the movement is along unchanged AS0.
Demand decreased: the higher price level at B is the result of reduced spending.
items.feedback: B is above and right of A, where AD1 intersects unchanged AS0. More demand raises both output and prices in this short-run diagram. Moving along AS0 does not mean that aggregate supply shifted.

items.stem: Aggregate demand rises while short-run aggregate supply falls. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Real output rises, while the price level is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output rises.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
Both the price level and real output fall.
items.feedback: Both shifts raise the price level, but aggregate demand raises output while adverse supply lowers it.

items.stem: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply rises. Which outcome is certain?
options: Real output falls, while the price level is uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output is uncertain.
items.feedback: A demand contraction and favorable supply shock both lower the price level, but they push output in opposite directions.

items.stem: After an adverse supply shock, policymakers use expansionary demand policy to restore output. Which risk remains?
options: The price level may rise further.
Unemployment must rise because aggregate demand increased.
Short-run aggregate supply automatically returns to its old position.
The economy must move below potential output.
items.feedback: Demand expansion can support output after a supply shock, but it adds inflation pressure rather than repairing supply.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: If banks lend more aggressively from excess reserves, the money supply rises mainly because
options: new loans create new deposits as funds are spent and redeposited
the Fed prints commodity money for each loan
M1 excludes bank deposits
borrowers destroy checking accounts when they borrow
items.feedback: Bank lending creates deposits as loan proceeds are spent and redeposited through the banking system.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: If the simple money multiplier falls from 10 to 4, what happened to the reserve ratio?
options: It rose from 10 percent to 25 percent.
It fell from 25 percent to 10 percent.
It rose from 4 percent to 10 percent.
It fell from 10 percent to 4 percent.
items.feedback: The reserve ratio is 1/multiplier. A multiplier of 10 means 10 percent; a multiplier of 4 means 25 percent.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: A bank has $1,000,000 in deposits and $140,000 in reserves. The reserve requirement is 10 percent. The bank lends all excess reserves, and that loan is redeposited in another bank facing the same reserve requirement. What is the second bank's maximum loan?
items.feedback: The first bank's required reserves are $100,000, so it lends $40,000. The second bank keeps 10 percent, or $4,000, and can lend $36,000.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: Use a hypothetical fixed-ratio reserve model with no currency drain: every loan payment is fully redeposited, credit demand is sufficient, and no other constraint binds. A bank has $5 million in deposits, $700,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It lends all excess reserves, and every later bank does the same. What is the maximum total money expansion created by the excess reserves?
options: $2 million
$5 million
items.feedback: Required reserves are $500,000, so excess reserves are $200,000. With multiplier 10, maximum expansion from excess reserves is $2 million.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: In a hypothetical system, a household deposits $10,000 of currency previously held outside banks. Banks initially meet a fixed 20 percent reserve ratio exactly, lend every new excess reserve dollar, and all loan payments are redeposited without currency drain. No other constraint binds. What are the first bank’s loan and the eventual net increase in currency plus checking deposits?
options: First loan $8,000; net money increase $40,000.
First loan $8,000; net money increase $50,000.
First loan $2,000; net money increase $40,000.
First loan $10,000; net money increase $50,000.
items.feedback: Required reserves on the initial deposit are $2,000, leaving an $8,000 first loan. Total deposits rise by $10,000/0.20 = $50,000, but public currency falls by $10,000. Net money creation is $40,000.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. Suppose the reserve ratio is 25 percent and a public cash deposit of $4,000 enters the banking system. What is the maximum total deposit expansion and the first bank's initial loan?
options: Maximum expansion = $16,000; initial loan = $3,000
Maximum expansion = $4,000; initial loan = $1,000
Maximum expansion = $3,000; initial loan = $16,000
Maximum expansion = $1,000; initial loan = $4,000
items.feedback: Multiplier is 1 / 0.25 = 4, so total expansion is $16,000. First bank keeps $1,000 and lends $3,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: The public deposits $120 of previously held currency in a system with rr=10%, no later currency leakage and no excess reserves. At the maximum deposit expansion predicted by this model, how does total deposit expansion compare with the net increase in M1?
options: Deposits can rise $1200, while net M1 rises $1080 because public currency initially falls $120
Deposits and net M1 both rise $1200; ignore the reduction in public currency
Deposits rise $1080 while net M1 rises $1200; subtract the currency from deposits only
Deposits and net M1 both rise $120; all subsequent loans transfer existing deposits only
items.feedback: The deposit maximum is 120/.1 = 1200. M1 includes public currency, which falls 120; net M1 change is 1200−120 = 1080. Deposit growth and net new money differ for an initial currency deposit.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: In a simplified system with a 20% reserve ratio, no currency leakage and no excess reserves, $180 of new reserves enters. A student calls the first bank's $144 initial loan the system's total deposit increase. What is wrong with that claim?
options: The maximum total deposit increase is $144; later deposits are excluded from money
The maximum total deposit increase is $180; banks cannot create deposits by lending
The maximum total deposit increase is $1080; add the original reserve injection to the multiplier result again
The maximum total deposit increase is $900; repeated lending and redepositing extends beyond the first loan
items.feedback: The simple maximum is ΔR/rr = 180/.20 = 900. The first-round loan is not the total expansion; the multiplier result already includes the deposits supported by the initial reserves.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: The public deposits $200 of previously held currency in a system with rr=10%, no later currency leakage and no excess reserves. At the maximum deposit expansion predicted by this model, how does total deposit expansion compare with the net increase in M1?
options: Deposits and net M1 both rise $200; all subsequent loans transfer existing deposits only
Deposits can rise $2000, while net M1 rises $1800 because public currency initially falls $200
Deposits and net M1 both rise $2000; ignore the reduction in public currency
Deposits rise $1800 while net M1 rises $2000; subtract the currency from deposits only
items.feedback: The deposit maximum is 200/.1 = 2000. M1 includes public currency, which falls 200; net M1 change is 2000−200 = 1800. Deposit growth and net new money differ for an initial currency deposit.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: Banks receive $140 in new reserves. The required reserve ratio is 10%, which would give a simple deposit multiplier of 10 if banks held no excess reserves. Banks also choose to hold excess reserves equal to 10% of deposits. With no currency leakage, what is the maximum deposit increase supported by the new reserves?
options: $2800 in total deposits; add the reciprocals of the two ratios
$280 in total deposits; multiply reserves by the percentage expressed as 2
$700 in total deposits; the effective reserve fraction is 20%
$1400 in total deposits; excess reserves never constrain lending
items.feedback: Required plus additional reserves total 20% of deposits. Thus deposits supported by 140 new reserves are 140/.20 = 700, rather than the required-ratio-only maximum.

items.topic: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
items.stem: In a simplified banking system, a new $100 deposit arrives and the reserve requirement is 20%. The bank holds only required reserves. How much can it lend in this first round?
items.feedback: The bank keeps $20 and can lend the remaining $80. That loan can support a later deposit if the funds are redeposited, but this question asks only for the first round.

items.stem: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence matches disinflation and expectations adjustment?
options: b to d to c
b to c to d
b to a to c
b to d to a
items.feedback: Disinflation moves from b to d in the short run; expected inflation falls and the economy moves to c.

items.stem: A central bank announces a gradual disinflation, but households and firms doubt that the plan will continue. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The natural unemployment rate immediately falls to zero.
High expected inflation can prolong the output and job losses.
The price level must begin falling throughout the adjustment.
Unemployment cannot rise because the disinflation is gradual.
items.feedback: If the plan lacks credibility, expected inflation can adjust slowly and make the disinflation more costly.

items.stem: A disinflation announcement is not credible, and wage contracts embed 6% inflation. What makes immediate costless adjustment unlikely?
options: Aggregate demand cannot affect inflation
Deflation is required before unemployment changes
Expected inflation and nominal contracts may adjust slowly
The LRPC must shift left before policy begins
items.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

items.stem: Two paths reach 2% inflation. The rapid path has a deep one-year recession; the gradual path has smaller gaps for several years. What must be compared?
options: The price levels at the start, without output data
Their cumulative output losses and inflation reductions
Only the largest annual unemployment rate
Only the final year’s output level
items.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

items.stem: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence best shows disinflation with temporary unemployment costs?
options: b to d to c
b to a to c
b to c to d
b to d to b
items.feedback: Disinflation lowers actual inflation first, moving to d, then expectations fall and the economy returns to c.

items.stem: What does the path b to d to c show about disinflation when expected inflation adjusts gradually?
options: Unemployment temporarily rises from U2 to U3, then returns to U2 as expectations fall.
Unemployment temporarily rises from U1 to U2, then returns to U1 as expectations fall.
Unemployment rises from U2 to U3 because disinflation permanently raises the natural rate.
Unemployment returns from U3 to U2 through a rise in demand along the unchanged upper SRPC.
items.feedback: The path first moves down SRPC2 from b to d, raising unemployment to U3. Falling expected inflation then shifts the short-run curve down, reaching c at the unchanged natural rate U2.

items.stem: Country A has a sacrifice ratio of 2, while Country B has a sacrifice ratio of 5. If both reduce inflation by 3 percentage points, which comparison is correct?
options: A loses about 15% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 6%.
Both lose about 3% of annual GDP because the inflation reduction is equal.
A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
A has no output loss because its sacrifice ratio is below the inflation reduction.
items.feedback: Cumulative output loss equals the sacrifice ratio times the inflation reduction: 2 × 3 = 6 for A and 5 × 3 = 15 for B.

items.stem: Inflation falls 3 points while cumulative output loss equals 6% of annual GDP. Unemployment later returns to its natural rate. What is the sacrifice ratio, and is the unemployment increase permanent?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 0.5, and unemployment stays permanently high
The ratio is 3, and LRPC shifts right permanently
The ratio is 6, and the price level must have fallen
The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
items.feedback: The sacrifice ratio is 6/3=2 percent of annual output per percentage-point inflation reduction. The given return to natural unemployment means the unemployment cost is temporary in this model; disinflation alone need not make the price level fall.

items.stem: An adverse supply shock has raised inflation and unemployment. Why can disinflation policy face a harder near-term tradeoff than after a demand boom?
options: The LRPC becomes downward sloping during supply shocks
Contraction shifts the SRPC downward with no demand effect
Contraction can lower inflation pressure while worsening an already weak output position
Supply shocks automatically lower the sacrifice ratio to zero
items.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

items.stem: Starting at b, policymakers reduce inflation. Why could the economy reach c directly instead of first passing through d?
options: Expectations and contracts adjust promptly, moving the short-run relationship from SRPC1 to SRPC2 before the demand restraint.
Expectations and contracts adjust promptly, moving the short-run relationship from SRPC2 to SRPC1 before the demand restraint.
Expectations remain fixed, but the lower actual inflation alone moves both unemployment and the short-run curve to c.
Demand restraint permanently lowers natural unemployment, shifting LRPC to c before expectations change.
items.feedback: The graph places c on the lower SRPC at the same natural unemployment rate as b. Reaching c immediately requires lower expected inflation and prompt contract adjustment; demand restraint with old expectations leads to d.

items.stem: Two plans each lower inflation four points. A rapid plan loses 8% of one year's output cumulatively; a gradual plan loses 6%. Which comparison is supported, and what is not established?
options: Ratios: gradual 0, rapid 2; spreading losses removes the gradual plan's cost.
Ratios: gradual 1.5, rapid 2; timing constraints still matter for selection.
Ratios: gradual 2, rapid 1.5; fewer calendar years establish lower cumulative cost.
Ratios: gradual 4, rapid 4; equal inflation reductions establish equal costs per point.
items.feedback: Using the stated cumulative-loss convention: rapid 8/4=2, gradual 6/4=1.5. Timing, uncertainty and other constraints are additional evaluation margins.

items.stem: A rapid disinflation loses 5% of annual output and cuts inflation 2 points. A gradual plan loses 6% and cuts inflation 3 points. Which plan has the lower cost per inflation point?
options: Rapid: 5 versus gradual 6; the inflation reductions are irrelevant
Both have ratio 1 because each plan reduces inflation
Gradual: 2 versus rapid 2.5, despite greater total loss
Rapid: 2.5 versus gradual 2, because a larger ratio is more efficient
items.feedback: Rapid 5/2=2.5, gradual 6/3=2. Different targets require comparison per point rather than total loss alone.

items.stem: Two countries announce identical demand restraint. In A, expectations fall promptly and wages can reset; in B, expectations remain high. What can be predicted about transition costs, without a numerical Phillips slope?
options: Both must have identical costs because the announced demand restraint is identical
A can face a smaller output cost, but an exact sacrifice-ratio difference is not identified
A must have exactly zero output cost because any credible announcement is costless
B must have the lower cost because higher expectations shift SRPC down
items.feedback: Faster downward expectations adjustment shifts A’s short-run tradeoff favorably. Without the relevant response sizes, that directional advantage does not identify an exact cost or prove zero cost.

items.stem: Which policy mix is most likely to support sustained productivity growth rather than only a temporary boost?
options: Education, investment, property rights, trade, and research support
One-time stimulus checks only
Price ceilings on all capital goods
Discouraging foreign investment and innovation
items.feedback: Sustained growth comes from policies that improve capital, skills, innovation, and institutions.

items.stem: With technology and other inputs fixed, successive increases in capital per worker produce smaller additions to output per worker. What does this imply for a policy that relies on capital accumulation alone?
options: It can raise the level of output, but sustaining productivity growth also requires improvements beyond physical capital alone.
It cannot raise output after the first investment because diminishing returns mean a zero marginal product.
It lowers output as soon as marginal gains become smaller than earlier gains.
It preserves the initial output growth rate indefinitely if the same amount of capital is added each year.
items.feedback: Capital deepening raises output per worker, but diminishing marginal returns limit repeated gains. Sustained productivity growth requires continuing improvements such as technology or human capital; additional physical capital does not become useless.

items.stem: A government uses a temporary spending surge that raises current output but does not change capital, worker skills, technology, or institutions. What is the main long-run limitation?
options: It permanently doubles output per worker even though productive capacity is unchanged
It guarantees a permanently lower natural unemployment rate without changing labor-market institutions
It eliminates diminishing returns to capital even though the capital stock is unchanged
It does not directly strengthen long-run productivity fundamentals
items.feedback: A temporary spending surge can raise current demand/output, but without stronger fundamentals it does not directly raise long-run productivity.

items.stem: A country funds education but blocks firms from adopting new technologies and discourages investment. What is the likely issue?
options: Skills need complementary capital and technology
Education alone guarantees growth
Technology restrictions raise productivity
Investment is unrelated to output per worker
items.feedback: Productivity growth usually requires complementary gains in skills, capital, and technology.

items.stem: A country saves heavily and imports machinery, yet productivity barely rises because schools are weak, power is unreliable, and contracts are insecure. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Capital alone may not deliver catch-up when complementary conditions are weak
High saving guarantees convergence even when schools, infrastructure, and institutions remain persistently weak
The country should restrict technological adoption so scarce capital continues to have a high marginal product
The catch-up effect requires poorer economies to have lower productivity growth than richer economies
items.feedback: Investment needs complementary human capital, infrastructure, technology, and secure institutions; capital alone may not deliver catch-up.

items.stem: A government subsidizes investment for five years, raising capital per worker, but it makes no lasting change to research, education, or institutions. Which long-run caution is most appropriate?
options: The temporary subsidy guarantees a permanently higher growth rate even after capital deepening slows
Research and education matter only for short-run aggregate demand
Institutions become irrelevant once the capital stock has increased
More capital raises output, but does not guarantee sustained productivity growth.
items.feedback: More capital can raise the output level, but continuing productivity growth requires ongoing gains in skills, technology, and institutions.

items.stem: A training subsidy is justified by skills that benefit future employers. Evidence shows the subsidized course teaches only a proprietary process unusable elsewhere. Which part of the original case weakens?
options: The private-benefit rationale disappears; proprietary skills cannot improve any firm's output.
The resource cost disappears; training limited to one employer uses no scarce inputs.
The external-benefit rationale strengthens automatically; less transferability means larger spillovers.
The external-benefit rationale weakens; most benefits may remain with the current employer.
items.feedback: The original subsidy rationale concerned benefits firms could not capture because skills were transferable. Firm-specific training weakens that particular externality argument, even though training can still have private value and resource costs.

items.stem: Saving rises and capital per worker grows, but each extra unit of capital adds less output under unchanged technology. A forecast extends the initial output-growth increase forever. Which correction is warranted?
options: Total output must decline immediately; diminishing marginal returns mean negative capital productivity.
Current consumption must rise immediately; higher saving creates resources without an opportunity cost.
Transition growth can slow as marginal returns diminish; permanently faster growth needs another sustained source.
Transition growth must accelerate; diminishing returns make each later unit more productive.
items.feedback: Capital deepening can increase the output level and speed growth during transition, while diminishing marginal returns reduce successive gains. It does not alone establish a permanently higher growth rate under unchanged technology.

items.stem: Reliable contract enforcement is established, but frequent electricity outages leave equipment idle. A proposal spends the entire growth budget on duplicating the legal reform. Which diagnosis challenges its priority?
options: More nominal spending alone supplies power; identifying the infrastructure bottleneck is unnecessary.
Power reliability is now the stated constraint; another legal reform does not directly operate idle equipment.
Contract enforcement is still necessarily the sole constraint; physical infrastructure cannot affect output.
Idle equipment proves labor skills are irrelevant; no policy can raise its productive use.
items.feedback: The binding constraint is context-dependent. With enforcement already reliable and outages idling machines, improving electricity availability addresses the specified barrier more directly than duplicating the legal reform.

items.stem: An economy is already at potential output but has weak incentives for innovation. Officials propose sustained demand stimulus as their only growth strategy. Which comparison is appropriate?
options: Stronger demand permanently raises capacity; innovation incentives affect only current prices.
Both policies affect only current prices; productive capacity cannot respond to innovation.
Both policies permanently raise capacity equally; higher nominal spending is real growth.
Stronger demand mainly pressures current prices; better innovation incentives can expand future capacity.
items.feedback: At potential, sustained demand expansion does not by itself supply more technology or resources. Innovation policy addresses a real source of future productive capacity, subject to its costs and effectiveness.

items.stem: A technology policy raises potential output for 240 workers but displaces some workers whose skills no longer match vacancies. Which package recognizes both the growth benefit and transition cost?
options: Use only demand stimulus and assume it reverses every permanent skill change
Block every productivity improvement because any displacement proves long-run output must fall
Support productive innovation and targeted retraining; higher potential output does not instantly rematch displaced workers
Stop measuring displaced workers so productivity and employment both improve by definition
items.feedback: Innovation can expand productive capacity while creating structural transition costs. Retraining/mobility address the mismatch; aggregate growth alone does not guarantee immediate employment for each displaced worker.

items.stem: A government must choose between accelerating a useful research program and temporary purchases during a demand slump. Does the slump prove the research program has no value?
options: Yes; temporary government purchases permanently determine the economy's research productivity.
No; stabilizing current demand and increasing future productive capacity are distinct benefits.
Yes; idle capacity makes every investment in future technology economically worthless.
No; research spending automatically eliminates the current output gap without a demand calculation.
items.feedback: A slump creates a demand-management concern, but does not eliminate future benefits from research. Budget allocation should compare timing, expected benefits and opportunity costs; neither policy's value follows mechanically from the other's objective.

items.stem: A low-capital economy could earn high marginal returns from investment, but unreliable contract enforcement deters investors. Why might improving enforcement alongside investment be more effective than subsidizing machines alone?
options: It addresses investors' ability to retain returns as well as the cost of adding capital.
Machine subsidies already eliminate any risk that investors will lose their returns.
Improved enforcement raises the capital stock immediately without requiring investment.
High marginal returns remove the need for either reliable institutions or investment finance.
items.feedback: High physical returns do not guarantee investment when investors cannot retain the proceeds. Better enforcement addresses that incentive constraint and complements capital accumulation; it does not itself create machines or guarantee catch-up.

items.stem: A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period. What is the central concern?
options: Whether the evidence generalizes to the current setting.
Whether the policy has a money price.
Whether economists may use models.
Whether positive analysis is always normative.
items.feedback: Policy advice must consider whether evidence is applicable to the target population and context.

items.stem: An economist is employed by an agency that benefits from a favorable estimate. What practice best protects credibility?
options: Publish the chosen model with full calculations, omitting the agency relationship to keep the report technical.
Disclose the agency interest, assumptions, alternatives and uncertainty so others can assess the estimate.
Have an agency colleague check the arithmetic, then report one point estimate to avoid confusing readers.
Report an interval from the chosen model, leaving model selection and other reasonable versions of the model to the agency.
items.feedback: Disclosure must address both the institutional interest and methodological discretion. Arithmetic review or an uncertainty interval alone does not reveal how model selection could favor the agency.

items.stem: A policy has a positive expected net benefit but a small chance of catastrophic loss. Which addition is necessary?
options: A claim that averages eliminate risk.
Removal of all low-probability outcomes.
Risk analysis beyond the expected-value calculation.
A conclusion based only on sunk costs.
items.feedback: Low-probability, high-cost outcomes may matter even when expected net benefits are positive.

items.stem: A pilot worked elsewhere but institutions differ locally. What is the key warning?
options: A successful pilot automatically generalizes to other settings
Institutional differences matter only for normative judgments
A large effect elsewhere guarantees a large local effect.
Evidence may not transfer to the new setting
items.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

items.stem: An efficient proposal conflicts with a legal-rights goal. What follows?
options: The efficient proposal must be adopted
Efficiency evidence does not uniquely decide social desirability
The legal-rights goal is irrelevant to policy evaluation
The conflict proves the proposal is economically inefficient.
items.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

items.stem: A recommendation changes under plausible assumptions. What should the economist do?
options: Report only the baseline estimate
Use the assumption that produces the most favorable result
Report sensitivity rather than one certain answer
Delay all advice until uncertainty is eliminated.
items.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

items.stem: Two advisers accept the same estimate: consolidating offices saves staff time but lengthens rural travel. One favors consolidation and the other opposes it. Which information best explains their different recommendations?
options: Which adviser used more decimal places in the shared estimate
Whether the two advisers agree that travel is measurable
Whether consolidation is being proposed by a public institution
How each weighs staff savings against rural access
items.feedback: Agreement about effects leaves room for different weights on efficiency and access. Those priorities can explain the recommendations without inventing a forecast disagreement.

items.stem: An economist recommends a policy because it maximizes total surplus, while citizens prioritize equal treatment. The disagreement is primarily about:
options: The arithmetic definition of surplus.
The normative criterion used to rank outcomes.
Whether incentives exist.
The distinction between micro and macro topics.
items.feedback: Economic analysis can measure consequences, but ranking competing values requires a normative criterion.

items.stem: Policy A creates $40 million of gains for high-income households and $10 million of losses for low-income households. Policy B creates $22 million of gains for low-income households and costs high-income households $5 million. With no other effects, which advice distinguishes efficiency from distribution?
options: A has the larger unweighted net gain, while B favors low-income households; the ranking depends on the stated social criterion.
B has the larger unweighted net gain, while A favors low-income households; efficiency alone therefore selects B.
A has the larger unweighted net gain, so it necessarily satisfies a goal of improving low-income households’ welfare.
B favors low-income households, so A cannot have a positive unweighted net gain even if its benefits exceed losses.
items.feedback: Unweighted net gains are 40-10=30 for A and 22-5=17 for B. Efficiency totals and incidence differ. Choosing between them requires stating how distribution enters the social ranking.

items.stem: A subsidy model estimated that firms would add 100 jobs when credit was available at 5%. Credit is now rationed and borrowing costs 12%; the model still predicts 100 jobs because it treats financing as fixed. What is the best next analysis?
options: Keep the 100-job forecast because the subsidy is unchanged; treat financing as an unrelated macroeconomic detail.
Reestimate firms’ financing responses and compare predictions under feasible credit conditions before transferring the old forecast.
Replace 100 jobs with the latest observed hiring total; that difference directly measures the subsidy’s causal effect.
Reject all subsidy models because one institutional change means simplified forecasts cannot provide policy evidence.
items.feedback: Credit conditions affect the mechanism through which firms finance expansion. The old forecast is conditional on assumptions that changed; observed hiring alone does not identify a counterfactual subsidy effect.

items.stem: Two advisers agree that a flood barrier yields $60 million in avoided damage, costs $35 million and relocates 200 households. One favors it; the other rejects involuntary relocation. Which further step would clarify rather than merely repeat their disagreement?
options: Collect a more precise construction-cost estimate until both advisers must adopt the same view of relocation.
Add the number of relocated households directly to the dollar cost and select the policy with the smallest sum.
State the relocation criterion, examine feasible less-displacing alternatives and show how each changes net benefits and affected households.
Treat the shared positive net benefit as evidence that objections to relocation are errors in economic forecasting.
items.feedback: The advisers share the main predictions but differ over a social criterion. Examining feasible alternatives and explicit tradeoffs informs the choice; greater forecast precision cannot itself settle the value judgment.

items.stem: A tool-rental shop compares two weekly rates. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $30 to $36 and quantity demanded from 400 to 360. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
options: About 0.58, inelastic; use $36 to earn $960 more.
About 0.58, inelastic; use $30 to earn $960 more.
About 1.73, elastic; use $30 to earn $960 more.
About 0.58, elastic; both prices earn the same revenue.
items.feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(360 - 400) / ((360 + 400) / 2)| divided by |(36 - 30) / ((36 + 30) / 2)|, about 0.58. Revenue is $12,000 at $30 and $12,960 at $36. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, price for specialty coffee subscriptions changes from $18 to $21 and quantity demanded changes from 800 to 680. What is price elasticity of demand?
items.feedback: The elasticity of demand is determined by the midpoint formula: |[(Q2 − Q1)/((Q1 + Q2)/2)] ÷ [(P2 − P1)/((P1 + P2)/2)]|. Substituting: |[(680 − 800)/740] ÷ [(21 − 18)/19.5]| ≈ 1.05. Demand is elastic over this interval.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, price for museum admissions changes from $14 to $11 and quantity demanded changes from 500 to 650. What is price elasticity of demand?
items.feedback: The elasticity of demand is determined by the midpoint formula: |[(Q2 − Q1)/((Q1 + Q2)/2)] ÷ [(P2 − P1)/((P1 + P2)/2)]|. Substituting: |[(650 − 500)/575] ÷ [(11 − 14)/12.5]| ≈ 1.09. Demand is elastic over this interval.

items.stem: A print service tests two poster prices. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $25 to $30 and quantity demanded from 480 to 360. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
options: About 1.57, elastic; use $30 to earn $1,200 more.
About 0.64, inelastic; use $30 to earn $1,200 more.
About 1.57, inelastic; both prices earn $12,000.
About 1.57, elastic; use $25 to earn $1,200 more.
items.feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(360 - 480) / ((360 + 480) / 2)| divided by |(30 - 25) / ((30 + 25) / 2)|, about 1.57. Revenue is $12,000 at $25 and $10,800 at $30. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, price for fitness memberships changes from $35 to $40 and quantity demanded changes from 900 to 765. What is price elasticity of demand?
items.feedback: The elasticity of demand is determined by the midpoint formula: |[(Q2 − Q1)/((Q1 + Q2)/2)] ÷ [(P2 − P1)/((P1 + P2)/2)]|. Substituting: |[(765 − 900)/832.5] ÷ [(40 − 35)/37.5]| ≈ 1.22. Demand is elastic over this interval.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, price for festival tickets changes from $50 to $44 and quantity demanded changes from 600 to 720. What is price elasticity of demand?
items.feedback: The elasticity of demand is determined by the midpoint formula: |[(Q2 − Q1)/((Q1 + Q2)/2)] ÷ [(P2 − P1)/((P1 + P2)/2)]|. Substituting: |[(720 − 600)/660] ÷ [(44 − 50)/47]| ≈ 1.42. Demand is elastic over this interval.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, price for meal-kit subscriptions changes from $60 to $66 and quantity demanded changes from 1000 to 850. What is price elasticity of demand?
items.feedback: The elasticity of demand is determined by the midpoint formula: |[(Q2 − Q1)/((Q1 + Q2)/2)] ÷ [(P2 − P1)/((P1 + P2)/2)]|. Substituting: |[(850 − 1000)/925] ÷ [(66 − 60)/63]| ≈ 1.70. Demand is elastic over this interval.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, price for airport parking days changes from $16 to $20 and quantity demanded changes from 1500 to 1170. What is price elasticity of demand?
items.feedback: The elasticity of demand is determined by the midpoint formula: |[(Q2 − Q1)/((Q1 + Q2)/2)] ÷ [(P2 − P1)/((P1 + P2)/2)]|. Substituting: |[(1170 − 1500)/1335] ÷ [(20 − 16)/18]| ≈ 1.11. Demand is elastic over this interval.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, the price of a professional exam-prep course falls from $250 to $225, and quantity demanded rises from 400 seats to 480 seats. What is the price elasticity of demand?
items.feedback: The elasticity of demand is determined by the midpoint formula: |[(Q2 − Q1)/((Q1 + Q2)/2)] ÷ [(P2 − P1)/((P1 + P2)/2)]|. Substituting: |[(480 − 400)/440] ÷ [(225 − 250)/237.5]| ≈ 1.73. Demand is elastic over this interval.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, price for premium headphones changes from $180 to $198 and quantity demanded changes from 700 to 560. What is price elasticity of demand?
items.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 2.33, so demand is elastic.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, the price of artisan bread loaves changes from $4 to $5 and quantity supplied changes from 900 to 1080. What is price elasticity of supply?
items.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 0.82, classified as inelastic.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, the price of rental bicycles changes from $12 to $15 and quantity supplied changes from 300 to 390. What is price elasticity of supply?
items.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 1.17, classified as elastic.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, the price of greenhouse tomatoes changes from $3 to $4 and quantity supplied changes from 1000 to 1180. What is price elasticity of supply?
items.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 0.58, classified as inelastic.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, the price of cloud-server capacity rises from $40 to $50 per unit, and quantity supplied rises from 500 to 700 units. What is the price elasticity of supply?
items.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 1.5, classified as elastic.

items.stem: Using the midpoint method, the price of hotel rooms rises from $150 to $180, and short-run quantity supplied rises from 800 to 840 rooms. What is the price elasticity of supply?
items.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 0.27, classified as inelastic.

items.stem: Using point elasticity, what are the elasticities at C and A? Why do they differ even though the demand curve has a constant slope?
options: 2 at C and 1/2 at A; the price-to-quantity ratio changes even though slope is constant.
3 at C and 1/3 at A; a constant slope means equal percentage responsiveness at both points.
2 at C and 1/2 at A; a constant slope means equal percentage responsiveness at both points.
3 at C and 1/3 at A; the price-to-quantity ratio changes even though slope is constant.
items.feedback: The intercepts show that quantity rises by 120/16 = 7.5 units for each $1 price decrease. Point elasticity is 7.5 times price divided by quantity: at C, 7.5 × 12/30 = 3; at A, 7.5 × 4/90 = 1/3. The same changes in dollars and units represent different percentage changes at different starting prices and quantities.

items.stem: A seller cuts price by 8 percent and quantity demanded rises by 5 percent. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Demand is inelastic and total revenue falls
Demand is elastic and total revenue rises
Demand is unit elastic and total revenue is unchanged
Demand is perfectly inelastic and quantity cannot change
items.feedback: Elasticity is about 0.625. With inelastic demand, a price cut reduces total revenue.

items.stem: A seller raises price by 6 percent and quantity demanded falls by 15 percent. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Demand is inelastic and total revenue rises
Demand is elastic and total revenue falls
Demand is unit elastic and total revenue is unchanged
Demand is income elastic
items.feedback: Elasticity is 2.5, so the proportionally larger quantity loss reduces revenue.

items.stem: A public transit agency faces inelastic peak demand but elastic off-peak demand. Which pricing strategy is most consistent with revenue management?
options: Raise peak fares and use discounts to attract off-peak riders
Cut peak fares and raise off-peak fares
Charge zero in both periods
Ignore elasticity because both services use the same buses
items.feedback: Higher prices fit the less elastic segment, while discounts can expand the more elastic segment.

items.stem: A product has many substitutes, but buyers have signed one-year contracts. Which statement is most defensible?
options: Demand must be perfectly elastic immediately
Short-run demand can be inelastic; renewal demand more elastic
Contracts make long-run demand less elastic
Substitutes matter only for supply elasticity
items.feedback: Contractual switching costs suppress short-run response but not necessarily later response.

items.stem: Two markets generate the same tax revenue. Market A has more elastic demand and supply than Market B. Which market likely loses more mutually beneficial trades?
options: Market A
Market B
Both necessarily lose the same number
The statutory payer determines the loss
items.feedback: More elastic quantities respond more strongly to the wedge, increasing the reduction in trade.

items.stem: A price floor creates a surplus. All else equal, which supply characteristic would make the surplus larger for a given increase in price?
options: More elastic supply
More inelastic supply
Perfectly inelastic demand alone
A smaller number of sellers by itself
items.feedback: More elastic suppliers expand quantity supplied more in response to the supported price.

items.stem: A binding price ceiling creates a shortage. Which demand characteristic makes quantity demanded rise more sharply at the controlled price?
options: More inelastic demand
More elastic demand
Perfectly inelastic supply
A larger tax wedge
items.feedback: More elastic demand responds more to the lower controlled price.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Using points C and B and midpoint percentages, which elasticity and revenue implication describe a move from C to B?
options: About 1.67, elastic; the price cut lowers total revenue.
About 0.60, inelastic; the price cut raises total revenue.
About 1.67, elastic; the price cut raises total revenue.
About 1.00, unit elastic; total revenue is unchanged.
items.feedback: C is P = 12, Q = 30 and B is P = 8, Q = 60. Midpoint elasticity is (30/45)/(4/10) = 1.67. Revenue rises from 360 to 480, so the elastic interval supports the price cut.

items.stem: For the B-to-A interval, calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand from the graph.
items.feedback: The percentage quantity change is 30/75 = 40% and the percentage price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving elasticity about 0.60.

items.stem: Across the full C-to-A interval, what midpoint price elasticity does the graph imply?
items.feedback: From C to A, quantity changes by 60 around an average of 60 and price changes by 8 around an average of 8, so both percentage changes are 100%.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Using the midpoint method, compare demand over the entire interval from C to A. Which conclusion follows? Use elasticity = |percentage change in quantity ÷ percentage change in price|, with average quantity and price as the bases.
options: Elasticity is 3; total revenue must rise between the endpoints.
Elasticity is 1; the endpoints have equal total revenue.
Elasticity is 1/3; total revenue must fall between the endpoints.
Elasticity is 1; demand has the same point elasticity everywhere.
items.feedback: At C, P = $12 and Q = 30; at A, P = $4 and Q = 90. Midpoint elasticity = |(60/60)/(−8/8)| = 1. Both endpoint revenues are $360. This interval result does not imply constant point elasticity.

items.stem: Using the two labeled points on D1, what is the midpoint price elasticity of demand?
items.feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 50/70 ≈ 71.4% and the price change is 4/8 = 50%, so elasticity is about 1.43.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the midpoint price elasticity of demand between the marked points on D2?
items.feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 20/45 ≈ 44.4% and the price change is 4/8 = 50%, so elasticity is about 0.89.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Using the labeled $10-to-$6 price change, which classification is correct?
options: Both D1 and D2 are elastic
D1 is elastic and D2 is inelastic
D1 is inelastic and D2 is elastic
Both D1 and D2 are unit elastic
items.feedback: The midpoint coefficients are about 1.43 for D1 and 0.89 for D2.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Using the black point where the two supply curves intersect and point A on the short-run supply curve, calculate the midpoint price elasticity of supply.
items.feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 10/65 ≈ 15.4% and the price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving PES ≈ 0.23.

items.stem: A garden workshop compares admission prices. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $40 to $48 and quantity demanded from 150 to 135. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
options: About 0.58, elastic; $40 raises revenue by $480.
About 0.58, inelastic; $48 raises revenue by $480.
About 1.73, elastic; $40 raises revenue by $480.
About 0.58, inelastic; $40 raises revenue by $480.
items.feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(135 - 150) / ((135 + 150) / 2)| divided by |(48 - 40) / ((48 + 40) / 2)|, about 0.58. Revenue is $6,000 at $40 and $6,480 at $48. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

items.stem: A digital lesson service compares subscription prices. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $9 to $12 and quantity demanded from 900 to 600. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
options: About 1.40, elastic; $9 earns $900 more than $12.
About 1.40, elastic; $12 earns $900 more than $9.
About 0.71, inelastic; $12 earns $900 more than $9.
About 1.40, unit elastic; the prices earn equal revenue.
items.feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(600 - 900) / ((600 + 900) / 2)| divided by |(12 - 9) / ((12 + 9) / 2)|, about 1.4. Revenue is $8,100 at $9 and $7,200 at $12. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

items.stem: A repair service can charge $50 for 120 jobs or $45 for 140 jobs, with enough capacity for either. Holding other demand factors fixed, use midpoint elasticity to choose the higher-revenue price.
