options: About 1.46, elastic; choose $50 because elastic demand favors a higher price.
About 0.68, inelastic; choose $50 because revenue is $6,300 rather than $6,000.
About 1.00, unit elastic; choose either because the revenues are equal.
About 1.46, elastic; choose $45 because revenue is $6,300 rather than $6,000.
items.feedback: The midpoint changes are 20/130 for quantity and 5/47.5 for price, giving about 1.46. Revenue is 45 × 140 = $6,300 versus 50 × 120 = $6,000. The price cut raises revenue over this interval.

items.stem: A tax is imposed in a market with very inelastic demand and very elastic supply. Which combination is most likely?
options: Consumers bear little of the tax and quantity rises
Consumers bear most of the tax and quantity falls relatively little
Producers bear most of the tax and quantity falls sharply
The burden is split equally and quantity cannot change
items.feedback: The less elastic demand side bears more burden, while limited quantity responsiveness restrains the decline in trade.

items.stem: A regulator compares two markets facing identical per-unit fees. In Market X, demand and supply are relatively inelastic; in Market Y, both are relatively elastic. Which claim is best?
options: Market Y is likely to have the larger quantity reduction and larger efficiency loss
Market X is likely to have the larger quantity reduction and larger efficiency loss
Both markets must have identical quantity reductions because the fee is identical
Elasticity affects tax incidence but never deadweight loss
items.feedback: Flatter, more elastic curves generate stronger behavioral responses and typically more lost trades.

items.stem: A firm sells a product with few substitutes today, but several close substitutes will enter next year. Holding other factors constant, what should happen to the firm’s pricing power over time?
options: It should strengthen as demand becomes more inelastic
It should be unchanged because substitutes do not affect elasticity
It should disappear only if supply becomes perfectly elastic
It should weaken as demand becomes more elastic

items.stem: A subsidy lowers the effective price of a product. Policymakers want a large increase in quantity consumed rather than mainly a transfer to existing buyers. Which market is the better candidate?

Elasticity is irrelevant to quantity response
A market with more elastic demand
A market with more inelastic demand
items.feedback: More elastic demand produces a larger quantity response to the lower effective price.

items.stem: A firm estimates elasticity using percentage changes from the original value and gets 1.20 for a price increase but 0.83 for the reverse price decrease. What caused the discrepancy?

Different base values; the midpoint method would produce one symmetric estimate
Elasticity cannot be measured between two points
The correct method always uses the larger endpoint
items.feedback: Conventional percentage changes depend on the chosen base, while midpoint percentages do not.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. As you move from C to B, how is demand best classified?

items.stem: A planning model assumes a 6 percent price increase with demand elasticity 1.8. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?

Quantity demanded rises about 10.8 percent

items.stem: A planning model assumes a 5 percent price cut with demand elasticity 0.4. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?

Quantity demanded falls about 2 percent

items.stem: A pharmaceutical patent expires and many close substitutes enter. Holding other determinants constant, what happens to the original brand’s demand elasticity and pricing power?
options: Demand becomes less elastic and markup rises
Demand becomes perfectly inelastic because medicine is necessary
Demand becomes more elastic and sustainable markup falls
Elasticity is unchanged because only price affects demand
items.feedback: Entry creates switching options, increasing responsiveness and limiting markup.

items.stem: Demand for a firm’s output becomes more elastic. What is the likely effect on the firm’s derived demand for an input used in production?
options: Input demand becomes perfectly inelastic
Input demand becomes unrelated to output price
Input supply becomes less elastic automatically
Input demand becomes more elastic
items.feedback: When customers readily reduce output purchases, firms more strongly reduce input use after cost increases.

items.stem: A linear supply curve intersects the quantity axis at a positive quantity. Along its positive-price region, supply elasticity tends to be:
options: Less than one
Greater than one
Exactly one at every point
Negative
items.feedback: With Q = a + bP and a > 0, bP/Q < 1.

items.stem: A linear supply curve has a negative quantity intercept and crosses the price axis above zero. Along its positive-quantity region, supply elasticity tends to be:
options: Less than one
Greater than one
Exactly zero
Negative because the intercept is negative
items.feedback: With Q = −a + bP, bP/Q exceeds one where Q is positive.

items.stem: Compare the C→B and B→A intervals on the graph. Why can their elasticity classifications differ?
options: The demand curve has different slopes in the two intervals
The percentage-change bases differ across the two intervals
Elasticity uses only the absolute quantity change
Elasticity is determined only by the direction of price
items.feedback: Elasticity depends on percentage changes, so identical absolute changes can produce different elasticities when the average price and quantity bases differ.

items.stem: Use the labeled intervals to calculate midpoint elasticity on D1 and D2. Which statement follows?
options: Only D1 is above the unit-elastic threshold
Only D2 is above the unit-elastic threshold
Both are exactly unit elastic
Neither curve can be classified
items.feedback: Elasticity above one is elastic; 1.43 exceeds one while 0.89 does not.

items.stem: A seller can supply at most 70 units. Compare charging the prices at B and A. At each price, sales equal the smaller of quantity demanded and capacity. Which choice correctly calculates revenue and identifies where capacity limits sales?
options: B earns $560 and A earns $360; neither price leaves unused capacity.
B earns $480 and A earns $360; only A is limited by capacity.
B earns $560 and A earns $280; both prices are limited by capacity.
B earns $480 and A earns $280; only A is limited by capacity.
items.feedback: B has P = 8, Qd = 60: sales are 60 and revenue $480. A has P = 4, Qd = 90: only 70 can be sold, earning $280. Capacity leaves B unconstrained but limits A. Demand elasticity describes desired purchases, not a seller’s capacity.

items.stem: For the marked price decrease, calculate total revenue before and after on D1 and D2. Which product could plausibly have more close substitutes, given the difference in responsiveness?
options: D1: $400→$520; D2: $300→$280. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D1’s greater responsiveness.
D1: $450→$570; D2: $350→$330. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D1’s greater responsiveness.
D1: $450→$570; D2: $350→$330. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D2’s lower responsiveness.
D1: $400→$520; D2: $300→$280. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D2’s lower responsiveness.
items.feedback: On D1, revenue goes from 10 × 45 = $450 to 6 × 95 = $570, and midpoint elasticity is 1.43. On D2 it goes from 10 × 35 = $350 to 6 × 55 = $330, with elasticity 0.89. More close substitutes can explain greater responsiveness on D1, although the graph alone cannot establish the cause.

items.stem: How much does quantity demanded rise for each $1 price decrease? Does this constant change in units mean that elasticity is constant?
options: 5 units; the constant unit response does not imply constant percentage responsiveness.
7.5 units; the constant unit response does not imply constant percentage responsiveness.
7.5 units; the constant unit response implies constant percentage responsiveness.
5 units; the constant unit response implies constant percentage responsiveness.
items.feedback: The line connects P = 16, Q = 0 to P = 0, Q = 120, giving 120/16 = 7.5 additional units per $1 decrease. Elasticity also uses P/Q, which varies along the line. Constant slope is not constant elasticity.

items.stem: Supply is Q = 10 + 3P. Price rises from $8 to $12. Use the midpoint method to calculate supply elasticity: percentage change in quantity divided by percentage change in price, using average values.
Supply is Q = −20 + 4P. Price rises from $8 to $12. What is midpoint supply elasticity, using average quantity and average price as the percentage-change bases?
items.feedback: Quantity rises from 12 to 28. Midpoint elasticity = [(28 − 12)/20] ÷ [(12 − 8)/10] = 0.80/0.40 = 2.

items.stem: A linear supply curve passes through the origin: Q = 5P. Compare price increases from $4 to $8 and from $8 to $12 using the midpoint method. What are the two supply elasticities?
options: 0 for both intervals
2 for the first and 0.5 for the second
0.5 for the first and 2 for the second
1 for both intervals
items.feedback: For $4 to $8: Q rises 20 to 40, so (20/30)/(4/6) = 1. For $8 to $12: Q rises 40 to 60, so (20/50)/(4/10) = 1. A linear supply curve through the origin is unit elastic.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Initially, price is $4 and quantity supplied is 60 in both time periods. Price then rises to $8. Point A shows the short-run outcome and point B the long-run outcome for that same price increase. How much does quantity supplied rise in each period, and why are the responses different?
options: 10 units in the short run and 40 in the long run; more adjustment time permits a larger response.
20 units in the short run and 60 in the long run; more adjustment time permits a larger response.
10 units in the short run and 40 in the long run; the longer horizon limits capacity adjustment.
70 units in the short run and 100 in the long run; the final quantities measure the increases.
items.feedback: Both comparisons begin at price $4 and quantity 60. At $8, short-run quantity is 70 at A and long-run quantity is 100 at B. The increases are 70 − 60 = 10 and 100 − 60 = 40 units. More time to adjust inputs and capacity allows a larger long-run response. A and B are alternative outcomes of the same price change, not the starting and ending points of that change.

Burden cannot change over time
The tax becomes a subsidy
items.feedback: As producers gain exit options, demand becomes relatively less elastic.

items.stem: A binding rent ceiling persists for years. Housing supply becomes more elastic over time. What happens to the shortage?
options: It disappears because supply is elastic
It remains identical
It grows as quantity supplied responds more to the below-market rent
Quantity demanded falls because rent is lower
items.feedback: Long-run supply contraction magnifies the shortage.

items.stem: A farm quota reduces quantity 5% and raises price 8%, with no other change. A student says fewer sales must lower revenue. Which correction is right using the exact stated percentage changes?
options: Revenue falls 5% because the price increase does not affect revenue per sale.
Revenue rises exactly 13% because the magnitudes of both percentage changes should be added.
Revenue stays unchanged because all quota policies imply unit elasticity.
Revenue rises about 2.6%; the price increase outweighs the quantity decrease.
items.feedback: Revenue is price times quantity. The new revenue factor is 1.08×0.95=1.026, so revenue rises 2.6%; a lower quantity alone does not determine revenue.

items.stem: A seller faces downward-sloping demand with absolute elasticity 0.8 at its current output. An analyst proposes a small output expansion to raise total revenue. Which response follows from elasticity, without needing a cost model?
options: Reject it; marginal revenue is negative, so a small output expansion reduces total revenue.
Accept the claim: any positive price makes marginal revenue positive regardless of elasticity.
Reject the claim because marginal revenue is zero whenever elasticity is below one.
Accept the claim because inelastic demand means quantity changes proportionately more than price.
items.feedback: In the inelastic range, expanding sales requires a proportionately large price reduction, reducing revenue. Thus MR is negative; the conclusion is about revenue rather than a complete profit choice.

items.stem: Supply is Q=20+2P. At P=$20, a planner uses the slope 2 as elasticity and forecasts a 20% quantity rise after a small 10% price increase. Which correction is correct?
options: Elasticity is 2 because slope and elasticity are equal for any straight line; the 20% forecast is correct.
Elasticity is 60/20=3; the quantity response is approximately 30%.
Elasticity is 2×20/60≈0.67; the approximate quantity response is 6.7%, not 20%.
Elasticity is 0.67, so quantity falls 6.7% when price rises.
items.feedback: At P=20, Q=60. Elasticity multiplies slope by P/Q: 2×20/60=2/3. The forecast quantity response is (2/3)×10%≈6.7%.

items.stem: A 10 percent price increase lowers quantity 20 percent. Cost per unit is unchanged. Which revenue-profit statement is best supported?
options: Both revenue and profit must rise
Profit must fall by exactly 10 percent
Revenue is unchanged
Revenue falls, but profit direction still requires cost information
items.feedback: Elasticity determines revenue direction, but profit also depends on costs.

items.stem: A rival’s 10% price cut reduces a firm’s sales by 15%, with its own price held fixed. Using the resulting cross-price elasticity, what would a small 4% rival price increase predict, and what relationship is indicated?
options: About a 6% sales increase; the goods are substitutes because the cross-price elasticity is +1.5.
About a 6% sales decline; the goods are complements because the original sales change was negative.
About a 1.5% sales increase; elasticity is already a percentage forecast.
About a 2.7% sales increase; use the reciprocal of the observed response ratio.
items.feedback: The ratio is (−15%)/(−10%)=+1.5. A 4% rival-price rise predicts 1.5×4%=6% more sales, consistent with substitution.

items.stem: Income falls 4% and product demand rises 6%, with prices and other determinants unchanged. If the estimated income elasticity applies to a subsequent small 2% income increase, what is the forecast and classification?
options: Demand rises about 3%; discard the negative sign when using income elasticity.
Demand falls about 3%; the good is inferior over the observed range.
Demand falls about 1.5%; the elasticity coefficient itself is the forecast percentage.
Demand rises about 8%; add the observed quantity change to the new income change.
items.feedback: Income elasticity is 6/(−4)=−1.5. Multiplying by the new +2% income change gives −3%. Its negative sign identifies an inferior good over this range.

items.stem: A tariff is placed on imports with highly elastic import demand. What is most likely?
options: Import quantity barely changes
Foreign supply becomes perfectly inelastic automatically
Import quantity falls sharply and tariff revenue may be fragile
Consumers bear no burden
items.feedback: Elastic import demand responds strongly to the tariff-inclusive price.

items.stem: A wage floor raises the wage employers pay by 10%. Estimated labor-demand elasticity is −1.4 in the short run and −2 in the long run. A forecast says employment must fall exactly 14% in both periods. Which correction follows from these estimates, holding other factors affecting labor demand constant?
options: The approximate declines are 1.4% and 2%; elasticity coefficients already state total percentage changes.
Employment rises 14% and 20% because labor supply slopes upward.
Employment falls 14% in both periods because the same wage change implies the same quantity response.
The approximate declines are 14% and 20%; longer-run substitution makes the second response larger.
items.feedback: Multiply each elasticity by +10%: −14% and −20%. These are local approximations, not exact universal predictions, and different horizons need not share one elasticity.

items.stem: A city’s congestion toll goal is quantity reduction, not revenue. Which companion policy improves effectiveness?
options: Expand close transit substitutes
Reduce transit availability
Shorten advance notice
Make parking cheaper downtown
items.feedback: Better substitutes make trip demand more elastic.

items.stem: A product is a necessity but one brand has many rivals. Which elasticity comparison is correct?
options: Both must be inelastic
Brand demand can be elastic while category demand remains inelastic
Category demand must be more elastic
Necessity eliminates market-definition effects
items.feedback: The relevant substitute set differs by market definition.

items.stem: A regression slope is −200 units per dollar. Why is this not enough to classify elasticity?
options: Negative slopes are always elastic
All slopes below −1 are elastic
Elasticity also requires the current price and quantity scale
Elasticity uses only units per dollar
items.feedback: Point elasticity scales the slope by P/Q.

items.stem: A market has relatively inelastic demand and supply. If the good is taxed, which combination is most likely?
options: Unstable revenue and large quantity distortion
No tax burden
Perfectly equal incidence
Relatively stable revenue and comparatively small quantity distortion
items.feedback: Low responsiveness preserves transactions and the tax base.

items.stem: A firm estimates the price elasticity of demand to be 2 near its current price. Why should it not assume the same responsiveness after a 50 percent price cut?
options: Elasticity can vary along the curve and outside the estimated range
Elasticity cannot be used for price cuts
Demand becomes vertical after large changes
Only income elasticity varies
items.feedback: Local estimates may not extrapolate to large changes.

items.stem: A seller segments customers by elasticity, but low-price customers can resell. What is the main problem?
options: Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
Arbitrage collapses the price separation
Marginal cost becomes negative
Income elasticity becomes zero
items.feedback: Resale undermines third-degree price discrimination.

items.stem: Demand is perfectly inelastic: quantity demanded remains at the same positive amount when market price increases. A student correctly computes zero midpoint demand elasticity, then concludes that total revenue is unchanged. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: Elasticity is zero, but selling the same quantity at a higher price raises revenue.
Zero elasticity also means zero price change, so equal revenue follows.
Zero elasticity means quantity rises enough to offset the price rise, so equal revenue follows.
A vertical demand curve has infinite elasticity, so the midpoint calculation must be reversed.
items.feedback: Quantity is unchanged while price increases, so the midpoint quantity-change numerator and demand elasticity are zero. Revenue is P×Q: with a positive fixed Q, the higher price produces higher revenue.

items.stem: Using the midpoint formula and the displayed short-run and long-run endpoints, which approximate pair correctly compares supply elasticity?
options: Short run 0.75; long run 0.23
Short run 1.00; long run 1.00
Short run 3.25; long run 0.75
Short run 0.23; long run 0.75
items.feedback: The short-run response is about 0.23 and the long-run response about 0.75, so long-run supply is more elastic.

items.stem: At a $20 minimum wage, what labor surplus does the graph show?
options: 400 workers
2,000 workers
6,000 workers
4,000 workers
items.feedback: Labor supplied is 6,000 and labor demanded is 2,000, leaving a surplus of 4,000 workers.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. A student says the wage floor creates an employment level of 6,000 workers. Which statement corrects this reasoning?
options: That is labor demanded; supply is 2,000
The floor creates 6,000 new jobs
That is labor supplied; firms demand only 2,000 workers
The competitive equilibrium is 6,000 workers
items.feedback: The right intersection measures people willing to work. Actual transactions are limited by the short side, labor demanded at 2,000.

items.stem: The nursing labor market begins where DL0 and SL0 intersect. Demand and supply then shift to DL1 and SL1. What new equilibrium does the graph show?
options: 4,000 nurses at $20 per hour
8,000 nurses at $40 per hour
6,000 nurses at $25 per hour
8,000 nurses at $20 per hour
items.feedback: The solid curves intersect at 80 hundreds of nurses, or 8,000, and the wage remains $20.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. By how much does nursing employment increase?
options: 400 nurses
2,000 nurses
4,000 nurses
8,000 nurses
items.feedback: Employment rises from 4,000 to 8,000 nurses, an increase of 4,000.

items.stem: The warehouse's next worker has an MPL of 5 orders, and output sells for $10 per unit. At a $44 wage, is the hire profitable?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Hire the worker because VMP exceeds the wage
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $50 per hour (5 × $10). Because $50 exceeds $44, the added value is greater than labor cost.

items.stem: A worker at a furniture shop adds 2 chairs per hour, each worth $30. The wage is $55. What should the competitive firm do?
options: Hire the worker because VMP exceeds the wage
Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $60 per hour (2 × $30). Because $60 exceeds $55, the added value is greater than labor cost.

items.stem: At a food truck, the marginal worker produces value from 10 extra meals sold for $5 apiece. How does a $46 wage affect the hiring decision?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
Hire the worker because VMP exceeds the wage
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $50 per hour (10 × $5). Because $50 exceeds $46, the added value is greater than labor cost.

items.stem: The bottling plant's next worker has an MPL of 12 cases, and output sells for $4 per unit. At a $45 wage, is the hire profitable?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Hire the worker because VMP exceeds the wage
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $48 per hour (12 × $4). Because $48 exceeds $45, the added value is greater than labor cost.

items.stem: A worker at a coffee roaster adds 4 batches per hour, each worth $16. The wage is $64. What should the competitive firm do?
options: The firm is at the marginal hiring condition because VMP equals the wage
Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $64 per hour (4 × $16). That equals the wage, which is the marginal hiring condition.

items.stem: A new scanner raises warehouse-worker productivity. How should the firm's labor-demand response be represented?
options: Movement along the original labor-demand curve
A rightward shift of labor demand
A shift of labor supply
No change in the firm's labor choice
items.feedback: The productivity changes the value of labor at a given wage, so the labor-demand curve shifts.

items.stem: Demand for printed catalogs falls. How should the firm's labor-demand response be represented?
options: Movement along the original labor-demand curve
A shift of labor supply
No change in the firm's labor choice
A leftward shift of printer labor demand
items.feedback: The product demand changes the value of labor at a given wage, so the labor-demand curve shifts.

items.stem: A drought lowers farm-worker marginal product. How should the firm's labor-demand response be represented?
options: Movement along the original labor-demand curve
A shift of labor supply
A leftward shift of farm labor demand
No change in the firm's labor choice
items.feedback: The productivity changes the value of labor at a given wage, so the labor-demand curve shifts.

items.stem: A software tool substitutes for routine bookkeeping labor. How should the firm's labor-demand response be represented?
options: Movement along the original labor-demand curve
A leftward shift of bookkeeping labor demand
A shift of labor supply
No change in the firm's labor choice
items.feedback: The substitute input changes the value of labor at a given wage, so the labor-demand curve shifts.

items.stem: A fall in airline travel reduces airlines' demand for baggage handlers. With labor supply unchanged, what happens in the competitive labor market?
options: The wage rises and employment falls
The equilibrium wage and employment both fall
The wage falls and employment rises
Only the number of workers willing to work changes
items.feedback: The event shifts labor demand left. With labor supply unchanged, the equilibrium wage and employment move in the same direction as labor demand.

items.stem: More restaurants open in a city and each demands kitchen labor. With labor supply unchanged, what happens in the competitive labor market?
options: Market labor demand shifts right, raising wage and employment
The wage rises and employment falls
The wage falls and employment rises
Only the number of workers willing to work changes
items.feedback: The event shifts labor demand right. With labor supply unchanged, the equilibrium wage and employment move in the same direction as labor demand.

items.stem: A warehouse installs robots that perform the same sorting tasks as entry-level workers. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: All factors must be substitutes
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
Robots substitute for those workers.
items.feedback: Robots substitute for that labor, so demand for those workers falls. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: More delivery trucks make drivers more productive. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: All factors must be substitutes
Truck capital and drivers are complements in the stated production process
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
items.feedback: Truck capital and drivers are complements in the stated production process. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: A factory replaces manual welding with fully automated welding cells. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: Automation substitutes for manual welders in this task
All factors must be substitutes
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
items.feedback: Automation substitutes for manual welders in this task. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: A hospital's nursing shortage leaves operating rooms idle. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: All factors must be substitutes
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
Scarce complementary labor can reduce the marginal value of operating-room capital
items.feedback: Scarce complementary labor can reduce the marginal value of operating-room capital. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: A licensing rule becomes more restrictive for dental hygienists. What happens to labor supply?
options: There is movement along an unchanged labor-supply curve
Labor demand necessarily shifts in the same direction
Worker productivity must fall
Hygienist labor supply shifts left
items.feedback: This nonwage determinant changes how many workers are willing or able to work at a given wage, shifting labor supply.

items.stem: Workers come to value flexible schedules offered by one occupation. What happens to labor supply?
options: There is movement along an unchanged labor-supply curve
Labor demand necessarily shifts in the same direction
Labor supply to that occupation shifts right
Worker productivity must fall
items.feedback: This nonwage determinant changes how many workers are willing or able to work at a given wage, shifting labor supply.

items.stem: The wage for delivery work falls with all supply determinants unchanged. What happens to labor supply?
options: The labor-supply curve shifts
Quantity of delivery labor supplied falls along the existing curve
Labor demand necessarily shifts in the same direction
Worker productivity must fall
items.feedback: A change in the occupation's wage causes movement along its labor-supply curve.

items.stem: Improved outside opportunities pull workers out of food processing. With labor demand unchanged, what happens to the equilibrium wage and employment?
options: Both wage and employment rise
Both wage and employment fall
The wage changes but employment cannot change
Food-processing wages rise while employment falls
items.feedback: A labor-supply change moves wage and employment in opposite directions when labor demand is unchanged.

items.stem: Consumers buy fewer printed newspapers. What is the labor-demand effect?
options: Only movement along the original demand curve occurs
Labor supply must shift in the same direction
Demand for press operators shifts left because derived output demand falls
Labor demand cannot respond to product markets
items.feedback: Lower demand for printed newspapers reduces the value of press operators’ output, shifting the derived demand for press operators left.

items.stem: A drought lowers the harvest produced by each field worker. What is the labor-demand effect?
options: Only movement along the original demand curve occurs
Farm labor demand shifts left as MPL falls
Labor supply must shift in the same direction
Labor demand cannot respond to product markets
items.feedback: The drought lowers workers’ marginal product and therefore their value of marginal product, shifting farm labor demand left.

items.stem: Industrial robots become cheaper and substitute for routine assembly labor. How does this affect demand for routine assembly labor?
options: Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Robot use rises and demand for routine assembly labor shifts left
Only factor supply can change
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
items.feedback: Robot use rises and demand for routine assembly labor shifts left. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: The greenhouse's next worker has an MPL of 7 plant trays, and output sells for $6 per unit. At a $38 wage, is the hire profitable?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Hire the worker because VMP exceeds the wage
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $42 per hour (7 × $6). Because $42 exceeds $38, the added value is greater than labor cost.

items.stem: At a machine shop, the marginal worker produces value from 3 extra parts sold for $24 apiece. How does a $68 wage affect the hiring decision?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
Hire the worker because VMP exceeds the wage
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $72 per hour (3 × $24). Because $72 exceeds $68, the added value is greater than labor cost.

items.stem: Refer to the monopsony graph. How much lower are wage and employment than under competition, and what hiring rule accounts for the difference?
options: $10 and 4,000 workers lower; monopsony equates MFC with MRP, then pays the supply-curve wage.
$5 and 2,000 workers lower; monopsony equates the wage itself with MRP to choose employment.
$5 and 2,000 workers lower; monopsony equates MFC with MRP, then pays the supply-curve wage.
$10 and 4,000 workers lower; monopsony equates the wage itself with MRP to choose employment.
items.feedback: MFC = MRP at 40 hundreds, with wage $20 on supply. Competition has supply = MRP at 60 hundreds and $25. Monopsony restricts hiring because marginal factor cost exceeds the wage.

items.stem: A proposal requires employment of 6,000 workers, with productivity and workers’ opportunity costs unchanged. At that employment level, compare the value of a worker’s output with the opportunity cost of working. Do these marginal hires increase total surplus?
options: Opportunity cost is $30 and product value $20; the marginal hires reduce surplus, and their wages are transfers.
Opportunity cost is $25 and product value $15; the marginal hires reduce surplus, and their wages are transfers.
Opportunity cost is $25 and product value $15; the wage payment itself proves that the marginal hires increase surplus.
Opportunity cost is $30 and product value $20; the wage payment itself proves that the marginal hires increase surplus.
items.feedback: At 60 hundreds of workers, supply is $25 and demand $15. Workers’ opportunity cost exceeds the value of their marginal output. A wage payment transfers income; it does not make a negative resource gain positive.

items.stem: The market begins where DL0 and SL intersect. A manager says the change shown was caused by more workers becoming available at each wage. What is the new equilibrium, and does the graph support that explanation?
options: $30 and 8,000 workers; greater labor demand, not a supply expansion alone, accounts for the change.
$25 and 6,000 workers; a supply expansion alone accounts for the higher wage and employment.
$30 and 8,000 workers; a supply expansion alone accounts for the higher wage and employment.
$25 and 6,000 workers; greater labor demand, not a supply expansion alone, accounts for the change.
items.feedback: The new intersection is $25 and 60 hundreds of workers, up from $20 and 40 hundreds on unchanged supply. Increased demand raises both wage and employment. Increased supply alone would lower the wage.

items.stem: Marginal product rises 25% while the competitive output price falls 10%. Which comparison of labor demanded at the $20 wage correctly evaluates whether these changes support the direction of the shift from DL0 to DL1?
options: Demand at $20 rises from 4,000 to 6,000 workers; the hypothetical 12.5% VMP increase supports the same shift direction.
Demand at $20 rises from 4,000 to 8,000 workers; VMP falls 10% because output price alone determines it.
Demand at $20 rises from 4,000 to 8,000 workers; the hypothetical 12.5% VMP increase supports the same shift direction.
Demand at $20 rises from 4,000 to 6,000 workers; VMP falls 10% because output price alone determines it.
items.feedback: At $20, DL0 gives 40 hundreds (4,000 workers) and DL1 gives 80 hundreds (8,000 workers). VMP = P × MP changes by 1.25 × 0.90 = 1.125, a 12.5% increase. This is consistent with the plotted rightward shift in labor demand, but does not establish the shift’s particular magnitude.

items.stem: Labor demand falls from DL0 to DL1, with SL unchanged. What is the new equilibrium employment? Could a 20% fall in every worker’s marginal product, combined with a 25% rise in the competitive output price, explain this shift?
options: The graph ends at 3,000 workers; the two changes alone leave VMP unchanged and do not produce that demand shift.
The graph ends at 2,000 workers; the productivity loss necessarily produces that shift regardless of fruit prices.
The graph ends at 3,000 workers; the productivity loss necessarily produces that shift regardless of fruit prices.
The graph ends at 2,000 workers; the two changes alone leave VMP unchanged and do not produce that demand shift.
items.feedback: The solid demand curve intersects supply at 20 hundreds, or 2,000 workers. But the hypothetical combined change multiplies VMP by 0.80 × 1.25 = 1. A productivity effect alone cannot establish the net derived-demand shift.

items.stem: Starting from the equilibrium in the graph, employment later reaches 6,000 at $25 per hour. An analyst reports that hourly payroll rises by 50% because employment rises by 50%. Which original payroll and correction are right?
options: Originally $60,000; payroll rises 150% because both wage and employment change.
Originally $80,000; payroll rises 87.5% because both wage and employment change.
Originally $80,000; payroll rises only 50% because wage changes do not affect payroll.
Originally $60,000; payroll rises only 50% because wage changes do not affect payroll.
items.feedback: The original point is 40 hundreds of workers at $20, giving $80,000 per hour. Final payroll is 6,000 × 25 = $150,000. The increase is 70,000/80,000 = 87.5%, not the employment percentage alone.

items.stem: The market begins where DL0 and SL intersect. The graph shows a productivity loss at an unchanged output price. A later output-price increase raises marginal revenue product by an unspecified amount. Which initial employment loss and conclusion about the later outcome are justified?
options: A loss of 1,000 workers; final employment relative to its original level remains uncertain.
A loss of 2,000 workers; final employment relative to its original level remains uncertain.
A loss of 2,000 workers; any output-price increase must exactly restore the original employment.
A loss of 1,000 workers; any output-price increase must exactly restore the original employment.
items.feedback: Employment falls from 40 to 20 hundreds, a loss of 2,000. A higher output price offsets some of the derived-demand decline, but without its magnitude the final level relative to the original 4,000 is undetermined.

items.stem: The market begins where SL0 and DL intersect. Expanded nursing programs cause the supply shift shown. Hospitals then face an increase in demand for care of unknown size. What wage results from the first shift? After both shifts, what can be concluded about wage and employment relative to the original equilibrium?
options: The first shift lowers wage to $10; after both shifts employment is higher, but the final wage relative to the original is ambiguous.
The first shift lowers wage to $15; after both shifts employment is higher, but the final wage relative to the original is ambiguous.
The first shift lowers wage to $15; after both shifts employment is higher and the final wage must remain below the original.
The first shift lowers wage to $10; after both shifts employment is higher and the final wage must remain below the original.
items.feedback: SL1 intersects demand at $15 and 6,000 workers. Added labor supply and later added labor demand both increase employment. Their wage effects oppose each other, so the final wage relative to the original $20 depends on shift sizes.

items.stem: A report calls every excess job seeker at the minimum wage a lost job. Calculate the decline in employment and the surplus of workers. Why are those numbers different?
options: Jobs fall by 1,000; excess labor supply is 2,000 because the higher wage also attracts additional job seekers.
Jobs fall by 2,000; excess labor supply is 4,000 because the higher wage also attracts additional job seekers.
Jobs fall by 2,000; excess labor supply is 4,000, and both figures measure the same decline in employment.
Jobs fall by 1,000; excess labor supply is 2,000, and both figures measure the same decline in employment.
items.feedback: Competitive employment is 40 hundreds. At the $20 floor, demand is 20 hundreds and supply 60 hundreds. Jobs lost = (40−20) × 100 = 2,000; excess supply = (60−20) × 100 = 4,000. The second includes new job seekers.

items.stem: How many more nurses would be hired under competition than under monopsony? Why would those additional hires create gains from trade?
options: 1,000 additional nurses; their marginal product value exceeds opportunity cost, while higher wages are transfers.
2,000 additional nurses; their marginal product value exceeds opportunity cost, while higher wages are transfers.
2,000 additional nurses; the larger wage payments themselves are the extra real resource gains.
1,000 additional nurses; the larger wage payments themselves are the extra real resource gains.
items.feedback: MFC = MRP gives monopsony employment of 40 hundreds; supply = MRP gives 60 hundreds. In between, MRP exceeds the opportunity cost on supply. The additional 2,000 hires recover gains from trade; wage transfers alone do not measure those gains.

items.stem: At a fixed price level, initial desired output is $500 billion. Government purchases rise by $40 billion and MPC is 0.5. Crowding out creates a total $20 billion AD offset, already including induced effects. Under the simple spending multiplier, what is the new quantity of output demanded?
options: $560 billion; subtract the already-total offset from the multiplied spending increase.
$540 billion; subtract the offset from purchases before multiplying both amounts.
$580 billion; the offset does not affect demand after the multiplier operates.
$620 billion; add the offset to the multiplied spending increase.
items.feedback: The spending multiplier is 2, so the gross demand increase is $80 billion. Subtract the already-total $20 billion offset once, leaving a $60 billion net increase and $560 billion demanded. Without supply information, this is not a prediction of equilibrium output.

items.stem: Fiscal expansion raises AD through the multiplier, but interest rates rise and investment falls. Which description best fits the final result?
options: Initial AD shift partly offset by crowding out
SRAS shift fully offset by lower taxes
LRPC shift partly offset by higher inflation
Money demand shift fully offset by M1
items.feedback: Fiscal expansion can be amplified by the multiplier but weakened by crowding out.

items.stem: If government spending rises, MPC is high, and interest rates do not rise, which effect dominates?
options: Multiplier effect
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
Adverse supply shock
items.feedback: A high MPC strengthens the multiplier, and little interest-rate increase means crowding out is weak.

items.stem: If government spending rises, MPC is low, and interest rates rise sharply, which concern dominates?
options: Weak multiplier with strong crowding out
Strong multiplier with no crowding out
Money neutrality with no AD change
Expected inflation with SRPC falling
items.feedback: A low MPC weakens the multiplier, while higher rates crowd out private investment.

items.stem: If government spending initially shifts AD right by $40 billion and MPC is 0.75, what is the total shift before crowding out?
options: $160 billion
$70 billion
$40 billion
$30 billion
items.feedback: With MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is 4. A $40 billion initial shift becomes $160 billion before crowding out.

items.stem: If the initial AD shift is $30 billion and the final shift is $150 billion, what MPC is implied by the simple multiplier?
items.feedback: The multiplier is 150/30 = 5. If 1/(1-MPC)=5, then MPC = 0.8.

items.stem: If the initial shift is $50 billion and MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.5, what happens to the final AD shift before crowding out?
options: It falls from $250 billion to $100 billion.
It rises from $100 billion to $250 billion.
It stays at $50 billion.
It falls from $250 billion to $50 billion.
items.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so $250 billion. MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so $100 billion.

items.stem: If policymakers expect the multiplier shift to close a recessionary gap exactly, but crowding out is stronger than expected, what is the likely result?
options: AD does not shift far enough right to fully close the gap.
AD shifts too far right because crowding out magnifies fiscal policy.
AD shifts left because government spending is not part of AD.
The multiplier becomes infinite.
items.feedback: Stronger crowding out reduces the net AD shift, so stimulus may fall short.

items.stem: Government purchases increase by $60 billion. MPC = 0.75; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $50 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. What is the net rightward AD shift?
options: $190 billion
$240 billion
$110 billion
$10 billion
items.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so the gross shift is $240 billion. Subtract $50 billion crowding out for a net $190 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

items.stem: A government spending increase raises income, consumption, and AD, but also raises interest rates and lowers investment. Which answer correctly names both effects?
options: Multiplier effect and crowding-out effect
Fisher effect and monetary neutrality
Liquidity trap and fiat money
Reserve requirement and inflation tax
items.feedback: The multiplier amplifies the AD increase; crowding out offsets part of it by reducing investment.

items.stem: A student says fiscal expansion raises AD and therefore can never crowd out investment. What is the best correction?
options: Fiscal expansion can raise AD while higher rates reduce private investment.
Fiscal expansion lowers rates because government borrowing reduces money demand.
Fiscal expansion shifts SRAS right because firms face lower costs.
Fiscal expansion eliminates the multiplier because taxes disappear.
items.feedback: Fiscal expansion can increase AD, but rising interest rates can reduce investment and offset part of the effect.

items.stem: A purchases change first moves AD1 to AD2; induced consumption then moves demand to AD3. Higher interest rates subsequently reduce private spending. Which account fits the directions shown?
options: The direct and induced effects expand demand; the interest-rate effect partly offsets that expansion.
The direct and induced effects contract demand; the interest-rate effect further reduces demand.
The direct and induced effects expand demand; the later private-spending decline is another multiplier expansion.
The first demand change is induced consumption; the second is the original purchases impulse.
items.feedback: AD2 is right of AD1 and AD3 farther right. The first shift is the direct purchases effect, the next is induced spending, and the reduction in private spending is crowding out. The initial impulse must not be confused with the rounds it induces.

items.stem: Government spending rises by $70 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct order of AD shifts before crowding out?
options: AD shifts right $70 billion directly and $350 billion in total.
AD first shifts right by $350 billion, then shifts back to $70 billion.
AD shifts left by $70 billion, then left by $350 billion.
AD does not shift because the multiplier only affects money demand.
items.feedback: The first AD shift is the direct $70 billion increase in G. With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so the final AD shift is $350 billion.

items.stem: Government spending rises by $60 billion and the final AD shift is $300 billion. What order of AD shifts and implied MPC fit these data?
options: AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts right first by $300 billion, then back to $60 billion; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts left first by $60 billion, then left by $300 billion; MPC = 0.2.
AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.6.
items.feedback: The multiplier is $300/$60 = 5. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 5, then MPC = 0.8.

items.stem: Government spending rises by $40 billion. If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, how do the initial and total increases in aggregate demand change?
options: The initial AD shift stays $40 billion, but the final shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion.
The initial AD shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion, but the final shift stays $40 billion.
Both the initial and final AD shifts stay $40 billion.
The initial AD shift becomes $200 billion and the final shift becomes $80 billion.
items.feedback: The initial shift is still $40 billion. With MPC = 0.5, multiplier is 2 and final shift is $80 billion. With MPC = 0.8, multiplier is 5 and final shift is $200 billion.

items.stem: Government purchases increase by $100 billion. MPC = 0.6; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $75 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. Which sequence separates the direct purchases, gross multiplier prediction, and net AD shift?
options: Direct increase: $100 billion; gross increase: $250 billion; net increase: $175 billion.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out increases it to $325 billion.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $250 billion, then crowding out leaves $175 billion.
AD shifts right $100 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
items.feedback: MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. The $100 billion initial shift becomes $250 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $175 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

items.stem: Two governments each increase purchases by $60 billion. Economy A has MPC 0.80 and a total $100 billion reduction in aggregate demand from crowding out; Economy B has MPC 0.60 and a total $20 billion reduction. These offsets already include induced spending effects. Using the simple spending multiplier, which comparison is correct?
options: Economy A has a $200 billion net AD increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy B.
Economy A has a $300 billion net increase and Economy B has a $150 billion net increase because crowding out does not affect AD.
Economy B has a $200 billion net increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy A.
Both economies have the same $180 billion net AD increase because the initial spending changes are equal.
items.feedback: A: 60/(1−0.80)−100 = 300−100 = $200 billion. B: 60/(1−0.60)−20 = 150−20 = $130 billion. A's net increase is $70 billion larger. Each stated crowding-out amount is already a total AD offset and is subtracted once, not multiplied again.

items.stem: Government purchases rise by $80 billion and MPC is 0.75. The observed net AD increase is $230 billion. Define crowding out here as the total reduction in AD after induced spending effects, not an autonomous investment change. How much of the gross spending-multiplier effect was offset?
options: $230 billion.
$320 billion.
$10 billion.
$90 billion.
items.feedback: The gross increase is 80/(1−0.75) = $320 billion. The total AD offset is 320−230 = $90 billion. It already incorporates induced spending effects and does not receive another multiplier.

items.stem: The graph shows aggregate demand before fiscal expansion (AD1), after the direct increase in government purchases (AD2), and after the multiplier effect (AD3). At price P, how large can a positive crowding-out effect be if final demand must remain strictly between AD2 and AD3?
options: Less than about half of the total increase.
Exactly half of the total increase.
More than half but less than the total increase.
Equal to the total increase.
items.feedback: At price P, the AD2-to-AD3 distance is approximately half of the full AD1-to-AD3 increase. Positive crowding out moves demand left from AD3. To remain strictly between AD2 and AD3, that reduction must be smaller than the AD2-to-AD3 distance, leaving some of the additional spending generated by the multiplier.

items.stem: Government purchases rise by $80 billion and MPC is 0.75. Crowding out reduces aggregate demand by a total of $100 billion after induced spending effects. Using the simple spending multiplier, what is the net increase in AD?
options: $220 billion
$300 billion
$320 billion
$420 billion
items.feedback: The gross AD increase is 80/(1−0.75) = $320 billion. Subtract the already-total AD offset once: 320−100 = $220 billion. Multiplying the $100 billion again would apply induced effects twice.

items.stem: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the simple multiplier and total AD increase before crowding out?
options: Multiplier = 4; AD increase = $320 billion
Multiplier = 3; AD increase = $240 billion
Multiplier = 0.75; AD increase = $60 billion
Multiplier = 1.33; AD increase = $106.4 billion
items.feedback: Multiplier = 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4. Total AD increase = 4 x $80 billion = $320 billion.

items.stem: If MPC = 0.9 and government spending increases by $25 billion, what is the simple multiplier effect on AD before crowding out?
options: $250 billion
$22.5 billion
$27.8 billion
$225 billion
items.feedback: With MPC = 0.9, the multiplier is 10. AD increases by 10 x $25 billion = $250 billion.

items.stem: In a simple fixed-price model with MPC 0.75, government purchases rise $20. Crowding out then reduces AD by a total $20 after induced effects. Which calculation avoids multiplying the offset twice?
options: Net AD rises $100: add the offset to the multiplier result
Net AD rises $60: 80 gross minus 20 total offset
Net AD is unchanged: multiply both stated amounts by four
Net AD rises $80: ignore the offset
items.feedback: Gross effect=20/.25=80. The offset is already total AD, so subtract 20 once: net=60.

items.stem: The desired net AD increase is $90. MPC is 0.5, and a total AD crowding-out offset of $30 is expected after induced effects. What purchases increase reaches the target?
options: $180; multiply the target by two, omitting the offset.
$60; divide target plus total offset by the multiplier.
$30; subtract the offset before reversing the multiplier.
$120; add the offset without reversing the multiplier.
items.feedback: 2ΔG−30=90, so ΔG=(90+30)/2=60. Reverse the net-effect equation; the offset is not an autonomous component to multiply again.

items.stem: An increase in government purchases of $40 raises AD by $160 before crowding out in the simple model. What MPC does this imply, and does it determine how much aggregate demand will rise after crowding out?
options: MPC: 0.75; the increase before crowding out does not establish the final increase.
MPC: 0.25; the saving share equals the marginal consumption share.
MPC: 4; the gross spending ratio equals the marginal consumption share.
MPC: 0.75; the increase before crowding out establishes the same final increase.
items.feedback: The spending multiplier is 4 = 1/(1 − MPC), so MPC = 0.75. This gives the demand increase before crowding out. Later crowding out can reduce the final increase.

items.stem: A government raises taxes and increases purchases by the same dollar amount. Which statement is most precise about the immediate AD effects?
options: The two actions must cancel exactly before behavior is considered.
Both actions shift AD right by the same amount.
Taxes enter AD directly as a negative component.
Purchases enter AD directly, while higher taxes reduce consumption indirectly.
items.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD; taxes work through disposable income and consumption.

items.stem: The government cuts purchases during a recession but also cuts taxes. Which conclusion is valid without knowing the magnitudes and household response?
options: Aggregate demand must rise.
The two policies always cancel exactly.
The net direction of aggregate demand is ambiguous.
Aggregate demand must fall.
items.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left, while a tax cut tends to shift it right; magnitudes matter.

items.stem: A tax cut occurs while households expect future taxes to rise and save much of the extra income. What happens to the tax multiplier?
options: It is weaker than simple models predict
It becomes infinite automatically
It shifts SRAS instead of AD
It eliminates crowding out
items.feedback: If households save much of the tax cut, the increase in consumption and AD is weaker.

items.stem: A fiscal package raises government purchases by $120 billion and taxes by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, the package’s first-round effect on AD is:
options: A $20 billion increase.
A $200 billion increase.
A $40 billion increase.
A $40 billion decrease.
items.feedback: Purchases add $120 billion; the tax increase reduces consumption by $80 billion.

items.stem: A government increases purchases by $50 billion and raises taxes by $50 billion. MPC is 0.75. Before subsequent multiplier rounds, the net first-round AD change is:
options: No change.
A $12.5 billion increase.
A $37.5 billion decrease.
A $100 billion increase.
items.feedback: Purchases add $50 billion; the tax increase cuts consumption by $37.5 billion.

items.stem: A tax cut raises disposable income by $160 billion. Households spend 60 percent of the increase initially. If later rounds follow a simple spending multiplier of 2.5, the total AD increase before other offsets is:
options: $400 billion.
$64 billion.
$240 billion.
$96 billion.
items.feedback: First-round consumption rises $96 billion; multiplying by 2.5 gives $240 billion.

items.stem: The government increases infrastructure purchases, but imports rise sharply because much of the equipment is purchased abroad. Relative to a package using domestic inputs, the increase in domestic aggregate demand is likely:
options: Leftward because any import increase reduces government purchases.
Identical because all government spending counts equally.
Smaller because part of the spending leaks into imports.
Larger because imports are part of domestic production.
items.feedback: Spending on imports does not directly purchase domestically produced output.

items.stem: Congress replaces $100 billion of government purchases with a $100 billion tax cut. Households have MPC 0.80. Holding other AD determinants fixed and looking only at the first round, what happens to aggregate demand?
options: AD is unchanged because the two fiscal changes are equal.
AD rises by $20 billion.
AD rises by $80 billion.
AD falls by $20 billion.
items.feedback: Government purchases enter AD directly, while tax changes affect AD through the share of disposable income households spend.

items.stem: In a fixed-price economy with idle resources and MPC 0.75, a tax cut of $20 and a purchases increase of $20 are considered separately. Which comparison distinguishes the initial and multiplied effects?
options: The purchases plan initially adds $20 and ultimately $80; the tax cut initially adds $15 and ultimately $60
Both plans initially add $20 and ultimately $80; households spend the entire tax cut
The purchases plan adds only $20; the tax cut adds $80 because taxes have the larger multiplier
Both plans contract AD by $20; taxes and purchases have the same sign
items.feedback: Purchases directly enter demand; only the MPC share of a tax cut initially becomes consumption. With multiplier 1/(1−.75)=4, the respective total effects are 4 G and 3×tax cut.

items.stem: Government raises purchases and lump-sum taxes by $30 each. Assume MPC 0.8, fixed prices, idle resources and no other leakage or crowding out. Which net demand effect follows?
options: $0; equal tax and purchase changes cancel their initial demand effects.
$150; apply the spending multiplier without the tax-induced consumption reduction.
−$120; apply the tax multiplier without the government purchases increase.
+$30; purchases exceed the initial tax-induced consumption reduction.
items.feedback: Initial net spending is 30−.8×30=.2×30; multiplier 5 yields a total increase of 30. Fiscal balance and demand balance are different comparisons.

items.stem: Government sends $40 in transfers rather than buying output. With MPC 0.6, how do government purchases and consumption initially change, and what is the total effect on aggregate demand in a simple fixed-price model with no other changes?
options: G: +$40; initial C: $0; total AD: +$100.
G: $0; initial C: −$24; total AD: −$60.
G: $0; initial C: +$24; total AD: +$60.
G: $0; initial C: $0; total AD: $0.
items.feedback: Transfers are not government purchases, but recipients can spend part of them. Initial C=.6×transfer; multiplying by 1/(1−.6)=2.5 gives total 1.5×transfer.

items.stem: Government raises purchases and lump-sum taxes by $70 each. Assume MPC 0.8, fixed prices, idle resources and no other leakage or crowding out. Which net demand effect follows?
options: $0; equal tax and purchase changes cancel their initial demand effects.
+$70; purchases exceed the initial tax-induced consumption reduction.
$350; apply the spending multiplier without the tax-induced consumption reduction.
−$280; apply the tax multiplier without the government purchases increase.
items.feedback: Initial net spending is 70−.8×70=.2×70; multiplier 5 yields a total increase of 70. Fiscal balance and demand balance are different comparisons.

items.stem: Country A has expected inflation of 8 percent and a real interest rate of 1 percent. Country B has expected inflation of 3 percent and a real interest rate of 5 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Country A must have a nominal rate exactly 5 points above Country B.
Country B must have the lower nominal interest rate because lower expected inflation always dominates any real-rate difference.
The Fisher effect says real interest rates are always identical across countries.
A one-for-one comparison of nominal rates cannot use expected inflation alone because the real rates differ too.
items.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

items.stem: A lender receives a 10 percent nominal rate that was set when expected inflation was 4 percent. Actual inflation is later 9 percent. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Expected inflation is irrelevant once a fixed nominal rate has been written.
The ex ante pricing reflected roughly a 6 percent real return, but the realized real return is much lower.
The Fisher effect predicted a 1 percent real return when the loan was made.
The nominal rate automatically rises to 15 percent after inflation is observed because fixed-rate contracts always adjust retroactively after the fact.
items.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

items.stem: Nominal interest rates rise from 7 to 11 percent at the same time expected inflation rises from 3 to 8 percent. Can we conclude the real rate was unchanged?
options: No. The nominal rate rose 4 points while expected inflation rose 5, so the implied real rate actually fell about 1 point.
Yes. Any rise in nominal rates alongside expected inflation proves the real rate is unchanged.
Yes. The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to rise exactly half as much as expected inflation regardless of changes in real rates.
No. The implied real rate rose about 9 percentage points.
items.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower signs a loan at 9 percent nominal interest when expected inflation is 4 percent. Actual inflation is 7 percent. What happened to the realized real interest rate compared with what the lender expected?
options: It fell from 5 percent expected to 2 percent realized.
It rose from 5 percent expected to 7 percent realized.
It stayed at 5 percent because nominal interest was fixed.
It fell from 9 percent expected to 4 percent realized.
items.feedback: Expected real rate was 9 - 4 = 5 percent. Realized real rate was 9 - 7 = 2 percent.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate is stable at 3 percent, what should happen to the nominal interest rate under the Fisher effect?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 12 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 3 percent.
It rises from 2 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 3 percent.
items.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 3 + 2 = 5 to 3 + 9 = 12 percent.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 11 percent. The real interest rate falls from 3 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 13 percent.
It rises from 4 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
items.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 3 + 4 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 11 = 13 percent.

items.stem: Money growth rises from 8 percent to 20 percent. Velocity growth is zero and output growth is 4 percent. If expected inflation adjusts fully, what happens to nominal rates when the real rate stays at 3 percent?
options: Nominal rates rise from about 7 percent to about 19 percent.
Nominal rates fall from 7 percent to 3 percent.
Nominal rates rise from 8 percent to 20 percent exactly.
Nominal rates stay at 3 percent.
items.feedback: Inflation rises from 8 - 4 = 4 percent to 20 - 4 = 16 percent. With real rate 3 percent, nominal rates rise from 7 to 19 percent.

items.stem: A country establishes a credible low-inflation regime. Expected inflation falls from 9 percent to 3 percent, while saving and investment conditions leave the long-run real interest rate near 2 percent. Which outcome best fits the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate tends to fall from about 11 percent to about 5 percent.
The nominal interest rate tends to rise from about 5 percent to about 11 percent.
The real interest rate must fall from 2 percent to negative 4 percent.
The nominal interest rate should stay near 11 percent because credibility affects only actual inflation.
items.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. The nominal interest rate is 11 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent. If actual inflation turns out to be 10 percent, what is the realized real interest rate?
options: 1 percent
4 percent
3 percent
21 percent
items.feedback: The realized real rate uses actual inflation: 11 - 10 = 1 percent.

items.stem: For a $260 loan, expected inflation rises from 2% to 5% while the required expected real return falls from 4% to 3%. Under the Fisher approximation, which nominal-rate comparison is correct?
options: The nominal rate rises from 6% to 9%; the real rate must be held fixed despite the supplied change
The nominal rate falls from 6% to 5%; subtract expected inflation from the required real return
The nominal rate remains 6%; opposite movements in components must cancel exactly
The nominal rate rises from 6% to 8%; the real-rate decline partly offsets the inflation-expectation increase
items.feedback: Initially i≈r+πe=4+2=6. Later i≈3+5=8. A one-for-one response to expected inflation requires a fixed real rate, which is not the case here.

items.stem: A fixed-rate loan was written when expected inflation was 2 percent, but actual inflation turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Expected inflation helped determine the original nominal rate; the surprise changes the realized real return.
The Fisher effect requires the bank to retroactively reset the nominal rate to actual inflation.
Unexpected inflation leaves the realized real return unchanged on a fixed-rate contract.
The nominal rate was based only on actual inflation, which was already known.
items.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

items.stem: A $280 fixed-rate loan has nominal interest 7% when expected inflation is 3%. Actual inflation later turns out to be 6%. Which pair separates the rate-setting prediction from the realized outcome?
options: The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contractual rate
The expected real return was about 4%; the realized real return is about 1%, without changing the contractual nominal rate
The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed
Both expected and realized real returns are 4% because the lender chose a fixed nominal rate
items.feedback: Fisher rate setting uses expected inflation at agreement; ex post purchasing power uses actual inflation. Thus 7−3=4% expected and 7−6=1% realized; the nominal contract remains 7%.

items.stem: Refer to the conceptual graph. Which event and equilibrium response fit the displayed demand shift?
options: Higher domestic NCO; the dollar depreciates and quantity rises
Weaker foreign demand for domestic exports; the dollar depreciates and quantity falls
More domestic purchases of foreign assets; the dollar appreciates and quantity falls
Stronger foreign demand for domestic exports; the dollar appreciates and quantity rises
items.feedback: D1 lies right of D0 with S0 fixed, consistent with stronger foreign demand for domestic output and a new intersection above and right of the old one.

items.stem: Refer to the conceptual graph. Which transaction change and equilibrium response fit the displayed supply shift?
options: Fewer domestic purchases of foreign assets; the dollar appreciates and quantity falls
Greater foreign demand for domestic currency; the dollar depreciates and quantity falls
More domestic purchases of foreign assets; the dollar depreciates and quantity rises
More foreign purchases of domestic goods; the dollar appreciates and quantity rises
items.feedback: S1 lies right of S0 with D0 fixed, consistent with more dollars supplied to purchase foreign assets and a new intersection below and right of the old one.

items.stem: In the market for U.S. dollars, demand and supply both increase. Demand slopes downward and supply slopes upward, and the exchange rate is measured in foreign currency per dollar. Without information about the relative size of the shifts, what can be determined?
options: The exchange rate falls while currency quantity is unchanged
Currency quantity rises, but the exchange-rate direction is ambiguous
Both currency quantity and the exchange rate rise
Currency quantity falls while the exchange rate rises
items.feedback: Both shifts raise equilibrium quantity. The demand increase raises the rate while the supply increase lowers it, so their relative sizes determine the rate.

items.stem: In the market for U.S. dollars, demand decreases while supply increases. Demand slopes downward and supply slopes upward, and the exchange rate is measured in foreign currency per dollar. What can be determined about the exchange rate and the quantity of dollars exchanged?
options: The exchange rate falls, while the quantity direction is ambiguous
The exchange rate rises and quantity falls
Both the exchange rate and quantity fall
Both outcomes are ambiguous
items.feedback: Both shifts lower the exchange rate. The demand decrease lowers quantity while the supply increase raises it, so quantity depends on relative shift sizes.

items.stem: In the conceptual graph, the market begins where D0 and S0 intersect. Demand shifts to D1 and supply shifts to S1. Which combined outcome is shown?
options: A larger dollar quantity with the exchange rate unchanged
A smaller dollar quantity with appreciation
A larger dollar quantity with depreciation
An unchanged dollar quantity with appreciation
items.feedback: The new D1-S1 intersection lies to the right of the original D0-S0 intersection at the same vertical position.

items.stem: In the market for U.S. dollars, demand and supply both decrease. Demand slopes downward and supply slopes upward. Why is the change in the exchange rate, measured in foreign currency per dollar, uncertain?
options: Both shifts push it down by different amounts
Supply determines only the rate and demand only quantity
Supply prevents any exchange-rate change
Lower demand pushes it down, while lower supply pushes it up
items.feedback: Lower demand reduces the exchange rate, while lower supply raises it. The relative size of these opposing effects determines the net change.

items.stem: The dollar market moves from A to B. An importer faces an unchanged foreign-currency price. How do the dollar, traded quantity and dollar cost of the import change?
options: The dollar depreciates 25%, quantity rises 50%, and the import costs about 33.3% more in dollars.
The dollar depreciates 20%, quantity rises 50%, and the import costs 20% more in dollars.
The dollar depreciates 20%, quantity rises 50%, and the import costs 25% more in dollars.
The dollar depreciates 20%, quantity rises about 33.3%, and the import costs 25% less in dollars.
items.feedback: The graph gives e: 1.0 to 0.8 and quantity: 100 to 150. Thus e falls 20% and quantity rises 50%. An unchanged foreign price costs 1/0.8 = 1.25 times as many dollars. Reciprocal percentage changes are not symmetric.

items.stem: A real depreciation makes domestic goods cheaper relative to foreign goods, and net exports rise. With other spending unchanged, what happens to aggregate demand?
options: It decreases.
It increases.
It stays unchanged because exports are foreign spending.
It changes only if government purchases also rise.
items.feedback: Net exports are a component of aggregate demand. Their increase adds to demand for domestic output.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: With constant tradeoffs per day, Fern can make 28 trays or 7 stools; Cove can make 18 trays or 9 stools. Which specialization and exchange can give both positive gains?
options: Fern makes stools, Cove makes trays; 3 trays per stool
Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 5 trays per stool
Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 1 tray per stool
Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 3 trays per stool
items.feedback: A stool costs Fern 4 trays and Cove 2. Cove has stool advantage and Fern tray advantage; a rate strictly between 2 and 4 trays per stool can benefit both.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Two studios have constant daily tradeoffs. Alder can make 21 prints or 7 models; Brook can make 20 prints or 10 models. Which proposal benefits both at the margin?
options: Brook exports models to Alder for 2.5 prints each
Alder exports models to Brook for 2.5 prints each
Brook exports models to Alder for 3.5 prints each
Brook exports models to Alder for 1.5 prints each
items.feedback: Alder gives up 3 prints per model; Brook gives up 2. Brook can supply models at a rate above 2 that still saves Alder prints compared with making models itself.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output. A proposed exchange gives all 40 extra units to one firm. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: Specialization created aggregate gains, but the proposed distribution may not benefit both firms
Comparative advantage is disproved whenever gains are unequal.
Any increase in combined output makes every exchange mutually beneficial
Equal gains are required before specialization can raise output
items.feedback: Higher combined output creates potential gains; terms of trade determine how those gains are divided.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: River can produce 18 X or 6 Y; Hill can produce 12 X or 8 Y. What is each producer’s opportunity cost of one unit of Y, measured in units of X?
options: River: 3 X; Hill: 1.5 X
River: one-third X; Hill: two-thirds X
River: 12 X; Hill: 18 X
River: 2 X; Hill: 3 X
items.feedback: River gives up 18/6 = 3 units of X per unit of Y; Hill gives up 12/8 = 1.5 units of X per unit of Y.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: North can make 20 chips or 10 sensors; South can make 12 chips or 12 sensors. A technology change lets North make 40 sensors with unchanged chip capacity. What changes?
options: North gains comparative advantage in sensors and South in chips
North keeps comparative advantage in chips because its chip output is unchanged
South gains comparative advantage in both goods
Equal opportunity costs eliminate specialization
items.feedback: Recompute relative opportunity costs after a change and respect the model limits.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Ava gives up 2 sacks to produce one crate; Ben gives up 5 sacks. If the terms of trade are exactly 2 sacks per crate, who gains from exchanging a crate?
options: Ava is indifferent and Ben can gain from buying the crate
Both receive positive gains from the trade.
Ben is indifferent and Ava captures every gain
The rate lies strictly between their opportunity costs
items.feedback: For both producers to be better off, the trading price must be above the lower opportunity cost and below the higher one.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: One bolt costs East 0.5 panel and West 1.25 panels. What range of trading prices, measured in panels per bolt, makes both producers better off than producing the goods themselves?
options: More than 0.5 but less than 1.25 panels per bolt
More than 2 but less than 4 bolts per panel.
At least 0.5 and at most 1.25 panels per bolt
Less than 0.5 panels per bolt only
items.feedback: Both producers gain when the trading price is above East’s opportunity cost of 0.5 panel per bolt and below West’s cost of 1.25 panels per bolt. At either endpoint, one producer only breaks even.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Specialization raises combined output, but a proposed exchange rate lies above both producers’ costs for the exported good. What follows?
options: Higher output creates potential gains, but this rate will not benefit both sides
Every feasible exchange must share the production gain.
The higher-cost producer now has comparative advantage
Both sides are strictly better off because specialization occurred
items.feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Coast’s opportunity cost of one unit of cocoa is 3 units of tea; Ridge’s is 6 units of tea. What range of trading prices, measured in units of cocoa per unit of tea, makes both producers better off?
options: More than one-sixth and less than one-third
More than one-third and less than one-sixth
More than 3 and less than 6
At least one-sixth and at most one-third
items.feedback: Both gain when one unit of cocoa trades for more than 3 but less than 6 units of tea. In cocoa per unit of tea, the range is greater than 1/6 and less than 1/3. At either endpoint, one producer only breaks even.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Alpha gives up 2 kits to make a machine, while Beta gives up 6. Both could trade at either 3 or 5 kits per machine. How would changing the terms of trade from 3 to 5 kits per machine affect their gains?
options: Both work, but 5 shifts more modeled gain to Alpha
