Only the 3-kit rate lies between the two opportunity costs.
Only the 5-kit rate is between costs
Both divide the gain equally
items.feedback: Total gains and their distribution are distinct; terms of trade allocate the modeled surplus.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: You know how much a producer makes after specializing and the rate at which it can trade. Can you calculate its consumption gain without knowing what it consumed before trade?
options: No; the autarky comparison is underdetermined
Yes; the trading rate determines the pre-trade consumption bundle.
Yes; combined output equals each gain
No; trade gains can never be measured
items.feedback: A consumption gain is the difference between the post-trade bundle and the pre-trade, or autarky, bundle. Specialization output and an exchange rate do not identify that missing baseline, so different autarky bundles could imply different numerical gains. Gains can be measured when the required consumption information is supplied.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: As producers specialize further, their opportunity costs rise. What does this imply about how much specialization is needed to gain from trade?
options: Both producers can gain through specialization without either specializing completely
Both producers must always specialize completely.
Opportunity cost becomes irrelevant after exchange
Absolute advantage fixes every output
items.feedback: With increasing opportunity cost, producing more of a good requires giving up progressively more of the other good. Reallocation can create gains while relative marginal costs differ, but the rising cost can make further specialization unattractive before either producer specializes completely. Absolute productivity alone does not determine that stopping point.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: A trading price exactly equals the exporter’s opportunity cost and is below the importer’s opportunity cost. How are the gains from this trade divided?
options: The exporter is indifferent while the importer captures the modeled gain
The exporter captures every gain because it supplies the good.
Both parties receive positive and exactly equal gains
Neither party can gain because the rate is on one boundary
items.feedback: At its own opportunity cost the exporter is indifferent; the importer still saves resources.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: A high-productivity surgeon is also the fastest typist in a clinic. The surgeon hires an assistant to type notes. What completes the economic explanation?
options: The assistant must have an absolute advantage in typing.
The surgeon cannot have comparative advantage in surgery.
Typing displaces more valuable surgical work.
Specialization matters only in international trade.
items.feedback: The surgeon delegates typing because the forgone value of surgical work makes typing costly for the surgeon.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Country A has comparative advantage in software. After trade opens, software employment rises but some hardware workers lose jobs. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: The job losses prove comparative advantage was calculated incorrectly.
All workers must gain for trade to be efficient.
Comparative advantage predicts no sectoral adjustment.
Aggregate gains can coexist with transition costs and distributional losses.
items.feedback: Trade can expand total gains while requiring adjustment and creating identifiable losers.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Combined consumption rises by 9 units, but one party gains 11 while the other loses 2. What is the correct evaluation?
options: Aggregate gain exists, but the trade is not mutually beneficial
Both parties gain because their combined consumption increases.
The losing party has advantage in both goods
Each gain must be reset to 4.5
items.feedback: Total gains and their distribution are distinct; terms of trade allocate the modeled surplus.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Nia can produce more of either good per hour than Sol. Yet each loaf costs Nia 2 shirts and Sol 1 shirt in forgone output. With constant tradeoffs and no trade costs, which proposed loaf-for-shirt exchange can benefit both?
options: Nia supplies loaves at 1.5 shirts per loaf.
Sol supplies loaves at 2.5 shirts per loaf.
Sol supplies loaves at 1.5 shirts per loaf.
Nia supplies loaves at 0.5 shirts per loaf.
items.feedback: Sol’s cost of a loaf is 1 shirt, below Nia’s 2. At 1.5 shirts, Sol receives 0.5 shirt above cost and Nia saves 0.5 shirt relative to making a loaf. Absolute productivity does not settle this comparison.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Specialization frees resources worth 60 units of output, but the proposed shipping plan uses 70 units. A different carrier would use 35 units and require 10 units of extra monitoring. Which plan increases net resources?
options: Both carriers: the original gains 60 units and the alternative gains 95.
Only the alternative carrier: the original loses 10 units and the alternative gains 15.
Only the original carrier: monitoring makes the alternative lose 45 units.
Neither carrier: any positive exchange cost eliminates specialization gains.
items.feedback: Net resources are 60-70=-10 under the original plan and 60-35-10=15 under the alternative. Real exchange and monitoring costs must be netted against production gains.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Opening trade yields consumer gains of $90 million and producer losses of $50 million. Moving displaced workers uses $12 million of real resources. A proposed $20 million domestic transfer to producers costs another $5 million to administer. Which evaluation includes efficiency and distribution?
options: Net national gain is $3 million; producers remain $30 million below their initial position after the transfer.
Net national gain is $43 million; producers recover fully because the transfer exceeds adjustment costs.
Net national gain is $23 million; producers remain $30 million below their initial position after the transfer.
Net national gain is $28 million; producers recover fully because aggregate consumer gains exceed their losses.
items.feedback: The domestic transfer redistributes rather than destroys surplus. Net gain is 90-50-12-5=23. Producers lose 50 and receive 20, leaving a 30 loss. Positive aggregate gains do not establish that compensation is complete.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: East can make 12 drones or 18 radios per day; West can make 6 drones or 24 radios. Costs are constant. West offers 1.5 radios per drone, then raises its offer to 2.5. Ignoring exchange costs, which evaluation is correct?
options: East exports drones; the first offer leaves East indifferent, while the second gives East 1 radio and West 1.5 radios of gain per drone.
West exports drones; the first offer leaves West indifferent, while the second gives West 1 radio and East 1.5 radios of gain per drone.
East exports drones; both offers give positive gains, and the second divides 2.5 radios of gain equally between the two producers.
East exports drones; the first offer benefits both, while the second makes West lose because the rate exceeds East’s opportunity cost.
items.feedback: East gives up 18/12=1.5 radios per drone; West gives up 24/6=4. At 1.5 East is indifferent. At 2.5 East gains 2.5-1.5=1 radio and West saves 4-2.5=1.5 radios.

items.topic: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
items.stem: Arden can make 12 machines or 24 tools; Bellora can make 6 machines or 12 tools. After training, Bellora can make 6 machines or 24 tools with the same resources. With constant costs, what changes in the case for specialization?
options: Initially costs are equal; after training Arden has machine advantage, Bellora has tool advantage, and a rate between 2 and 4 tools per machine can benefit both.
Initially Arden has both advantages; after training Bellora has both advantages, and any positive tools-per-machine rate can benefit both.
Initially costs are equal; after training Bellora has machine advantage, Arden has tool advantage, and a rate between 2 and 4 tools per machine can benefit both.
Initially costs are equal; after training costs remain equal because Bellora’s machine capacity is unchanged, so no range of trading prices that makes both producers better off appears.
items.feedback: Initially both sacrifice 2 tools per machine. Training raises Bellora’s machine opportunity cost to 4 tools while Arden remains at 2. Arden should specialize relatively more in machines and Bellora in tools; positive gains for both producers require a rate between 2 and 4.

items.stem: A government sends $1,000 unemployment checks to households, and households spend the full amount on groceries. What is the GDP effect?
options: The transfer is excluded; grocery purchases count as consumption
Both the transfer and groceries count, so GDP rises by $2,000
Neither counts because government is involved
Only the transfer counts as government purchases
items.feedback: Transfer payments are not purchases of current goods and services, but later household spending can count as consumption.

items.stem: A U.S. household buys a $40,000 car produced in Germany. In U.S. GDP accounting, what happens?
options: Consumption: +$40,000; net exports: −$40,000; GDP: unchanged
Consumption rises and GDP rises by $40,000
Investment rises and imports are ignored
Government purchases rise and GDP is unchanged
items.feedback: Imported consumer goods enter consumption but are subtracted through imports in net exports, so domestic GDP does not rise.

items.stem: A household buys a $2,000 imported laptop, a firm buys a $5,000 domestic machine, and the government sends a $1,000 benefit check. What directly adds to domestic GDP?
options: $5,000 from the domestic machine
$8,000 from all three transactions
$7,000 from the laptop and machine
$6,000 from the machine and benefit
items.feedback: The domestic machine adds $5,000 of business investment. The imported laptop is offset by imports, and the benefit check is a transfer rather than a purchase of current output.

items.stem: A city buys $3 million of domestic buses and sends $2 million in transfers. Recipients spend $1.5 million on imported services. What is the direct increase in domestic GDP?
options: $5 million
$4.5 million
$3 million
$6.5 million
items.feedback: Domestic buses contribute 3 million to G. Transfers themselves are excluded. Recipients’ imported services add 1.5 million to C and subtract 1.5 million through imports, leaving zero domestic contribution. Total domestic GDP rises 3 million.

items.stem: A domestic software firm exports $4 million of services, imports $1.5 million of servers, and adds $0.5 million of current domestic output to inventory. What is the direct contribution to domestic GDP?
options: $2.5 million
$4.5 million
$6 million
$3 million
items.feedback: The $4 million export and $0.5 million of inventory are current domestic production. The imported servers do not add domestic production, so the direct contribution is $4.5 million.

items.stem: Consumption is $9T, investment is $3T, government purchases are $4T, exports are $2T, and imports are $3T. Then households buy $1T more imported goods, with no change in domestic production. What happens to measured GDP?
options: It does not change
It rises by $1T because consumption rises
It falls by $1T because imports rise
It rises by $2T because trade increases
items.feedback: Imported consumption raises C but lowers NX by the same amount, so domestic GDP is unchanged.

items.stem: A government spends $100B hiring workers to build bridges and also sends $100B in Social Security payments. If recipients spend all Social Security payments on current domestic goods, what is the maximum direct GDP increase described?
items.feedback: Bridge spending is government purchases, and household spending from transfers can count as consumption. The transfer itself is not counted separately.

items.stem: If C = $15T, I = $4T, G = $6T, imports = $5T, and GDP = $23T, what are exports?
A household buys a newly built condo for $250,000 and pays $3,000 in property taxes. Which is the best GDP treatment?
options: The condo counts as investment; the tax is excluded
Both count as consumption
The condo is consumption and the tax is government purchases
Neither counts
items.feedback: New residential construction is investment. A tax payment is not itself government purchase of a final good or service.

items.stem: A household buys a newly built house for $300,000, a used car for $15,000, and $5,000 of groceries. What amount is added to GDP from these purchases?
items.feedback: The new house and groceries count. The used car resale does not add to current GDP, so GDP rises by $305,000.

items.stem: A firm adds $85 of current unsold output to inventories while a household buys a newly built domestic home for $255. A student classifies only the firm's inventory as investment. Which correction is needed?
options: Both are financial saving; neither is production until resold
Both are investment; their combined GDP contribution is $340
Only the home is investment; inventories count when sold later
The home is consumption and inventory is investment; GDP excludes the home
items.feedback: Inventory accumulation and new residential construction are both investment in the GDP accounts. Their current production adds 85+255 = $340. Buying an existing home would differ.

items.stem: GDP is $900, C is $540, G is $180, exports are $90, and imports are $180. What are investment and net exports?
options: Investment must be $270; net exports are −$90
Investment must be $90; subtracting imports would count them twice
Investment must be $90; net exports are +$90
Investment must be $450; subtract both imports and exports from spending

items.stem: Government buys $5 million of foreign equipment and $4 million of domestic road repair, then sends $3 million in transfers whose recipients spend $2 million on domestic services. What raises domestic GDP?
options: $14 million: every payment and purchase
$11 million: government purchases plus domestic services
$9 million: both government purchases only
$6 million: road repair plus recipients’ domestic services
items.feedback: Imported equipment adds 5 million to G and subtracts 5 million through imports. Domestic road repairs add 4 million to G. The 3 million transfer itself is excluded; recipients’2 million domestic service purchases enter C. Domestic GDP rises 4+2=6 million.

items.stem: A restaurant buys $300 of ingredients and receives $900 from customers for meals, including $100 in tips. Ignoring other complications, how much final restaurant service enters GDP?
items.feedback: The $300 of ingredients are intermediate inputs. The full $900 customer payment, including the $100 in tips, is final expenditure on restaurant service.

items.stem: A country reports $18T in consumption, $5T in investment, $6T in government purchases, $4T in exports, and $5T in imports. Separately, income data show $20T in wages, $4T in rents and interest, and $4T in profits plus other production income. What is the best conclusion?
options: The expenditure and income approaches both imply GDP of $28T
The expenditure approach implies $38T while income implies $28T
Imports should be added, so GDP is $38T
Income cannot be used to measure GDP
items.feedback: Expenditure GDP = 18 + 5 + 6 + (4 - 5) = 28. Income also totals 20 + 4 + 4 = 28.

items.stem: A firm produces $1M of output, sells $800,000 to customers, and adds $200,000 to inventory. It pays $600,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $100,000 in interest, and has $200,000 in profit. Which statement is correct?
options: GDP rises by $1M and income generated also totals $1M
GDP rises only by $800,000 because inventories are unsold
GDP rises by $1.2M because inventory is added to sales
GDP rises by wages only
items.feedback: Unsold output is inventory investment, so all $1M counts; income payments also total $1M.

items.stem: A U.S. household buys a new $30,000 car built in Mexico, while a Mexican household buys a new $40,000 car built in Michigan. What is the net effect on U.S. GDP from these two transactions?
options: U.S. GDP rises by $40,000
U.S. GDP rises by $70,000
U.S. GDP rises by $10,000
U.S. GDP is unchanged
items.feedback: Only the car produced in Michigan counts in U.S. GDP. The imported car affects consumption and imports but not domestic production.

items.stem: A firm imports $500,000 of parts, adds $300,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final good domestically for $800,000. What is the contribution to domestic GDP?
items.feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported inputs are not domestic production.

items.stem: A country produces only two goods. In 2025 it produces 100 meals at $20 and 50 laptops at $1,000. It imports 10 additional laptops at $900 each for households. What domestic production value is counted in GDP?
items.feedback: GDP counts domestic production: 100($20) + 50($1,000) = $52,000. Imported laptops are not domestic production.

items.stem: A firm imports $200,000 of components, adds $150,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final product domestically for $350,000. How much does this production add to domestic GDP?
items.feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported components are not domestic production.

items.stem: A household buys a $98 newly produced domestic computer and a $73 existing corporate share. A broker supplies a new service charging $58. Which revision to a report counting all three payments is correct?
options: Subtract the $58 service; the computer and share contribute $171
Subtract the $98 computer; financial transactions contribute $131
Subtract both the share and service; only $98 counts
Subtract the $73 share transfer; the computer and brokerage service contribute $156
items.feedback: The share is a financial-asset transfer. The current computer and brokerage service are production, totaling 98+58 = $156. A service is not excluded merely because it accompanies finance.

items.stem: A producer reports $100 of final output. A supplier's $60 input is already embodied in it. The national accounts also record $75 of unrelated domestic services. Which proposed GDP total counts each unit of current output once?
options: $115; subtract the input from final output even though it was never added
$100; services are excluded when goods have intermediate inputs
$175; count final output and unrelated services, without adding its embodied input
$235; every observed sale is added
items.feedback: The final good already embodies the supplier's contribution. GDP is 100+75 = $175; neither add the input again nor subtract it from final expenditure.

items.stem: A domestic farm sells grain for $62 to a domestic mill, which sells flour for $77 to a domestic bakery. The bakery sells all bread to households for $102. No inventories change. What is the contribution to GDP, and how does it compare with the sum of value added?
options: Count $179; exclude the farm but retain the mill's intermediate sale
Count $102; summing each producer's value added gives the same final-output value
Count $241; every sale is separate current output
Count $25; only the bakery creates final value
items.feedback: Value added is 62 + (77−62) + (102−77) = $102, equal to the bread's final sale. Adding gross intermediate sales counts embedded production repeatedly.

items.stem: A tax credit for home improvements is claimed by many households that would have renovated anyway. Why might the credit generate relatively little additional renovation?
options: The credit has no budget cost.
A large share of payments does not change marginal behavior.
Households never respond to prices.
The policy creates a price floor.
items.feedback: An incentive is effective at the margin only when it changes decisions that otherwise would differ.

items.stem: The same dollar penalty sharply changes behavior for low-income households but barely affects high-income households. What does this show?
options: All people respond identically to a given dollar amount.
The penalty is not an incentive.
Responses depend on constraints and the size of the incentive relative to resources.
Income has no role in marginal choices.
items.feedback: A fixed incentive can have different marginal importance for different decision-makers.

items.stem: A hospital is paid for each procedure but penalized for readmissions. Which response best reflects both incentives?
options: It may increase profitable procedures while investing in follow-up that lowers readmissions
It must reduce every procedure because penalties dominate rewards
It will ignore follow-up entirely because only direct procedure payments can ever affect hospital behavior
The payment design guarantees the socially optimal treatment mix
items.feedback: Procedure payments and readmission penalties act on different behavioral margins.

items.stem: A school rewards high test pass rates. Administrators shift tutoring toward students just below the cutoff and away from students far behind. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: A threshold metric changes where effort has the highest measured payoff
The reward guarantees equal gains for every student
Tutoring shifts prove the pass-rate reward was not an incentive
The stated goal determines behavior more than the measured target
items.feedback: Effort near the pass threshold produces the largest measured return, even if broader learning is the goal.

items.stem: An environmental fee applies only when emissions exceed a monthly cap. A factory shifts production between months to remain below the cap without lowering annual emissions. What happened?
options: The threshold changed timing rather than the underlying annual outcome
The fee created no incentive because annual emissions stayed constant
Any legal response must satisfy the policy’s broader objective
A fee cannot affect production timing
items.feedback: The incentive altered the monitored margin while leaving annual emissions unchanged.

items.stem: An office awards contracts to the lowest bidder but later faces frequent requests for costly changes to the work. How could it change its selection rule to address this incentive problem?
options: Evaluate expected total cost and performance, not the opening bid alone
Raise the reward for submitting any low opening bid regardless of later changes to the work
Ignore later requests for changes because the opening bid was lower
Require every bidder to choose the same production method
items.feedback: Considering total cost and performance reduces the incentive to submit an artificially low opening bid and recover the difference through later changes.

items.stem: A deductible rises from $100 to $1,000. Which prediction is best without knowing patient income, health risk, or alternatives?
options: Use of covered services tends to fall, but response size can vary widely
Every patient reduces covered care by exactly the same percentage after the deductible change
No response is possible because insurance already exists
The higher deductible guarantees better health decisions
items.feedback: The higher out-of-pocket cost creates directional pressure, while circumstances shape magnitude.

items.stem: A police department rewards citation counts. Citations rise, public trust falls, and serious-case work receives less time. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: The metric changed behavior but did not capture the department’s full objective
Falling trust proves the citation reward cannot influence officer behavior or case priorities in any meaningful way
More citations establish that public safety necessarily improved
Economic analysis requires moral approval of the reward
items.feedback: The reward affects behavior, but the observed metric omits trust and case importance.

items.stem: Why can a small probability of a severe penalty sometimes have little deterrent effect?
options: People may discount unlikely enforcement or misperceive the risk.
Only rewards influence behavior.
The expected cost is always equal to the maximum penalty.
Penalties have no opportunity cost.
items.feedback: Behavior depends on the expected and perceived consequence, not just the statutory maximum.

items.stem: A university raises parking fines. Students respond by arriving earlier, carpooling more, and contesting tickets more often. What principle ties these reactions together?
options: People respond to incentives, including responses the university did not intend
People ignore incentives when rules are created by institutions
Opportunity cost disappears when penalties are legal
Markets allocate resources only when prices are zero
items.feedback: A changed penalty changes behavior, including responses the policy designer may not have wanted.

items.stem: A congestion charge is announced, but drivers believe cameras identify only 5% of violators. Which factor most limits deterrence?
options: The low perceived probability of paying the charge
The charge is negative rather than positive
Driving has benefits as well as costs
A legal charge cannot change expected costs
items.feedback: The expected cost depends on both the charge and the chance it is imposed.

items.stem: A housing program withdraws $1 of aid for each $1 of additional earnings over a threshold. Which behavioral pressure follows?
options: Earning just above the threshold may provide little immediate net gain
Every recipient stops working completely
The rule rewards every additional dollar of earnings with an equal dollar of net income
Aid withdrawal is an outcome rather than an incentive
items.feedback: The phaseout can sharply reduce the net benefit of crossing the earnings threshold.

items.stem: A charity matches the first $100 of each donation. A donor planning to give $300 still gives $300. How should the match be evaluated for that donor?
options: It transfers funds but does not change this donor’s marginal giving decision
It necessarily causes an additional $100 donation
The donor did not face an incentive because the entire planned gift amount was chosen before the match
The match reduces the benefit of donating
items.feedback: The match applies to the gift, but this donor’s amount is unchanged relative to the alternative.

items.stem: A transit agency offers off-peak discounts. Flexible riders shift trips, while shift workers cannot. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: The price incentive changes trip timing mainly for riders with feasible alternatives
The discount is not an incentive because some riders cannot respond
All riders receive identical benefits from changing travel time
The policy guarantees total ridership will rise
items.feedback: The discount changes relative prices, but schedule constraints determine who can act on it.

items.stem: A streaming service removes a cancellation fee but adds a loyalty reward after twelve months. Which decision does the rule most directly influence?
options: Whether subscribers stay through the twelfth month
The quality of every program on the service
The certainty that all subscribers remain
Subscribers’ moral judgment of loyalty programs
items.feedback: The reward changes the benefit of remaining until a specific time threshold.

items.stem: A warranty pays repair shops a flat amount per claim. Shops begin avoiding complex claims and completing simple ones quickly. What caused the pattern?
options: A uniform payment changes the payoff differently for low-cost and high-cost claims
The flat payment guarantees equal service across claims
Avoiding difficult cases proves payments cannot affect selection
Claim complexity is irrelevant whenever prices are fixed
items.feedback: Simple claims become more profitable relative to complex ones, encouraging selection.

items.stem: A sports contract pays a large bonus for games played. An injured athlete returns early and performs poorly. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: The bonus increased pressure to play but did not guarantee a beneficial outcome
The poor performance proves the bonus was not an incentive
Bonuses influence effort but never participation decisions
Playing establishes that the athlete approved of the contract design
items.feedback: The bonus changed the payoff to participation, while health and performance remained uncertain.

items.stem: A delivery platform guarantees a minimum hourly payment only while drivers are actively carrying orders. Which response is plausible?
options: Drivers may favor longer trips or avoid unpaid waiting when choosing orders
Every driver accepts the shortest available trip
The guarantee removes all opportunity costs of time
Payment rules cannot change which orders drivers select
items.feedback: The rule changes which activities count as paid time, altering the relative payoff to orders.

items.stem: A city raises water prices after a monthly allowance and also publishes neighborhood conservation rankings. What response should be expected?
options: Price and status pressures may reduce use by different amounts across households
The ranking is irrelevant because only prices are incentives
Every household cuts water use by the same quantity
Lower use is guaranteed wherever both incentives exist
items.feedback: Both monetary cost and social comparison can affect use, with varied strength.

items.stem: A hospital bonus rewards low average treatment cost. Managers discharge patients earlier, but readmissions rise. Which redesign best aligns the incentive with patient outcomes?
options: Include readmissions and health outcomes alongside treatment cost
Increase the reward for low initial cost alone
Judge success only by the number of discharges
Remove monitoring because outcomes vary across patients
items.feedback: A broader measure reduces the payoff to cost cutting that shifts expense or harm into readmissions.

items.stem: A fine rises from $100 to $500 while the actual probability of detection falls from 80% to 10%. Drivers are risk neutral and understand those probabilities. Reform C instead keeps the $500 fine and restores detection to 20%. Which comparison of expected penalties is correct?
options: The initial change lowers expected penalty from $80 to $50; C raises it to $100, strengthening deterrence relative to both earlier rules.
The initial change raises expected penalty from $80 to $500; C lowers it to $100 because more detection reduces risk.
The initial change leaves expected penalty at $80; C leaves it unchanged because headline fines determine all deterrence.
The initial change lowers expected penalty from $100 to $50; C restores it only if every violator is detected.
items.feedback: Expected penalty equals probability times fine: 0.8×100=80, 0.1×500=50 and 0.2×500=100. Under the stated behavior assumptions, the headline fine increase can weaken deterrence if detection falls sufficiently.

items.stem: A university funds departments for graduates employed within 30 days. Programs steer students toward quick-placement jobs and away from longer searches for better matches. What is the central design problem?
options: The measured deadline rewards placement speed rather than match quality
Employment funding cannot influence advising behavior
Quick placement guarantees the best long-run outcome
The stated career goal prevents any unintended response
items.feedback: Departments gain from hitting the short deadline even if longer searches would improve matches.

items.stem: A conservation policy combines a usage fee, public recognition, and exemptions for medical needs. Which assessment is most defensible?
options: Different households face different effective incentives, so response and burden will vary
The usage fee guarantees identical reductions for all households
Recognition is irrelevant because it is not money
Exemptions prove the policy has no behavioral effect
items.feedback: Prices, status, and exemptions change payoffs differently across households.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. After policy, by approximately how many percentage points does the top 20 percent's income share fall relative to before policy?
options: About 5 percentage points
About 20 percentage points
About 10 percentage points
About 35 percentage points
items.feedback: The graph shows the bottom 80 percent receiving about 55 percent before and 65 percent after, leaving about 45 percent and 35 percent for the top quintile—a decrease of about 10 percentage points.

items.stem: Two households each earn $50,000 from work. One inherits $100,000 and invests it at 4% per year; the other receives no inheritance. Ignoring taxes and other income, how do next year’s labor earnings and total incomes compare?
options: Labor earnings differ by $100,000; total income is equal.
Labor earnings are equal; the inheriting household has $4,000 more total income.
Labor earnings are equal; total income differs by $100,000 each year.
Both labor earnings and total income differ by $4,000.
items.feedback: An inheritance is an asset stock; its 4% return produces a $4,000 annual income flow without changing labor earnings.

items.stem: A recipient’s preferred bundle after a $100 cash grant contains only $40 of food. A $100 nonresalable food voucher replaces the grant at the same prices. What restriction matters?
options: The voucher can be spent entirely on rent.
The voucher excludes the preferred $40-food bundle.
The voucher reduces all prices by 60%.
The voucher offers more options than equal cash.
items.feedback: The voucher is binding because desired food spending under cash is below $100; it cannot be exchanged for the preferred nonfood purchases.

items.stem: A redistribution proposal raises the poorest group’s income from 10 to 14 and lowers total income from 100 to 94. One evaluator supports it; another rejects it solely because the total falls. What explains the disagreement?
options: They disagree about whether 14 exceeds 10.
The proposal is mathematically impossible.
They both apply maximin but calculate the same minimum differently.
They apply different normative criteria: the minimum versus total income.
items.feedback: The stated facts allow improved minimum income alongside a smaller total. The disagreement concerns what to value, not the arithmetic.

items.stem: A household holds assets of $180,000 and debt of $70,000, including an inherited asset worth $40,000 already included in total assets. What is its net wealth?
items.feedback: Net wealth equals assets minus debt: $180,000 − $70,000 = $110,000. Adding the inheritance again would double-count it.

items.stem: A recipient would spend $200 on food with a $100 cash grant. Instead the program offers a nonresalable $100 food voucher, with identical prices and no transaction costs. What can be inferred?
options: Every restriction must reduce welfare.
The voucher raises cash income by $200.
The voucher limits food spending to $100.
The preferred cash bundle remains affordable.
items.feedback: The intended food spending exceeds the voucher amount. The voucher can replace $100 of spending the recipient would already make, leaving the cash-optimal bundle feasible.

items.stem: Policy A yields group incomes (12, 100); B yields (18, 70). A third policy C yields (18, 90). Under a rule that first maximizes the minimum and breaks ties by total income, which policy is selected?
options: A
B
All three tie
C
items.feedback: B and C share the highest minimum, 18. The stated tie-break then selects C, whose total is 108 rather than 88.

items.stem: A benefit phaseout takes $0.60 per extra earnings dollar and an earnings tax takes $0.20, both calculated independently on gross earnings. Reducing the phaseout to $0.30 leaves the tax unchanged. What happens to the net return from an extra $100 earned?
options: It rises from $40 to $70.
It falls from $80 to $50.
It rises from $20 to $50.
It stays at $20.
items.feedback: Initially the household keeps 100 − 60 − 20 = $20; afterward it keeps 100 − 30 − 20 = $50.

items.stem: Two households have equal labor earnings. Household A inherits productive assets, while B does not. A proposal equalizes their current labor earnings but leaves asset ownership and returns unchanged. Which evaluation is justified?
options: The proposal eliminates the wealth gap because equal annual earnings imply equal asset stocks.
The wealth gap and associated capital-income gap remain.
The proposal removes capital income by holding labor earnings equal.
The proposal increases labor productivity in B by transferring ownership of A’s assets.
items.feedback: A stock of inherited assets can persist and yield income independently of equal labor earnings. A labor-income rule alone does not transfer that stock.

items.stem: A hypothetical poverty measure counts cash income but excludes food vouchers. A household has $25,000 in cash and $3,000 in vouchers; its threshold is $27,000. Replacing the vouchers with $3,000 cash changes no prices. Which conclusion follows?
options: Measured status remains below because transfers never enter cash income.
Measured status changes from above to below because vouchers are counted twice.
Measured status remains above because the original vouchers already count as cash.
Measured status changes from below to above; well-being requires a separate assessment.
items.feedback: The measure initially counts $25,000 and then $28,000. Classification changes mechanically; the economic value of relaxing spending restrictions is a separate question.

items.stem: Two households each have $31,000 measured income. The threshold is $30,000 for the smaller household and $34,000 for the larger. An analyst classifies both as above poverty because their incomes match. What is the error?
options: The analyst should classify both below poverty because their incomes match.
The analyst should compare the smaller household with the larger household’s threshold only.
The analyst should average the thresholds before classifying either household.
The analyst ignores different applicable thresholds; only the smaller household is above its threshold.
items.feedback: Each household must be compared with its own specified threshold. Equal measured income need not imply equal classification.

items.stem: One policy restores property proven to have been stolen; another redistributes legitimately acquired property to equalize incomes. Both lower inequality. What follows under an entitlement framework?
options: Both must be rejected because an entitlement framework prohibits any change in ownership.
The first may rectify a rights violation; the common distributional result does not make the two policies equivalent.
Both must be accepted because lower inequality is the sole entitlement criterion.
Neither can be assessed without knowing whether aggregate income rises.
items.feedback: Rectification of unjust acquisition differs from compulsory equalization of legitimate holdings. A shared effect on inequality does not erase that distinction.

items.stem: A program replaces a $1,000 benefit cliff at one earnings cutoff with a $0.20 reduction per dollar over the next $5,000. Which assessment is correct?
options: The cliff disappears, but earnings face a 20% phaseout over a wider range.
All work disincentives disappear because there is no longer a cliff.
The phaseout removes the benefit after only $200 of additional earnings.
Recipients throughout the phaseout keep every additional earnings dollar.
items.feedback: Spreading $1,000 over $5,000 produces a 20% phaseout. It smooths the discontinuity while applying a marginal benefit loss over the range.

items.stem: For the bottom 40% of households, express average income as a percentage of the economy-wide average. Why must the group’s income share be adjusted for its population share?
options: 50% of the overall mean; divide the group’s income share by its population share.
37.5% of the overall mean; divide the group’s income share by its population share.
37.5% of the overall mean; use the group’s income share without adjusting for its population share.
50% of the overall mean; use the group’s income share without adjusting for its population share.
items.feedback: The bottom 40% receives 15% of total income. Its mean relative to the overall mean is 0.15/0.40 = 0.375. A cumulative income share alone is not a relative group mean.

items.stem: Total income is $100 million in economy A and $400 million in B. How much does the bottom 40% receive in each? Does the economy giving this group the larger share also give it more dollars?
options: A: $20 million; B: $24 million. A gives the group a larger share, but B gives it more dollars.
A: $22 million; B: $28 million. A’s larger share proves the group receives more dollars in A.
A: $20 million; B: $24 million. A’s larger share proves the group receives more dollars in A.
A: $22 million; B: $28 million. A gives the group a larger share, but B gives it more dollars.
items.feedback: At the bottom 40%, A has 22% of income and B 7%. Thus group income is $22 m in A and 0.07 × 400 = $28 m in B. A relative share and an absolute dollar total answer different questions.

items.stem: In economy B, the income outside the bottom 80% belongs to which group? What is that group’s average income relative to the economy-wide average?
options: About twice the overall mean for the top 20%; use the complement’s income and population shares.
About three times the overall mean for the top 40%; the complement of 80% is 40%.
About three times the overall mean for the top 20%; use the complement’s income and population shares.
About twice the overall mean for the top 40%; the complement of 80% is 40%.
items.feedback: B’s bottom 80% receives about 40% of income. The remaining 60% belongs to the top 20%, giving a relative group mean of 60/20 = 3. Cumulative shares must be complemented on both axes.

items.stem: An analyst claims that the middle quintile in economy A earns twice the overall average income. Which income-share and relative-mean calculation correctly evaluates the claim?
options: Share: 16%; mean: 0.8 of the overall mean; claim rejected.
Share: 18%; mean: 0.9 of the overall mean; claim rejected.
Share: 40%; mean: 2.0 times the overall mean; claim supported.
Share: 18%; mean: 2.0 times the overall mean; claim supported.
items.feedback: A’s cumulative shares at population 40% and 60% are about 22% and 40%. The middle quintile receives 40 − 22 = 18%, and 18/20 = 0.9 of the overall mean, so the twice-average claim is false. The upper cumulative endpoint includes earlier quintiles.

items.stem: Calculate the change in the Gini coefficient shown. Could cutting every household’s income by the same 10% produce this change? Explain.
options: A decline of 0.100; no, proportional income changes leave relative shares and the Gini unchanged.
A decline of 0.128; yes, a common proportional reduction makes relative income shares more equal.
A decline of 0.100; yes, a common proportional reduction makes relative income shares more equal.
A decline of 0.128; no, proportional income changes leave relative shares and the Gini unchanged.
items.feedback: The plotted decline is 0.380−0.252 = 0.128. Multiplying every income and the total by 0.9 leaves all income shares unchanged, so it cannot generate the plotted Lorenz or Gini change.

items.stem: Average real income falls from $20,000 to $18,000 while the Gini changes as shown. Calculate both changes. Does the lower Gini prove that every group has a higher standard of living?
options: Gini falls 0.100 and mean income 10%; lower relative inequality does not prove every group is better off.
Gini falls 0.128 and mean income 10%; lower relative inequality does not prove every group is better off.
Gini falls 0.128 and mean income 10%; the Gini decline proves every group’s real income rises.
Gini falls 0.100 and mean income 10%; the Gini decline proves every group’s real income rises.
items.feedback: The Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252, or 0.128, while mean income falls 2,000/20,000 = 10%. Relative inequality and the level of income are distinct; a better Gini does not establish universal welfare gains.

items.stem: Suppose the CPI systematically overstates the rise in the true cost of living. What can happen to a benefit that is fully indexed to the CPI?
options: The nominal benefit must decline every year.
The benefit can become too generous in real terms.
The real value remains exactly constant by definition.
Indexing removes every possible measurement problem.
items.feedback: If the CPI overstates cost-of-living growth, full CPI indexation can overcompensate recipients in real terms.

items.stem: A retiree benefit is indexed to overall CPI, but retirees buy a systematically different basket. What limitation remains?
options: The benefit should be deflated with the GDP deflator only
CPI cannot measure any consumer prices
The chosen index may not match the retiree’s actual cost changes
Indexation guarantees identical costs for every household
items.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

items.stem: A salary adjustment uses last year’s CPI while inflation accelerates this year. What can happen before the next adjustment?
options: Current inflation becomes irrelevant
Purchasing power can temporarily fall
Real value must rise because the contract is indexed
The nominal salary must decline
items.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

items.stem: A stipend pays $1,800 at CPI 150. At CPI 165 it rises to $1,920. How much additional monthly pay would restore the original purchasing power, and why?
options: $60; full indexation requires $1,980
$180; the CPI increased by 10%, so add 10% again
$120; any increase exactly restores purchasing power
$0; the stipend already rose in dollars
items.feedback: Maintaining the initial purchasing power requires 1,800 × 165/150 = 1,980. The actual 1,920 is short by 60. A positive nominal raise may still fall short of price growth.

items.stem: A pension is fully CPI-indexed, but quality gains make CPI overstate true living-cost growth. What is the likely real effect?
options: The pension must lose nominal value throughout the entire inflation-adjustment period
Indexation eliminates quality measurement issues
The GDP deflator must rise by the same amount
The pension can gain purchasing power relative to the true cost of living
items.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

items.stem: A $150 monthly benefit is fully indexed to a 5% CPI rise, but its recipient's actual fixed basket rises 8%. Which conclusion distinguishes index protection from household purchasing power?
options: CPI-adjusted value falls 3%; household purchasing power is preserved
Both measures rise 13% because the index and basket changes add
CPI-adjusted value is preserved; purchasing power over this household basket falls about 2.8%
Both CPI-adjusted and household purchasing power are preserved because the contract is indexed
items.feedback: The contract preserves value relative to CPI, not every household basket. For this basket the real factor is 1.05/1.08, or about a 2.78% decline.

items.stem: A past monthly payment was $160 when CPI was 100. A current payment is $208 when CPI is 125. Which comparison uses common purchasing-power units?
options: The payments have equal purchasing power; both CPI and the payment increased
The current payment is $8 higher in current dollars; the past payment converts to $200
The current payment is $48 higher in real terms; compare unadjusted dollar amounts
The past payment is $8 higher in current dollars; deflate the past payment again
items.feedback: The past payment in current dollars is 160×125/100 = 200. The current payment exceeds it by 8.

items.stem: A $170 indexed benefit resets once annually. Immediately after a reset, prices rise while the next reset is six months away. Which proposal addresses the specific loss without promising complete protection against a mismatched household basket?
options: Reset more frequently to reduce the lag; index mismatch can still leave real-value differences
Reset less frequently to reduce the lag; a CPI rule eliminates all household mismatch
Replace the index with the original nominal amount; fixed payments follow current prices
Use the GDP deflator regardless of consumption; domestic output prices always equal each household basket
items.feedback: More frequent adjustment can shorten the timing gap. Even prompt CPI indexation cannot guarantee unchanged purchasing power for a different household consumption basket.

items.stem: A lender expected 2 percent inflation and charged 6 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 5 percent. Who is helped by the surprise, and why?
options: Borrowers, because they repay with dollars worth less than expected.
Lenders, because they receive dollars worth more than expected.
Borrowers, because the nominal interest rate rises after the loan is signed.
Lenders, because real repayment rises automatically.
items.feedback: Unexpectedly high inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders because repayment occurs in less valuable dollars.

items.stem: A lender expected 6 percent inflation and charged 10 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 2 percent. Who is helped by the surprise?
options: Lenders
Borrowers
Both equally because nominal interest was fixed
Neither because inflation never redistributes wealth
items.feedback: Lower-than-expected inflation helps lenders because they are repaid with dollars worth more than expected.

items.stem: If all prices rise but incomes rise by the same percentage, why can inflation still be costly?
options: It causes shoe-leather and menu costs, tax distortions, distorted relative-price signals, and redistribution.
It has no costs if incomes rise at all.
It only affects people who never buy goods.
It permanently raises real wages.
items.feedback: Inflation can still impose real costs through behavior changes, price adjustment costs, distortions, and redistribution.

items.stem: A fixed-rate lender expected 3 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 8 percent. At the same time firms repeatedly update prices. Which statement separates the two costs?
options: Unexpected inflation benefits the borrower; repricing uses real resources even when inflation is anticipated.
Both effects are examples only of shoeleather costs.
The surprise benefits the lender, while repricing raises real output automatically.
Neither effect is an inflation cost unless the price level actually falls, because rising prices cannot redistribute purchasing power or use real resources.
items.feedback: The surprise redistributes purchasing power toward the borrower, while repeated price changes are menu costs that use real resources even when inflation is anticipated.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 6 percent inflation and charged 11 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 3 percent. Who gains from the surprise and what is the realized real rate?
options: Lender gains; realized real rate is 8 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 14 percent.
items.feedback: Actual inflation was lower than expected, so the lender gains. Realized real rate is 11 - 3 = 8 percent.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower expected 3 percent inflation on a loan with a 7 percent nominal rate. Actual inflation was 10 percent. Who gains and what is the realized real rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -3 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 4 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 7 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -3 percent.
items.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. The realized real rate is 7 - 10 = -3 percent.

items.stem: A student says inflation makes everyone poorer because all prices rise. What is the best response?
options: Incomes can rise too; inflation still causes costs and redistribution.
Inflation never has costs if any wage rises.
Inflation only affects creditors and no one else.
Inflation lowers all nominal incomes by definition.
items.feedback: Rising prices alone do not establish that everyone loses purchasing power: nominal incomes and fixed contracts matter. Inflation can still use resources, distort decisions and redistribute wealth.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 3 percent inflation and charged 8 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 12 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -4 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 8 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -4 percent.
items.feedback: Actual inflation exceeded expected inflation, so borrowers gain. The realized real rate is 8 - 12 = -4 percent.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 8 percent inflation and charged 13 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 2 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real rate?
options: Lender gains; realized real rate is 11 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 11 percent.
items.feedback: Actual inflation was lower than expected, so lenders gain. The realized real rate is 13 - 2 = 11 percent.

items.stem: Two economies each have $140 in fixed nominal contracts. One unexpectedly raises inflation; the other credibly announces the same inflation before new contracts are written. Which difference is supported?
options: Both paths must have identical redistribution regardless of contract timing and indexation
The surprise creates more unexpected redistribution on existing contracts; the anticipated path can still create resource costs
The anticipated path must be economically costless because contracts can price every resource cost away
The surprise benefits all borrowers and lenders equally because the price level rises for both
items.feedback: Contract timing and expectations determine surprise redistribution. Anticipation allows adjustment but does not generally remove repricing, cash-management or tax-distortion costs.

items.stem: A $280 fixed nominal debt was agreed with expected inflation 2%, but actual inflation is 7%. At the same time, firms incur real repricing costs. Which combined assessment is correct?
options: Unexpected inflation benefits the lender relative to the borrower, while repricing consumes real resources
Borrower gains exactly equal a social resource gain, so repricing cannot reduce welfare
Repricing redistributes debt obligations but uses no real resources, so it is the same as surprise inflation
Unexpected inflation benefits the borrower relative to the lender, while repricing consumes real resources
items.feedback: A lower-than-expected real repayment transfers purchasing power toward borrowers. Repricing is a resource cost, so redistribution and efficiency costs are conceptually different.

items.stem: Two economies each have $300 in fixed nominal contracts. One unexpectedly raises inflation; the other credibly announces the same inflation before new contracts are written. Which difference is supported?
options: The surprise benefits all borrowers and lenders equally because the price level rises for both
Both paths must have identical redistribution regardless of contract timing and indexation
The surprise creates more unexpected redistribution on existing contracts; the anticipated path can still create resource costs
The anticipated path must be economically costless because contracts can price every resource cost away
items.feedback: Contract timing and expectations determine surprise redistribution. Anticipation allows adjustment but does not generally remove repricing, cash-management or tax-distortion costs.

items.stem: A saver earns a nominal $320 return that only compensates for inflation. The tax system taxes the entire nominal return without inflation adjustment. Which inference follows?
options: The nominal return is all a real gain because inflation compensation counts as extra purchasing power
Tax can reduce real principal despite a zero pre-tax real gain; nominal income and real income differ
No tax distortion is possible because a zero real gain implies a zero nominal tax base
The tax increases the saver's real return because it is charged in nominal dollars
items.feedback: A tax on nominal interest can tax inflation compensation as though it were real income. After-tax purchasing power can therefore fall even when the pre-tax real return is zero.

items.stem: A household keeps a fixed $720 cash balance while the price of a representative basket of goods rises from $1.20 to $1.50 during money-financed government spending. How many fewer baskets can the household buy with that unchanged cash balance?
options: 120 baskets.
180 baskets.
144 baskets.
No baskets, because the nominal balance is fixed.
items.feedback: The cash initially buys 720/1.20 = 600 baskets and later buys 720/1.50 = 480 baskets. The loss is 120 baskets. An unchanged cash balance need not preserve purchasing power.

items.stem: A country uses money creation to finance deficits, inflation rises, and nominal interest rates rise with expected inflation. Which two ideas are linked?
options: Inflation tax and Fisher effect
Crowding out and SRAS
Multiplier and LRPC
M1 and sacrifice ratio
items.feedback: Printing money can act as an inflation tax, and higher expected inflation raises nominal interest rates through the Fisher effect.

items.stem: A country raises money growth from 5 percent to 25 percent while real output growth stays at 3 percent and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 2 percent to about 22 percent.
It rises from about 5 percent to about 25 percent exactly.
It falls from 25 percent to 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth is unchanged.
items.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth: initially 2 percent, then 22 percent.

items.stem: Deflation lowers the price level from 200 to 180. What happens to the value of money, and why can this matter for debtors?
options: The value of money rises; debtors repay with dollars worth more.
The value of money falls; debtors repay with dollars worth less.
The value of money is unchanged; debtors are unaffected.
The value of money rises; debtors repay with dollars worth less.
items.feedback: Deflation raises the value of money. Fixed nominal debts become harder for debtors to repay.

items.stem: A country uses seigniorage heavily during a fiscal crisis. Which combination is most likely if confidence erodes?
options: Rapid money growth, rising expected inflation, and higher nominal interest rates
Falling money growth, falling expected inflation, and lower nominal interest rates
No change in inflation because money is neutral in the short run
Lower price levels and higher money value immediately
items.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations, and higher expected inflation pushes nominal interest rates up.

items.stem: A government prints money to finance deficits. Money growth rises from 6 percent to 26 percent, output growth remains 3 percent, and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 3 percent to about 23 percent.
It rises from about 6 percent to about 26 percent exactly.
It falls from about 23 percent to about 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth did not change.
items.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth. It rises from 3 percent to 23 percent.

items.stem: A government finances purchases by creating money. Expected inflation rises, and nominal interest rates rise. Which economic concepts explain how these events are connected?
options: Inflation tax, expected inflation, and the Fisher effect
Crowding out, reserve requirements, and commodity money
Menu costs, M1, and fiscal multipliers
Liquidity trap, real wage, and barter
items.feedback: Printing money can create inflation expectations, and the Fisher effect links expected inflation to nominal interest rates.

items.stem: A government prints money to finance spending, expected inflation rises, and households reduce desired real cash balances. Which concern is most complete?
options: Households holding less money automatically raises real output enough to offset the inflation-tax burden and preserve seigniorage revenue.
Inflation-tax finance can erode real balances and become harder to sustain as people avoid holding money.
Lower money demand guarantees a stable price level despite continued money creation.
Printing money eliminates the need to consider inflation because seigniorage is a real resource.
items.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations and reduce desired real money balances, making continued reliance on seigniorage increasingly disruptive.

items.stem: A household holds $260 in currency while the price level rises 25%. No interest is paid. Which loss and interpretation fit the inflation-tax mechanism?
options: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
Nominal cash falls 25%; inflation removes currency through an implicit tax bill.
Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
Real purchasing power is unchanged; holding the same nominal cash preserves its value.
items.feedback: Real balances are M/P. With nominal currency fixed and prices multiplied by 1.25, purchasing power becomes 1/1.25=.8 of its original level, a 20% loss.

items.stem: A borrower owes a fixed $1,000. Compare a 10% price-level increase with a 10% price-level decrease, from an initial index 100. Which real-debt comparison uses the correct denominators?
options: Exactly $1,000 in both; a fixed nominal contract is also fixed in real terms
About $909 after inflation and $1,111 after deflation; equal opposite price percentages have asymmetric real-debt effects
Exactly $900 and $1,100; subtract the percentage directly from the debt
About $1,111 and $909; inflation increases the real debt burden
items.feedback: Real debt is 1000/1.1≈909 and 1000/.9≈1111. A fixed nominal promise changes purchasing-power value when the price level changes.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An insurer charges the same premium to applicants who privately know their own risks. Why might repeated premium increases drive the average risk of those insured even higher?
options: Low-risk customers leave as premiums rise.
Insured customers take more risks after buying coverage.
High-risk customers leave before low-risk customers.
Higher premiums reveal each customer’s exact risk.
items.feedback: Selection occurs through enrollment: a worsening risk pool raises costs and can drive out additional low-risk customers.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Buyers initially think 75% of devices are good, worth $120, and 25% are bad, worth $40. Good sellers require $90. If the good share falls to 50%, how does participation change at expected-value prices?
options: The offer rises from $80 to $100, attracting good sellers.
The offer falls from $120 to $40, but good sellers still accept.
The offer stays at $90 because reservation values determine expected quality.
The offer falls from $100 to $80, causing good sellers to withdraw.
items.feedback: The initial expectation is 0.75(120)+0.25(40)=$100; the new expectation is $80, below the good seller’s $90 reservation value.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A warranty provider introduces a reliable pre-purchase fragility test but does not monitor care after purchase. Which problem does this change directly address?
options: Postpurchase moral hazard, while fragility remains hidden.
Adverse selection from hidden fragility, while postpurchase moral hazard can remain.
Both problems completely, because any test makes behavior enforceable.
Neither problem, because information never affects contracting.
items.feedback: The test reveals precontract type; it does not reveal or change the enforceability of later care.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An insurer can perfectly verify how carefully a driver behaves but cannot make enforceable contract terms or penalties depend on that behavior. Does observing the driver’s behavior alone remove the incentive to take less care?
options: Yes; seeing an action automatically changes the driver’s payoff.
Yes; observation refunds every premium.
No; the remaining issue must be hidden precontract type only.
No. Verified behavior still needs enforceable rewards or penalties.
items.feedback: Observation and enforceability are separate. Verified actions need enforceable consequences to change the described incentive.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A small study reports that a reminder improves saving. A larger, preregistered replication with comparable conditions finds an estimate near zero and a confidence interval excluding the original large effect. What is the best response?
options: Discard the replication because it disagrees with the first result.
Reduce confidence in the original large effect while considering both studies’ uncertainty and designs.
Conclude reminders must reduce saving in every setting.
Treat the first estimate as certain because it was published first.
items.feedback: The replication supplies contrary evidence about the claimed magnitude. It need not prove an exactly zero effect everywhere to weaken the original claim.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A program switches its default at the same time it increases the employer subsidy. Participation rises. Why can the increase not be attributed entirely to the default from this comparison alone?
options: Defaults cannot influence behavior when a subsidy exists.
Participation is unrelated to incentives.
An increase in participation proves the subsidy had no effect.
The subsidy changed too, creating a competing explanation.
items.feedback: Two relevant conditions changed together. Without further evidence their contributions cannot be separated.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Two studies estimate an intervention effect at 4 and 5 percentage points, each with an uncertainty interval from −2 to 10. Does the one-point difference establish conflicting effects?
options: Yes; any different point estimates establish different underlying effects.
No; the estimates are close relative to their reported uncertainty.
Yes; overlapping intervals prove opposite mechanisms.
No; the true effect is necessarily exactly 4.5 points.
items.feedback: Sampling variation can produce nearby estimates. Their uncertainty does not support treating the one-point difference as a demonstrated conflict.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A person rejects a fair gamble. Why does that fact alone not establish loss aversion?
options: Loss aversion requires accepting every fair gamble.
Ordinary risk aversion can also explain rejection; evidence about gains and losses around a reference point is needed.
Risk aversion and loss aversion are identical definitions.
Rejecting a gamble proves probability judgments are accurate.
items.feedback: Risk aversion concerns curvature over outcomes; loss aversion concerns asymmetric valuation of gains and losses relative to a reference point. A single rejection need not distinguish them.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Two groups see the same accident-rate table; one also sees a vivid anecdote. Random assignment yields higher risk estimates only in the anecdote group. What does this design add?
options: It proves the true accident rate rose in the anecdote group.
It changes the table’s sample size for one group.
It establishes loss aversion rather than a judgment effect.
It isolates the anecdote’s effect while holding the statistical information fixed.
items.feedback: Holding the table constant and randomly varying the anecdote supports an effect of salience on risk judgment.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A rule violates independence of irrelevant alternatives in one example. Does that alone imply that every voter’s ranking is cyclic?
options: Yes; IIA is the definition of individual transitivity.
No; the collective rule can violate IIA even when each individual ranking is transitive.
Yes; adding an alternative necessarily changes every pairwise preference.
No; IIA places no restriction on a social ranking rule.
items.feedback: IIA concerns how a collective pairwise ranking responds to preference profiles; it is distinct from consistency of each individual’s ranking.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: One-third ranks A>B>C, one-third B>C>A, and one-third C>A>B. What happens under pairwise majority voting?
options: A is a Condorcet winner
Every pair ties
Majority preferences form a cycle: A > B > C > A.
The median option always wins
items.feedback: Two-thirds prefer A to B, two-thirds prefer B to C, and two-thirds prefer C to A. This creates a majority cycle even though each voter has a transitive ranking.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Two office-seeking candidates care only about winning and voters choose the closer one on a single policy dimension. What tendency follows?
options: Both move toward opposite extremes
Policy location becomes irrelevant
The candidate at the mean always loses
Both tend toward the median voter.
items.feedback: Moving toward the median can capture pivotal voters without losing those on the candidate's outer side.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: After a recent burglary, residents become more worried. Local data also show a sustained increase in burglaries. Why is increased concern alone insufficient to diagnose availability bias?
options: A recent event prevents any rational response.
Availability bias requires no memorable events.
Statistical evidence cannot influence perceived risk.
The concern may reflect the documented rise in risk.
items.feedback: A changed belief is not automatically a bias when relevant risk evidence also changes. The two explanations require discrimination.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Sellers claim their products are reliable. An independent test accurately identifies reliability and results are disclosed before buyers choose. Which mechanism could improve trade?
options: The test changes every unreliable product into a reliable one.
The test prevents all buyers from considering prices.
The test creates adverse selection by hiding quality that was formerly disclosed.
Verified quality lets reliable sellers distinguish their products.
items.feedback: Credible disclosure separates qualities rather than improving the physical product itself; good products need not be priced as though they were average.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Two warranty markets differ only in information. In A, fragility is privately known before purchase; in B, fragility is verified and priced, but postpurchase care is unobserved. Which pairing is correct?
options: A: moral hazard; B: adverse selection
A: adverse selection; B: moral hazard
Both: adverse selection only
Both: moral hazard only
items.feedback: A concerns who selects coverage based on hidden type. B concerns hidden actions after coverage begins.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A bank expects rescue only if its losses become very large. Managers respond by choosing a riskier portfolio after financing is obtained. What makes this a moral-hazard mechanism?
options: The rescue reveals the bank’s hidden precontract type with certainty.
The risk increase is a fixed characteristic that cannot respond to incentives.
Rescue expectations raise the bank’s share of every possible loss.
The rescue expectation reduces the downside the bank bears and changes its later risk-taking.
items.feedback: Sharing or shifting losses can weaken incentives to avoid them; the stated change is in behavior after financing.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A borrower offers collateral as a signal of repayment confidence. Suppose both high-risk and low-risk borrowers face the same expected collateral loss and obtain the same loan benefit. What follows?
options: Collateral necessarily separates types even when their incentives match.
The stated costs and benefits do not give the two types different signaling incentives.
Equal incentives reveal every borrower to be low risk.
Equal incentives convert the signal into perfect lender screening.
items.feedback: A separating signal needs an incentive difference that makes mimicking unattractive for one type. The stated identical payoffs provide none.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A warranty initially costs good sellers $2 and bad sellers $20 to honor. Third-party insurance then makes the warranty cost $3 for either type. Holding the price premium fixed, does the warranty become a stronger or weaker signal of product quality, and why?
options: It strengthens because identical costs reveal quality more accurately.
It weakens because the warranty no longer imposes a higher signaling cost on bad sellers.
It is unchanged because signaling never depends on imitation incentives.
It reverses physical quality, making bad products good.
items.feedback: Equalizing the cost removes the original reason bad sellers would be less willing to mimic the warranty.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Automatic enrollment raises participation, but some workers later opt out and report that the plan did not fit their needs. Which conclusion follows?
options: The opt-outs prove defaults have no effect on initial choices.
Higher participation establishes unanimous informed preference for the plan.
The plan must yield lower returns solely because opt-outs occur.
The default changes choices; higher participation alone does not establish that every affected worker benefits.
items.feedback: Choice effects and welfare effects are separate. Some people may remain enrolled because of inertia rather than a plan that best fits their circumstances.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A trial finds that a default raises participation by 20 points among new employees. A firm plans to apply the same estimate to long-serving workers who already made active choices. What limitation matters?
options: Random assignment guarantees an identical effect in every population.
Prior choices make the trial’s result mathematically impossible.
A 20-point effect means participation must double in every group.
The effect may differ for workers who already made active choices.
items.feedback: Internal evidence from one group does not guarantee the same response in a different decision context.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Two identical outcomes are framed as keeping $80 of an endowed $100 or losing $20 of it. A decision changes with the framing. Which explanation is consistent with this evidence, without claiming it is uniquely proven?
options: The frames produce different final wealth by definition.
Reference-dependent evaluation can make the loss frame more salient despite identical final wealth.
The change proves the person has different income in the two descriptions.
The frames eliminate any role for a reference point.
items.feedback: The monetary outcome is the same. A difference in response is consistent with framing and reference dependence, though it alone does not uniquely identify a mechanism.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A policy analyst predicts that a $50 rebate framed as avoiding a loss will work identically for people who expected the rebate and people who did not. What does reference dependence suggest?
options: Equal rebates should create identical expectations.
Different expectations may produce different responses.
Only the final dollar amount affects the response.
The rebate’s legal value depends on expectations.
items.feedback: Expectations can affect whether an outcome is experienced as a gain or avoidance of a loss, limiting the prediction of identical responses.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Three equal-sized groups rank A>B>C, B>C>A and C>A>B. Under sequential pairwise voting with sincere votes, compare agenda 1 (A versus B, then the winner versus C) with agenda 2 (B versus C, then the winner versus A).
options: Both agendas select A.
Agenda 1 selects B; agenda 2 selects C.
Both agendas select C.
Agenda 1 selects C; agenda 2 selects A.
items.feedback: A beats B but then loses to C. B beats C but then loses to A. The cycle makes the final result depend on the agenda.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A median-voter prediction was derived for single-peaked preferences on one policy dimension. The election then adds a second independent policy dimension. What conclusion is warranted?
options: The arithmetic median on the first dimension must still win every multidimensional comparison.
Adding a dimension guarantees unanimous agreement.
The original theorem’s assumptions no longer suffice to guarantee a median policy winner.
All individual preferences must become cyclic.
items.feedback: The one-dimensional ordering supports the median-voter result. Moving to multiple dimensions removes that guarantee without proving that a cycle must occur.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: High-productivity applicants value a job at $30,000 more than their alternative and face a $5,000 certificate cost. Low-productivity applicants gain $10,000 and face a $15,000 cost. With the job available only to certificate holders, can certification separate the two types under these payoffs?
options: No; both types gain because the job is valuable.
No; both types lose because certification is costly.
