Yes; low types gain $5,000 while high types lose $25,000.
Yes; high types gain $25,000 net while low types would lose $5,000.
items.feedback: High types have benefit minus cost 30,000 − 5,000 = 25,000; low types have 10,000 − 15,000 = −5,000. Their incentives differ as separation requires.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Several small studies report a large behavioral effect, while a well-designed large replication reports a smaller positive effect. Which conclusion best combines magnitude and replication evidence?
options: Any smaller effect proves the underlying mechanism does not exist.
The evidence may support a positive effect while weakening the claim that it is as large as first reported.
A positive effect in the replication confirms the original magnitude exactly.
The number of small studies alone makes sample size and design irrelevant.
items.feedback: Replicating a direction does not establish the original magnitude. Assessing both size and uncertainty can support a more modest conclusion.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A vivid report raises perceived accident risk, while a large representative dataset shows that the rate has not changed. Which response most directly corrects an availability-based inference?
options: Increase the estimated frequency further because the story is memorable.
Ignore both the story and the dataset because no probability can be estimated.
Treat the single report as more representative than the large dataset.
Use the representative frequency data while distinguishing vividness from prevalence.
items.feedback: Representative base-rate evidence addresses frequency; vividness alone does not show a change in that frequency.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A designer claims that Arrow’s theorem proves no useful election rule can exist. Which correction best states the limitation of that claim?
options: The theorem guarantees all voting rules satisfy every fairness condition.
A useful rule may relax one of the theorem’s conditions.
The theorem applies only when there are exactly two alternatives.
The theorem says individual preferences cannot be transitive.
items.feedback: An impossibility result about jointly meeting conditions is not a claim that every rule is useless. Practical design involves which conditions to retain or relax.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: In this setting, policy is multidimensional and voters' preferences are not single-peaked. Can median-voter convergence be assumed?
options: No; the theorem's key assumptions may fail
Yes, it holds under every preference domain
Yes, because mean and median are identical
No, because majority voting is impossible
items.feedback: The result depends on a one-dimensional policy space, single-peaked preferences, majority rule, and strategic conditions.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A marketplace makes product quality observable before purchase and makes seller effort observable and enforceable after purchase. Pollution from production still harms nearby residents. Which assessment separates the problems?
options: Better information removes the pollution cost as well as the hidden-information problems, so no other distortion remains.
Only hidden action can be addressed; observing quality before purchase cannot affect selection into trade.
Better information can reduce hidden-type and hidden-action problems, but it does not itself make sellers bear the pollution cost.
Only pollution can be addressed; making information shared cannot improve the contracting problems.
items.feedback: Observable quality improves type-based contracting; enforceable effort improves action incentives. Pollution is an external cost, so it can remain even when information is shared.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Two borrowers seek identical loans, but only they know their project risks before signing. A lender charges a pooled interest rate. Safer borrowers increasingly decline the loans, while riskier borrowers remain. Which diagnosis and response fit the timing?
options: Moral hazard worsens the borrower pool; monitoring effort only after lending directly reveals the original hidden types.
Adverse selection worsens the borrower pool; verified pre-loan risk information can support risk-specific offers.
Adverse selection improves the pool; increasing the pooled rate must bring safer borrowers back.
Moral hazard improves the pool; a uniform rate removes differences in project risk before contracting.
items.feedback: Private risk is a hidden type before the contract. If safer borrowers exit, the remaining pool becomes riskier; screening before lending targets that mechanism.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Both sides can verify a product’s quality and enforce promised actions, but only the seller knows its private reservation price. Which statement is correct?
options: All private information is eliminated because quality is verifiable.
Enforceable actions necessarily create moral hazard.
Quality and effort are verifiable; private valuations can still differ.
Private reservation prices imply the product’s quality cannot be verified.
items.feedback: Information about quality, actions and valuations are different. Removing two asymmetries does not logically eliminate the third.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Buyers value a verified reliable product at $120, and its seller’s resource cost is $100. Without verification, buyers offer only $80 because quality is hidden. Independent verification costs $10 and reliably identifies quality. Which conclusion follows?
options: Verification cannot restore trade because the original pooled offer is below the seller’s cost.
Verification restores trade and creates $40 of net gains, measured by the rise from the pooled offer to buyer value.
Verification leaves $20 of net gains because a real verification cost is only a transfer.
Verification can restore the reliable-product trade and leave $10 of net gains after its resource cost.
items.feedback: Without verification the $80 offer cannot cover the reliable seller’s $100 cost. With verification, willingness to pay $120 exceeds cost $100 plus verification $10, leaving $10 of net surplus.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Before lending, a bank can verify a borrower’s past defaults but cannot observe the risk of its new project. What can the bank conclude about information asymmetry?
options: All private information disappears once any history is verified.
One source has been reduced, but private information about the new project can remain.
Verification creates hidden past defaults that were previously observable.
The remaining problem must concern actions taken after the loan, not hidden current project quality.
items.feedback: Verifying one observable history does not reveal every relevant private characteristic. The new project’s risk remains hidden before contracting.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A buyer and contractor can observe quality but cannot enforce a promised effort level in court. A proposal merely publishes the observed effort, while another makes payment contingent on a verified effort measure. Which is more directly targeted at hidden-action incentives?
options: Publication alone, because observing an action necessarily makes all promised penalties enforceable.
Neither, because incentives matter only for hidden types before contracting.
Contingent payment links verified effort to enforceable incentives.
The contingent-payment contract only if it prevents buyers from observing quality.
items.feedback: Information and enforceability are distinct. Making payment contingent on a verified action changes the incentive to exert effort; observation alone does not establish that contractual consequence.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Half of used devices are reliable and worth $120 to buyers; half are defective and worth $40. Reliable sellers require at least $100 and defective sellers $20. Buyers cannot distinguish quality. What happens if they initially offer the expected value and then update after sellers decide whether to participate?
options: The initial offer is $80; reliable sellers stay because $80 exceeds defective sellers’ $20 requirement.
The initial offer is $160; both types stay because values should be added without weighting.
The initial offer is $100; defective sellers withdraw because buyers prefer reliable products.
The initial offer is $80; reliable sellers withdraw, so the remaining pool supports only $40.
items.feedback: The pooled value is 0.5×120+0.5×40=$80. That is below reliable sellers’ $100 reservation value. Their exit leaves defective products valued at $40, illustrating adverse selection.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Customers privately know device fragility before buying insurance; after purchase some reduce care. The insurer proposes a durability test before purchase and a deductible on each claim. Which assessment correctly separates the purposes?
options: The test addresses moral hazard after purchase; the deductible identifies the device’s original hidden type without affecting care.
The test addresses hidden type and adverse selection; the deductible can preserve care incentives after purchase and reduce moral hazard.
Both target only adverse selection because all insurance problems arise before purchase.
Both target only moral hazard because private fragility is an action chosen after purchase.
items.feedback: Fragility at purchase is a type; care after coverage is an action. Screening and cost sharing address distinct information and incentive problems.

items.stem: A binding minimum wage raises pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces hiring for low-skill labor. What is the strongest policy interpretation?
options: The policy eliminates scarcity in labor markets
The policy guarantees higher employment and higher wages for all workers
The policy only changes CPI and has no employment effects
The policy creates a tradeoff between higher wages for some and job loss for others
items.feedback: A binding wage floor can help workers who remain employed while making it harder for others to find jobs.

items.stem: A city imposes rent control below equilibrium. Rent is lower for some tenants, but apartments become scarce and quality declines. Which chain is best?
options: Binding ceiling → shortage → rationing and weaker maintenance
Binding floor → surplus → higher apartment quality
Tax wedge → higher seller revenue → no shortage
CPI bias → labor force exit → real wage growth
items.feedback: A binding ceiling creates shortages and changes incentives, often producing waiting, rationing, black markets, or quality decline.

items.stem: A price ceiling is imposed during an inflation spike. Official prices stop rising, but buyers wait longer and pay side fees. What is the best interpretation?
options: Inflation is fully eliminated because the listed price cannot rise
The posted price is capped, but the full economic cost to buyers may still rise.
The good becomes less scarce because the posted price is lower.
The CPI must perfectly capture waiting time
items.feedback: A price ceiling can hide costs in waiting time, side payments, lower quality, or black markets.

items.stem: A tax is placed on a good with very inelastic demand and elastic supply. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Sellers bear most of the burden and quantity rises
Buyers and sellers split the burden exactly equally by law
Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
The tax has no effect because supply is elastic
items.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. With inelastic demand, buyers bear more and quantity changes less.

items.stem: A tax on sellers shifts supply upward, raises the price buyers pay, lowers the price sellers receive, and reduces quantity. What is the best overall description?
options: The tax creates a price floor and expands the market
The tax only affects sellers because they mail the check
The tax eliminates deadweight loss
The tax creates a wedge and shrinks the market
items.feedback: A tax wedge separates buyer and seller prices and reduces the equilibrium quantity traded.

items.stem: Why do a tax on buyers and an equal tax on sellers lead to similar market outcomes?
options: Both create the same wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive
Only seller taxes reduce quantity
Only buyer taxes change demand
The legal taxpayer always bears the full burden
items.feedback: Whether the tax is legally placed on buyers or sellers, the market adjusts around the wedge between buyer and seller prices.

items.stem: The economy has high inflation but unemployment is also above natural. Which policy problem is most likely?
options: Supply-side inflation, not simple excess demand
Pure demand boom with no supply issue
Money neutrality in the short run
A permanent Phillips curve improvement
items.feedback: High inflation with above-natural unemployment points toward an adverse supply shock or worsened expectations, not a clean demand boom.

items.stem: Output and inflation are falling while unemployment is rising. Which diagnosis and policy pairing is strongest?
options: Negative AD shock; expansionary policy can shift AD back right.
Adverse supply shock; expansionary policy shifts SRAS right.
Positive AD shock; contractionary policy shifts AD farther right.
Favorable supply shock; contractionary policy raises output.
items.feedback: Falling output and falling inflation point to weak aggregate demand, which maps to higher unemployment and lower inflation.

items.stem: The Fed wants lower inflation. Expected inflation is slow to adjust because the policy lacks credibility. Which assessment is strongest?
options: Disinflation likely carries a higher sacrifice ratio.
Disinflation likely lowers unemployment immediately.
Expected inflation shifts SRPC downward instantly.
The long-run Phillips curve becomes downward sloping.
items.feedback: If expected inflation adjusts slowly, reducing inflation requires more output and employment pain.

items.stem: The Fed announces disinflation, wage contracts adjust quickly, and expected inflation falls before output drops much. Which assessment is strongest?
options: The sacrifice ratio is likely lower than with slow expectations adjustment.
The sacrifice ratio is likely higher because credibility raises unemployment.
The LRPC shifts right because inflation expectations fall quickly.
The SRPC shifts upward because disinflation reduces actual inflation.
items.feedback: Credibility can lower the cost of disinflation by moving expected inflation down faster.

items.stem: A student says a tax cut always creates the full multiplier effect. Which correction is best?
options: The final AD shift depends on MPC, saving, expectations, and crowding out.
The final AD shift ignores MPC because taxes only affect SRAS.
The final AD shift must equal zero because fiscal policy cannot shift AD.
The final AD shift becomes infinite when interest rates rise.
items.feedback: The simple multiplier can be weakened by saving behavior, expectations, and crowding out.

items.stem: Congress expands spending during a recession, but the Fed tightens to fight inflation expectations. Which assessment is strongest?
options: Fiscal stimulus may be offset because higher rates weaken investment and AD.
Fiscal stimulus must fully work because monetary policy cannot affect AD.
Fiscal stimulus shifts SRAS right because higher rates lower production costs.
Fiscal stimulus lowers expected inflation because government spending always reduces prices.
items.feedback: Monetary tightening can offset fiscal expansion by raising interest rates and reducing investment.

items.stem: The economy has high inflation and unemployment above natural. The Fed expands AD to lower unemployment. What danger follows?
options: Unemployment may improve temporarily, but inflation and expectations can worsen.
Inflation must fall because higher AD lowers production costs.
Unemployment must stay below natural because expectations cannot change.
The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is higher.
items.feedback: AD expansion can reduce unemployment temporarily but may worsen inflation and expected inflation.

items.stem: A country doubles money growth, but output growth also rises sharply and velocity falls. Which warning is strongest?
options: Do not infer inflation from money growth alone when V and Y change.
Inflation must double because money growth always maps one-for-one.
Inflation must be zero because output growth always dominates.
Inflation must equal velocity growth because money is neutral.
items.feedback: The quantity equation requires considering money growth, velocity growth, and real output growth together.

items.stem: A government finances deficits by printing money. Inflation rises, nominal rates rise, and real balances lose value. Which memo is strongest?
options: The inflation tax reduces money value and expected inflation raises nominal rates.
The policy raises real output permanently because money growth lowers real wages forever.
The policy lowers nominal rates because inflation makes borrowing cheaper for all lenders.
The policy leaves money value unchanged because fiat money has no intrinsic value.
items.feedback: Printing money can impose an inflation tax, and higher expected inflation raises nominal rates through the Fisher effect.

items.stem: The Fed lowers reserve requirements, but few households or firms want to borrow and banks are cautious about lending. Why might the actual increase in the money supply be smaller than the simple model predicts?
options: The potential multiplier rises, but actual money creation may remain weak.
The actual multiplier must rise fully because reserve rules changed.
The money supply must fall because lower reserves reduce deposits.
The natural rate must fall because banks can lend more.
items.feedback: A lower reserve requirement increases lending potential, but actual lending depends on banks and borrowers.

items.stem: The economy is above potential, inflation is rising, and unemployment is low. Which policy assessment is strongest?
options: Tighten demand or allow SRAS adjustment; output above potential is not a stable long-run position.
Expand demand further because low unemployment proves the natural rate has fallen.
Hold policy fixed because high inflation guarantees permanently low unemployment.
Shift money demand right because higher rates raise investment.
items.feedback: Above-potential output creates inflation pressure and eventually triggers expectation adjustment.

items.stem: Inflation has been high for several years. The Fed wants lower inflation but households and firms doubt the policy will last. How might their doubts affect the output cost of reducing inflation?
options: The SRPC may not shift down quickly, so disinflation likely requires more output loss.
The LRPC shifts left immediately because credibility is low and inflation is high.
The SRPC shifts up less because doubt makes expected inflation fall faster.
The sacrifice ratio becomes zero because policy announcements replace output adjustment.
items.feedback: If expected inflation remains high, disinflation is more costly.

items.stem: Aggregate demand is rising, output is above potential, unemployment is below the natural rate, and expected inflation is beginning to rise. Which concern is most important?
options: The short-run gain is becoming a long-run inflation problem.
The economy has permanently increased natural output.
The SRPC is shifting downward because inflation rose.
The money multiplier has eliminated unemployment.
items.feedback: A demand-driven boom can reduce unemployment temporarily, but rising expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward and erodes the gain.

items.stem: The economy begins at natural output. A stock-market boom raises consumption and investment, while expected prices have not yet adjusted. Which conclusion is most accurate?
options: AD shifts right, output rises above potential, and inflation rises in the short run.
SRAS shifts right, output rises above potential, and inflation falls in the short run.
LRAS shifts right, unemployment falls permanently, and inflation stays fixed.
AD shifts left, output falls below potential, and inflation rises in the short run.
items.feedback: A stock market boom can raise spending and shift AD right, raising output and prices in the short run.

items.stem: The economy begins at natural output. A major input shortage raises production costs. Why is this not a typical demand-side recession?
options: Output falls, but the price level rises, so the shock is supply-side stagflation.
Output falls and the price level falls, so the shock is weak aggregate demand.
Output rises and inflation rises, so the shock is expansionary demand pressure.
Output rises and inflation falls, so the shock is favorable supply growth.
items.feedback: A negative supply shock lowers output while raising prices, which creates stagflation.

items.stem: A recessionary gap appears after aggregate demand falls. Can waiting restore output?
options: Yes, if wages and expected prices fall enough to shift SRAS right.
Yes, if expected prices rise enough to shift SRAS left.
No, because output gaps cannot close without fiscal expansion.
No, because LRAS must shift left to meet actual output.
items.feedback: A recessionary gap can close over time if lower wages and expected prices shift SRAS right.

items.stem: An expansionary gap appears after aggregate demand rises. Why can unemployment not remain below the natural rate forever?
options: Rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left and return output to potential.
Falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right and increase output further.
The LRPC shifts right because unemployment was temporarily low.
The money multiplier rises and permanently lowers the natural rate.
items.feedback: When output is above potential, wages and expected prices rise, shifting SRAS left and restoring natural output.

items.stem: The economy is below potential, but the main cause is an oil shock rather than weak spending. Which mistake should be avoided?
options: Treating the problem as a simple AD shortfall with no inflation tradeoff.
Recognizing that output is weak while prices are under upward pressure.
Seeing that fiscal stimulus may help output but worsen inflation.
Noting that the Phillips curve tradeoff has likely worsened.
items.feedback: An oil shock is not a clean demand recession; policy must account for inflation pressure.

items.stem: High inflation is caused by an adverse supply shock rather than demand growth. Which response is most defensible?
options: Contraction may reduce inflation pressure but risks deeper output losses.
Expansion must lower inflation because it raises aggregate demand.
Contraction must raise output because lower AD reduces firm costs.
Expansion shifts SRAS right because government spending increases productivity.
items.feedback: With supply-shock inflation, contraction can fight prices but may worsen unemployment and output losses.

items.stem: An unexpected oil-supply disruption raises firms' costs. With aggregate demand initially unchanged, output falls and inflation rises; natural unemployment is unchanged. How does the shock map across AD-AS and Phillips curves, and what tradeoff would demand tightening create?
options: SRAS shifts left and SRPC shifts up; tightening can lower inflation pressure but worsen the output loss
AD shifts left and the economy moves down SRPC; tightening can lower inflation pressure but worsen the output loss
SRAS shifts left and LRPC shifts right; tightening can lower inflation and restore output simultaneously
SRAS shifts right and SRPC shifts down; tightening can lower inflation and restore output simultaneously
items.feedback: The locally stated adverse supply shock shifts SRAS left and worsens the short-run inflation-unemployment relation, shifting SRPC up. It does not by itself change the stated natural rate. Demand tightening reduces inflation pressure at the cost of lower output and higher unemployment in the short run.

items.stem: In the simple deposit-expansion model, a reserve injection supports less deposit expansion than the no-leakage maximum because banks keep additional reserves. At the same time, government borrowing puts upward pressure on interest rates, partly offsetting the downward rate pressure from monetary expansion. Why can investment rise less than a prediction that ignores both effects?
options: Additional reserve holding raises the deposit multiplier, while government borrowing weakens the fall in rates that would encourage investment.
Additional reserve holding limits deposit expansion, and government borrowing weakens the fall in rates that would encourage investment.
Additional reserve holding limits deposit expansion, while government borrowing reinforces the fall in rates and crowds investment in.
Both effects operate only after investment rises, so neither can weaken the transmission from monetary policy to spending.
items.feedback: Reserve retention weakens the reserve-to-deposit link. Government borrowing can crowd out investment by pushing rates up relative to the monetary-expansion-only case. These constraints affect different steps, so the simple prediction overstates the investment response.

items.stem: A planned 3-point disinflation has sacrifice ratio 2. After credibility improves, the projected cumulative loss falls from 6% to 3% with the same target. Which updated ratio should be used?
options: 1; the cost per inflation point has halved
2; the original ratio is fixed by definition
3; cumulative loss itself is the ratio
6; divide the original loss by the new loss and multiply the target
items.feedback: The revised ratio is 3/3=1, compared with 6/3=2 before the forecast change. Fixed targets do not imply fixed transition costs.

items.stem: Nominal GDP rises 5% while the GDP deflator rises 7%. What happened to real GDP?
options: Real output falls 7%; the price-index increase is the contraction.
Real output falls about 1.9%; this is a real contraction.
Real output rises 5%; nominal spending establishes real expansion.
Real output rises 12%; combining nominal growth and inflation gives expansion.
items.feedback: Real growth=1.05/1.07−1≈−1.87%. The nominal increase is more than explained by prices.

items.stem: The economy is below potential. Congress increases purchases, but the resulting rise in interest rates reduces private investment. Which conclusion best combines the multiplier, crowding out, and AD-AS effects?
options: Aggregate demand can still rise, but crowding out makes the increase smaller than the simple multiplier predicts.
Crowding out guarantees aggregate demand falls below its starting position after every increase in government purchases.
The fiscal multiplier becomes exactly zero whenever market interest rates rise after expansionary policy.
Higher government purchases shift long-run aggregate supply right by the full amount of the simple multiplier.
items.feedback: Fiscal expansion pushes AD right, but higher interest rates can crowd out some private investment, making the realized AD increase smaller than the simple multiplier predicts.

items.stem: An oil-price shock lowers real output while raising inflation and unemployment. Why is this a harder stabilization problem than an ordinary demand-side recession?
options: Supporting output can worsen inflation, while restraining inflation can deepen the output and unemployment loss.
Supporting output can reduce unemployment, but because inflation originated from aggregate demand, inflation will necessarily fall as output recovers.
Demand restraint can lower inflation without an additional output cost because the original loss of output came from supply.
Because inflation and unemployment rise together, policymakers can stabilize both by returning aggregate demand to its original level.
items.feedback: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while reducing output and employment. Supporting demand can limit the output loss but add inflation pressure; restraining demand can reduce inflation pressure but deepen the output loss. The fact that the original shock came from supply does not remove the output cost of demand restraint.

items.stem: Which statement best links an AD expansion to the Phillips curve in the short run?
options: AD rises, output rises, unemployment falls, inflation rises
AD rises, output falls, unemployment rises, inflation falls
AD falls, output rises, unemployment falls, inflation rises
AD falls, output falls, unemployment falls, inflation rises
items.feedback: Expansionary AD raises output and inflation, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation on SRPC.

items.stem: Which statement best links an adverse supply shock across models?
options: SRAS shifts left and SRPC shifts up-right
SRAS shifts right and SRPC shifts down-left
AD shifts right and SRPC shifts down-left
LRAS shifts right and LRPC shifts right
items.feedback: An adverse supply shock raises prices, lowers output, and worsens the Phillips curve tradeoff.

items.stem: A central bank accommodates an adverse supply shock with more AD. What is the likely tradeoff?
options: Output loss may shrink but inflation rises more
Inflation falls and unemployment rises less
SRAS shifts right and prices fall
LRPC shifts left and inflation vanishes
items.feedback: Accommodation can support output but usually worsens inflation pressure.

items.stem: A central bank refuses to accommodate an adverse supply shock. What is the likely tradeoff?
options: Inflation pressure is restrained but output loss remains
Output rises and inflation disappears
Unemployment falls and prices fall
SRAS shifts right immediately
items.feedback: Not accommodating helps restrain inflation, but the economy still suffers lower output and higher unemployment.

items.stem: A recession lowers output below potential and inflation also falls. Which model pairing fits?
options: AD shifts left and movement down-right on SRPC
SRAS shifts left and SRPC shifts up-right
AD shifts right and movement up-left on SRPC
LRAS shifts right and LRPC shifts right
items.feedback: A negative AD shock lowers output and prices, mapping to higher unemployment and lower inflation.

items.stem: A boom raises output above potential and inflation rises. Which model pairing fits?
options: AD shifts right and movement up-left on SRPC
SRAS shifts left and SRPC shifts up-right
AD shifts left and movement down-right on SRPC
LRAS shifts left and LRPC shifts right
items.feedback: A positive AD shock raises output and inflation, mapping to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

items.stem: In the short run, how does a demand expansion affect output, unemployment and inflation in the AD-AS and Phillips-curve models?
options: AD shifts right; output rises; unemployment falls; inflation rises
AD shifts left; output rises; unemployment falls; inflation falls
SRAS shifts left; output rises; unemployment falls; inflation falls
LRAS shifts right; unemployment rises; inflation rises
items.feedback: A demand expansion raises output and inflation in AD-AS, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation on the SRPC.

items.stem: The domestic government auctions all import licenses competitively with no administrative costs. What is the value of rectangle R in the quota graph, and how does it enter domestic welfare?

R is $200 of deadweight loss because domestic firms pay it to the government.
R is $200 of government revenue, a domestic transfer rather than deadweight loss.
R is $100 of deadweight loss because domestic firms pay it to the government.
items.feedback: Rectangle R has height $40 - $30 = $10 and width 40 - 20 = 20 imported units, so its value is $200. A competitive domestic government auction collects this rent as government revenue. The payment transfers income within the country; it is not destroyed surplus or deadweight loss.

$25 thousand

125 thousand

items.stem: The quota raises domestic production from 75 thousand to 150 thousand. What is the production-side deadweight loss in the displayed trade graph?

$75 thousand
$150 thousand.

options: $50 thousand
$112.5 thousand
$150 thousand.
$225 thousand

items.stem: At an unchanged world price, domestic mills supply 68 units and residents buy 44. After opening to trade, which combination is consistent with this competitive small-country market?
options: 24 imports, a price below autarky, and a gain to domestic consumers
68 exports, since all domestic output is sold abroad
24 exports, a price below autarky, and a loss to domestic producers
24 exports, a price above autarky, and a gain to domestic producers
items.feedback: The excess of supply over domestic demand is 24 exports. With upward supply and downward demand, this occurs at a world price above autarky, benefiting domestic producers.

items.stem: A small country initially imports steel at a world price below its autarky price. Domestic demand then falls sharply while domestic supply is unchanged. What could happen if the shift is large enough?
options: The country cannot change trade status once it opens
The country could import less or even switch to exporting
The country must import more because world price is fixed
The world price must rise to the old autarky price
items.feedback: At the fixed world price, a large demand decrease reduces excess demand and can create excess supply.

items.stem: A small country initially exports wheat because the world price exceeds its autarky price. A productivity improvement shifts domestic supply strongly right. Holding world price fixed, the most likely effect is:
options: Exports increase
Exports decrease because supply rose
The country becomes an importer automatically
World price falls because the small country controls it
items.feedback: At the fixed world price, greater domestic supply increases the excess supply available for export.

items.stem: A tariff and a voluntary export restraint each allow 45 imports at a domestic price of $27; the world price stays $23. Foreign firms get the VER rights free. How much higher is importing-country surplus under the tariff, holding quantities and other costs equal?
options: $0, because identical prices imply identical national welfare
$1,215, because all spending on imports is government revenue
$180, because the tariff removes both distortion losses
$180, because the price-wedge receipts stay in the importing country
items.feedback: Both restrictions have the same production and consumption distortions. The difference is $4 × 45 = $180: tariff receipts stay domestic while the specified VER rents go abroad.

items.stem: A quota is set at the current free-trade import quantity and is fully binding only if import demand later rises. Compared with a fixed tariff, what feature makes the quota potentially more restrictive after a demand increase?
options: The tariff fixes import quantity while the quota fixes price
A quota cannot affect price after it is set
The quota fixes import quantity while the domestic price can rise further
The quota automatically lowers the world price to zero
items.feedback: A quantitative ceiling does not expand automatically when import demand rises, so the domestic price can adjust upward.

items.stem: A proposed tariff would save 2,000 jobs in one industry but raise costs for downstream firms and millions of consumers. What is the best economic evaluation?
options: Compare protected wages with tariff revenue, treating higher input prices as transfers that cannot affect downstream output.
Compare protected jobs with downstream jobs, treating consumer purchasing-power losses as irrelevant when employment rises.
Compare protected-job benefits with consumer, downstream, retaliation and efficiency costs before judging the policy.
Compare imports before and after the tariff, treating fewer imports as the net national benefit of protection.
items.feedback: Saved jobs are one effect. Consumer costs, input-using industries, retaliation and resource distortions can offset benefits; import reductions or selected employment counts do not measure net welfare.

items.stem: An industry requests “temporary” protection but has received it for 25 years and has no measurable productivity improvement. What does this evidence do to the infant-industry argument?
options: It proves consumers receive the tariff revenue
It weakens it because the promised temporary learning benefit has not materialized
It strengthens it because longer protection proves the industry is important
It is irrelevant because infant-industry protection should be permanent
items.feedback: Persistent protection without learning or an exit condition undermines the standard infant-industry rationale.

items.stem: A country imposes a tariff to reduce dependence on a strategic input, but domestic production cannot expand and allied suppliers are available. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: If domestic output cannot expand, the tariff may do little to make supply more reliable; compare buying from several allied suppliers with the tariff’s added costs.
Higher producer prices establish greater resilience immediately, even if domestic capacity cannot expand.
Lower import dependence is sufficient for resilience, regardless of whether the remaining supply comes from one supplier.
Allied suppliers remove every security risk, making evaluation of diversification costs and reliability unnecessary.
items.feedback: The tariff cannot quickly create the missing domestic capacity. Buying from several reliable allied suppliers may address the specific risk at lower cost, but its reliability and costs still require comparison.

items.stem: A tariff raises domestic producer surplus by $60 million, government revenue by $20 million, and lowers consumer surplus by $105 million. Ignoring other effects, what is the strongest conclusion?
options: National surplus rises by $185 million because all three figures should be added
National surplus rises by $25 million because producer gains exceed revenue
The tariff is efficient because government receives revenue
National surplus falls by $25 million even though protected producers gain
items.feedback: The net change is +60 +20 -105 = -25 million; distributional gains do not erase the aggregate loss.

items.stem: A protection proposal benefits a small organized industry by $50 per person while costing a very large number of consumers $2 each. Why can the policy still attract strong political support?
options: Small individual consumer losses establish a smaller total cost, so support reflects a necessarily positive net benefit.
A large consumer population creates stronger per-person lobbying incentives even when each person loses only a little.
A larger individual stake gives beneficiaries stronger organizing incentives even when small dispersed losses sum to more.
Organized support reveals higher aggregate willingness to pay, so the policy’s national efficiency follows from its passage.
items.feedback: Concentrated stakes can make organizing worthwhile for beneficiaries while small individual losses discourage consumers from organizing. Political support does not establish aggregate net benefits.

items.stem: Why is the tariff production-side deadweight loss a social loss?
options: Domestic firms receive revenue
Consumers buy imported goods
The government collects tariff revenue
Higher-cost domestic units replace lower-cost imported units
items.feedback: The resource cost rises for units shifted to less efficient domestic production.

items.stem: Why is the tariff consumption-side deadweight loss a social loss?
options: Consumers stop buying units valued above the world resource cost
Domestic firms sell more units
Government revenue rises
All imported units disappear
items.feedback: The tariff prevents mutually beneficial consumption.

items.stem: An import quota is administered by first-come, first-served licenses. What additional concern arises?
options: The quota cannot bind
License allocation may reward speed or connections rather than lowest distribution cost
Consumers receive all rents automatically
Domestic price must equal zero
items.feedback: Administrative allocation can create inefficiency and rent-seeking.

items.stem: Assuming quota rents remain domestic, what total deadweight loss is shown by the displayed trade graph?
options: $112.5 thousand
$150 thousand
$225 thousand
$450 thousand
items.feedback: The two $112.5-thousand distortion triangles sum to $225 thousand.

items.stem: Which statement correctly treats potential compensation from trade?
options: Losers are automatically compensated through prices
Gains can fund compensation, but policy must deliver it.
Potential compensation proves no one loses
Compensation is impossible whenever trade raises total surplus
items.feedback: A Kaldor-Hicks gain does not itself transfer resources.

items.stem: Which statement about a trade deficit is economically valid?
options: It does not by itself measure whether individual trades create gains from exchange
It proves imports have zero consumer value
It proves every domestic industry is shrinking
It equals tariff deadweight loss
items.feedback: The trade balance is not the surplus test for a particular market.

items.stem: A quota-holder spends resources lobbying to obtain import rights. How does rent seeking affect welfare?
options: It turns all rents into consumer surplus
It can dissipate some quota rents and create additional social cost
It removes the domestic price increase
It guarantees efficient license allocation
items.feedback: Resources spent capturing rents can add to the policy cost.

items.stem: Which comparison best tests whether protection is the least-cost response to worker displacement?
options: Compare it with wage insurance, retraining, mobility aid, and targeted income support
Compare only protected-firm profits
Compare only import quantity before and after
Assume no alternative policies exist
items.feedback: Adjustment goals can be pursued through policies with different efficiency costs.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why lower-cost imports raise total surplus?
options: They guarantee every producer survives
They force demand to equal domestic supply
They convert all producer surplus into tariff revenue
They replace some high-cost domestic production and enable additional consumption valued above world cost
items.feedback: Both production efficiency and consumption expansion generate gains.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why exports raise total surplus?
options: Sales to higher-value buyers and expansion of production with value above cost.
Domestic consumers buy more at a lower price
All exports have zero production cost
Producer gains never exceed consumer losses
items.feedback: The higher world price reveals gains from serving higher-value buyers.

items.stem: Which statement about domestic producer losses from imports is strongest?
options: They should be omitted because consumers gain
They prove imports are inefficient
They equal the country’s total loss
They are genuine distributional losses even when total surplus rises
items.feedback: A complete analysis recognizes both aggregate and group effects.

items.stem: Which statement about domestic consumer losses from exports is strongest?
options: They are genuine distributional losses even when producer gains create a larger total gain
They prove exports destroy national wealth
They are always exactly equal to producer gains
They disappear because foreign consumers pay
items.feedback: Export gains can coexist with domestic consumer losses.

items.stem: Arden has a straight demand curve with a price-axis intercept of $80. Before trade, price is $50 and quantity is 30. With exports, price rises to $70 and domestic consumption becomes 10. What is the change in consumer surplus?

A loss of $800
A loss of $400
No change

items.stem: Bellora has a straight demand curve with a price-axis intercept of $94. Before trade, price is $60 and quantity is 34. With exports, price rises to $76 and domestic consumption becomes 18. What is the change in consumer surplus?
options: A gain of $416
A loss of $256
No change
A loss of $416

items.stem: Caspia has a straight demand curve with a price-axis intercept of $72. Before trade, price is $42 and quantity is 30. With exports, price rises to $60 and domestic consumption becomes 12. What is the change in consumer surplus?
options: A loss of $378
A gain of $378
A loss of $324
No change
items.feedback: Before: ½ × (72 − 42) × 30 = $450. After: ½ × (72 − 60) × 12 = $72. Consumer surplus falls by $378.

items.stem: Arden has a straight supply curve with a price-axis intercept of $20. Before trade, price is $50 and quantity is 30. With exports, price rises to $70 and domestic production becomes 50. What is the change in producer surplus?
items.feedback: Before: ½ × (50 − 20) × 30 = $450. After: ½ × (70 − 20) × 50 = $1250. Producer surplus rises by $800.

items.stem: Bellora has a straight supply curve with a price-axis intercept of $26. Before trade, price is $60 and quantity is 34. With exports, price rises to $76 and domestic production becomes 50. What is the change in producer surplus?
items.feedback: Before: ½ × (60 − 26) × 34 = $578. After: ½ × (76 − 26) × 50 = $1250. Producer surplus rises by $672.

items.stem: Caspia has a straight supply curve with a price-axis intercept of $12. Before trade, price is $42 and quantity is 30. With exports, price rises to $60 and domestic production becomes 48. What is the change in producer surplus?
items.feedback: Before: ½ × (42 − 12) × 30 = $450. After: ½ × (60 − 12) × 48 = $1152. Producer surplus rises by $702.

items.stem: Arden has straight demand and supply curves with price-axis intercepts of $80 and $20. Without trade, price is $50 and quantity is 30. Free trade lowers price to $30; consumption becomes 50 and domestic production 10. What is the gain in total surplus from trade?

Bellora has straight demand and supply curves with price-axis intercepts of $94 and $26. Without trade, price is $60 and quantity is 34. Free trade lowers price to $42; consumption becomes 52 and domestic production 16. What is the gain in total surplus from trade?

Caspia has straight demand and supply curves with price-axis intercepts of $72 and $12. Without trade, price is $42 and quantity is 30. Free trade lowers price to $20; consumption becomes 52 and domestic production 8. What is the gain in total surplus from trade?
Arden imposes an $8 tariff and imports 24 units after the tariff. Calculate tariff revenue.
items.feedback: Revenue is $8×24=$192.

items.stem: Bellora imposes a $10 tariff and imports 16 units after the tariff. Calculate tariff revenue.
items.feedback: Revenue is $10×16=$160.

items.stem: In Arden, an $8 tariff raises domestic production from 10 to 18. Calculate the production-side deadweight loss.
items.feedback: The triangle is ½×$8×8=$32.

items.stem: In Bellora, a $10 tariff raises domestic production from 16 to 26. Calculate the production-side deadweight loss.
items.feedback: The triangle is ½×$10×10=$50.

items.stem: An $8 tariff reduces domestic consumption from 50 to 42. Calculate the consumption-side deadweight loss.
items.feedback: The triangle is ½×$8×8=$32.

items.stem: A binding quota permits 24 imports and creates a $7 price gap. Calculate total quota rent.
items.feedback: Quota rent is $7×24=$168.

items.stem: A small importing country imposes a $5 per-unit tariff. Domestic production rises from 20 to 38 units and domestic consumption falls from 70 to 48 units. Demand and supply are linear. What is total deadweight loss?
items.feedback: Production distortion = ½ × $5 × (38 − 20) = $45. Consumption distortion = ½ × $5 × (70 − 48) = $55. Total DWL = $100.

items.stem: In a small importing country, Qd=80-P and Qs=P-20. World price is $30 with unlimited foreign supply. Compare tariffs of $10 and $15 per unit, both with positive imports. What happens to revenue?
options: It rises from $200 to $300: the higher rate applies to the original 20 imports.
It rises from $400 to $525: apply the tariff to all domestic purchases.
It falls from $200 to $150: imports shrink from 20 to 10 despite the higher unit tariff.
It falls from $400 to $150: the initial tariff is collected on both imports and domestic production.
items.feedback: At P=40, Qd=40 and Qs=20, so imports=20 and revenue=10×20=200. At P=45, Qd=35 and Qs=25, so imports=10 and revenue=15×10=150. A higher rate does not guarantee more revenue.

items.stem: Refer to the tariff graph. What is the production-side deadweight loss?
items.feedback: The production-distortion triangle has area ½ × $10 × 10 = $50.

items.stem: Refer to the tariff graph. What is the consumption-side deadweight loss?
items.feedback: The consumption-distortion triangle has area ½ × $10 × 10 = $50.

items.stem: Refer to the tariff graph. In this small country, world price stays $30 and the linear domestic demand and supply curves remain unchanged. The displayed tariff is cut from $10 to $5 per unit. Relative to the displayed outcome, how do deadweight loss and government revenue change?
options: Deadweight loss falls by $50; revenue falls by $100.
Deadweight loss falls by $75; revenue rises by $50.
Deadweight loss falls by $75; revenue falls by $50.
Deadweight loss falls by $50; revenue rises by $50.
items.feedback: At a $5 tariff, price is $35, Qs=15 and Qd=45, so imports are 30 and revenue is $150 rather than $200. Each distortion triangle is 0.5 x $5 x 5 = $12.50; total DWL is $25 rather than $100. Thus DWL falls $75 and revenue falls $50. Revenue is a domestic transfer, not part of DWL.

items.stem: A binding quota permits 20 imports and raises domestic price $10 above world price. One-quarter of the licenses are given to foreign exporters; the rest go to domestic residents. Production and consumption distortions total $100, and no resources are spent obtaining licenses. What is the domestic welfare loss?
options: $300: $100 of distortions plus every $200 of quota rents, regardless of ownership.
$100: rent ownership never affects domestic welfare because all rents are transfers worldwide.
$250: $100 of distortions plus $150 of rents retained by domestic residents.
$150: $100 of distortions plus $50 of rents going abroad; $150 of rents stay domestic.
items.feedback: Total rent is 20×10=200. Foreign recipients receive 0.25×200=50, while domestic recipients retain 150. For domestic welfare, add exported rents to the 100 resource distortion loss: 150.

items.stem: Two binding quota systems create the same $200 of rents and $100 of production/consumption distortions. A costless government auction captures all rents. Free domestic licenses instead induce $30 of real lobbying expenses. Which comparison is correct?
options: Auction loss is $100 and free-license loss $130; the ownership transfer is not a resource loss, but lobbying dissipates resources.
Auction loss is $300 and free-license loss $130; government revenue must be added to deadweight loss.
Auction loss is $100 and free-license loss -$70; private rents are an extra national gain over the auction.
Both losses are $100; lobbying uses money and therefore cannot consume real resources.
items.feedback: Auction receipts and domestic private rents are domestic transfers. With identical market distortions, only the $30 real lobbying difference changes national loss: 100 versus 130.

items.stem: A quota generates $200 of rents that currently go to foreign exporters, plus $100 of domestic production/consumption distortions. A reform auctions all rights domestically without changing price or imports, but uses $60 of real administrative resources. What is the change in domestic welfare?
options: A $300 gain: recover foreign rents and eliminate both distortion triangles even though price and imports are unchanged.
A $140 gain: recover $200 in foreign-held rents, then subtract $60 of administration; the $100 distortion remains.
A $60 loss: rent ownership cannot affect domestic welfare, so only administration changes.
A $240 loss: auction payments and administration must both be subtracted from consumers’ unchanged position.
items.feedback: The market distortion is unchanged. National loss falls from 100+200=300 to 100+60=160, an improvement of 140. Capturing previously foreign rents changes domestic income even though the physical allocation stays fixed.

items.stem: A small country has Qs=P-20, initial Qd=80-P and world price $30. A $10 tariff initially produces the same imports as a quota of 20. Demand then becomes Qd=100-P. Which comparison follows?
options: With the tariff, P=$50 and imports=20; with the quota, P=$40 and imports=40.
Both policies keep P=$40 and imports=20 because they were initially equivalent.
With the tariff, P=$40 and imports=40; with the quota, P=$50 and imports=20.
Both policies raise P=$50 and imports=40 because demand increases equally under each.
items.feedback: The nonprohibitive tariff keeps P=30+10=40; new imports are (100-40)-(40-20)=40. The quota fixes Qd-Qs=20: 100-P-(P-20)=20, giving P=50. Initial equivalence does not imply equal responses to shocks.

items.stem: A small country has Qd=100-P, Qs=P-20 and a binding quota of 20 imports. World price falls from $30 to $20 while domestic schedules and the quota are unchanged. What happens to domestic price and quota rents?
options: Domestic price falls from $50 to $40; rents stay $400 because a quota fixes the price wedge.
Domestic price stays $50; rents fall from $400 to $200 because import cost is lower.
Domestic price falls to $20; unlimited foreign supply removes the binding quota automatically.
Domestic price stays $50; total rents rise from $400 to $600 because the import-right price gap widens.
items.feedback: The quota-clearing equation 100-P-(P-20)=20 gives P=50 at either world price. Rents rise from (50-30)×20=400 to (50-20)×20=600. The quantity cap, not a fixed wedge, is held constant.

items.stem: Demand rises in a small importing country. Under a nonprohibitive fixed tariff, unlimited foreign supply holds domestic price at world price plus tariff. Under a binding quota, the maximum imports cannot rise. Which adjustment difference is most accurate?
options: Tariff imports absorb the extra demand at the unchanged price; quota price rises, inducing more domestic output and restraining consumption.
Tariff price must rise because imports are fixed; quota imports absorb the change because its price wedge is fixed.
Both domestic prices must rise equally; greater demand determines price independently of the trade-policy instrument.
Quota price rises only if domestic supply is vertical; otherwise domestic firms can absorb any demand increase at the same price.
items.feedback: At a fixed tariff-inclusive world price, imports can expand. A binding quota prevents that import response, so price adjusts until more domestic supply and less quantity demanded close the gap. Upward-sloping domestic supply does not keep price fixed.

items.stem: A tariff lowers domestic consumer surplus by $500, raises producer surplus by $180 and raises government revenue by $200. Administering it uses $20 of additional real resources. What is the net effect on national welfare after including all of these gains and costs?
options: National welfare falls $520; producer gains and revenue do not offset any part of consumer loss.
National welfare falls $140; producer gains and revenue are domestic transfers, while the residual distortion and administration are real losses.
National welfare falls $340; government revenue is a social loss because consumers fund it.
National welfare rises $360; add producer gains and revenue and subtract administration without counting consumer loss.
items.feedback: Before administration, national change is -500+180+200=-120. Additional resource cost gives -140. Revenue and producer gains offset portions of consumer loss rather than being counted again as deadweight loss.

items.stem: Protection would preserve 2,000 jobs for a year at a real efficiency cost of $60 million to consumers and firms that use the protected product, with no other benefits in this exercise. A targeted transition program costs $20 million and enables 1,500 workers to obtain equally valued jobs that year. How do the two policies compare in cost per worker helped and number of workers helped?
options: Protection costs $13,333 per preserved job; transition costs $30,000 per worker and leaves no employment gap.
Protection is necessarily best because it preserves all 2,000 jobs; consumer and downstream costs are irrelevant to an employment goal.
Protection costs $30,000 per preserved job; transition costs about $13,333 per reemployed worker but leaves 500 more workers needing help.
Transition is necessarily best because its total cost is lower; differences in the number of workers helped need not be reported.
items.feedback: Protection costs 60000000/2000=30000 per job-year, versus 20000000/1500≈13333. The targeted program costs less per worker but reaches fewer. Advice should state both the efficiency comparison and the remaining distributional need.

items.stem: A strategic input faces an outage risk. A broad tariff costs $40 million in expected efficiency losses and would reduce expected outage losses by $15 million. A reserve program costs $12 million and would reduce those losses by $25 million. Both estimates already include operating costs. Which evaluation is best on the stated evidence?
options: The tariff nets $55 million while reserves net $37 million; security benefits should be added to policy costs.
The reserve program nets $25 million while the tariff nets $15 million; resource costs are irrelevant once security is the objective.
The tariff is preferable whenever it reduces imports, even if the reserve program has larger net security benefits.
The reserve program nets $13 million while the tariff nets -$25 million; a real security concern does not establish that broad protection is the best instrument.
items.feedback: Net expected benefits are 25-12=13 million for reserves and 15-40=-25 million for the tariff. The national-security goal is evaluated by the policy’s actual risk reduction and resource cost, not the protection label.

items.stem: Temporary protection was justified by a forecast that three years of learning would cut unit resource cost from $12 to $8, below a $9 world price. After five years, audited cost remains $12. Firms request renewal based only on past subsidies and current jobs. Which evidence would most strengthen a renewed learning case?
options: A credible, independently testable mechanism and timetable for additional learning gains exceeding the new consumer and resource costs.
The total subsidy already spent, because recovering sunk public expenditure establishes future learning benefits.
The number of years protection has lasted, because longer duration demonstrates that costs are approaching the target.
Current protected employment alone, because retaining jobs proves unit productivity has improved despite the audited cost.
items.feedback: The promised cost reduction has not occurred, weakening the original rationale. Renewal requires prospective, credible learning evidence and a comparison with additional costs. Sunk subsidies, duration and employment do not establish future productivity gains.

items.stem: A proposed tariff is estimated to create $40 million of domestic producer gains, $25 million of revenue and $80 million of consumer losses. Retaliation would additionally reduce domestic exporters’ net surplus by $20 million. These export losses are additional to the gains and losses already listed. What is the overall effect on national welfare?
options: Net gain is $5 million; retaliation can be ignored because export firms are outside the protected industry.
Net loss is $35 million; retaliation adds a separate export-market loss to the initial $15 million tariff loss.
Net loss is $60 million; government revenue is an extra resource loss rather than a domestic transfer.
Net loss is $15 million; every export loss is automatically included in consumer losses from the original tariff.
items.feedback: The initial national change is 40+25-80=-15 million. Adding the explicitly separate export loss gives -35 million. Revenue is a domestic transfer, while retaliation can impose additional losses in other markets.

items.stem: Refer to the tariff-regions graph. An analyst counts rectangle B as deadweight loss and excludes the two side triangles. Which correction uses the plotted quantities and prices?
options: B is $400 of revenue; the two $100 side triangles total $200 of deadweight loss.
B is $200 of deadweight loss; the side triangles are domestic producer transfers.
B is $200 of revenue; the two $50 side triangles total $100 of deadweight loss.
B is $100 of revenue; the two side triangles total $200 of deadweight loss.
items.feedback: The wedge is 40-30=10 and post-tariff imports are 40-20=20, so B=200. Each distortion base is 10 units, giving 0.5×10×10=50 on each side. Domestic revenue is a transfer; the distortion triangles sum to 100.

items.stem: In the quota-rent graph, import licenses are initially given free to foreign firms. The domestic government instead sells all licenses at a costless competitive auction, with the quota and prices unchanged. What domestic welfare gain follows, and how much deadweight loss remains relative to free trade?
options: Gain of $100; remaining deadweight loss $100
Gain of $200; remaining deadweight loss $200
Gain of $400; remaining deadweight loss $200
Gain of $200; remaining deadweight loss $100
items.feedback: Rectangle R has height $40-$30=$10 and width 40-20=20 imports, so the auction brings $200 home instead of transferring it abroad. Each distortion triangle is half of $10 times 10 units, or $50. Their $100 total remains because prices and quantities are unchanged.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Which quantity combination is correct under the import quota?
options: Qs = 75 thousand; Qd = 275 thousand; imports = 200 thousand
Qs = 200 thousand; Qd = 150 thousand; exports = 50 thousand
Qs = Qd = 175 thousand; imports = 0
Qs = 150 thousand; Qd = 200 thousand; imports = 50 thousand
items.feedback: At the quota-induced price of $6, domestic supply is 150 thousand and demand is 200 thousand, leaving 50 thousand imports.

items.stem: Output is $2.4 trillion, consumption is $1.5 trillion, investment is $0.4 trillion, and government purchases are $0.6 trillion. What are NX and NCO?
options: Both are $0.1 trillion
NX is −$0.1 trillion and NCO is $0.1 trillion
NX is $0.5 trillion and NCO is −$0.1 trillion
Both are −$0.1 trillion
items.feedback: NX = Y − C − I − G = 2.4 − 1.5 − 0.4 − 0.6 = −0.1 trillion; NX = NCO.

items.stem: Private saving is $420 billion, public saving is −$80 billion, and domestic investment is $390 billion. What follows?
options: National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are $50 billion
National saving is −$50 billion, so NCO and NX are −$390 billion
National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are −$50 billion
National saving is $500 billion, so NCO and NX are $110 billion
items.feedback: National saving is $420 billion − $80 billion = $340 billion. Subtracting $390 billion of investment gives NCO = NX = −$50 billion.

items.stem: A student says a trade deficit proves imports destroyed an equal amount of domestic output. Which correction is best?
options: The deficit proves national saving exceeds domestic investment
It shows imports exceed exports, without establishing the change in domestic output
The claim is correct because imports are subtracted from GDP
A trade deficit means domestic consumption must be falling
items.feedback: Imports are subtracted to exclude foreign production from GDP. The trade balance alone does not show how domestic output changed.

items.stem: Exports rise by $40 billion and imports rise by $65 billion while other GDP components are unchanged. How do NX and GDP change?
options: Both fall by $25 billion
Both rise by $105 billion
NX falls by $25 billion while GDP rises by $25 billion
NX rises by $25 billion while GDP is unchanged
items.feedback: Net exports change by $40 billion − $65 billion = −$25 billion, so the expenditure identity lowers measured GDP by $25 billion when other components are fixed.

items.stem: Across two consistently measured periods, foreign purchases of domestic bonds rise while domestic purchases of foreign assets are unchanged. Which accounting change follows, without identifying how quickly trade adjusts?
options: NCO is unchanged, while NX falls
NCO falls, while NX must rise
NCO falls, and NX must be lower in the accounts
NCO rises, and NX must be higher
items.feedback: The larger foreign-purchase flow lowers NCO. NX must match NCO in consistent period accounts; this identity alone does not establish an immediate trade response to a particular bond purchase.

items.stem: National saving rises by $70 billion, domestic investment rises by $30 billion, exports rise by $55 billion, and imports rise by $15 billion. Are the changes mutually consistent?
options: Yes; both balances rise by $70 billion
Yes; both NCO and NX rise by $40 billion
No; NCO rises by $100 billion while NX rises by $40 billion
No; NCO falls by $40 billion while NX rises by $70 billion
items.feedback: ΔNCO = ΔS − ΔI = $40 billion, and ΔNX = ΔX − ΔM = $40 billion, so the identities reconcile.

items.stem: Private saving rises $40 billion, public saving falls $15 billion, and domestic investment rises $10 billion. The trade accounts report exports up $20 billion and imports up $10 billion. Under S−I=NX, with no statistical discrepancy and all saving/investment figures held fixed, which correction makes the trade figures consistent with saving and investment?
options: NX must rise $35 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must fall $15 billion
NX must fall $15 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must rise $35 billion
NX must rise $15 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must rise $5 billion
NX must rise $10 billion; revise saving down $5 billion despite the instruction to hold it fixed
items.feedback: National saving rises 40−15=25; subtract investment growth 10 to obtain NX growth 15. Since ΔNX=ΔX−ΔM, 15=20−ΔM implies imports rise 5. The original trade report's $10 billion NX increase fails the identity under the stated constraints.

items.stem: Imports rise by $70 billion and exports rise by $20 billion, while consumption rises by $70 billion entirely because of the new imports. Other domestic spending is unchanged. What happens to GDP?
options: GDP is unchanged
GDP rises by $20 billion
GDP falls by $50 billion
GDP rises by $70 billion
items.feedback: The import-driven $70 billion rise in consumption is offset by imports; the $20 billion export increase adds domestic production.

items.stem: A country has positive NCO but a reported trade deficit. Within the same consistently measured period, which statement is correct?
options: At least one reported balance is inconsistent with the accounting identity
The combination is expected whenever saving is high
Positive NCO mechanically creates a trade deficit
The signs can differ whenever exchange rates float
items.feedback: The identity NX = NCO requires the two balances to share the same value and sign.

items.stem: National saving exceeds domestic investment. How does that fact connect to the foreign-exchange market?
options: The saving gap raises demand for domestic currency through imports
Positive NCO removes domestic currency from exchange markets
The saving gap fixes the nominal exchange rate
The positive NCO supplies domestic currency as residents acquire foreign assets
items.feedback: S − I is positive NCO. Residents exchange domestic currency to purchase foreign assets, creating foreign-exchange supply.

items.stem: A binding minimum wage raises hourly pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces low-skill employment. What is the strongest economic interpretation?
options: Higher wages for some, fewer opportunities for others
The policy must help every worker equally
The policy eliminates structural unemployment
The policy has no effect if firms dislike it
items.feedback: A binding wage floor can raise wages for some workers while creating a labor surplus.

items.stem: Unemployment insurance increases from 12 weeks to 40 weeks. What is the likely tradeoff?
options: Better income protection, but longer searches and more frictional unemployment
Lower income protection and shorter unemployment spells only
Immediate elimination of structural unemployment
A guaranteed fall in labor force participation to zero
items.feedback: Unemployment insurance helps workers smooth income but can reduce urgency to accept work quickly.

items.stem: Unemployment benefits become more generous while a new matching platform sharply improves the quality and speed of job referrals. What is the best prediction for frictional unemployment?
options: The net effect is ambiguous because the two changes work in opposite directions
It must rise because matching services cannot offset the weaker search incentives created by benefits
It must fall because unemployment benefits never change search incentives when matching technology improves
Only structural unemployment can change because neither policy affects normal search and matching
items.feedback: More generous benefits can lengthen search by reducing urgency, putting upward pressure on frictional unemployment. Faster and better referrals shorten matching time, putting downward pressure on it. Without their relative magnitudes the net effect is ambiguous.

items.stem: A firm raises wages above equilibrium and worker effort rises enough to improve productivity, but fewer workers are hired at the higher wage. Which interpretation is most complete?
options: Higher productivity guarantees every worker seeking a job will be hired despite the higher wage
The wage increase must be a legally binding minimum wage rather than a voluntary firm decision
The policy can raise worker effort only when cyclical unemployment has already fallen to zero
Efficiency-wage benefits can coexist with a labor surplus and fewer job opportunities
items.feedback: An efficiency wage can raise effort and productivity, but if it is above equilibrium, firms may hire fewer workers, creating a labor surplus.

items.stem: A wage floor is $16. At that wage, 112 workers seek jobs and firms hire 88. A demand increase raises desired hiring to 100 while the wage and labor supply stay fixed. What happens to the labor surplus?
options: It falls from 24 to 12; higher labor demand reduces the excess supply
It stays at 24 because the statutory wage did not change
It rises from 24 to 36 because firms want more labor
It disappears because any increase in demand makes a floor nonbinding
items.feedback: Initially the surplus is 112 - 88 = 24. With hiring demand of 100, it is 112 - 100 = 12. The wage floor can remain binding even as the size of the labor surplus changes.

items.stem: A recession increases layoffs, while unemployment insurance helps workers avoid immediate hardship but lengthens some searches. Which pair of concepts is involved?
options: Cyclical unemployment and frictional unemployment incentives
Only structural unemployment
GDP deflator and CPI
Natural resources and capital deepening
items.feedback: The recession creates cyclical unemployment; unemployment insurance affects job-search incentives.

items.stem: A binding wage floor raises pay for retained workers in a competitive labor market, but firms offer fewer jobs and more people seek work at the higher wage. What do these wage and employment changes tell us about workers' total earnings?
options: Wages rise for workers who keep their jobs, but fewer people work; total earnings depend on the sizes of both changes.
Wages rise for workers who keep their jobs, and fewer people work; total earnings rise by the same percentage as wages.
Wages rise for workers who keep their jobs, and fewer people work; total earnings fall by the same percentage as employment.
Wages rise and more people work; the higher wage shows that labor demand increased.
items.feedback: A binding floor changes the wage paid and the quantity employed along demand. Winners among retained workers do not establish an aggregate earnings gain; employment quantities matter.

items.stem: A firm voluntarily pays above the market wage to reduce turnover and improve effort among workers. Which comparison distinguishes an efficiency wage from a union-negotiated wage without denying either employment tradeoff?
options: Firm incentives drive efficiency wages; bargaining drives union wages; only unions can exceed clearing.
Bargaining drives efficiency wages; firm incentives drive union wages; either can exceed clearing.
Firm incentives drive efficiency wages; bargaining drives union wages; either can exceed clearing.
Legal wage floors drive both wage types; neither depends on productivity or bargaining.
items.feedback: Efficiency wages arise from employer incentives such as effort and turnover; union wages arise from bargaining. They differ in mechanism even if both can leave job seekers unmatched at the wage.

items.stem: A benefit reform gives 120 unemployed workers more time to search for good matches. Search duration rises, while later job retention also improves. Which policy assessment recognizes the tradeoff?
options: Longer job searches are costly, and improved retention provides no offsetting benefit, so welfare must fall.
Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.
Improved retention provides a benefit, and longer job searches have no cost, so welfare must rise.
Longer searches raise cyclical unemployment, while improved retention affects only structural unemployment.
items.feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.

items.stem: A state increases unemployment benefits but also improves job-placement services. What is the most careful prediction?
options: Benefits slow search; placement services speed it
Frictional unemployment must rise
Frictional unemployment must fall
Only structural unemployment can change
items.feedback: Two forces move in opposite directions, so the net effect is not automatic.

items.stem: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 130 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
options: Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
items.feedback: Faster matching shortens spells; waiting longer can lengthen them. Both involve the search component, so relative magnitudes are needed for the net rate.

items.stem: Above-market wages improve effort among 140 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
options: Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium
items.feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.

items.stem: At a binding wage floor, 120 workers seek jobs and firms hire 90. A productivity gain raises hiring to 110 with the wage and labor supply unchanged. Which claim about the labor surplus is correct?
options: Surplus falls from 30 to zero; increased demand fully removes the wage-floor constraint.
Surplus falls from 30 to 10; twenty additional jobs still leave ten workers unable to find a job.
Surplus rises from 10 to 30; productivity gains displace twenty previously employed workers.
Surplus stays at 30; the unchanged wage fixes the number of available jobs.
items.feedback: Surplus initially 120−90=30, later 120−110=10. The fixed wage does not prevent labor demand changing; the remaining positive surplus still matters.

items.stem: A nonunion firm pays above the clearing wage to reduce quits. Turnover falls but hiring also falls. What do lower turnover and lower hiring tell us about the effects of the higher wage?
options: The firm can retain more workers while offering fewer jobs; an efficiency wage above the market-clearing wage can leave some willing workers without jobs.
Lower turnover proves employment increased; retaining existing workers and hiring new workers measure the same change.
Fewer jobs prove a union imposed the wage; a firm cannot voluntarily choose to pay an efficiency wage.
Lower turnover eliminates job shortages; an efficiency wage necessarily brings labor supply and labor demand into balance.
items.feedback: An efficiency wage is chosen for productivity or retention incentives. Those benefits do not establish that all willing workers obtain jobs at the higher wage; the effect on hiring must also be considered.

items.stem: A benefit reform gives 170 unemployed workers more time to search for good matches. Search duration rises, while later job retention also improves. Which policy assessment recognizes the tradeoff?
options: Longer job searches are costly, and improved retention provides no offsetting benefit, so welfare must fall.
Improved retention provides a benefit, and longer job searches have no cost, so welfare must rise.
Longer searches raise cyclical unemployment, while improved retention affects only structural unemployment.
Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.
items.feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.

items.stem: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 180 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
options: Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
