Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
items.feedback: Faster matching shortens spells; waiting longer can lengthen them. Both involve the search component, so relative magnitudes are needed for the net rate.

items.stem: Above-market wages improve effort among 190 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
options: Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium
items.feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.

items.stem: A firm voluntarily raises wages above market rates. Its wage bill rises $12,000, turnover costs fall $8,000 and improved effort adds $7,000 to revenue. Which evaluation goes beyond looking only at wages?
options: Profit falls $3,000 because cost savings reduce revenue
Profit rises $3,000 under these estimates; the efficiency gains exceed the wage cost
Profit falls $12,000 because only payroll affects profitability
Profit rises $15,000 because higher payroll is not a cost
items.feedback: Net profit change=−12000+8000+7000=3000. The stated efficiency-wage channels can justify higher pay; that is conditional on the estimates.

items.stem: Better monitoring lets a firm obtain the same effort at a lower wage. A proposal instead keeps its old above-market wage solely to deter shirking. Which inference follows from the changed constraint?
options: The efficiency-wage premium may become less valuable; monitoring substitutes for part of its incentive role.
The efficiency-wage premium must rise; monitoring raises the minimum wage set by law.
The union wage must rise; monitoring automatically creates collective bargaining coverage.
The market-clearing wage becomes irrelevant; a lower effort cost fixes employment mechanically.
items.feedback: If monitoring delivers the same effort at lower pay, part of the original anti-shirking reason for a wage premium weakens. The observation does not establish a legal or union wage requirement or a mechanical employment change.

items.stem: A benefit reform gives 220 unemployed workers more time to search for good matches. Search duration rises, while later job retention also improves. Which policy assessment recognizes the tradeoff?
options: Longer job searches are costly, and improved retention provides no offsetting benefit, so welfare must fall.
Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.
Improved retention provides a benefit, and longer job searches have no cost, so welfare must rise.
Longer searches raise cyclical unemployment, while improved retention affects only structural unemployment.
items.feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.

items.stem: Which scenario best shows why GDP per person is more useful than total GDP for comparing living standards?
options: A country’s total GDP rises while its population remains unchanged
A country’s real GDP per person rises while total GDP remains fixed
A country’s GDP doubles while its population triples
A country’s GDP and population both double over the same period
items.feedback: If population grows faster than GDP, average income may fall even though total GDP rises.

items.stem: Pollution causes more medical and cleanup spending, raising measured output. Why can the welfare conclusion differ from the GDP change?
options: Medical and cleanup services are excluded whenever pollution caused the demand
GDP subtracts the environmental damage and then subtracts cleanup spending again
Any increase in measured cleanup output proves the original damage improved welfare
GDP counts the services produced but not the full damage that made them necessary
items.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

items.stem: Workers choose shorter workweeks, measured output falls, and leisure rises. Which inference is justified?
options: GDP stays unchanged because added leisure replaces every lost unit of production
The leisure gain is automatically valued and added to business investment
GDP falls, but well-being could rise or fall
Both measured GDP and total well-being must decline by the same amount
items.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

items.stem: Country A has higher market output but more pollution and inequality; Country B has more leisure and unpaid household production. Which comparison is defensible?
options: Country A must have higher well-being because its recorded market GDP is higher
Country B must have higher measured GDP after valuing every hour of leisure
GDP is useless because it measures neither legal market goods nor services
GDP compares market production, but these facts do not settle overall well-being
items.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

items.stem: A storm destroys productive assets, followed by a surge in rebuilding services. What distinction is essential?
options: Higher rebuilding output proves the storm created a net gain for every household
Current production can rise while lost wealth and hardship leave welfare lower
Rebuilding services cannot enter GDP because the storm destroyed assets first
The destroyed productive assets are added to current household consumption spending
items.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

items.stem: Real GDP per person rises 16% while leisure falls and air quality deteriorates. What can be concluded about output per person and well-being?
options: Output per person increased, but the net welfare change requires valuing the omitted losses
Output per person increased, so welfare must have increased by exactly the same percentage
Output per person decreased because environmental damage is automatically deducted from GDP
Output per person is unknown because GDP cannot be measured when leisure changes
items.feedback: Real GDP per person measures average production, not a complete welfare index. Leisure and environmental quality can offset some or all benefits; their values are not supplied.

items.stem: Two countries have the same real GDP per person of $20700. One has greater inequality and poorer health outcomes. Which conclusion respects both the production data and their limits?
options: Every resident has equal income; different health outcomes therefore cannot change the ranking
The less equal country has lower real GDP per person once inequality is read into the given measure
The data establish neither output nor welfare because all averages exclude distribution
Average measured output is equal; distribution and health can still support different welfare rankings
items.feedback: Equal GDP per person establishes equality of average measured production, not individual incomes or a complete welfare ranking. Distribution and health are separate evidence.

items.stem: A storm destroys existing homes. Rebuilding produces $18 million of current construction, while families lose housing services during repairs. Which GDP-versus-welfare comparison is correct?
options: Rebuilding is excluded because it replaces old assets; neither GDP nor welfare changes
Destruction is automatically subtracted from GDP by the replacement value; GDP equals the net welfare effect
Rebuilding adds to current GDP; loss of existing wealth and services prevents treating it as a net welfare gain
Destruction and rebuilding both add to current GDP; their sum measures the welfare gain
items.feedback: Current reconstruction is production. Destruction of existing assets is a wealth loss, not automatically a negative final purchase; lost services also matter for welfare.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: If the price level rises, what happens in the money market under the interest-rate effect?
options: Money demand rises, interest rates rise, and investment falls.
Money demand falls, interest rates fall, and investment rises.
Money supply rises, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
Money demand rises, interest rates fall, and investment rises.
items.feedback: Higher prices increase money demand, which raises interest rates and reduces investment.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Why does a lower price level increase the quantity of goods and services demanded?
options: Lower prices reduce money demand, lower interest rates, and increase investment.
Lower prices increase money demand, raise interest rates, and lower investment.
Lower prices reduce money supply and shift AD left.
Lower prices eliminate the need for investment.
items.feedback: Lower prices reduce money demand, which lowers interest rates and raises investment spending.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: If income rises and the Fed prevents interest rates from rising, what policy shift is needed?
options: Increase money supply as money demand rises
Decrease money supply as money demand rises
Increase money demand as money supply falls
Decrease money demand as interest rates rise
items.feedback: Higher income raises money demand; to hold rates down, the Fed must increase money supply.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: If the Fed cuts money supply while money demand rises, what happens to the interest rate pressure?
options: It rises from both forces
It falls from both forces
It rises from supply but falls from demand
It falls from supply but rises from demand
items.feedback: Lower money supply and higher money demand both push the interest rate upward.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Money demand increases while the money supply remains fixed. What is the likely effect on the interest rate and interest-sensitive investment?
options: r rises and investment falls.
r falls and investment rises.
r rises and investment rises.
r falls and investment falls.
items.feedback: With fixed money supply, a rightward shift in money demand raises the interest rate, which lowers investment.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Money demand shifts left while money supply remains fixed. What chain follows?
options: r falls, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
r rises, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
r falls, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
r rises, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
items.feedback: Lower money demand reduces the equilibrium interest rate, which supports investment and AD.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: If an increase in Y raises money demand and the Fed wants to prevent r from rising, what should the Fed do?
options: Increase money supply to match the higher money demand.
Decrease money supply to reduce money demand.
Raise taxes because money supply cannot shift.
Reduce government spending to make MD vertical.
items.feedback: If money demand rises, increasing money supply can prevent the equilibrium interest rate from rising.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: A student says a fall in the nominal interest rate from 8% to 6%, with income and the price level unchanged, shifts the money-demand curve right. What is the error?
options: The rate change increases quantity demanded along the existing money-demand curve.
The rate change increases money demand at every interest rate, shifting the entire curve.
The rate change directly increases the fixed money supply while money demand remains constant.
The rate change shifts both money supply and money demand by the same amount.
items.feedback: The nominal interest rate is the opportunity cost represented on the money-demand curve. A rate change alters quantity demanded along that curve; a change in income or prices would shift it.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: A student says the fall in the interest rate from 4 percent to 2 percent proves money demand shifted left. What does the graph actually show?
options: MD0 shifts left while money supply remains fixed at MS0 throughout.
MD0 and money supply both shift right to separate new curves.
MD0 is fixed; MS shifts right and equilibrium moves along MD0.
Neither money demand nor money supply changes in the diagram.
items.feedback: MD0 is unchanged. The new equilibrium is reached by moving along the same money-demand curve after MS shifts right.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Income rises, money demand shifts right, and the Fed holds money supply fixed. What memo is strongest?
options: Interest rates rise unless the Fed increases money supply.
Interest rates fall because higher income lowers money demand.
Interest rates stay fixed because money demand cannot shift.
Interest rates fall because fixed money supply means more lending.
items.feedback: Higher income raises money demand; with fixed money supply, interest rates rise.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Money demand rises because income rises, while the Fed cuts the money supply. Which memo is strongest?
options: Both forces push interest rates upward and pressure AD downward.
Both forces push interest rates downward and pressure AD upward.
Money demand raises rates, but lower money supply lowers rates.
Money demand lowers rates, but lower money supply raises rates.
items.feedback: Higher money demand and lower money supply both raise interest rates, weakening investment and AD.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Money demand falls while the Fed expands money supply. Which memo is strongest?
options: Both forces push interest rates downward and support AD.
Both forces push interest rates upward and weaken AD.
Money demand lowers rates, but higher money supply raises rates.
Money demand raises rates, but higher money supply lowers rates.
items.feedback: Lower money demand and higher money supply both push interest rates down, supporting investment and AD.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. If the Fed wants to prevent the resulting interest-rate increase, what should it do?
options: Increase money supply enough to offset the rightward money-demand shift.
Decrease money supply to reinforce the money-demand shift.
Raise taxes because taxes directly shift money demand left.
Do nothing because r must fall when money demand rises.
items.feedback: A rightward money-demand shift raises r if MS is fixed. Increasing MS can offset that pressure.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Real income rises and the central bank increases the money supply enough to leave the equilibrium interest rate unchanged. What must be true?
options: Money demand stayed fixed even though higher income increased transaction volume.
The money supply shifted left by enough to offset the rise in money demand.
The price level fell to zero and eliminated the need to hold transaction balances.
The money-supply increase offset the rise in money demand.
items.feedback: Higher income raises money demand. A sufficiently large increase in money supply can offset that pressure and leave the equilibrium interest rate unchanged.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Suppose the nominal interest rate is temporarily 8% while the displayed money supply stays fixed. What adjustment would move this market toward equilibrium?
options: People want more money than they hold, so bond sales lower bond prices and push the interest rate up.
People hold more money than they want, so bond purchases raise bond prices and push the interest rate down.
People hold more money than they want, so they sell bonds and push the interest rate up.
People want more money than they hold, so the imbalance automatically shifts money supply right.
items.feedback: At 8%, MD0 shows quantity demanded below the fixed supply of 100. People try to exchange excess balances for bonds. Bond prices rise and yields fall toward the plotted equilibrium rate of 6%.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Starting from the money-market change shown, which downstream effect would normally follow?
options: Lower rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Higher rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
Higher rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
items.feedback: The standard transmission channel runs from more money to lower interest rates to more interest-sensitive spending and higher aggregate demand.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: After the money-supply change from MS0 to MS1 shown in the graph, which spending-and-AD response should follow?
options: Higher rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
Higher rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
items.feedback: The standard contractionary chain runs from less money to higher interest rates to less interest-sensitive spending and lower aggregate demand.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Which transmission mechanism explains the changes from A to B in both panels?
options: Money supply rises, lowering the rate; stronger interest-sensitive spending expands AD and raises output and prices.
Money demand rises, raising the rate; weaker interest-sensitive spending contracts AD and lowers output and prices.
Money demand rises, raising the rate; lower output reflects a contraction of SRAS rather than lower spending.
Money supply falls, raising the rate; weaker interest-sensitive spending contracts AD and lowers output and prices.
items.feedback: The supply of money stays fixed while MD shifts right. Higher rates reduce spending, shifting AD left along fixed SRAS. The fourth account has a valid transmission direction, but its money-supply trigger is not the one drawn.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD2 and MS2, the equilibrium is point d at r3. If the interest rate is temporarily at point b on MS2 at r4, what adjustment should occur?
options: There is excess money demand, so households sell interest-bearing assets; bond prices fall and the interest rate rises farther above r4 before the market can clear.
Point b is already the equilibrium because it lies on MS2.
Money demand must shift right again before the interest rate can change.
Excess money supply prompts asset purchases, lowering interest toward r3.
items.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD1 and MS1, equilibrium is point e at r2. If the interest rate is temporarily at r1, what pressure moves the market back toward equilibrium?
options: The market remains at r1 because a vertical money-supply curve prevents interest-rate adjustment.
The central bank must reduce the fixed money supply before households can obtain enough money balances and the interest rate can move back toward equilibrium.
Excess money demand prompts asset sales, raising the interest rate toward r2.
Quantity of money supplied exceeds money demanded, so asset purchases push the interest rate lower.
items.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: The central bank increases the money supply and the equilibrium interest rate falls while income and the price level are unchanged. A student says, “Money demand shifted left.” What is the best correction?
options: A lower interest rate means movement along money demand, unless another determinant changed.
The student is correct because any fall in interest rates shifts the entire money-demand curve left at every quantity, even when income and the price level are unchanged.
Money demand shifts right whenever money supply increases.
Money demand becomes horizontal after an expansionary money-supply change.
items.feedback: A change in the interest rate causes movement along a given money-demand curve. Income or the price level can shift the money-demand curve.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: In the liquidity-preference model, money demand rises while money supply increases. What can be concluded about the equilibrium interest rate?
options: Higher money demand pushes the rate down and higher supply pushes it down; the effects reinforce
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it down; opposite directions ensure an unchanged rate
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it down; relative shifts determine the result
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it up; the effects reinforce
items.feedback: When money demand and money supply both increase, the interest-rate effect depends on which shift is larger.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Transaction demand for money increases at every rate in an economy with money supply 20. The central bank wants to hold the interest rate fixed in the standard liquidity-preference model. Which response and curve distinction are correct?
options: Leave supply fixed because higher demand is only movement along the original curve
Shift money demand back by redefining the unchanged nominal supply as a demand curve
Raise money supply enough to meet the added demand at that rate; the demand curve still shifted
Reduce money supply to match the higher demand; the interest rate then stays fixed
items.feedback: At the old rate, higher money demand creates excess demand. Increasing supply to meet it can keep the rate unchanged; a fixed observed rate does not prove no demand shift.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: Income rises while the price level falls in an economy with nominal money supply fixed. Which additional evidence is needed to determine whether the interest rate rises or falls?
options: Income alone: higher income pushes rates up, prices do not affect money demand.
Relative demand effects: income pushes rates up, lower prices pull rates down.
Prices alone: lower prices pull rates down, income does not affect money demand.
Neither effect: opposite demand forces imply equal offsets and an unchanged rate.
items.feedback: Both determinants shift money demand. Their effects oppose, and fixed supply translates the net demand effect into the rate change; magnitudes are required.

items.topic: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
items.stem: At the current interest rate, desired money holdings exceed fixed supply by 40. Which portfolio adjustment and rate direction restore equilibrium in the standard model?
options: People try to sell bonds for money, lowering bond prices and raising the interest rate
People try to buy bonds with unwanted money, raising bond prices and lowering the interest rate
The central bank must create money automatically; the interest rate cannot adjust
Bond prices and interest rates rise together until money demand is unchanged
items.feedback: Excess money demand motivates asset sales. Lower bond prices correspond to higher yields, which reduce money demand toward fixed supply. Individual attempts cannot change aggregate money supply by themselves.

items.stem: Real GDP rises from $1.20 trillion to $1.32 trillion while population rises from 40 million to 42 million. Approximately how does real GDP per person change?
options: It rises from $30,000 to $33,000, a gain of exactly 10 percent.
It rises from $30,000 to about $31,429, a gain of roughly 4.8 percent.
It falls from $30,000 to about $28,571 as population increases.
It stays at $30,000 because both real GDP and population rose.

items.stem: Country A has real GDP per person of $20,000 and grows at 2%. Country B has real GDP per person of $10,000 and grows at 6%. Using the Rule of 70, what is the strongest long-run implication?
options: B can catch up because it doubles much faster than A
A must always remain richer because it starts ahead
B cannot grow because it is poorer
Both double every 35 years
items.feedback: A doubles in about 35 years; B doubles in about 11.7 years, so B can catch up if growth persists.

items.stem: A poor country grows quickly after gaining stable property rights, schools, and foreign investment. Which explanation is strongest?
options: Catch-up potential plus growth-supporting institutions
Growth must be caused only by inflation
Poor countries grow automatically regardless of policy
Property rights reduce investment
items.feedback: Catch-up growth is more likely when institutions support investment, human capital, and technology adoption.

items.stem: Real GDP per person rises, but average leisure falls sharply and pollution worsens. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Market output per person rose, but overall well-being may have changed differently.
Living standards rose by exactly the same rate because GDP per person captures all welfare changes.
GDP per person becomes unusable whenever leisure or environmental quality changes.
Pollution and lost leisure are already fully subtracted from measured real GDP.
items.feedback: Real GDP per person is useful for material output, but it does not fully capture leisure, environmental quality, distribution, or nonmarket activity.

items.stem: Country A grows at 2% and Country B grows at 5%. Using the Rule of 70, how much sooner does Country B double its income?
options: About 21 years sooner
About 3 years sooner
About 35 years sooner
About 70 years sooner
items.feedback: Country A doubles in about 35 years; Country B doubles in about 14 years, so B doubles about 21 years sooner.

items.stem: A country with initial real GDP per person $240 sustains 4% growth instead of 2%. Another policy raises the level once by 4% but leaves later growth at 2%. Which comparison recognizes the long-run distinction?
options: Sustained growth changes only the level; the level increase shortens subsequent doubling time.
Both shorten subsequent doubling time equally; each policy specifies the same 4% figure.
Sustained growth compounds faster; the level increase leaves subsequent doubling time unchanged.
Neither changes the future path; percentage changes affect nominal measures rather than output.
items.feedback: A growth-rate change repeatedly changes the path, whereas a one-time level gain shifts the starting point. Under Rule of 70, sustained 4% growth implies roughly 17.5-year doubling versus 35 at 2%.

items.stem: Real GDP is initially $250 billion. It grows 6%, while population grows 8%. Which statement reconciles aggregate growth and average output?
options: Aggregate output falls because population growth exceeds GDP growth
Aggregate real output rises, but real GDP per person falls about 1.9%
Both aggregate and per-person real output rise 6%
Per-person output rises 14% because output and population growth add
items.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.06/1.08−1≈−1.85%. A larger economy can have lower average output if population grows faster.

items.stem: Country A begins at $40260 real GDP per person and grows 2% annually; B begins at half that level and grows 7%. Using the Rule of 70, which warning corrects the claim that B catches A in ten years?
options: B doubles in ten years; A also grows, delaying catch-up.
B doubles in ten years; A's starting level establishes catch-up then.
A doubles in ten years; B doubles in thirty-five, preventing catch-up.
B doubles in five years; doubling its growth rate halves catch-up time.
items.feedback: 70/7≈10 years doubles B's starting level; 70/2≈35 years doubles A's. A is a moving target, so B reaching A's initial level is not the same as reaching A's contemporaneous level.

items.stem: Real GDP is initially $100 billion. It grows 6%, while population grows 8%. Which statement reconciles aggregate growth and average output?
options: Aggregate real output rises, but real GDP per person falls about 1.9%
Both aggregate and per-person real output rise 6%
Per-person output rises 14% because output and population growth add
Aggregate output falls because population growth exceeds GDP growth
items.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.06/1.08−1≈−1.85%. A larger economy can have lower average output if population grows faster.

items.stem: A larger budget deficit lowers public saving while private-saving behavior and investment determinants remain unchanged. Which complete loanable-funds sequence follows?
options: National saving falls, investment demand shifts left, and both the rate and quantity fall
National saving rises, supply shifts right, and investment falls along demand
National saving is unchanged because public saving is not part of the supply of loanable funds
Supply shifts left, raising the rate and reducing investment
items.feedback: Public saving is part of national saving, which supplies loanable funds. A deficit lowers that supply, raises the equilibrium real interest rate, and crowds out investment along unchanged demand.

items.stem: Households become more willing to save at every real interest rate. The resulting equilibrium rate falls, and firms undertake more projects. Which description separates the initial cause from the response?
options: Investment demand shifts right first; saving rises through movement along unchanged supply
Both the supply of loanable funds and investment demand shift right merely because their quantities rise
The supply of loanable funds shifts right; investment rises through movement down along unchanged demand
The lower rate shifts the supply of loanable funds left and shifts investment demand right
items.feedback: Greater willingness to save shifts supply right. The lower equilibrium rate then makes more projects profitable, increasing investment as movement along the original investment-demand curve.

items.stem: A retirement incentive increases saving at every real rate, while improved technology raises expected returns on investment. Which conclusion follows without knowing shift sizes?
options: Only the supply of loanable funds shifts right, so the real rate must fall
Both curves shift right and equilibrium quantity rises; the real-rate direction is ambiguous
Both curves shift right and the real rate must remain unchanged
The supply of loanable funds shifts left while investment demand shifts right, so quantity is ambiguous
items.feedback: The saving incentive shifts supply right, while improved technology shifts investment demand right. Both changes raise equilibrium quantity, but their pressures on the real interest rate oppose one another.

items.stem: A higher real return encourages households to postpone consumption, while a new retirement incentive increases saving at every real rate. How should these effects be represented?
options: Both changes shift the supply of loanable funds right because each raises observed saving
Movement along supply, followed by a rightward supply shift
The higher rate shifts supply right, while the incentive causes movement along the curve
Both changes cause movement along the original saving curve because neither affects demand
items.feedback: The current real rate determines a quantity supplied on a given curve. A retirement incentive changes saving behavior at every real rate, so it shifts the whole curve.

items.stem: A saving incentive shifts the supply of loanable funds right. The lower equilibrium real rate makes more investment projects profitable, and firms also become more optimistic about future sales. Which description is complete?
options: Both investment increases are movements along demand because firms ultimately borrow more
Both investment increases shift demand because the equilibrium rate changes
The saving incentive shifts investment demand right, while optimism moves firms along that curve
Movement along demand, followed by a separate rightward demand shift
items.feedback: The saving shock lowers the rate and causes movement along the existing investment-demand curve. Optimism changes desired investment at every rate, so it separately shifts demand right.

items.stem: Government purchases fall while output is fixed and the consumption schedule is unchanged at each real rate. Which account connects this policy to the move from A to B?
options: Higher national saving lowers the rate from 8% to 6%, raising investment from 80 to 120 along D0.
Higher national saving lowers the rate from 8% to 4%, raising investment from 80 to 160 along D0.
Higher national saving lowers the rate from 8% to 6%; investment rises to 120 because D0 shifts right.
The fall from 8% to 6% first raises government saving, so the observed supply shift is a response to the rate.
items.feedback: With Y and consumption at each rate fixed, lower G raises national saving. The supply increase moves equilibrium from 80/8 to 120/6. The resulting investment response is along unchanged D0, not an independent demand shift.

items.stem: How should the increase in investment from A to B in the graph be classified?
options: Investment rises by 80 units along D0 because increased saving lowers the interest rate.
Investment rises by 40 units because a lower rate shifts D0 right at every real rate.
Investment rises by 40 units because stronger project profitability shifts D0 while S0 stays fixed.
Investment rises by 40 units along D0 because increased saving lowers the interest rate.
items.feedback: The equilibrium quantity rises from 80 to 120 on unchanged D0, a 40-unit increase. The initiating shift is in saving supply; lower financing costs induce movement along investment demand.

items.stem: In the graph, the equilibrium quantity of loanable funds falls from 100 to 80. Does this mean the supply of loanable funds shifted left by 20 units?
options: No. At a common interest rate, supply shifts left by 60 units.
No. At a common interest rate, supply shifts left by 40 units.
Yes. With investment demand fixed, the equilibrium decline measures the supply shift.
No. The 40-unit horizontal difference measures a shift in investment demand.
items.feedback: At rate 8%, S0 supplies 120 and S1 supplies 80, a 40-unit shift. A to B changes equilibrium quantity from 100 to 80. The higher rate induces movement along the schedules, so the equilibrium decline is not the fixed-rate shift.

items.stem: At every given real interest rate, public saving falls by $30 billion while planned private saving rises by $10 billion. With investment demand unchanged, what follows?
options: Supply shifts left, raising the rate and reducing investment
National saving rises $40 billion, shifting supply right and increasing investment
National saving falls $20 billion, shifting investment demand left and lowering the rate
National saving remains unchanged because private saving always offsets a deficit
items.feedback: The component changes sum to −$20 billion. Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left, which raises the equilibrium real rate and reduces investment along demand.

items.stem: Saving behavior is unchanged as the market moves from A to B. Which economic change is consistent with the pattern shown?
options: Lower expected project profitability reduces investment demand at each real rate.
Higher expected project profitability increases investment demand at each real rate.
The higher real rate itself shifts investment demand right rather than causing movement along it.
A larger public deficit shifts the supply of loanable funds left while investment demand stays fixed.
items.feedback: Both the rate and quantity rise on unchanged S0, with D1 right of D0. Greater project profitability can shift investment demand. A higher rate is part of the equilibrium response, not the cause of a demand shift.

items.stem: With saving behavior unchanged, what could explain the move from A to B?
options: Firms expect stronger future sales, increasing planned investment at each real rate.
The lower real rate itself reduces planned investment at every real rate.
Households become more willing to save, shifting the supply of funds right.
Firms expect weaker future sales, reducing planned investment at each real rate.
items.feedback: B has a lower rate and smaller quantity on unchanged S0. D1 is left of D0, consistent with weaker expected sales. Lower borrowing costs alone would move along investment demand rather than shifting it.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. The market moves from A to B with the supply of loanable funds fixed. Which change could have caused this outcome?
options: A tax credit raises expected investment profitability
Households become more willing to save at every real rate
Firms expect weaker future demand for their output
A deficit reduces public saving while investment determinants remain fixed
items.feedback: Weaker expected sales reduce desired investment at every real interest rate, shifting demand left from D0 to D1 and lowering both equilibrium variables.

items.stem: The real interest rate and equilibrium quantity both fall while the supply of loanable funds is unchanged. Which explanation is most consistent with those observations?
options: Households became more willing to save at every real rate
Weaker expected sales reduced investment demand at every real rate
A larger deficit reduced public and national saving
The lower real rate caused investment demand to shift left
items.feedback: With supply fixed, a leftward shift in investment demand lowers both equilibrium variables. Weaker sales expectations provide the causal determinant; the rate change itself produces movement along demand.

items.stem: The market begins at A. Both the supply of loanable funds and investment demand increase, moving equilibrium to B. Which statement distinguishes the general prediction from the plotted outcome?
options: Quantity must rise; the rate is generally ambiguous, and the plotted rate rises.
Quantity must rise; the rate is generally ambiguous, but the plotted rate is unchanged.
Quantity rises and the rate is unchanged; every pair of rightward saving and investment shifts has that rate result.
Quantity is generally ambiguous; the unchanged plotted rate means national saving did not rise.
items.feedback: Both shifts raise quantity, but they exert opposing pressures on the rate. A and B are both at 6%, so those pressures offset in this drawing. That particular offset is not a universal rule.

items.stem: Which pair of events could produce the changes from the solid to the dashed curves?
options: Households plan less saving, and firms expect investment projects to be less profitable.
Households plan more saving, while firms expect investment projects to be less profitable.
The higher quantity itself shifts both schedules, without any change in saving or investment plans.
Households plan more saving, and firms expect investment projects to be more profitable.
items.feedback: S1 is right of S0 and D1 is right of D0. Higher planned saving explains the supply shift, while higher expected project returns explain investment demand. Equilibrium quantity is a result, not a determinant that shifts both curves.

items.stem: The market changes from A to B after saving and investment plans both change. What explains the interest-rate outcome shown?
options: Investment demand dominates here, raising the rate to 8%; different relative shifts could change the rate.
The rate stays at 6% because every equal-direction pair of supply and demand shifts leaves the rate fixed.
The opposing pressures offset here, leaving the rate at 6%; different relative shifts could change the rate.
The rate stays at 6% because a doubling of quantity prevents any change in the price of loanable funds.
items.feedback: Both marked equilibria are at 6%, though quantity rises from 40 to 80. Greater saving puts downward pressure on the rate and greater investment demand puts upward pressure on it. Their offset is specific to the drawn shifts.

items.stem: A saving incentive raises planned national saving at every real rate, while weaker expected sales reduce desired investment at every real rate. With an upward-sloping supply curve for loanable funds and a downward-sloping investment demand curve, which conclusion and information requirement are correct?
options: The real rate falls; investment quantity must fall because only the demand shift affects quantity
The real rate falls; the relative shift magnitudes are needed to determine the investment-quantity change
Investment quantity rises; the relative shift magnitudes are needed to determine the real-rate change
The real rate rises; investment quantity must rise because the saving incentive finances more projects
items.feedback: More saving shifts supply right, while weaker sales shift demand left. Both changes lower the real rate. The supply change raises equilibrium quantity and the demand change lowers it, so their relative magnitudes determine the net investment response.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Improved technology raises investment demand, while households also become more willing to save. What limitation matters when using this graph for that scenario?
options: It depicts the saving shift but keeps investment demand fixed
It depicts both shifts and therefore proves the real rate must rise
It cannot show investment demand because D1 is a saving curve
It omits the shift in the supply of loanable funds from household saving
items.feedback: The graph cleanly represents technology through D0 shifting to D1. The scenario also requires the supply of loanable funds to shift right, but S0 remains fixed, so the full combined outcome is not shown.

items.stem: Technology improves expected project returns, but the equilibrium real interest rate subsequently rises. Which statement correctly separates the two effects on investment?
options: Technology moves firms along demand, while the higher rate shifts the entire curve left
Both changes shift demand right because equilibrium investment initially rises
The higher rate shifts the supply of loanable funds left and leaves investment demand unchanged
Demand shifts right; the higher rate partly offsets the increase
items.feedback: Improved technology changes profitability at every rate and shifts investment demand right. The endogenous rate increase makes fewer marginal projects profitable along the new curve, partly offsetting the initial increase.

items.stem: In a closed-economy loanable-funds model, expected investment profitability falls while a larger budget deficit reduces planned national saving at every real interest rate. What must happen, and what remains uncertain?
options: The real rate falls, while equilibrium quantity is ambiguous
Quantity falls; the real-rate direction is ambiguous
Both the real rate and quantity must rise
The real rate must remain unchanged, while quantity falls
items.feedback: Investment demand shifts left and loanable-funds supply shifts left. Both changes reduce equilibrium quantity, but demand puts downward pressure on the rate while supply puts upward pressure on it.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output
items.stem: A productivity improvement lowers production costs and raises potential output over time. Which curves are most likely affected?
options: SRAS right and LRAS right
AD left and SRAS left
SRPC up and AD left
MD right and MS left
items.feedback: Higher productivity can shift SRAS right and increase long-run aggregate supply.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output
items.stem: A permanent labor-force increase raises productive capacity and tends to expand short-run supply. A simultaneous temporary energy-price spike tends to reduce short-run supply. No relative magnitudes are given. What can be concluded about LRAS and the net SRAS shift?
options: LRAS shifts right; the net SRAS direction is not determined.
LRAS shifts right; SRAS necessarily shifts left.
LRAS shifts left; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
LRAS stays fixed; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
items.feedback: The labor-force increase raises potential output, shifting LRAS right. The two events exert opposing pressures on SRAS, so their relative effects are needed to determine its net direction. A temporary energy-price spike does not by itself remove productive capacity.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output
items.stem: A permanent tax credit raises capital investment, while a temporary wage subsidy lowers current labor costs. Which supply changes are most likely?
options: LRAS shifts right over time and SRAS shifts right immediately.
SRAS shifts left because subsidies raise wages
LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
Only AD shifts right
items.feedback: More capital raises potential output, while the subsidy lowers short-run production cost.

items.topic: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output
items.stem: A larger permanent labor force adds productive capacity and supports short-run supply, but a temporary oil-price spike pushes short-run supply in the opposite direction. Before their relative sizes are known, which conclusion should an AD-AS analysis carry forward?
options: LRAS shifts right; SRAS necessarily shifts left.
LRAS shifts left; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
LRAS shifts right; the net SRAS direction is not determined.
LRAS stays fixed; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
items.feedback: The labor-force increase raises potential output, shifting LRAS right. The two events exert opposing pressures on SRAS, so their relative effects are needed to determine its net direction. A temporary energy-price spike does not by itself remove productive capacity.

items.stem: At AD2-AS2, demand and productive capacity remain unchanged. How would wage adjustment move the economy toward long-run equilibrium?
options: Wages rise; SRAS contracts, bringing output toward Y1 and prices toward P3.
Wages fall; SRAS expands, bringing output toward Y2 and prices toward P1.
Wages rise; demand contracts, bringing output toward Y1 and prices toward P3.
Wages fall; lower production costs bring output toward Y1 while LRAS shifts left.
items.feedback: The starting output Y2 exceeds potential Y1. Upward wage and expected-price pressure shifts SRAS from AS2 toward AS1. On AD2 the long-run endpoint is Y1/P3; capacity and demand need not change.

items.stem: The economy is at AD1-AS1. If demand and potential output do not change, how would flexible wages help close the gap shown?
options: Lower wages shift SRAS right, raising output from Y3 toward Y1 and lowering prices toward P1.
Higher wages shift SRAS left, lowering output from Y2 toward Y1 and raising prices toward P3.
Lower wages shift LRAS right, raising potential output from Y3 to Y1.
Lower wages shift AD right, moving output from Y3 to Y1 at a higher price level.
items.feedback: The graph places current output at Y3, left of potential Y1. Lower wage costs move AS1 toward AS2. The resulting Y1/P1 is reached along AD1, without a capacity change.

items.stem: A negative AD shock lowers output and prices. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
options: Wages and expected prices fall
Wages and expected prices rise
Money demand rises permanently
LRPC shifts right
items.feedback: Lower wages and expected prices shift SRAS right and help output return to natural.

items.stem: A positive AD shock pushes output above potential. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
options: Wages and expected prices rise
Wages and expected prices fall
SRAS shifts right immediately
LRAS shifts to AD2
items.feedback: Higher wages and expected prices shift SRAS left and return output to potential.

items.stem: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts right until output reaches Y3
AD shifts right until output reaches Y2
LRAS shifts right until it reaches Y2
items.feedback: At Y2, output is above natural output, so rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left toward long-run equilibrium.

items.stem: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts right until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y3
AD shifts left until output returns to Y3
LRAS shifts left until it reaches Y3
items.feedback: At Y3, output is below natural output, so falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right toward long-run equilibrium.

items.stem: A one-time aggregate-demand decline that remains in place lowers output below potential. With no policy response and flexible wages and expected prices over time, what is the long-run outcome?
options: SRAS shifts right and output returns to potential at a lower price level.
Output remains permanently below potential with the original price level.
LRAS shifts left until productive capacity matches the recession output.
Aggregate demand automatically shifts right because unemployment increased.
items.feedback: Falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right, restoring natural output while leaving the price level lower.

items.stem: Demand has moved the economy to AD2-AS2. With AD2 and productive capacity unchanged, how do the short-run and long-run outcomes compare?
options: Output falls from Y2 to Y1 as wage costs adjust; the price level rises from P2 to P3.
Output rises from Y3 to Y1 as wage costs adjust; the price level falls from P2 to P1.
Output falls from Y2 to Y1 because potential output falls; the price level rises from P2 to P3.
Output stays at Y2 because the demand expansion permanently raises capacity; prices stay at P2.
items.feedback: Y2 is above the fixed potential level Y1. Wage and expectation adjustment contracts SRAS toward AS1, leaving output at Y1 and prices at P3. The short-run demand-driven output gain is temporary.

items.stem: Two economies have identical recessionary gaps. In Economy A, most wages can be reset monthly; in Economy B, most wages are fixed by three-year contracts. With no policy response, which prediction best follows from the long-run adjustment model?
options: Economy B should self-correct faster because longer wage contracts make SRAS respond more quickly to the recessionary gap.
Both economies must return to potential at exactly the same speed because a vertical LRAS fixes the timing as well as the destination.
Neither economy can self-correct without an aggregate-demand policy change because wage and cost adjustment cannot move SRAS.
Economy A should tend to self-correct faster because wages and production costs can adjust sooner.
items.feedback: Long-run adjustment can take time because wage contracts, input costs, and price expectations may change gradually.

items.stem: A demand boom raises output 30 above potential. The central bank does not respond and AD stays fixed. What adjustment is predicted if wages and expected prices rise?
options: SRAS shifts left, output returns toward potential, and the price level rises further
SRAS shifts right, output rises farther above potential, and prices fall
LRAS shifts right until it reaches the temporary boom output without new resources
AD shifts left automatically because wage increases directly lower the demand schedule
items.feedback: Higher wage/cost expectations shift SRAS left. The return to real potential need not restore the old price level; under fixed AD the price level can rise further.

items.stem: Demand has moved AD1→AD2 while supply remains AS2. Compare fixed AD2 with a policy that reverses demand to AD1 before expected wages rise. Which final price/output pairs follow?
options: Fixed AD2: P1/Y1; quick reversal: P3/Y1.
Fixed AD2: P2/Y2; quick reversal: P2/Y2.
Fixed AD2: P3/Y1; quick reversal: P1/Y1.
Fixed AD2: P2/Y3; quick reversal: P2/Y3.
items.feedback: The first path moves AS2→AS1 with AD2 fixed. The second returns to AD1-AS2 before the supply response. Both recover potential, but at different price levels.

items.stem: Inflation rises permanently after repeated demand expansion, but labor-market structure is unchanged. Which long-run statement is strongest?
options: Unemployment remains permanently below natural after expectations fully adjust
The LRPC shifts right because the price level rose over time
Unemployment returns toward the same natural rate on an unchanged LRPC
The LRPC shifts left because higher inflation permanently improves job matching
items.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

items.stem: The natural rate falls because job search becomes faster. How should SRPC and LRPC reasoning be separated?
options: LRPC stays fixed while unemployment permanently departs from its vertical location
LRPC shifts left; short-run curves may also reposition around the new natural rate
The economy merely moves upward along the old LRPC as inflation changes
Only inflation expectations can shift LRPC in the long-run model
items.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

items.stem: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which comparison best captures the long-run result of higher expected inflation?
options: b and c have same unemployment but different inflation
a and b have same unemployment but different inflation
c and d have same inflation but different unemployment
a and d have same inflation but different unemployment
items.feedback: Both b and c lie on the LRPC at U2, but b has higher inflation.

items.stem: Suppose actual inflation is held at B's rate while expectations adjust to it. With supply conditions and the natural rate unchanged, what adjustment does this graph predict?
options: SRPC shifts upward, and unemployment returns to the natural rate of 5%.
SRPC shifts downward, and unemployment returns to the natural rate of 5%.
SRPC shifts upward, permanently raising the natural rate from 3% to 5%.
LRPC shifts left, allowing unemployment to remain at B's 3% once expectations catch up.
items.feedback: B is above A's inflation rate and left of LRPC. Expectations catch up to the higher actual rate, shifting SRPC upward. At that sustained inflation, unemployment returns to the unchanged natural rate 5%.

items.stem: Actual inflation is held at B's rate while expectations gradually adjust to it. With the natural rate and supply conditions unchanged, which long-run adjustment fits the figure?
options: SRPC shifts upward, and unemployment returns from 3% toward 5%.
SRPC shifts downward, permanently reducing the natural rate from 7% to 5%.
SRPC shifts downward, and unemployment returns from 7% toward 5%.
LRPC shifts right to 7%, making the demand-induced unemployment increase permanent.
items.feedback: B has unemployment 7 and inflation 1.5, compared with A at natural unemployment 5 and inflation 2.5. Adapting to lower inflation shifts SRPC down; the eventual return to 5 does not change the natural rate.

items.stem: An unexpected monetary expansion temporarily lowers unemployment. Inflation expectations then fully adjust while the higher inflation rate persists. What is the long-run result?
options: Unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate.
Unemployment remains permanently below the natural rate.
Unemployment rises permanently above the natural rate.
Inflation returns automatically to its original rate while unemployment stays low.
items.feedback: The short-run unemployment effect disappears when expectations adjust, leaving higher inflation and natural-rate unemployment.

items.stem: Economy A lowers its natural rate through better job matching; Economy B only creates an unexpected demand boom. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both economies permanently shift LRPC left because unemployment initially declines
Only Economy B changes long-run unemployment by raising aggregate demand
Neither economy can affect unemployment at either a short or long horizon
A can shift LRPC left; B can only move unemployment below natural temporarily
items.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

items.stem: A labor-market reform lowers the natural unemployment rate from 6.4% to 5.6%. At the same time, an unexpected demand expansion pushes actual unemployment down to 4.9%. After inflation expectations fully adjust, the reform remains in place and there are no new demand surprises. How much did the natural rate change, how large was the temporary unemployment gap, and where does unemployment settle in the long run?
options: Natural rate falls 1.5 points; no temporary gap; long-run unemployment is 4.9%.
Natural rate is unchanged; temporary gap is 1.5 points; long-run unemployment is 6.4%.
Natural rate falls 0.8 point; temporary gap is 0.7 point; long-run unemployment is 4.9%.
Natural rate falls 0.8 point; temporary gap is 0.7 point; long-run unemployment is 5.6%.
items.feedback: The structural shift is 6.4 − 5.6 = 0.8 percentage point. Actual unemployment is temporarily 5.6 − 4.9 = 0.7 point below the new natural rate. Once the demand surprise disappears, the long-run anchor is 5.6, not the old 6.4 or temporary 4.9.

items.stem: A government insists on holding unemployment below the natural rate after inflation expectations have adjusted. What does the long-run Phillips-curve model predict?
options: A stable inflation rate will permanently sustain lower unemployment.
The policy requires continuously accelerating inflation.
Unemployment will fall to zero without further inflation.
The natural rate automatically falls whenever aggregate demand rises.
items.feedback: Once expected inflation catches up, maintaining below-natural unemployment requires repeated new inflation surprises.

items.stem: Officials promise a constant inflation rate above the public's former expectation and permanently lower unemployment. Expectations eventually equal the promised rate. Which component of the promise fails under unchanged labor-market structure?
options: The unemployment gain strengthens; correctly anticipated inflation creates a larger surprise.
The permanent unemployment gain fails; fully anticipated inflation leaves unemployment at natural.
The constant inflation rate is impossible; natural unemployment requires zero inflation.
The natural unemployment benchmark disappears; anticipated inflation determines productive capacity.
items.feedback: Once expected inflation equals actual inflation, the original surprise disappears. Under unchanged labor-market structure, the long-run benchmark remains natural unemployment; positive steady inflation is compatible with it.

items.stem: Matching reform reduces natural unemployment from 6% to 5% in a labor force of 200. Aggregate-demand policy separately raises sustained inflation after expectations adjust. Which graph distinction is correct?
options: Reform shifts LRPC left; inflation selects another point on that new curve.
Reform moves along LRPC; inflation shifts the entire curve to the left.
Reform shifts LRPC left; inflation shifts it right by reversing the reform.
Reform and inflation both move along the same downward-sloping long-run curve.
items.feedback: Structural changes in matching affect the natural rate and shift LRPC. A different sustained inflation rate with expectations adjusted does not itself determine natural unemployment.

items.stem: A firm can produce units with marginal benefits of $20, $16, $12, and $8 and marginal costs of $6, $10, $13, and $15. How many units maximize net benefit?
options: Two units.
Four units.
One unit.
Three units.
items.feedback: The first two units add net benefit; the third and fourth would reduce it.

items.stem: A city has spent $4 million on a stadium design. Construction will cost another $30 million and generate benefits valued at $24 million. What should marginal analysis recommend?
options: Build because total benefits are positive.
Do not build because the future cost exceeds the future benefit.
Ignore construction cost because design work is complete.
Build because abandoning the design wastes $4 million.
items.feedback: The $4 million is sunk; the relevant comparison is $24 million in benefits versus $30 million in future cost.

items.stem: A clinic can extend hours. The first extra hour has MB $5,000 and MC $2,000; the second has MB $3,000 and MC $2,500; the third has MB $1,500 and MC $2,200. The optimal extension is:
options: Zero hours.
Three hours.
One hour.
Two hours.
items.feedback: Extend through the second hour and stop before the third, where MC exceeds MB.

items.stem: A company’s average profit per customer is positive, but the next customer is expected to cost $140 to serve and generate $110 in revenue. The company should:
options: Accept the customer to spread fixed costs over more customers
Accept because average profit is positive
Accept because total revenue will increase.
Reject the next customer because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
items.feedback: The next customer lowers profit by $30.

items.stem: A farmer has already applied fertilizer. One additional unit raises crop value by $45 and costs $38, but also causes $10 in expected runoff damage. Including the external cost, the farmer should:
options: Ignore runoff because it is not paid directly by the farmer.
Apply because total crop value is positive.
Apply because private marginal cost is only $38.
Not apply the additional unit because marginal social cost is $48.
items.feedback: The added social cost is $38 plus $10, which exceeds the $45 marginal benefit.

items.stem: An airline can sell one more seat for $240. Added catering and handling cost $35, and carrying the passenger means giving up $170 in net earnings from cargo. What is net marginal benefit?
items.feedback: The added passenger brings $240 in revenue, costs $35 to serve, and replaces cargo that would have earned $170 net. The net marginal benefit is $240 - $35 - $170 = $35.

items.stem: A city considers a third congestion-reduction measure. Driver time savings are $1.4 million, implementation costs $900,000, and added neighborhood noise costs $600,000. What should it do?
options: Reject because marginal social cost is $1.5 million
Adopt because private implementation cost is below benefit
Adopt because total time savings remain positive
Reject only if average program cost rises
items.feedback: Implementation plus noise costs exceed the next measure’s benefit.

items.stem: Total revenue at 200 units is $18,000 and at 201 units is $18,075. Total cost rises from $14,400 to $14,482. Should unit 201 be produced?
options: No, because marginal revenue $75 is below marginal cost $82
Yes, because total revenue remains above total cost
Yes, because average profit is positive
No, because total cost rises when the unit is produced
items.feedback: Unit 201 reduces profit by $7.

items.stem: A hospital can add a night shift. Expected benefit is $31,000; added payroll is $22,000; and using the nurses displaces training worth $11,000. Which decision is best?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $33,000
Add it because payroll alone is below benefit
Add it because total hospital benefit is large
Do not add it because any displaced activity is sunk
items.feedback: Payroll plus forgone training exceeds the shift’s expected benefit.

items.stem: A research grant has spent $2 million. Another experiment costs $180,000 and has a 40% chance of producing evidence worth $600,000. Ignoring other outcomes, should it run?
options: Run because expected marginal benefit is $240,000
Stop because the $600,000 benefit is uncertain
Run only to justify the $2 million already spent
Stop because total spending would rise
items.feedback: Expected added benefit exceeds the $180,000 experiment cost.

items.stem: A retailer’s first three added inventory batches have net marginal benefits of $6,000, $2,000, and -$1,500. A fourth would have +$500 only if the third is purchased. How many additional batches should the retailer buy?
options: Buy two batches
Buy four batches
Buy three batches
Buy one batch
items.feedback: Buying batches three and four together would reduce net benefit by $1,000.

items.stem: A nonprofit is considering one more meal-delivery route. The route would generate $900 in attributable donations, cost $620 for food and fuel, and use volunteer time that would otherwise provide tutoring worth $310. Should the nonprofit add the route?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $930
Add it because direct cost is below donations
Add it because volunteer time is unpaid
Do not add it because total program costs are high
items.feedback: Direct plus forgone volunteer value exceeds added donations.

items.stem: A factory’s next three pollution-control units have marginal benefits of $90, $70, and $45 and marginal costs of $40, $65, and $60. How many units should be installed?
options: One unit.
Three units.
Zero units.
Two units.
items.feedback: The first two units have MB at least as large as MC; the third does not.

items.stem: A hospital considers one more diagnostic test. Expected patient benefit is $420, direct test cost is $250, and expected false-positive follow-up cost is $190. Taking all the listed benefits and costs into account, should the hospital add the test?
options: Ignore false-positive costs because they occur later.
Do not add the test because total marginal cost is $440.
Add because the direct cost is below the benefit.
Add because some patients benefit.
items.feedback: Relevant marginal cost includes direct and expected follow-up costs.

items.stem: A pollution rule’s next reduction step yields $4.8 million in health benefits, costs firms $3.6 million, and reduces recreational value by $1.5 million. Based on social marginal analysis, should the additional reduction be required?
options: Do not require it because social marginal cost is $5.1 million
Require it because compliance cost alone is below benefit
Require it because total prior health benefits are large
Do not require it because all environmental policy is costly
items.feedback: The next step’s combined social costs exceed its benefit.

items.stem: A utility considers one more conservation rebate. Expected energy savings are $130, rebate administration costs $90, and customer hassle is valued at $45. What is the social decision?
options: Do not offer it because marginal social cost is $135
Offer it because administrative cost is below savings
Offer it because total energy savings remain positive
Do not offer it because rebates are transfers
items.feedback: The next rebate’s social cost exceeds its benefit by $5.

items.stem: An emergency agency can pre-position one more team. Expected response benefit is $500,000, deployment costs $320,000, and the team’s best alternative assignment is worth $210,000. What should it do?
options: Do not deploy because relevant marginal cost is $530,000
Deploy because direct cost is below expected benefit
Deploy because emergency benefits are not monetary
Do not deploy because prior readiness spending is sunk
items.feedback: Direct plus opportunity cost exceeds expected response benefit.

items.stem: A farm’s next fertilizer application raises crop value by $1,100, costs $760, and increases expected water cleanup by $390. Which statement is correct?
options: Do not apply because marginal social cost exceeds benefit by $50
Apply because private marginal profit is $340
Apply because total crop revenue is positive
Do not apply because fertilizer cost is sunk
items.feedback: Combined marginal cost is $1,150, above the $1,100 benefit.

items.stem: A data center’s next cooling upgrade saves $140,000 in expected outages, costs $100,000, and uses technicians who could complete security work worth $50,000. What should it do?
options: Do not upgrade because relevant marginal cost is $150,000
Upgrade because outage savings exceed direct cost
Upgrade because technicians are already salaried
Do not upgrade because total cooling spending is high
items.feedback: Direct and opportunity costs exceed the expected outage savings.

items.stem: A school can offer a class with a gross benefit of 44 points, a delivery cost of 30 points, and a teacher fatigue cost of 9 points. A later class would yield a gross benefit of 50 points but requires this class first. Should the school offer or skip the first class?
options: Deliver the next class because its net marginal benefit is 5
Skip to the later class because its gross benefit is higher
Stop because combined cost is positive
Deliver only if average class benefit rises
items.feedback: The current required class has positive net marginal benefit.

items.stem: A firm already spent $5,000 designing a product. It can spend $1,200 more to launch it and earn $1,700 in revenue. What should it do if it is using marginal reasoning?
options: Launch, because the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost by $500
Do not launch, because total spending is $6,200
Do not launch, because the $5,000 sunk cost is too large
Launch only if total revenue exceeds all past costs
items.feedback: The $5,000 is sunk. The launch decision compares the extra $1,200 cost with the extra $1,700 revenue.

items.stem: MB values for units 1 through 4 are 30, 22, 14, and 8; MC values are 10, 16, 15, and 12. Which production plan is optimal?
options: Produce only unit 1
Produce all four units
Produce the first three units
Produce the first two units
items.feedback: Units 1 and 2 add net benefit; unit 3 would reduce it.

items.stem: A project has spent $5 million irreversibly. Finishing now costs $3 million and produces $2 million in future benefits. Abandoning it costs $1.5 million in required restoration, with no future benefits. Delaying changes neither future cost nor benefit. Which choice minimizes the remaining loss?
options: Abandon: $2 million of benefits is below $3 million of cost, regardless of the restoration alternative.
Finish: the $5 million already spent must be counted as an additional benefit from completion.
Finish: the $1 million future loss is smaller than the $1.5 million abandonment loss.
Delay: postponement removes the restoration cost even though the stated future alternatives are unchanged.
items.feedback: Finishing nets 2-3=-1 million. Abandoning nets -1.5 million. Finishing is preferable by 0.5 million, despite its negative standalone future net value, because the feasible alternative is worse. Sunk spending is irrelevant.

items.stem: A firm can accept a rush order for $30,000 or decline it. Internal production requires $16,000 in materials and labor plus $2,000 in extra maintenance, and displaces a job with $9,000 net profit. Outsourcing costs $24,000 plus $1,000 for inspection and leaves that other job intact. A $6,000 design fee is already paid and nonrefundable under every choice. Both production methods are feasible and give the same revenue. Which plan maximizes incremental private profit?
options: Produce internally; incremental profit is $12,000.
Outsource production; incremental profit is $5,000.
Reject the order; the best production option loses $1,000.
Produce internally; incremental profit is $3,000.
items.feedback: Internal production adds $30,000 - $16,000 - $2,000 - $9,000 = $3,000 after accounting for the displaced job. Outsourcing adds $30,000 - $24,000 - $1,000 = $5,000 and preserves that job, so outsourcing is best. The $6,000 design fee is sunk and does not enter either comparison.

items.stem: A project has $10 million in sunk spending. Completion costs $3 million, yields $3.4 million, and displaces another project worth $0.6 million. What is the decision?
options: Do not complete because relevant marginal cost is $3.6 million
Complete because future revenue exceeds direct cost
Complete to recover the $10 million
Do not complete because total project cost is high
items.feedback: Direct plus opportunity cost exceeds future benefit.

items.stem: One more factory inspection avoids expected losses of $95,000, costs $62,000, and creates $38,000 in delay costs for customers. What is the social choice?
options: Skip it because marginal social cost is $100,000
Perform it because direct cost is below avoided loss
Perform it because total quality benefit is positive
Skip it because all delay costs are sunk
items.feedback: The inspection’s combined added cost exceeds avoided loss.

items.stem: Demand increases while supply decreases, and the observed equilibrium quantity is unchanged. Which inference best reconciles the two shifts with that observation?
options: Equilibrium price rises, and the opposing quantity effects happen to offset
Equilibrium price falls, and the two shifts reinforce the quantity effect
Equilibrium quantity is unchanged because neither curve shifts
Equilibrium price is unchanged because the demand and supply shifts are equal
items.feedback: A demand increase and supply decrease both raise equilibrium price. Their quantity effects oppose one another, and the observed unchanged quantity indicates that those effects offset in this case.

items.stem: Demand decreases while supply increases. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium quantity falls
items.feedback: Both shifts push price down, but quantity is ambiguous.

items.stem: Demand and supply both increase. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity falls
items.feedback: Both shifts increase quantity, but price depends on which shift is larger.

items.stem: Demand and supply both decrease. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity rises
items.feedback: Both shifts reduce quantity, but price is ambiguous.

items.stem: A drought reduces wheat supply while a health trend increases demand for wheat bread. Explain which equilibrium effect is certain and which depends on the relative shift sizes.
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects
Price falls; quantity rises because both shifts increase purchases
Price rises; quantity rises because demand determines both outcomes
Price is ambiguous; quantity falls because supply determines both outcomes
items.feedback: The demand increase and supply decrease both raise price. Demand raises quantity while the supply decrease lowers it, so quantity depends on the relative magnitudes.

items.stem: Production technology lowers costs while consumer interest in the good falls. Explain which equilibrium effect is certain and which depends on the relative shift sizes.
options: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects
Price rises; quantity falls because both shifts reduce market availability
Price falls; quantity rises because supply determines both outcomes
Price is ambiguous; quantity falls because demand determines both outcomes
items.feedback: The supply increase and demand decrease both lower price. Supply raises quantity while the demand decrease lowers it, so quantity depends on the relative magnitudes.

items.stem: Demand and supply both increase, taking the market from D1/S1 to D2/S2. Which statement distinguishes what theory guarantees from the particular outcome shown?
options: Quantity must rise; price could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q3.
Quantity must rise; price could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2.
Quantity must rise; price must stay unchanged. Here price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q3.
Quantity must rise; price must stay unchanged. Here price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2.
items.feedback: A demand increase raises equilibrium price and quantity; a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Quantity therefore rises for certain, but price depends on the relative shifts. Here D1/S1 is (P2,Q1) and D2/S2 is (P2,Q3): price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q3.

items.stem: Demand increases from D1 to D2 while supply decreases from S2 to S1. Which statement distinguishes what theory guarantees from the particular outcome shown?
options: Price must rise; quantity could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price rises from P1 to P3 and quantity stays Q2.
Price must rise; quantity could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price rises from P2 to P3 and quantity stays Q2.
Price must rise; quantity must stay unchanged. Here price rises from P1 to P3 and quantity stays Q2.
Price must rise; quantity must stay unchanged. Here price rises from P2 to P3 and quantity stays Q2.
items.feedback: Higher demand and lower supply both raise price, but demand raises quantity while lower supply reduces it. Quantity is therefore ambiguous in general. Here D1/S2 is (P1,Q2) and D2/S1 is (P3,Q2): price rises from P1 to P3 while the quantity effects offset at Q2.

items.stem: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. Starting from D2/S1, demand decreases to D1 while supply increases to S2. What happens?
options: Price falls and quantity stays the same
Price rises and quantity stays the same
Price stays the same and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
items.feedback: D2/S1 gives P3 and Q2. D1/S2 gives P1 and Q2. Price falls while quantity remains Q2.

items.stem: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. If demand and supply both increase, what does this graph show is possible?
options: Quantity rises while price stays the same
Quantity rises while price rises because the demand shift has the larger price effect
Quantity rises while price falls because the supply shift has the larger price effect
Price rises while quantity stays the same because the shifts have equal quantity effects
items.feedback: The graph shows D1/S1 to D2/S2. Both demand and supply increase, quantity rises, and price remains unchanged.

items.stem: Compare the equilibrium at D1/S2 with the equilibrium at D2/S1. Which outcome is shown when demand increases and supply decreases?
options: Price rises from P1 to P3; quantity stays Q2
Price rises from P1 to P3; quantity rises from Q1 to Q2
Price rises from P1 to P3; quantity falls from Q3 to Q2
Price rises from P2 to P3; quantity stays Q2
