items.feedback: The graph places D1/S2 at (P1,Q2) and D2/S1 at (P3,Q2). The price increase is from P1 to P3; the two shifts have offsetting quantity effects here.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Calculate the disequilibrium at $1 per gallon and explain the price pressure that follows from buyers' and sellers' incentives.
options: A 200-thousand surplus; downward price pressure
A 50-thousand shortage; no price pressure
A 250-thousand surplus; upward price pressure
A 200-thousand shortage; upward price pressure
items.feedback: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by 200 thousand gallons. A shortage gives buyers an incentive to bid price upward toward equilibrium.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. How do equilibrium price and quantity change from A to B?
options: Price rises 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand
Price rises 4 dollars; quantity rises 200 thousand
Price falls 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand
Price stays 10 dollars; quantity falls 4 thousand
items.feedback: The quantity effects offset while price rises from 10 to 14 dollars.

items.stem: With supply fixed at S0, which transition is an increase in demand?
options: D to A
A to B
C to B
D to C
items.feedback: D is D0-S0 and C is D1-S0.

items.stem: With supply fixed at S1, which transition isolates increased demand?
options: D to A
D to C
A to B
C to B
items.feedback: A is D0-S1 and B is D1-S1.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Tastes shift demand from D1 to D2 while supply remains S1. Which explanation uses both intersections to distinguish the demand shift from the market's movement along supply?
options: Demand shifts right, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2
Supply shifts right, and equilibrium moves along D1 from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2
Demand shifts left, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P3, Q2 to P2, Q1
Supply shifts left, and equilibrium moves along D2 from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2
items.feedback: The taste change shifts the entire demand curve from D1 to D2. Because S1 is fixed, the new intersection is also a movement along S1 to a higher price and quantity.

items.stem: A market price is above equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
options: Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
No pressure because high prices clear every market
Downward pressure on quantity demanded because demand shifts left
items.feedback: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus, so sellers have an incentive to lower price.

items.stem: A market price is below equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
options: Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
No pressure because buyers prefer low prices
A supply increase because the legal price is low
items.feedback: A price below equilibrium creates a shortage, so buyers compete and push price upward.

items.stem: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D2 and S1, supply increases to S2 while demand stays at D2. What happens?
options: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2.
Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2.
items.feedback: A supply increase shifts supply right from S1 to S2, lowering price and raising quantity.

items.stem: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D1 and S2, supply decreases to S1 while demand stays at D1. What happens?
options: Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q1.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2.
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2.
Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
items.feedback: A decrease in supply shifts supply left, raising price and lowering quantity.

items.stem: In a market with Qd = 300 - 10P and Qs = 10P, price is initially $12. Diagnose the disequilibrium and calculate the price toward which an unregulated market adjusts.
options: A shortage of 60; price rises toward $15
A surplus of 60; price falls toward $9
A shortage of 120; price rises toward $18
A surplus of 120; price falls toward $6
items.feedback: At $12, Qd = 180 and Qs = 120, so the shortage is 60. Setting 300 - 10P = 10P gives the equilibrium price of $15, toward which the shortage pushes price.

items.stem: In a market with Qd = 410 - 10P and Qs = -10 + 10P, price is initially $25. Diagnose the disequilibrium and calculate the price toward which an unregulated market adjusts.
options: A surplus of 80; price falls toward $21
A shortage of 80; price rises toward $29
A surplus of 40; price falls toward $23
A shortage of 40; price rises toward $27
items.feedback: At $25, Qs = 240 and Qd = 160, so the surplus is 80. Setting the schedules equal gives P = $21, and seller competition pushes price downward toward it.

items.stem: Demand increases while supply decreases. Which equilibrium outcome is certain?
options: The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.
The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.
items.feedback: Both shifts raise price, while demand raises quantity and lower supply reduces quantity.

items.stem: Both demand and supply shift left in the same market. Which equilibrium result can be stated without knowing the shift sizes?
options: The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.
The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.
items.feedback: Both shifts reduce equilibrium quantity, but their price effects oppose each other.

items.stem: At the current price, quantity demanded is 400 and quantity supplied is 520. Which explanation diagnoses the imbalance and traces the adjustment along the existing curves without a price control?
options: A surplus pushes price down, raising quantity demanded and lowering quantity supplied until they converge
A shortage pushes price up, lowering quantity demanded and raising quantity supplied until they converge
A surplus shifts demand right while price remains fixed until inventories clear
A shortage shifts supply left while buyers reduce quantity demanded
items.feedback: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by 120, creating a surplus. Falling price moves the market along both curves: quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls toward equilibrium.

items.stem: At the next unit of a competitive product, a buyer values it at $18, the producer uses $14 of resources, and pollution harms neighbors by $6. Which outcome does a $6 per-unit tax encourage?
options: Forgo the unit: private gains are $4 but net social benefit is -$2.
Produce the unit: the $4 private gain measures its full social benefit.
Produce the unit: $6 of tax revenue makes its net social benefit $4.
Forgo the unit: every taxed unit has zero social benefit.
items.feedback: The trade has a private gain of 18 - 14 = $4, but net social benefit is 18 - 14 - 6 = -$2. A $6 tax makes the relevant private cost $20, above willingness to pay. Revenue is a transfer, not an extra resource benefit.

items.stem: Why can a common resource be overused?
options: It is nonrival and nonexcludable.
Users receive the private benefit while sharing depletion costs with others.
Its price is always above marginal cost.
No one can access it.
items.feedback: Common resources are rival but difficult to exclude, creating overuse incentives.

items.stem: A dominant seller withholds an additional unit that a buyer values at $25 even though producing it uses $18 of resources. There are no externalities. Which mechanism explains the lost efficiency?
options: The withheld trade creates a $7 external pollution cost paid by a third party.
The seller’s lost sales revenue equals the social gain, regardless of production cost.
Restricting output can preserve the seller’s price while forgoing a trade with $7 of social gains.
Any price above resource cost proves that expanding output would reduce total surplus.
items.feedback: The omitted unit has willingness to pay above marginal resource cost by 25 - 18 = $7. Market power can make restricting output privately attractive even though the unit would add social surplus. No third-party spillover is required.

items.stem: A seller knows a used car’s quality, but buyers cannot distinguish good cars from bad ones. What problem can result?
options: A public-good free-rider problem.
A positive production externality.
A binding price floor by definition.
Adverse selection from asymmetric information.
items.feedback: Hidden quality can drive high-quality goods from the market.

items.stem: A product is expensive because its inputs are scarce. Is that alone market failure?
options: No; high cost alone does not identify an efficiency wedge
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
A high price by itself establishes market failure
items.feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

items.stem: A city dislikes unequal restaurant access. What must be shown to establish market failure?
options: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
A mechanism causing private incentives to diverge from social efficiency
A high price by itself establishes market failure
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
items.feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

items.stem: A lake is rival in use but access is difficult to restrict. Which problem fits?
options: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
A common-resource overuse problem
It is nonrival but easy to exclude
items.feedback: Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.

items.stem: An insurer cannot observe customers’ risk types before pricing. What issue fits?
options: Both sides possess the same relevant information
The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain
A spillover harms an unrelated third party
Asymmetric information may distort participation
items.feedback: Asymmetric information means one side holds relevant information the other lacks.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the original deadweight loss in the fast-fashion garments market?
options: $480 million
$960 million
$240 million
$1,440 million
items.feedback: The distortion is 80 million garments and the marginal external effect is $6 per garment. The triangular loss is one-half times those values, or $240 million.

items.stem: Regulators want to reach the efficient outcome by setting a quantity limit rather than changing the price through a tax or subsidy. According to the graph, what quantity of fast-fashion garments should they allow?
options: 240 million garments
80 million garments
400 million garments
160 million garments
items.feedback: The socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 160 million garments and $15. A correctly calibrated quantity rule would therefore set the target at 160 million garments.

items.stem: What tax per garment would correct the externality shown? Explain how it changes the producer’s incentive.
options: A $6 tax; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $4 tax; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $6 tax collected as a fixed fee from each firm; it creates the same marginal incentive as charging $6 on each garment.
A $15 per-garment tax; producers should pay the full social marginal cost in addition to their private marginal cost.
items.feedback: At the efficient 160-million-garment quantity, MSC is $15 and MPC $9. A $6 per-unit tax aligns the producer’s marginal incentive with social cost. A fixed fee does not change marginal cost, while a $15 tax would count private cost twice.

items.stem: If affected parties could bargain costlessly over the fast-fashion garments spillover, which quantity on the graph would be their efficient target?
options: 240 million garments
160 million garments
80 million garments
Equal gains for every party regardless of rights
items.feedback: The socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 160 million garments and $15. Under the Coase assumptions, bargaining can reach that quantity, although the initial rights assignment still affects who compensates whom.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the original deadweight loss in the disposable-vapes market?
options: $80 thousand
$160 thousand
$560 thousand
$720 thousand
items.feedback: The distortion is 40 thousand vapes and the marginal external effect is $4 per vape. The triangular loss is one-half times those values, or $80 thousand.

items.stem: Regulators want to reach the efficient outcome by setting a quantity limit rather than changing the price through a tax or subsidy. According to the graph, what quantity of disposable vapes should they allow?
options: 180 thousand vapes
140 thousand vapes
40 thousand vapes
320 thousand vapes
items.feedback: The socially efficient outcome occurs where MPC intersects MSB, at 140 thousand vapes and $8. A correctly calibrated quantity rule would therefore set the target at 140 thousand vapes.

items.stem: What tax per vape would correct the externality shown? Explain how it changes the consumer’s incentive.
options: A $2 tax; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $4 tax makes private and social benefits equal by raising consumers’ underlying willingness to pay by $4.
A $4 tax; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $12 tax; the full marginal private benefit is the external harm.
items.feedback: At the efficient 140-thousand-vape quantity, MPB is $12 and MSB $8. A $4 tax reduces the private net incentive to consume by the external harm; it does not raise underlying willingness to pay.

items.stem: If affected parties could bargain costlessly over the disposable vapes spillover, which quantity on the graph would be their efficient target?
options: 180 thousand vapes
40 thousand vapes
Equal gains for every party regardless of rights
140 thousand vapes
items.feedback: The socially efficient outcome occurs where MPC intersects MSB, at 140 thousand vapes and $8. Under the Coase assumptions, bargaining can reach that quantity, although the initial rights assignment still affects who compensates whom.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the original deadweight loss in the native-plant gardens market?
items.feedback: The distortion is 50 gardens and the marginal external effect is $5 per garden. The triangular loss is one-half times those values, or $125.

items.stem: The council sets a maximum of 150 gardens but offers no subsidy or purchase commitment. How many gardens will the private market provide, and why does the cap have that effect?
options: 125 gardens remain privately supported; the cap permits expansion but provides no incentive for it.
100 gardens remain privately supported; a maximum of 150 forces private production up to the maximum.
125 gardens remain privately supported; a maximum of 150 forces private production up to the maximum.
100 gardens remain privately supported; the cap permits expansion but provides no incentive for it.
items.feedback: MPC and MPB intersect at 100 gardens, while the social intersection is 150. A maximum of 150 is nonbinding at the private quantity. Internalizing the benefit or arranging provision is needed to induce expansion.

items.stem: What subsidy per garden would correct the externality shown? Explain how it changes the producer’s incentive.
options: A $5 producer subsidy; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $3 producer subsidy; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $5 subsidy guarantees a $5 net social gain from every garden, including those already produced.
A $15 subsidy per garden; government must reimburse the whole private marginal cost.
items.feedback: At 150 gardens, MPC is $15 and MSC $10. The $5 external benefit justifies a matching subsidy. The subsidy itself is a transfer, not a guaranteed $5 net social gain on every existing garden.

items.stem: If affected parties could bargain costlessly over the native-plant gardens spillover, which quantity on the graph would be their efficient target?
options: 100 gardens
150 gardens
50 gardens
Equal gains for every party regardless of rights
items.feedback: The socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 150 gardens and $10. Under the Coase assumptions, bargaining can reach that quantity, although the initial rights assignment still affects who compensates whom.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the original deadweight loss in the public-transit rides market?
options: $50 thousand per day
$100 thousand per day
$300 thousand per day
$400 thousand per day
items.feedback: The distortion is 50 thousand rides per day and the marginal external effect is $2 per ride. The triangular loss is one-half times those values, or $50 thousand per day.

items.stem: A transport authority wants to achieve the socially efficient quantity in the graph. Which policy and explanation directly support that target?
options: A $1 rider subsidy; it internalizes the marginal external benefit and supports 175 thousand rides.
A $2 rider subsidy; it internalizes the marginal external benefit and supports 200 thousand rides.
An upper limit of 200 thousand rides; merely permitting that quantity forces riders to choose it.
An upper limit of 175 thousand rides; merely permitting that quantity forces riders to choose it.
items.feedback: MSB and MPC meet at 200 thousand rides; the gap above MPB there is $2. A matching rider subsidy rewards the external benefit. A maximum above private demand does not itself induce more trips.

items.stem: What subsidy per transit ride would correct the externality shown? Explain how it changes the rider’s incentive.
options: A $1 rider subsidy; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $2 rider subsidy makes the subsidy payment itself the extra social benefit of each ride.
A $2 rider subsidy; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $6 rider subsidy; the entire marginal social benefit must be added to the private incentive.
items.feedback: At 200 thousand rides, MSB is $6 and MPB $4. A $2 subsidy closes the incentive gap. The external benefit exists independently of the subsidy payment, which is a transfer.

items.stem: If affected parties could bargain costlessly over the public-transit rides spillover, which quantity on the graph would be their efficient target?
options: 150 thousand rides per day
50 thousand rides per day
Equal gains for every party regardless of rights
200 thousand rides per day
items.feedback: The socially efficient outcome occurs where MPC intersects MSB, at 200 thousand rides per day and $6. Under the Coase assumptions, bargaining can reach that quantity, although the initial rights assignment still affects who compensates whom.

items.stem: Based on the graph, by how much must the quantity of fast-fashion garments change to move from the unregulated market outcome to the corrected outcome?
options: 80 million garments
240 million garments
160 million garments
400 million garments
items.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 240 million garments and $12. The socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 160 million garments and $15. The difference is 80 million garments, so the market has overproduction.

items.stem: What per-unit gap between private and social incentives must the policy internalize in the fast-fashion garments market?
options: $2 per garment
$6 per garment
$4 per garment
$5 per garment
items.feedback: The relevant private and social marginal curves are $6 per garment apart. Matching that vertical gap makes the private decision reflect the marginal external cost.

items.stem: Which corrective instrument and per-unit amount shown on the graph would move fast-fashion garments to the efficient quantity?
options: a $1 corrective tax per unit
a $6 per garment subsidy
a $6 corrective tax per garment
a quantity target at 240 million garments
items.feedback: The tax makes producers face the $6 marginal external cost, aligning private marginal cost with MSC and moving quantity to 160 million garments. Therefore the graph's optimal instrument is a $6 corrective tax per garment.

items.stem: At the corrected quantity shown for fast-fashion garments, how much tax revenue does the per-unit policy generate?
options: $240 million
$320 million
$1440 million
$960 million
items.feedback: The corrected quantity is 160 million garments and the policy is $6 per garment. Multiplying the per-unit amount by quantity gives $960 million in tax revenue.

items.stem: After the optimal corrective tax internalizes the spillover, what quantity of fast-fashion garments is produced or consumed?
options: 160 million garments
240 million garments
80 million garments
400 million garments
items.feedback: The tax makes producers face the $6 marginal external cost, aligning private marginal cost with MSC and moving quantity to 160 million garments. The corrected quantity is therefore 160 million garments.

items.stem: Based on the graph, by how much must the quantity of disposable vapes change to move from the unregulated market outcome to the corrected outcome?
options: 180 thousand vapes
40 thousand vapes
140 thousand vapes
320 thousand vapes
items.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 180 thousand vapes and $10. The socially efficient outcome occurs where MPC intersects MSB, at 140 thousand vapes and $8. The difference is 40 thousand vapes, so the market has overconsumption.

items.stem: What per-unit gap between private and social incentives must the policy internalize in the disposable vapes market?
options: $2 per vape
$5 per vape
$4 per vape
$6 per vape
items.feedback: The relevant private and social marginal curves are $4 per vape apart. Matching that vertical gap makes the private decision reflect the marginal external cost.

items.stem: Which corrective instrument and per-unit amount shown on the graph would move disposable vapes to the efficient quantity?
options: a $1 corrective tax per unit
a $4 per vape subsidy
a quantity target at 180 thousand vapes
a $4 corrective tax per vape
items.feedback: The tax makes consumers face the $4 marginal external cost, aligning their private incentive with MSB and moving quantity to 140 thousand vapes. Therefore the graph's optimal instrument is a $4 corrective tax per vape.

options: $560 thousand
$80 thousand
$280 thousand
$720 thousand
items.feedback: The corrected quantity is 140 thousand vapes and the policy is $4 per vape. Multiplying the per-unit amount by quantity gives $560 thousand in tax revenue.

options: 180 thousand vapes
140 thousand vapes
40 thousand vapes
320 thousand vapes
items.feedback: The tax makes consumers face the $4 marginal external cost, aligning their private incentive with MSB and moving quantity to 140 thousand vapes. The corrected quantity is therefore 140 thousand vapes.

options: 100 gardens
150 gardens
50 gardens
250 gardens
items.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 100 gardens and $12. The socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 150 gardens and $10. The difference is 50 gardens, so the market has underproduction.

items.stem: What per-unit gap between private and social incentives must the policy internalize in the native-plant gardens market?
options: $2 per garden
$4 per garden
$6 per garden
$5 per garden
items.feedback: The relevant private and social marginal curves are $5 per garden apart. Matching that vertical gap makes the private decision reflect the marginal external benefit.

items.stem: Which corrective instrument and per-unit amount shown on the graph would move native-plant gardens to the efficient quantity?
options: a $5 producer subsidy per garden
a $1 producer subsidy per unit
a $5 per garden tax
a quantity target at 100 gardens
items.feedback: The producer subsidy rewards the $5 marginal external benefit, aligning the producer's effective cost with MSC and moving quantity to 150 gardens. Therefore the graph's optimal instrument is a $5 producer subsidy per garden.

items.feedback: The corrected quantity is 150 gardens and the policy is $5 per garden. Multiplying the per-unit amount by quantity gives $750 in subsidy expenditure.

options: 100 gardens
50 gardens
150 gardens
250 gardens
items.feedback: The producer subsidy rewards the $5 marginal external benefit, aligning the producer's effective cost with MSC and moving quantity to 150 gardens. The corrected quantity is therefore 150 gardens.

options: 150 thousand rides per day
200 thousand rides per day
350 thousand rides per day
50 thousand rides per day
items.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 150 thousand rides per day and $5. The socially efficient outcome occurs where MPC intersects MSB, at 200 thousand rides per day and $6. The difference is 50 thousand rides per day, so the market has underconsumption.

options: $2 per ride
$4 per ride
$5 per ride
$6 per ride
items.feedback: The relevant private and social marginal curves are $2 per ride apart. Matching that vertical gap makes the private decision reflect the marginal external benefit.

items.stem: Which corrective instrument and per-unit amount shown on the graph would move public-transit rides to the efficient quantity?
options: a $1 rider subsidy per unit
a $2 rider subsidy per ride
a $2 per ride tax
a quantity target at 150 thousand rides per day
items.feedback: The rider subsidy rewards the $2 marginal external benefit, aligning the rider's private incentive with MSB and moving quantity to 200 thousand rides per day. Therefore the graph's optimal instrument is a $2 rider subsidy per ride.

items.stem: At the corrected quantity shown for public-transit rides, how much subsidy expenditure does the per-unit policy generate?
options: $50 thousand per day
$400 thousand per day
items.feedback: The corrected quantity is 200 thousand rides per day and the policy is $2 per ride. Multiplying the per-unit amount by quantity gives $400 thousand per day in subsidy expenditure.

items.stem: After the optimal rider subsidy internalizes the spillover, what quantity of public-transit rides is produced or consumed?
options: 150 thousand rides per day
50 thousand rides per day
350 thousand rides per day
200 thousand rides per day
items.feedback: The rider subsidy rewards the $2 marginal external benefit, aligning the rider's private incentive with MSB and moving quantity to 200 thousand rides per day. The corrected quantity is therefore 200 thousand rides per day.

items.stem: Why can equating MPB with MPC fail when consumption creates an external cost?
options: MPB exceeds MSB, so some privately chosen units have social cost above social benefit
MPC necessarily exceeds MSC
External cost raises MSB above MPB
Efficiency never uses marginal analysis
items.feedback: Efficiency compares social marginal benefit and cost. The market uses MPB, but efficiency uses MSB for a consumption externality; confusing those curves overstates the value of marginal consumption.

items.stem: Market quantity is 90, efficient quantity is 60, and marginal external cost is $8. What triangular DWL results?
items.feedback: DWL is 0.5 x 30 x $8 = $120. The inefficient quantity range is 30 units, and the triangular welfare loss uses one-half of that base rather than the full rectangle.

items.stem: A plant saves $90 by evading one required emissions-control action. An inspection detects evasion with probability 0.20 and triggers a $300 fine. For a risk-neutral plant, which change would deter this evasion without changing the emissions standard?
options: Keep the current fine because $300 exceeds the $90 saving.
Reduce detection to 0.10 while retaining the $300 fine.
Raise the fine above $450 while keeping detection at 0.20.
Announce the same standard again without changing detection or penalties.
items.feedback: The expected penalty is 0.20 x 300 = $60, below the $90 saving. Deterrence requires 0.20 x fine > 90, or a fine above $450. A written standard alone does not change that comparison.

items.stem: A regulator knows the emissions target but not each firm's abatement cost. What design issue matters?
options: Every firm must have identical technology
Initial permit allocation determines the fixed cap
An output subsidy is required
Flexibility may reach the target at lower total cost
items.feedback: Flexibility can allocate reductions toward lower-cost sources. Flexibility lets low-cost firms undertake more abatement and high-cost firms less, potentially preserving the target while lowering total compliance cost.

items.stem: Before a corrective tax, a market sells 800 units. A $3 per-unit tax reduces sales to 500 units. What revenue is collected, and why does it differ from taxing the original sales volume?
options: $2,400, because revenue uses the 800 units sold before intervention.
$900, because only the 300 discouraged trades form the tax base.
$1,500, because the tax applies to the 500 units still traded.
$450, because revenue is the triangle over the quantity reduction.
items.feedback: Post-tax revenue is 3 x 500 = $1,500. The forgone 300 units pay no tax. A welfare triangle and a revenue rectangle measure different things.

items.stem: Marginal external cost is $7, but corrective tax is $4. What wedge remains?
options: $4 per unit
$7 per unit
$11 per unit
$3 per unit
items.feedback: The remaining wedge is $7 - $4. The $4 tax internalizes only part of the $7 marginal harm, so decision-makers still omit $3 of social cost on each unit.

items.stem: A regulator retires 10% of outstanding permits. What changes directly?
options: The cap loosens
Only initial wealth changes
Abatement incentives disappear
The aggregate emissions cap tightens
items.feedback: Fewer permits authorize less emissions. Retiring permits reduces the legal quantity of emissions, requiring additional aggregate abatement if regulated demand for emissions is otherwise unchanged.

items.stem: Two plants must jointly reduce emissions by two tons. Each can remove at most one ton at each successive cost: Plant A, $20 then $30; Plant B, $60 then $90. With enforceable tradable permits and no trading costs, how should the two-ton reduction be allocated?
options: A removes both tons for $50, saving $30 relative to one ton each.
Each removes one ton for $80, because equal cuts minimize total cost.
B removes both tons for $150, because high-cost plants should abate first.
A removes one ton and B removes one for $50, because only the cheaper costs count.
items.feedback: The two cheapest feasible marginal reductions are A’s $20 and $30 tons: total $50. Equal cuts cost 20 + 60 = $80. Trading permits can reallocate abatement without changing the aggregate target.

items.stem: Suppose a coastal barrier protects all shoreline residents, nonpayers cannot be excluded, and protecting another household does not reduce anyone else's protection. How is it classified?
options: Private good
Common resource
Club good
Public good
items.feedback: The barrier is nonexcludable because shoreline nonpayers still receive protection and nonrival because protecting another household does not reduce protection for others.

items.stem: Use the graph. An analyst uses North’s benefit alone to recommend reducing fireworks below four displays. At four displays, what is the total marginal benefit, and how should the neighborhoods’ benefits be combined to evaluate the recommendation?
options: Total MB = $50,000, equal to MC; add both neighborhoods’ benefits from the shared marginal display.
Total MB = $40,000, equal to MC; add both neighborhoods’ benefits from the shared marginal display.
Total MB = $50,000, equal to MC; average the two neighborhoods’ benefits to value the shared display.
Total MB = $40,000, equal to MC; average the two neighborhoods’ benefits to value the shared display.
items.feedback: North’s MB is $30,000 and South’s $20,000 at four displays, summing to the $50,000 MC. The public-good decision compares the sum of marginal benefits with cost, not one person’s benefit or their average.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is MSB at 40 hours after vertically summing the two groups' marginal benefits?
options: $1,000 per hour
$2,000 per hour
$4,000 per hour
$6,000 per hour
items.feedback: At Q = 40, Group A MB is $3,000 and Group B MB is $1,000. Their vertical sum gives MSB of $4,000 per hour.

items.stem: A gallon of gasoline is available only to a paying buyer and is gone after that buyer burns it. Which classification applies?
options: Public good
Private good
Common resource
Club good
items.feedback: Payment makes gasoline excludable and burning a gallon prevents anyone else from consuming that gallon, so it is rival.

items.stem: A missile-defense shield protects residents whether or not they contribute, and protecting one resident does not reduce protection for others. What is it?
options: Private good
Common resource
Public good
Club good
items.feedback: Noncontributors are difficult to exclude and protection is nonrival, so the shield has the defining characteristics of a public good.

items.stem: Herders may graze animals on unfenced public land, and added grazing leaves less forage for other herds. What is the land's use category?
options: Public good
Private good
Club good
Common resource
items.feedback: The open land is difficult to exclude, while forage is rival because one herd's consumption reduces what remains.

items.stem: A theater can check tickets at the door. What makes a performance excludable?
options: One audience member enjoys the performance
People without valid tickets can be denied entry
Several theaters compete for customers
The performance has a cultural benefit
items.feedback: Excludability asks whether access can feasibly be denied. Ticket inspection lets the theater prevent nonpayers from entering.

items.stem: Why does legal ownership not by itself guarantee excludability for offshore fish stocks?
options: Ownership makes fish nonrival
Legal rights eliminate migration
The boundary must also be monitored and enforced
Excludability depends only on market price
items.feedback: A right changes access only when violations can be detected and prevented. Mobile fish and costly monitoring can limit practical exclusion.

items.stem: An apartment building's rooftop is accessible only with a resident key. What does the key establish?
options: Nonrivalry at every crowding level
A lack of scarcity
Competition among landlords
Excludability
items.feedback: The key lets the building deny access to nonresidents. Whether resident use is rival depends on capacity and congestion.

items.stem: A swimming pool is nearly empty in the morning but packed in the afternoon. Which conclusion is best?
options: The pool is rival only when membership fees rise
Rivalry can emerge when congestion reduces swimming space
Excludability disappears when crowded
Its classification can never change during the day
items.feedback: With spare capacity, another swimmer may impose little cost. When crowded, added use reduces space and quality for others, making use rival.

items.stem: A public lecture is livestreamed with unlimited server capacity. Which use is nonrival?
options: Occupying the final seat in the hall
Taking the only printed handout
Watching the stream
Using the speaker's time for a private meeting
items.feedback: Another online viewer does not reduce the stream available to others, unlike scarce seats, handouts, or private time.

items.stem: A shared warning service costs $600 and will be provided only if fully funded. Four households each value it at $200; nonpayers cannot be excluded. Three have irrevocably contributed $150 each. What is the fourth household’s best choice if it cares only about its own net benefit?
options: Contribute the remaining $150: its contribution is pivotal and leaves a $50 net benefit.
Contribute nothing: a nonpayer can enjoy the service even if it is never funded.
Contribute $200: full willingness to pay is the minimum needed to finish funding.
Contribute nothing: total social benefit below $600 makes the service inefficient.
items.feedback: The shortfall is 600 - 3 x 150 = $150. Without that payment the service is not provided; paying leaves 200 - 150 = $50. Nonexcludability creates free-riding incentives, but a pivotal contribution can still be privately worthwhile.

items.stem: A city asks households to report benefits from a proposed siren network before setting voluntary fees. What bias should analysts anticipate?
options: Households must overstate benefits because sirens are rival
Households may understate benefits to avoid paying
Reported benefits automatically equal MSB
Only businesses can free ride
items.feedback: A household may hope others finance the network while it still receives warnings, so stated willingness to pay can be biased downward.

items.stem: A voluntary radio drive raises enough for 30 hours even though listeners collectively value 50 hours above cost. What explains the gap?
options: The radio hours are depleted by listening
Marginal social benefit must be below private benefit
Private contributions omit some benefits enjoyed by noncontributors
The fundraiser makes the signal excludable
items.feedback: Free riding causes revealed private contributions to fall short of total social willingness to pay, so funded programming can remain below the efficient amount.

items.stem: Why might a donation-funded flood barrier be smaller than the efficient barrier?
options: Individual donations may not capture benefits received by noncontributors
Flood protection is consumed by one donor at a time
Donations make marginal cost negative
Efficient provision ignores social benefits
items.feedback: Noncontributors still receive protection, so voluntary revenue can understate total social willingness to pay and finance too little protection.

items.stem: Why is cost-benefit analysis difficult when a public good has no ordinary market price?
options: Public goods have no opportunity cost
Marginal benefit cannot be positive
Analysts lack a direct price signal revealing beneficiaries' willingness to pay
Market prices always overstate social value
items.feedback: Without ordinary purchases and prices, analysts must estimate benefits that market transactions do not directly reveal.

items.stem: Which statement best compares efficient provision of a public good with an ordinary private good?
options: Public goods ignore marginal cost
Private goods require vertical summation of all buyers at one quantity
Public goods are efficient whenever government supplies them
Both use marginal benefit versus marginal cost, but public-good benefit is harder to observe and aggregate
items.feedback: The same marginal efficiency principle applies, but nonexcludability, free riding, dispersed benefits, and missing market prices make public-good MSB harder to estimate.

items.stem: A shared irrigation canal has ample water this month, but supply is scarce during drought. Which statement is best?
options: The canal is always nonrival because it is shared
Drought automatically creates excludability
Government ownership eliminates depletion
Rivalry can become important when withdrawals reduce water available to others
items.feedback: When water is scarce, one user's withdrawal directly reduces availability for others, strengthening common-resource incentives.

items.stem: An open-access fishery is biologically sustainable at 1,000 tons, but total intended catch is 1,400 tons. What is the current issue?
options: The fishery is underprovided by 400 tons
Planned harvest exceeds the sustainable shared-resource limit
Fish consumption is nonrival
Private firms cannot harvest fish
items.feedback: Total intended catch exceeds the sustainable amount by 400 tons, consistent with open-access incentives for excessive harvest.

items.stem: A lake's water quality falls as unrestricted boat traffic rises. Which fact is necessary for a common-resource diagnosis?
options: A government agency owns the lake
Boat makers compete
Some visitors dislike boating
Additional use reduces the quality available to other users
items.feedback: The diagnosis requires rival use: added traffic must diminish water quality or enjoyment available to others while access remains difficult to exclude.

items.stem: A fishery announces a total catch limit, but fishers can hide landings at unmonitored docks. Which complementary change most directly addresses the reason actual harvest can exceed the announced limit?
options: Allocate paper quotas equally while leaving all landings unobserved.
Measure landings across docks and enforce catch rights against unreported harvest.
Let quota holders trade on paper while leaving hidden catches unpenalized.
Pay a subsidy per landed fish while keeping detection unchanged.
items.feedback: A limit constrains actual use only if catches are measured and violations matter. Equal allocations and trading can affect distribution or compliance cost, but neither resolves this stated monitoring gap by itself.

items.stem: How can enforceable fishing rights reduce overharvesting?
options: Right holders bear more of the loss from depleting the future stock
Rights make fish nonrival
Rights eliminate every monitoring cost
Rights guarantee equal income for fishers
items.feedback: A secure claim to future harvest gives the holder a reason to preserve stock value rather than race to take fish before others do.

items.stem: A village assigns each household a monitored groundwater allowance. What incentive changes?
options: Groundwater becomes nonrival
Future scarcity disappears
Households face a clearer limit on the opportunity cost of withdrawal
Every household must pump its full allowance
items.feedback: A monitored allowance replaces unrestricted access with enforceable use rights, reducing the incentive to pump before others do.

items.stem: A regulator says any tax that reduces sales will fully correct the externality. What tax per garment is appropriate here, and why is reducing quantity alone insufficient?
options: $6 per unit; the tax must match the marginal external cost, so direction alone is insufficient.
$4 per unit; the tax must match the marginal external cost, so direction alone is insufficient.
$6 per unit; any positive tax is equally efficient once it reduces quantity.
$4 per unit; any positive tax is equally efficient once it reduces quantity.
items.feedback: MPC–MPB Q = 240; MSC–MPB Q = 160; at Q = 160, MSC = $15 and MPC = $9. The required wedge is $6. A smaller tax leaves excess quantity; a larger one can overcorrect. The regulator must calibrate size as well as direction.

items.stem: A regulator says any tax that reduces sales will fully correct the externality. What tax per vape is appropriate here, and why is reducing quantity alone insufficient?
options: $2 per unit; the tax must match the marginal external cost, so direction alone is insufficient.
$4 per unit; the tax must match the marginal external cost, so direction alone is insufficient.
$4 per unit; any positive tax is equally efficient once it reduces quantity.
$2 per unit; any positive tax is equally efficient once it reduces quantity.
items.feedback: MPB–MPC Q = 180; MSB–MPC Q = 140; at Q = 140, MPB = $12 and MSB = $8. The required wedge is $4. A smaller tax leaves excess quantity; a larger one can overcorrect. The regulator must calibrate size as well as direction.

items.stem: Based on the graph, how much overconsumption remains after the imperfect $2 vaping tax?
options: 40 thousand vapes
140 thousand vapes
20 thousand vapes
160 thousand vapes
items.feedback: The tax reduces consumption to 160 thousand vapes, while efficiency requires MPC to intersect MSB at 140 thousand. The remaining overconsumption is 20 thousand vapes.

items.stem: A permit system has a fixed cap but severe monitoring failures. What risk follows?
options: Monitoring guarantees lower costs
Permit price becomes a subsidy
Initial allocation repairs enforcement
Unrecorded emissions can exceed the legal cap
items.feedback: The cap requires enforceable emissions records. A cap is effective only when emissions are measured and permits are enforced; unrecorded emissions break the link between permits and actual pollution.

items.stem: Why can community norms reduce an externality without guaranteeing full efficiency?
options: Norms always make marginal social benefit equal marginal social cost
Norms eliminate all transaction costs
Coverage and enforcement may be incomplete
Voluntary action cannot affect spillovers
items.feedback: Private institutions can help without fully internalizing harm. Norms can change behavior, but incomplete participation and weak enforcement can leave some marginal external harm outside private decisions.

items.stem: A pollution bargain has poor information and strategic holdouts among thousands. Which Coase condition is weakest?
options: Scarcity
Downward demand
Low transaction and bargaining costs
Government tax collection
items.feedback: Information, coordination, and holdouts make bargaining costly. Poor information, many participants, and strategic holdouts raise the cost of reaching and enforcing agreement, undermining the low-transaction-cost assumption.

items.stem: A county hires a private contractor to operate emergency sirens. Does private operation make the warning a private good?
options: Yes; any privately produced service is a private good
Yes; contracts make warnings rival
No; all government purchases are common resources
No; classification still depends on excludability and rivalry
items.feedback: Who produces or purchases the service is separate from its consumption characteristics. An area-wide warning can remain nonexcludable and nonrival.

items.stem: An analyst values a public-health information campaign using only benefits to people who completed a survey. What may be missing?
options: The campaign's excludability must be zero
Every unobserved benefit is a cost
Benefits to affected people who were not identified or surveyed
Only the producer's profit matters
items.feedback: Public-good benefits can be dispersed, so failing to identify all affected beneficiaries understates marginal social benefit.

items.stem: A fishery uses quotas, but regulators cannot observe illegal catch. What complicates the remedy?
options: Enforcement and information constraints affect performance
Any intervention is automatically costless
Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
Administrative incentives and information do not matter
items.feedback: Compare feasible responses, administrative costs, information limits, and unintended effects.

items.stem: A poor neighborhood lacks groceries because operating costs are high. Why is failure not automatic?
options: Undesirability alone does not prove an efficiency wedge
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
A high price by itself establishes market failure
items.feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

items.stem: A password is shared widely and the provider cannot identify unauthorized users. What limits effective excludability?
options: Authorized use becomes rival automatically
The access rule is difficult to enforce
The service has no marginal cost
The provider is privately owned
items.feedback: A nominal password rule does not create strong exclusion when unauthorized use cannot be detected or stopped.

items.stem: The graph shows a corrective tax that reduces output from the unregulated equilibrium to the socially efficient level. How much more do buyers pay, how much less do sellers receive, and how is the tax burden shared?
options: Buyers pay $2 more and sellers receive $4 less; sellers bear two-thirds of the tax.
Buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less; sellers bear the entire tax.
Buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less; the burden is shared equally.
Buyers pay $2 more and sellers receive $4 less; buyers bear two-thirds of the tax.
items.feedback: Before the tax, price is $12. At the efficient quantity, buyers pay $15 and sellers receive $9. Each side bears $3 of the $6 tax, so the burden is shared equally.

items.stem: A regulator says the dashed, tax-adjusted curve achieves full efficiency because it intersects MPC. How much of the private-social benefit gap remains, and how far is the resulting quantity from the efficient quantity?
options: It remains $2 above MSB and yields 160 rather than 140 thousand vapes; private equilibrium need not be socially efficient.
It remains $1 above MSB and yields 150 rather than 140 thousand vapes; private equilibrium need not be socially efficient.
It remains $2 above MSB and yields 160 rather than 140 thousand vapes; any intersection with MPC establishes full efficiency.
It remains $1 above MSB and yields 150 rather than 140 thousand vapes; any intersection with MPC establishes full efficiency.
items.feedback: The dashed curve is $2 above MSB. Its intersection with MPC is 160 thousand rather than the social 140 thousand. Clearing a market with a remaining private-social gap does not remove the externality distortion.

items.stem: Compare the taxed quantity with the unregulated and socially efficient quantities. How much overconsumption remains, and has the tax partly or fully corrected the problem?
options: 10 thousand vapes remain above the efficient quantity; the tax improves efficiency without fully restoring it.
20 thousand vapes remain above the efficient quantity; any reduction from the private quantity proves full efficiency.
10 thousand vapes remain above the efficient quantity; any reduction from the private quantity proves full efficiency.
20 thousand vapes remain above the efficient quantity; the tax improves efficiency without fully restoring it.
items.feedback: The private quantity is 180 thousand, the taxed quantity 160 thousand and social efficiency 140 thousand. The tax reduces the distortion but leaves 20 thousand excess vapes and a residual welfare loss.

items.stem: A crop price rises after a drought reduces harvests. A separate processing plant also discharges unpriced waste into a river. Which diagnosis and targeted response distinguish scarcity from market failure?
options: Drought: scarcity; unpriced waste: external cost; target the waste.
Drought and waste: market failures; a price ceiling corrects both.
Drought and waste: efficient outcomes; neither needs a policy response.
Drought: asymmetric information; waste: a transfer; target the information gap.
items.feedback: A supply loss can raise a competitive price without creating a distortion. Unpriced harm omits social cost from the private decision and calls for a response to that specific wedge.

items.stem: Buyers cannot observe product risk before purchase. Mandatory disclosure accurately reports it, but only in a format most buyers cannot interpret. A simplified tested label helps buyers compare risks at lower reading cost. Which comparison is defensible?
options: Both formats necessarily eliminate the information problem because both are accurate.
Both address the information gap; the tested label makes risk information more usable.
The unreadable format corrects an externality; the label creates monopoly power.
Neither addresses market failure because information costs cannot affect gains from trade.
items.feedback: The original problem is an information gap about risk. Disclosure must be usable to affect choices; evidence about comprehension and behavior distinguishes formal disclosure from an effective remedy.

items.stem: A corrective policy would prevent $120 of external harm while using $35 of compliance resources and $100 of administrative resources. A simpler policy prevents $80 of harm and uses $20 in total resources. Which recommendation follows from these estimates alone?
options: Full policy: +$85; simpler policy: +$60; choose the full policy.
Full policy: +$60; simpler policy: +$60; either policy is equally good.
Full policy: −$15; simpler policy: +$60; choose the simpler policy.
Full policy: −$15; simpler policy: −$20; choose neither policy.
items.feedback: Net benefits are 120−35−100=−15 and 80−20=60. The scale of the original failure does not make every proposed correction worthwhile.

items.stem: Suppose the community currently has 30 emergency sirens. What does the graph imply about one more siren?
options: Its marginal cost exceeds its marginal social benefit
Its marginal social benefit is zero
Its marginal social benefit exceeds its marginal cost
Its provision cannot affect net social benefit
items.feedback: At 30 sirens, the graph shows MSB of $25,000 and MC of $20,000. Another siren adds more social benefit than cost, so expanding provision raises net social benefit.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the MC curve in the emergency-sirens graph?
options: Total siren cost is fixed at $20,000
Marginal cost falls by $500 per siren
Only the first siren has a cost
Each additional siren costs $20,000 over the shown range
items.feedback: The horizontal MC curve is at 20 on an axis measured in thousands of dollars per siren, so each additional siren costs $20,000; total cost is not fixed.

items.stem: Based on the two intersections shown in the graph, how much lower is private provision than efficient provision?
options: 40 hours per week
20 hours per week
60 hours per week
80 hours per week
items.feedback: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours while MSB intersects MC at 80 hours. The underprovision gap is 80 - 40 = 40 hours.

items.stem: For nonexcludable radio programming, which change could let a private organization provide more programming despite free riding?
options: Making the signal more nonexcludable
A sponsorship contract that pays for audience-wide benefits
Ignoring benefits to noncontributors
Assuming every listener voluntarily reveals full willingness to pay
items.feedback: A sponsorship contract supplies an alternative revenue mechanism that can capture some audience-wide benefit even when nonpayers cannot be excluded from the signal.

items.stem: A fall in aggregate demand reduces national output, while some firms cut employment more than others. What levels of analysis are present?
options: Only microeconomic analysis because the firms are the ones changing employment.
Macro analysis of the overall contraction and micro analysis of firm responses.
Only macro analysis.
Neither, because both use employment data.
items.feedback: The aggregate shock is macroeconomic; heterogeneous firm choices are microeconomic.

items.stem: A tax changes one product’s price and also affects total consumer spending. Why might both fields be needed?
options: The tax eliminates the distinction between fields.
Only macroeconomics is needed because total consumer spending changes.
Macroeconomics studies only government budgets.
Microeconomics studies the product market; macroeconomics studies aggregate spending.
items.feedback: One event can have market-level and economy-wide consequences.

items.stem: A tariff raises prices in one steel market, while a second study estimates its effect on the overall price level. How do the studies differ?
options: The first is micro; the second is macro
Both are micro because both use prices
The first is macro; the second is micro
Both are macro because a tariff is policy
items.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

items.stem: A drought reduces one region’s wheat supply and later contributes to national food inflation. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Inflation is always one-market analysis
The event has market-level and aggregate dimensions
Weather makes the question noneconomic
Food prices are always only microeconomic
items.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

items.stem: One factory closes while the national unemployment rate falls. What prevents a contradiction?
options: Macroeconomic data exclude factory workers
Firm closures always raise national employment
A single firm outcome need not match the national aggregate
The unemployment rate describes only one industry
items.feedback: Macro conclusions require appropriate aggregation across people, firms, and markets.

items.stem: Which research design is most clearly microeconomic despite using a very large dataset?
options: Estimating how individual consumers respond to a change in one product’s price.
Measuring national inflation over time, because all price questions are economy-wide
Explaining long-run growth in real GDP per person.
Forecasting the economy-wide unemployment rate.
items.feedback: Microeconomics can use massive data while focusing on individual choices and specific markets.

items.stem: Which statement best characterizes the boundary between micro and macro?
options: Microeconomics studies prices and firms, while macroeconomics studies government policy
The distinction concerns the level and aggregation of the question, not an absolute separation of topics.
Any government policy is automatically macroeconomic
Firm-level outcomes cannot contribute to macroeconomic outcomes.
items.feedback: Many issues can be studied at both individual-market and aggregate levels.

items.stem: A study uses records from every firm to estimate how individual managers choose training. Another totals the resulting output changes across the economy. Which distinction is defensible?
options: The first is macro and the second micro because totals hide choices
The first asks a micro question; the second asks an aggregate macro question
Both are macro because the dataset covers the whole country
Both are micro because firms supply the observations
items.feedback: The question and unit of explanation determine scope. Nationwide firm records can support micro analysis; combining output changes to study the economy is macro analysis.

items.stem: A housing subsidy raises rents locally and changes national construction spending. What is the best approach?
options: Analyze both the market response and aggregate effect
Use macro only because spending is measured
Use micro only because rents change
Treat the two outcomes as unrelated
items.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

items.stem: One industry loses jobs while national employment grows. Which explanation is valid?
options: National employment excludes changes that occur within individual industries.
Sector change can differ from the aggregate
The industry result disproves the aggregate
Job data cannot cross levels
items.feedback: Macro conclusions require appropriate aggregation across people, firms, and markets.

items.stem: A federal rule applies to a narrowly defined appliance market. What determines its field?
options: The number of pages in the rule
Whether policymakers support it
The outcome and aggregation being studied
The federal source of the rule alone
items.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

items.stem: A delivery study predicts how adding a loading bay affects waiting time, holding staffing fixed. The depot adds a bay and hires loaders. Why can the observed change differ from the prediction?
options: The observation combines two changes; the model isolates one
The fixed-staffing assumption says loaders cannot affect waiting
A useful model must predict the combined change from the bay alone
Any difference shows loading space has no effect
items.feedback: Holding staffing fixed isolates the bay effect. Hiring loaders changes another influence, so the observed combined effect need not equal that conditional prediction.

items.stem: A model fits historical data but fails after institutions change. Which limitation is most relevant?
options: Relationships estimated under old rules may not remain stable.
Historical data can never be useful.
Institutions are outside economics.
Model assumptions matter only for graphs.
items.feedback: Institutional change can alter incentives and the parameters of a model.

items.stem: A service model favors shorter forms when training is unchanged, but favors the current forms when a plausible training delay is included. What should the analyst report?
options: A definite preference for shorter forms because simplification is the model's purpose
The ranking depends on the training assumption and needs evidence about that condition
Only the original ranking because the delay is not certain
An average recommendation without identifying why the ranking changed
items.feedback: A plausible change in training conditions reverses the result. Report that sensitivity and seek evidence about the condition instead of presenting either conditional ranking as guaranteed.

items.stem: A highly detailed model predicts poorly because many parameters are estimated imprecisely. What does this illustrate?
options: Simple models always predict perfectly.
Parameters have no role in models.
More complexity can add noise and does not guarantee better prediction.
Prediction quality depends only on graphics.
items.feedback: Extra detail can create estimation problems and overfitting.

items.stem: A housing model estimated where construction is flexible is applied where zoning is strict. What is the central concern?
options: Zoning makes housing demand irrelevant
A more detailed model must automatically be correct
The supply assumption may not transfer across cities
Historical estimates are always invalid elsewhere
items.feedback: Strict zoning violates the flexible-construction condition, so transferring the housing estimate may produce poor predictions.

items.stem: Two labor models fit past employment equally well. One predicts a wage rule raises jobs; the other predicts a decline. What evidence is most useful?
options: The policy outcome preferred by the researcher
Evidence from a setting where their predictions differ
More old observations both models already explain
The number of variables included in each model
items.feedback: Evidence from a wage-rule change targets the models’ conflicting employment predictions and is more informative than another shared-fit observation.

items.stem: A transit model worked before remote work became common but now overpredicts commuting. What should be reconsidered?
options: Whether any historical data can ever be useful
Whether commuting belongs in economics
Whether assumptions matter only in graphs
Whether the old behavioral relationship remains stable
items.feedback: Remote work changed the commuting relationship, so the model’s stability and workplace-attendance assumptions need reassessment.

items.stem: A model uses an unrealistic assumption but predicts well in a narrow setting. What is the strongest evaluation?
options: Judge whether the abstraction serves that narrow purpose
Reject the model because every assumption must be literal
Accept the model for all settings without further checks
Treat predictive fit as proof of the assumed mechanism
items.feedback: A simplifying assumption need not be literally realistic if the model predicts well for the narrow question and setting in which it is used.

items.stem: A complex model predicts purchases accurately, while a simpler model identifies a price mechanism. Which model should be preferred?
options: Always choose the simple model regardless of performance
Average the models because mechanisms cannot be tested
Choose according to whether prediction or explanation is the goal
Always choose the complex model because it has better fit
items.feedback: Forecast accuracy favors the complex model for prediction, while the simpler model may be better for identifying and communicating the price mechanism.

items.stem: Two models fit past data, but only one predicts behavior after a new fee. What evidence best separates them?
options: The recommendation preferred by the policymaker
Evidence from the new fee setting where predictions differ
More past outcomes both models already reproduce
The relative length of the two model descriptions
items.feedback: The new fee creates an out-of-sample case where the models disagree, so observed post-fee behavior can distinguish them.

items.stem: A policy conclusion disappears when one plausible assumption changes. What is the strongest evaluation?
options: The conclusion is sensitive and should be qualified
The original conclusion remains fully robust
The alternate assumption should be hidden from users
The model is useless for every other question
items.feedback: A conclusion that disappears under one plausible assumption is fragile and should be reported with that sensitivity clearly stated.

items.stem: A larger model fits old data better but predicts new data worse. What does this show?
options: Historical fit proves the larger model is superior
Prediction quality depends only on equation length
The smaller model must omit every relevant mechanism
Added complexity can overfit rather than improve transfer
items.feedback: Better historical fit paired with worse new-data prediction is evidence of overfitting rather than a general gain from complexity.

items.stem: During a panic, banks hold excess reserves and households withdraw deposits into currency. What happens to the money multiplier?
options: It falls below the simple multiplier prediction.
It rises above the simple multiplier prediction.
It becomes equal to the reserve requirement.
It becomes unrelated to bank behavior.
items.feedback: Both excess reserves and currency withdrawals weaken deposit creation, so the actual multiplier falls.

items.stem: If the public suddenly deposits more currency into banks and banks lend excess reserves, what happens to the banking system's ability to create money?
options: It increases because deposits and reserves available for lending rise.
It decreases because deposits destroy reserves.
It stays unchanged because deposits are never lent.
It disappears because money becomes fiat.
items.feedback: When currency becomes bank deposits, banks have more deposits and reserves to support lending.

items.stem: A central bank wants to expand lending but banks are already holding large excess reserves. Which issue is most relevant?
options: Bank willingness to lend may limit money creation.
Commodity money must replace fiat money.
M1 must exclude checking deposits.
Velocity must be exactly zero.
items.feedback: More reserves do not guarantee more lending if banks are unwilling to lend.

items.stem: A Fed bond purchase increases reserves, but households convert much of the new deposits into currency. What is the likely result?
options: The money supply rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply rises by more than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply cannot rise at all because bonds were purchased.
Currency holdings make the reserve requirement negative.
items.feedback: Currency drain limits redepositing, so the multiplier effect is weaker.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why banks cannot make society rich simply by creating more money through lending?
options: Creating money does not automatically create real goods and services.
Every bank loan creates new factories instantly.
Money creation permanently increases real output without limits.
The money supply is unrelated to prices or output.
items.feedback: Banks can help create money, but real wealth depends on real goods, services, labor, capital, and productivity.

items.stem: A bank receives new deposits, the Fed pays higher interest on reserves, and banks choose to hold more excess reserves. What is the likely result?
options: Money creation weakens because lending falls
Money creation strengthens because deposits rose
The multiplier becomes unrelated to reserves
M1 falls because deposits are excluded
items.feedback: Deposits increase lending potential, but higher interest on reserves can make banks hold reserves instead of lending them.

items.stem: The Fed buys bonds during a banking panic, but households increase currency holdings and banks increase excess reserves. What should students infer?
options: Fed control is limited by depositor and bank behavior
The money multiplier must rise to its maximum
Open-market purchases cannot affect reserves
Currency holdings are excluded from M1
items.feedback: Fed purchases add reserves, but currency withdrawals and excess reserve holdings can weaken money creation.

items.stem: The Fed buys $30 million in bonds. The reserve ratio is 10 percent, but banks hold half of new reserves as excess reserves. Which answer best describes the actual result compared with the simple multiplier maximum?
options: The actual money increase is less than the $300 million simple multiplier maximum.
The actual money increase equals exactly $300 million.
The actual money increase exceeds $300 million because excess reserves multiply faster.
The money supply must fall because bond purchases are contractionary.
items.feedback: The simple maximum would be $30 million x 10 = $300 million, but excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

items.stem: A student says, 'If the Fed lowers reserve requirements, the money supply must always rise by the maximum multiplier amount.' What is the best correction?
options: The maximum depends on banks lending excess reserves and borrowers redepositing funds.
Lower reserve requirements always eliminate excess reserves.
The money supply must fall when reserve requirements fall.
Reserve requirements affect only fiscal policy.
items.feedback: The simple multiplier is a maximum under strict assumptions. Banks and the public can weaken the actual money creation process.

items.stem: The public withdraws $50 million from checking deposits into currency. The reserve ratio is 10 percent. Why can the final money supply fall by more than $50 million?
options: The withdrawal removes reserves from banks and reduces further deposit creation.
Currency automatically multiplies faster than deposits.
Banks gain excess reserves from the withdrawal.
Reserve requirements become negative.
items.feedback: A currency drain reduces bank reserves and shrinks the base for additional lending, so the total effect can exceed the initial withdrawal.

items.stem: If the Fed buys $100 million in bonds but the public holds all proceeds as currency instead of depositing them, which part of the simple multiplier process breaks?
options: Redepositing into banks, which limits further lending.
The initial Fed injection, which never occurs.
The definition of fiat money.
The unit of account function.
items.feedback: The money enters the public's hands, but if it is not deposited, banks cannot use it as reserves for further lending.

items.stem: Which answer best explains why lowering the discount rate may not create much lending during a crisis?
options: Banks may still consider borrowers too risky.
Lower borrowing costs always force banks to lend.
The discount rate controls tax rates, not bank borrowing.
Lower discount rates automatically create commodity money.
items.feedback: Lowering the discount rate helps only if banks are willing to borrow and lend.

items.stem: The Fed buys $80 million in bonds. The simple reserve ratio is 20 percent, but banks hold 25 percent of new reserves as excess reserves instead of lending them. Which answer best describes the result?
options: The money supply rises by less than the $400 million simple multiplier maximum.
The money supply rises by exactly $400 million.
The money supply rises by more than $400 million because excess reserves multiply.
The money supply falls because bond purchases are contractionary.
items.feedback: The simple multiplier maximum is 1/0.20 = 5, so $80 million could become $400 million. But excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

items.stem: The Fed sells $75 million in bonds. The multiplier is 4, but the public responds by moving additional funds out of banks into currency. What should we expect relative to the simple multiplier result?
options: The contraction may exceed $300 million because currency drain further weakens deposit creation.
The contraction must equal exactly $300 million.
The money supply must increase because bond sales add reserves.
The contraction must be smaller because currency drain raises bank reserves.
items.feedback: The simple contraction is $75 million x 4 = $300 million, but currency drain can make the banking contraction larger.

items.stem: A bank has a reserve shortfall of $20,000. The Fed lowers the discount rate, but the bank still refuses to borrow because it fears insolvency. What does this show?
options: Risk concerns can outweigh the incentive of cheaper borrowing.
The discount rate only affects fiscal policy.
Lower discount rates always force borrowing.
Reserve shortfalls increase lending capacity.
items.feedback: The Fed can make borrowing cheaper, but banks may still avoid borrowing or lending when risk dominates.

items.stem: A new $100,000 deposit enters the banking system. The required reserve ratio is 10 percent, but the public withdraws 20 percent of every new loan as currency before redepositing the rest. What happens relative to the simple multiplier?
options: The final expansion is smaller than the simple $1,000,000 maximum.
The final expansion equals exactly $1,000,000.
The final expansion is larger because currency leakage increases reserves.
The money supply must contract because deposits increase.
items.feedback: The simple maximum is $100,000 x 10 = $1,000,000, but currency leakage reduces redeposits and weakens money creation.

items.stem: Why can the actual increase in bank deposits be smaller than the simple money multiplier predicts?
options: Banks may hold excess reserves, and the public may hold some funds as currency.
Fractional reserve banking gives the Fed exact control over the quantity of bank deposits.
The simple money multiplier applies only when banks lend commodity money to the public.
Currency withdrawn by the public adds to bank reserves and allows banks to lend more.
items.feedback: Fractional-reserve banking can multiply deposits, but excess reserves and currency holdings can make the actual expansion smaller than the simple model predicts.

items.stem: A bank has $2 million in assets and $120,000 in capital. If asset values fall by 4 percent, capital falls to:
items.feedback: A 4 percent asset loss is $80,000, so capital falls from $120,000 to $40,000.

items.stem: Households withdraw $220 from checking into currency while the total of M1 initially stays constant. In a bank-reserve model, which change can still weaken later deposit expansion?
options: Bank capital automatically rises by the currency withdrawal, raising lending capacity
M1 must fall initially because currency held by households is outside money
Banks lose reserves and deposits; unchanged initial M1 does not imply unchanged bank lending capacity
Banks gain reserves and deposits; currency withdrawals expand the redepositing base
items.feedback: Checking falls while public currency rises, initially preserving M1. The banking system loses reserves and a deposit liability; less reserve availability can constrain later deposit creation despite unchanged initial money.

items.stem: Two otherwise comparable banking systems receive $240 in reserves. In A, banks lend available funds and payments are redeposited. In B, banks hold additional reserves and customers retain more currency. Which comparison is supported?
options: A's expansion must be zero because redepositing cancels every loan
A can support a larger deposit expansion; the simple multiplier is less descriptive of B's behavior
B must support a larger expansion because holding reserves is itself lending
Both expansions must be equal because the required reserve ratio alone determines actual lending
items.feedback: Extra reserve holdings and currency retention reduce successive lending/redepositing rounds. The same reserve injection and formal required ratio need not produce the same actual multiplier.

items.stem: A simple deposit-expansion model with a 10% required reserve ratio predicts a $2600 deposit maximum from $260 in new reserves. Actual deposits rise only $1040. Which diagnosis and inference are justified?
options: Reserve hoarding or currency leakage can lower the expansion; the effective multiplier here is 4
The required ratio must be 25%; behavior can never lower expansion below the reciprocal rule
The banks must have created negative reserves because every prediction is an accounting identity
The shortfall proves the central bank cannot create reserves in the first place
items.feedback: Observed deposit growth divided by new reserves is 1040/260=4. The 1/rr rule is a maximum under restrictive assumptions, not a behavioral guarantee; the data alone do not uniquely identify which leakage caused the shortfall.

items.stem: A monetary expansion raises output temporarily, but years later output returns to its prior real trend while the price level remains permanently higher. Why is this consistent with monetary neutrality?
options: Neutrality describes the long-run separation of nominal changes from real output, not the absence of short-run real effects.
Neutrality requires the price level to return fully to its original level after every monetary expansion, even in the long run.
Neutrality means real output must remain permanently above trend after money growth.
Neutrality applies only when both output and prices are unchanged at every horizon.
items.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

items.stem: Nominal GDP rises 12 percent while real GDP rises 5 percent. What happened to the price level, and which kind of variable changed?
options: The price level rose about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level rose about 17 percent; that is a real change.
The price level fell about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level was unchanged; only real output changed.
items.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price growth is about 12 - 5 = 7 percent. The price level is nominal.

items.stem: A worker's nominal wage rises from $24 to $30 while the price level rises from 6 to 10. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls from 4 units to 3 units.
It rises from 4 units to 5 units.
It stays at 4 units.
It rises from 6 units to 10 units.
items.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It falls from 24/6 = 4 to 30/10 = 3 units.

items.stem: All nominal prices double except wages, which rise only 50 percent. What happens to real wages?
options: Real wages fall because nominal wages rise less than the price level.
Real wages rise because nominal wages rose.
Real wages are unchanged because all prices rose.
Real wages double because prices doubled.
items.feedback: Real wages depend on wages relative to prices. If wages rise 50 percent while prices double, real wages fall.

items.stem: A country's price level rises from 100 to 140, nominal wages rise from $20 to $24, and workers complain their purchasing power fell. What happened to real wages?
