options: They fell because wages rose 20 percent while prices rose 40 percent.
They rose because nominal wages rose.
They stayed the same because both wages and prices rose.
They doubled because the price level rose.
items.feedback: Nominal wages rose 20 percent, but prices rose 40 percent. Real wages fell.

items.stem: A student says, 'Since money is neutral, monetary policy cannot affect output during recessions.' Which correction is strongest?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run sticky prices allow AD effects on output.
Neutrality means money changes output permanently but not prices.
Neutrality applies only to fiscal policy and never to money.
Neutrality means the Phillips curve slopes downward in the long run.
items.feedback: Money is neutral in the long run, but monetary policy can affect output in the short run through aggregate demand.

items.stem: A worker's nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 while the price level rises from 4 to 5. What happens to the real wage?
options: It rises from 5 to 6 units of output.
It falls from 5 to 4 units of output.
It stays at 5 units of output.
It rises from 4 to 5 units of output.
items.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It rises from 20/4 = 5 to 30/5 = 6.

items.stem: The price of coffee rises from $4 to $8 while the price of tea rises from $2 to $3. What happens to the relative price of coffee in terms of tea?
options: It rises from 2 teas to about 2.67 teas.
It stays at 2 teas.
It falls from 2 teas to 1.5 teas.
It becomes 8 teas.
items.feedback: Coffee was 4/2 = 2 teas. It becomes 8/3, or about 2.67 teas.

items.stem: Assume stable velocity, unchanged real productive capacity, and monetary neutrality in the long run. Using the quantity theory of money, how does a permanent increase in money growth differ from a one-time increase in the money supply?
options: Faster money growth and a one-time increase both raise sustained inflation equally.
Faster money growth raises sustained inflation; a one-time increase raises the price level.
Faster money growth raises sustained real growth; a one-time increase raises real capacity.
Faster money growth and a one-time increase leave both nominal price measures unchanged.
items.feedback: Levels and growth rates differ: a lasting growth-rate change can sustain inflation, whereas a one-time level change is not ongoing faster money growth. Real capacity remains determined by the stated real factors.

items.stem: A worker initially earns $260 while the consumption-price index is 100. In a long-run monetary-neutrality comparison, nominal wages and all prices double while real technology and resources are unchanged. Which conclusion respects both nominal and real measures?
options: Nominal pay doubles while the real wage and long-run productive capacity can remain unchanged
The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double
Productive capacity doubles because a larger money stock is itself more real capital
Nominal pay is unchanged because neutrality freezes every monetary variable
items.feedback: A real wage is nominal wage divided by prices; doubling both preserves the ratio. Long-run neutrality permits nominal changes without corresponding changes in real productive capacity.

items.stem: The central bank unexpectedly expands money, real activity rises for a time, and later output returns to potential while nominal prices remain higher. Which statement best reconciles the episode?
options: Long-run neutrality is disproved whenever any short-run real effect occurs.
Neutrality requires output to remain permanently above potential.
The episode can be neutral only if the price level eventually falls below its starting point.
Short-run real effects can coexist with long-run monetary neutrality.
items.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

items.stem: Which sequence best describes a contractionary open-market operation?
options: Sell bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Buy bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Sell bonds, reserves rise, lending expands
Buy bonds, reserves rise, lending contracts
items.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, weakens lending, and reduces money creation.

items.stem: The Fed raises the discount rate and also raises interest on reserves. Which combined effect is most likely?
options: Banks borrow less from the Fed and may hold more reserves.
Banks borrow more from the Fed and lend every reserve.
Households automatically hold fewer dollars because taxes fall.
The money multiplier becomes infinite.
items.feedback: A higher discount rate discourages bank borrowing, and higher interest on reserves can encourage banks to hold reserves.

items.stem: The Fed adds reserves to support easier credit but raises the interest rate paid on reserve balances. Why might the higher reserve rate work against its objective?
options: It raises the return banks require from alternative lending.
It automatically removes the newly added reserve balances.
It lowers the return banks require from alternative lending.
It reduces the reserve requirement on bank deposits.
items.feedback: A higher return on reserve balances raises the opportunity cost of alternative lending and puts upward pressure on short-term rates. Adding reserves therefore does not by itself establish that credit conditions will ease.

items.stem: The Fed wants the money supply to fall by $180 million. If the money multiplier is 6 and banks fully lend according to the simple model, what open-market operation should the Fed conduct?
options: Sell $30 million in bonds.
Buy $30 million in bonds.
Sell $180 million in bonds.
Buy $1.08 billion in bonds.
items.feedback: To reduce money by $180 million with a multiplier of 6, the Fed sells $30 million in bonds.

items.stem: The Fed buys bonds while raising the interest rate paid on reserve balances. Which conclusion follows?
options: Reserves rise, but the reserve-rate increase pushes short-term rates upward.
Reserves fall, and both actions push short-term rates downward.
Reserves rise, so short-term rates must fall despite the reserve-rate increase.
Reserves stay fixed because the higher reserve rate cancels the purchases.
items.feedback: Bond purchases add reserve balances. Raising the rate paid on those balances puts upward pressure on short-term market rates. The reserve increase alone does not establish the net effect on lending or spending.

items.stem: In a hypothetical scarce-reserves system with a binding reserve requirement, which package combines actions that reduce lending capacity with incentives to reduce lending?
options: Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds and lowers the discount rate.
Fed lowers reserve requirements and buys bonds.
items.feedback: Bond sales reduce reserves and a higher reserve requirement reduces lending capacity in this model. A higher return on reserve balances also makes alternative lending less attractive.

items.stem: In a hypothetical scarce-reserves system with a binding reserve requirement, which package combines actions that expand lending capacity with incentives to expand lending?
options: Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds and raises the discount rate.
Fed raises reserve requirements and pays banks more to hold reserves.
items.feedback: Bond purchases add reserves and a lower reserve requirement increases lending capacity in this model. A lower return on reserve balances also makes alternative lending more attractive.

items.stem: A bank has $400,000 in deposits and $80,000 in reserves. The required reserve ratio rises from 10 percent to 20 percent. What happens to excess reserves?
options: They fall from $40,000 to $0.
They rise from $40,000 to $80,000.
They fall from $80,000 to $40,000.
They stay at $80,000.
items.feedback: At 10 percent, required reserves are $40,000 and excess reserves are $40,000. At 20 percent, required reserves are $80,000 and excess reserves are $0.

items.stem: A bank has $400,000 in deposits and $80,000 in reserves. The required reserve ratio falls from 20 percent to 10 percent. What new lending capacity is created?
items.feedback: Required reserves fall from $80,000 to $40,000, creating $40,000 in excess reserves.

items.stem: If the Fed sells bonds and the public pays with checking deposits, what is the direct effect on bank reserves and the money supply process?
options: Bank reserves fall, weakening deposit creation.
Bank reserves rise, strengthening deposit creation.
Bank reserves stay fixed, but taxes rise.
Bank reserves become commodity money.
items.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, payment leaves bank deposits and reserves fall, reducing money creation.

items.stem: If the Fed buys bonds from the public and sellers deposit the proceeds, what is the direct effect on bank reserves and the money supply process?
options: Bank reserves rise, supporting deposit creation.
Bank reserves fall, weakening deposit creation.
Taxes rise, reducing consumption.
Reserve requirements automatically rise to 100 percent.
items.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, money enters bank deposits and reserves rise, supporting lending and deposit creation.

items.stem: A bank has $2,400,000 in deposits, $360,000 in reserves, and a reserve requirement of 10 percent. The reserve requirement then rises to 15 percent. What happens to excess reserves?
options: They fall from $120,000 to $0.
They rise from $120,000 to $360,000.
They fall from $360,000 to $240,000.
They rise from $0 to $120,000.
items.feedback: At 10 percent, required reserves are $240,000, so excess reserves are $120,000. At 15 percent, required reserves are $360,000, leaving zero excess reserves.

items.stem: The Fed cuts the discount rate, buys bonds, and lowers interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Bank borrowing and reserves rise, lending incentives strengthen, and the money supply tends to expand.
Bank reserves fall, lending incentives weaken, and the money supply contracts.
Taxes fall, consumption rises, and fiscal policy expands.
The money supply is unaffected because only fiscal policy matters.
items.feedback: All three actions push toward monetary expansion: cheaper Fed borrowing, more reserves, and less reward for holding reserves idle.

items.stem: The Fed raises the discount rate, sells bonds, and raises interest on reserves. Overall, what effect does this policy package tend to have?
options: Bank borrowing and deposit creation weaken.
Bank borrowing and deposit creation expand.
Government spending rises and taxes fall.
Money demand falls to zero.
items.feedback: That policy package tightens money through costlier borrowing, fewer reserves, and stronger incentives to hold reserves.

items.stem: A bank has $10 million in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It holds $1.4 million in reserves. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 12 percent and banks lend all remaining excess reserves. How much can the bank lend after the change?
options: $1.2 million
$1.4 million
items.feedback: New required reserves are 0.12 x $10 million = $1.2 million. With $1.4 million in reserves, the bank can lend $200,000.

items.stem: A hypothetical bank has $600,000 in deposits and $90,000 in reserves. The required-reserve ratio rises from 10 to 15 percent. The bank cannot obtain new reserves, and any additional loan payment would settle at another bank. Which conclusion distinguishes its reserve position from its ability to expand?
options: It meets the new requirement exactly, but has no excess reserves for an outgoing loan.
It has a $30,000 reserve deficit and must obtain reserves just to comply.
It retains $30,000 of excess reserves because deposits have not changed.
It must shrink deposits by $90,000 even if it makes no new loan.
items.feedback: Required reserves rise from $60,000 to $90,000, exactly equal to actual reserves. The bank is compliant but the specified settlement constraint prevents further outgoing lending without adjustment.

items.stem: In a simplified reserve-ratio exercise, a bank has deposits of $3000 and reserves of $600. The required ratio rises from 10% to 15%, with balances otherwise unchanged. Which result and limitation are correct?
options: Excess reserves: $300→$150; actual lending must fall by exactly $150.
Excess reserves: $300→$450; the higher ratio releases $150 for additional lending.
Excess reserves: $300→$150; actual lending also depends on bank and borrower responses.
Capital: $300→$150; the higher reserve requirement writes down assets by $150.
items.feedback: Old required reserves=300; new required reserves=.15×3000=450. Excess falls from 300 to 150. Balance-sheet capacity is not a complete behavioral lending forecast.

items.stem: A policy package supplies $320 of reserves but also increases the return banks can earn by holding reserves. What can be concluded about bank lending?
options: Reserve capacity increases, holding reserves becomes more attractive; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity increases, holding reserves becomes more attractive; the net lending response remains uncertain.
Reserve capacity decreases, holding reserves becomes more attractive; both changes discourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity increases, the return on reserves is irrelevant; a fixed multiplier determines lending.
items.feedback: Reserve availability and the incentive to hold reserves are different margins. Their combination does not determine lending without the relevant behavior, risk, demand and magnitudes.

items.stem: In an explicitly simplified scarce-reserves model, a central bank buys $340 of securities from banks while the required ratio is unchanged. Which balance-sheet change begins the expansionary transmission?
options: Bank securities fall and reserves rise; easier reserve conditions can support lower short-term rates and lending
Bank securities rise and reserves fall; tighter reserve conditions support lower short-term rates
Bank capital rises by the purchase amount; no reserve or securities asset changes
Government tax liabilities fall by the purchase amount; reserves are unaffected
items.feedback: The purchase exchanges securities for reserve balances on bank balance sheets. Under the stated scarce-reserves model, greater reserve availability eases money-market conditions; it is not a fiscal tax cut or automatic equity gain.

items.stem: A central bank wants to close a recessionary AD gap without fiscal policy. Which chain is most accurate?
options: Buy bonds, lower rates, raise investment, shift AD right
Sell bonds, lower rates, raise investment, shift AD right
Buy bonds, raise rates, reduce investment, shift AD left
Sell bonds, raise rates, raise investment, shift AD left
items.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy buys bonds, increases money supply, lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

items.stem: Which chain best explains expansionary monetary policy in the short run?
options: Fed buys bonds, money supply rises, interest rate falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
Fed sells bonds, money supply rises, interest rate falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
Fed buys bonds, money supply falls, interest rate rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
Fed raises taxes, money demand falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
items.feedback: Buying bonds increases money supply, lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

items.stem: Which chain best explains contractionary monetary policy in the short run?
options: Fed sells bonds, money supply falls, interest rate rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
Fed buys bonds, money supply falls, interest rate rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
Fed sells bonds, money supply rises, interest rate falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
Fed cuts taxes, interest rates rise, AD shifts left.
items.feedback: Selling bonds reduces money supply, raises interest rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

items.stem: If the Fed reduces the money supply, which sequence is most likely?
options: Money supply shifts left, interest rates rise, and AD shifts left.
Money supply shifts right, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
Money demand shifts left, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
Money supply shifts left, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
items.feedback: A lower money supply raises interest rates, reduces investment, and shifts AD left.

items.stem: If the Fed increases money supply, which sequence is most likely?
options: Money supply shifts right, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
Money supply shifts left, interest rates rise, and AD shifts left.
Money demand shifts right, interest rates rise, and AD shifts left.
Money supply shifts right, interest rates rise, and AD shifts left.
items.feedback: A higher money supply lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

items.stem: A stock market crash reduces household wealth and aggregate demand. Which Fed response best stabilizes output?
options: Increase money supply and lower interest rates.
Decrease money supply and raise interest rates.
Raise taxes and lower government spending.
Sell bonds to reduce investment.
items.feedback: A negative AD shock calls for expansionary monetary policy if the goal is stabilizing output.

items.stem: An economy is overheating because aggregate demand is too high. Which Fed response best reduces inflation pressure?
options: Reduce money supply and raise interest rates.
Increase money supply and lower interest rates.
Buy bonds to raise investment.
Lower reserve requirements to shift AD right.
items.feedback: To reduce inflation pressure from excessive AD, the Fed can tighten money and raise interest rates.

items.stem: Which explanation fits A to B across the two panels?
options: Less money supply raises the rate, restrains interest-sensitive spending and lowers output and prices through AD.
More money supply lowers the rate, stimulates interest-sensitive spending and raises output and prices through AD.
More money demand raises the rate, restrains spending and lowers output and prices through AD.
More money supply lowers the rate and raises output by shifting SRAS right rather than changing spending.
items.feedback: The left panel shows MS increasing and the rate falling from 6% to 4%. The right panel shows higher AD, output and prices on unchanged SRAS. This is spending transmission, not a supply-capacity change.

items.stem: What explains the changes from A to B in the two panels?
options: Money demand increases; higher borrowing costs restrain spending, shifting AD left on unchanged SRAS.
Money supply expands; lower borrowing costs stimulate spending, shifting AD right on unchanged SRAS.
Money supply contracts; lower productive capacity directly shifts SRAS left while AD stays fixed.
Money supply contracts; higher borrowing costs restrain spending, shifting AD left on unchanged SRAS.
items.feedback: MS1 lies left of MS0, raising the rate from 2.75% to 4% on unchanged MD0. Spending and AD fall, producing lower output and prices along the same SRAS. Higher money demand could give similar rate pressure, but is not the change shown.

items.stem: Which explanation connects the changes from MS1 to MS2 and AD1 to AD2?
options: Money supply falls, raising the rate and reducing investment and aggregate demand.
Money supply rises, lowering the rate and increasing investment and aggregate demand.
Money demand rises, raising the rate and reducing investment and aggregate demand.
Money supply falls, raising the rate and lowering output by reducing long-run productive capacity.
items.feedback: MS2 is left of MS1, with the rate rising from r 1 to r 2. Lower investment then reduces demand from AD1 to AD2. The money-demand curve and productive capacity are not the mechanisms that changed.

items.stem: If the Fed shifts money supply right, which chain correctly reaches aggregate demand?
options: MS rises, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MS rises, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MS falls, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MD rises, r rises, investment rises, AD shifts right.
items.feedback: More money lowers the interest rate, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

items.stem: If the Fed shifts money supply left, which chain correctly reaches aggregate demand?
options: MS falls, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MS falls, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MS rises, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MD falls, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
items.feedback: Less money raises the interest rate, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

items.stem: If the Fed increases money supply but investment barely responds to the lower interest rate, what happens to the AD shift?
options: AD shifts right by less than usual because the investment channel is weak.
AD shifts right by more because investment does not matter.
AD must shift left because lower r reduces investment.
AD cannot move because money supply changed.
items.feedback: Monetary policy works through investment. If investment barely responds, AD shifts right less.

items.stem: If the economy is in a liquidity trap, which part of the normal expansionary monetary-policy chain weakens?
options: Lowering interest rates enough to stimulate investment
The identity that AD includes investment
The fact that money demand exists
The ability of government spending to enter AD
items.feedback: In a liquidity trap, additional money may not lower interest rates enough to stimulate investment.

items.stem: If money supply rises and AD shifts right, what is the correct distinction between the money-market movement and the AD-AS outcome?
options: The money market shows r falling; the AD-AS model shows higher demand for output at each price level.
The money market shows P falling; the AD-AS model shows money demand disappearing.
The money market shows taxes falling; the AD-AS model shows reserves rising.
The money market shows real output fixed by bank reserves.
items.feedback: The money market determines the interest rate. The AD-AS model then reflects how lower rates raise spending and shift AD.

items.stem: A student says the central bank directly chose the real-output level at B. Which explanation uses the mechanism and evidence in both panels?
options: Money supply falls from 125 to 100, raising the rate from 2.75% to 4%; lower spending then reduces output.
Money supply falls from 150 to 100, raising the rate from 4% to 6%; lower spending then reduces output.
Money supply falls from 125 to 100; matching money and output quantities means the bank directly sets real GDP.
Money supply falls from 125 to 100, and output falls because the policy directly reduces productive capacity.
items.feedback: The monetary instrument changes money supply, not an output quota. The left panel supplies the rate response; borrowing costs affect investment and AD, with the output result determined by the right-panel intersection.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What policy movement is shown across the two panels?
options: Money supply falls; interest rises; AD falls; output falls.
Money supply rises; interest falls; AD rises; output rises.
Money demand falls; interest falls; investment rises; AD rises.
The price level falls and the economy moves along AD1 from Y1 to Y2.
items.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy: MS shifts left, r rises, AD shifts left, and output falls.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. If the investment change caused by the MS1 to MS2 movement is $80 billion and MPC = 0.6, what is the correct full AD effect?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $200 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $80 billion.
items.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left and r rising, so investment falls. MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5, so AD falls by $200 billion.

items.stem: A monetary contraction raises interest rates and reduces aggregate demand by $240 billion. MPC is 0.75, and investment is the only autonomous spending component that changes. What investment change accounts for the total demand loss?
options: Investment fell $960 billion after rates rose; divide the total loss by MPC
Investment fell $60 billion after rates rose; the multiplier converts that impulse to the total AD loss
Investment fell $240 billion before rates changed; the AD loss is the autonomous impulse
Investment rose $60 billion after rates fell; the money shift is expansionary
items.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4. Dividing the $240 billion total demand loss by 4 gives a $60 billion autonomous investment decline, occurring after the rate increase and before induced spending falls.

items.stem: The interest rate rises by the same amount in two economies. Investment falls by $20 billion in A and $5 billion in B. Both have MPC = 0.8 and no other shocks. What explains the difference in their total demand responses?
options: AD falls $25 billion in A and $100 billion in B; weaker investment sensitivity magnifies the effect
AD falls $100 billion in both; identical rate changes guarantee identical spending changes
AD falls $100 billion in A and $25 billion in B; B has weaker investment sensitivity to the rate change
AD falls $20 billion in A and $5 billion in B; the multiplier is irrelevant to rate-induced spending
items.feedback: Both multipliers equal 5, giving demand declines of $100 billion and $25 billion. With the same rate increase and multiplier, the difference reflects investment sensitivity, not reserve accounting.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. A student says the graph shows a movement along AD caused by a lower price level. What is the best correction?
options: The graph shows AD shifting left because money supply falls and r rises.
The graph shows AD shifting right because money supply rises and r falls.
The graph shows a lower price level causing movement along AD1.
The graph shows fiscal expansion through higher government spending.
items.feedback: This is not movement along AD. It is a leftward AD shift caused by tighter monetary policy.

items.stem: What economic response connects the move from A to B in the two panels?
options: Money supply rises and the rate falls; stronger spending raises output and the price level on unchanged SRAS.
Money supply falls and the rate rises; weaker spending lowers output and the price level on unchanged SRAS.
Money demand rises and the rate rises; weaker spending lowers output and the price level on unchanged SRAS.
Money supply falls and the rate rises; output falls because policy shifts LRAS left.
items.feedback: The graph shows a leftward money-supply shift at fixed money demand, followed by lower AD. Higher rates restrain spending; output and prices fall along unchanged SRAS. This does not establish a loss of productive capacity.

items.stem: In a scarce-reserves model, a student says, 'If the Fed buys bonds, inflation must rise immediately and real output cannot move.' Which correction is strongest?
options: In the short run, lower rates can raise AD and output before long-run price adjustment dominates.
Bond purchases only change fiscal spending, so inflation and output are unaffected.
Bond purchases lower AD because reserves rise and lending must fall.
In the long run, bond purchases permanently reduce unemployment.
items.feedback: In this scarce-reserves model, bond purchases lower interest rates and can raise aggregate demand and output while prices are sticky. Long-run monetary neutrality does not rule out that short-run response.

items.stem: In the standard short-run model, monetary easing lowers interest rates, making $20 in investment more attractive. However, weaker expected sales offset that incentive. Why might aggregate demand respond only weakly to the monetary easing?
options: Monetary easing failed to lower interest rates, despite the observed decline.
Investment cannot affect aggregate demand because capital spending is excluded from it.
An unreported increase in reserve requirements restricted lending despite the monetary easing.
Weaker expected sales can reduce investment despite lower interest rates.
items.feedback: Lower interest rates affect aggregate demand only if spending responds. Weaker expected sales can make firms reluctant to invest even when borrowing becomes cheaper.

items.stem: Suppose monetary easing lowers the interest rate and increases investment by $30. At the same time, fiscal tightening reduces aggregate demand by a total of $60 after induced effects. If the spending multiplier on the investment increase is 3, what is the net effect on aggregate demand?
options: AD falls by $90.
AD rises by $150.
AD rises by $30.
AD falls by $30.
items.feedback: The $30 increase in investment raises AD by 3 × $30 = $90. The $60 fiscal contraction is already stated as a total effect, so subtract it once. Net AD rises by $30.

items.stem: A central bank adds $40 to bank reserves, but banks hold the added balances and qualified borrowers do not expand borrowing. What happened to reserves, credit and spending?
options: Reserves stayed fixed; weak borrowing proves no injection occurred.
Reserves rose; credit and spending responses remain limited.
Reserves rose; aggregate demand rises by the same amount.
Reserves rose; the natural unemployment rate therefore falls permanently.
items.feedback: Reserve implementation, lending behavior and expenditure are distinct stages. Weak later links can limit aggregate-demand effects without undoing the initial reserve operation.

items.stem: Currency held by the public rises because households withdraw funds from checking accounts. What happens to banks' ability to create deposits, other things equal?
options: It falls because banks have fewer deposits to support lending.
It rises because currency held by the public becomes excess reserves.
It is unchanged because currency and deposits are identical for banks.
It becomes unlimited because reserve requirements no longer matter.
items.feedback: When households hold more currency and fewer deposits, banks have fewer deposits available to support loans.

items.stem: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A table lists public currency as $600, checkable deposits as $1,400, savings deposits as $1,800, small time deposits as $500, and retail money market mutual funds as $300. What are M1 and M2?
items.feedback: M1 is currency plus checkable deposits: $600 + $1,400 = $2,000. M2 adds savings, small time deposits, and retail money market funds: $4,600.

items.stem: Currency held by the public rises by $20 billion, checking deposits fall by $20 billion, and small time deposits are unchanged. What happens to M1 and M2?
options: M1 rises by $20 billion while M2 remains unchanged because currency is broader money.
Both aggregates are unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
M1 and M2 both fall by $20 billion because checking deposits decline.
M1 remains unchanged while M2 rises by $20 billion because currency increases.
items.feedback: Currency and checking deposits are both in M1 and M2. An equal transfer between them changes composition but not either total.

items.stem: A new digital wallet stores claims on bank checking deposits and the same balances are still reported as checking deposits. How should statisticians avoid double counting?
options: Count both the checking deposit and the wallet claim as separate M1 balances.
Exclude the checking deposit and count only the wallet claim as part of M2.
Count the underlying deposit once and do not add the wallet claim again.
Remove both records because digitally accessed balances cannot qualify as money.
items.feedback: A wallet claim backed one-for-one by an already-counted checking deposit is another access channel, not a second stock of money.

items.stem: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A table lists currency held by the public as $900, checkable deposits as $1,600, savings deposits as $2,000, small time deposits as $700, and retail money market funds as $300. What are M1 and M2?
items.feedback: M1 = currency + checkable deposits = $2,500. M2 = M1 + savings + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $5,500.

items.stem: A household holds $200 in checking, $400 in savings, and $200 in a small time deposit. Under current U.S. definitions, it transfers the time deposit into savings. Which M1/M2 changes follow?
options: M1 is unchanged; M2 rises $200
Both M1 and M2 rise $200
M1 falls $200; M2 is unchanged
M1 rises $200; M2 is unchanged
items.feedback: Current M1 includes savings but not small time deposits. The transfer moves funds into M1 while remaining inside M2, so it is a reclassification within broad money, not an M2 increase.

items.stem: A store quotes a $220 price in dollars but accepts a card that transfers dollars from a deposit account. A student calls the card a fourth function of money. Which correction connects the instrument and functions?
options: Quote: store of value; deposit: transfer instrument; card: unit of account.
Quote: payment medium; deposit: unit of account; card: money-creation instrument.
Quote: unit of account; deposit: payment medium; card: transfer instrument.
Quote: unit of account; deposit: outside money; card: commodity payment medium.
items.feedback: Distinguish the monetary unit and balances from the technology used to access them. Quoting prices uses a unit of account; paying transfers money through the card system.

items.stem: An economy has currency $240, checking $480, savings $720, and small time deposits $240. Using current U.S. definitions, what are M1 and M2?
items.feedback: M1 = 240+480+720 = 1440. M2 adds the time deposit once: 1440+240 = 1680. Savings already inside M1 must not be added again.

items.stem: Seabrook Repair sells a differentiated service. Its MR and rising MC intersect at 48 units; demand at that quantity gives a price of $39, and ATC is $31. What are its profit margin and total economic profit?
options: $8 per unit; $1872 total
$8 per unit; $384 total
$39 per unit; $1872 total
$31 per unit; $1488 total
items.feedback: Use the MR = MC quantity, obtain price from demand, and subtract ATC: 39 - 31 = 8 per unit. Multiplying by 48 gives $384; revenue and total cost are not profit.

items.stem: Cairn Tailoring sells a differentiated service. Its MR and rising MC intersect at 36 units; demand at that quantity gives a price of $56, and ATC is $42. What are its profit margin and total economic profit?
options: $14 per unit; $2016 total
$56 per unit; $2016 total
$42 per unit; $1512 total
$14 per unit; $504 total
items.feedback: Use the MR = MC quantity, obtain price from demand, and subtract ATC: 56 - 42 = 14 per unit. Multiplying by 36 gives $504; revenue and total cost are not profit.

items.stem: Grove Pottery sells a differentiated service. Its MR and rising MC intersect at 65 units; demand at that quantity gives a price of $28, and ATC is $24. What are its profit margin and total economic profit?
options: $4 per unit; $1820 total
$4 per unit; $260 total
$28 per unit; $1820 total
$24 per unit; $1560 total
items.feedback: Use the MR = MC quantity, obtain price from demand, and subtract ATC: 28 - 24 = 4 per unit. Multiplying by 65 gives $260; revenue and total cost are not profit.

items.stem: Willow Tours sells a differentiated service. Its MR and rising MC intersect at 28 units; demand at that quantity gives a price of $75, and ATC is $54. What are its profit margin and total economic profit?
options: $21 per unit; $2100 total
$75 per unit; $2100 total
$54 per unit; $1512 total
$21 per unit; $588 total
items.feedback: Use the MR = MC quantity, obtain price from demand, and subtract ATC: 75 - 54 = 21 per unit. Multiplying by 28 gives $588; revenue and total cost are not profit.

items.stem: Ember Design sells a differentiated service. Its MR and rising MC intersect at 42 units; demand at that quantity gives a price of $63, and ATC is $38. What are its profit margin and total economic profit?
options: $25 per unit; $2646 total
$25 per unit; $1050 total
$63 per unit; $2646 total
$38 per unit; $1596 total
items.feedback: Use the MR = MC quantity, obtain price from demand, and subtract ATC: 63 - 38 = 25 per unit. Multiplying by 42 gives $1050; revenue and total cost are not profit.

items.stem: North Quay Roasting sells a differentiated service. Its MR and rising MC intersect at 55 units; demand at that quantity gives a price of $34, and ATC is $29. What are its profit margin and total economic profit?

$34 per unit; $1870 total
$29 per unit; $1595 total
$5 per unit; $275 total
items.feedback: Use the MR = MC quantity, obtain price from demand, and subtract ATC: 34 - 29 = 5 per unit. Multiplying by 55 gives $275; revenue and total cost are not profit.

items.stem: At Q1, calculate the markup over marginal cost. Does the firm earn economic profit, and is it producing at minimum ATC?
options: $20; zero economic profit coexists with excess capacity.
$15; zero economic profit coexists with excess capacity.
$20; a positive markup guarantees positive economic profit and production at efficient scale.
$15; a positive markup guarantees positive economic profit and production at efficient scale.
items.feedback: Q1 = 20 has P = ATC = 70 and MC = 50, giving markup 20 and zero profit. The minimum-ATC output is Q2 = 34.64, above Q1, so excess capacity remains.

items.stem: Demand shifts outward so buyers will pay $5 more at every quantity. Costs stay fixed. If the firm initially keeps output at Q1, what profit does it earn? How would entry then affect incumbent demand?
options: $120; entry can reduce incumbent demand after short-run profit appears.
$100; entry can reduce incumbent demand after short-run profit appears.
$100; demand must return immediately to its original position before entry occurs.
$120; demand must return immediately to its original position before entry occurs.
items.feedback: Initially Q1 = 20 and P = ATC = $70. At the same output after the shift, price is $75, so profit is (75−70) × 20 = $100. This profit can attract entry, which adds substitutes and reduces incumbent demand over time.

items.stem: The graph shows the long-run result after profit attracted entry. What price does the firm charge, and how did entry eliminate its economic profit?
options: $76; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
$72; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
$76; entry eliminates the price–MC markup whenever it eliminates economic profit.
$76; entry shifts each incumbent’s marginal cost down until its existing demand curve becomes tangent to ATC.
items.feedback: At Q = 24, P = ATC = $76 while MC = $49.60. Entry reduces incumbent demand until profit is zero, but markup and output below minimum ATC remain. Entry need not shift the firm’s cost curves.

items.stem: Calculate the markup at Q1. Why can the firm earn zero economic profit while still being allocatively inefficient?
options: $16.20; price exceeds marginal cost, so P = ATC does not establish marginal efficiency.
$12.20; price exceeds marginal cost, so P = ATC does not establish marginal efficiency.
$16.20; price equaling ATC automatically establishes marginal efficiency despite P exceeding MC.
$12.20; price equaling ATC automatically establishes marginal efficiency despite P exceeding MC.
items.feedback: At Q1 = 18, price and ATC are $64 and MC is $47.80. The markup is $16.20. P = ATC means zero profit; allocative efficiency requires price, a marginal willingness to pay, to equal MC.

items.stem: Use the graph. After entry restores the plotted long-run equilibrium, which markup and profit combination can persist?
options: A $16.20 markup with zero economic profit; price exceeds MC but equals ATC.
A $12.20 markup with zero economic profit; price exceeds MC but equals ATC.
A $16.20 markup with zero economic profit; any markup must also be economic profit per unit.
A $12.20 markup with zero economic profit; any markup must also be economic profit per unit.
items.feedback: The graph gives P = ATC = 64 and MC = 47.8 at Q1. Markup is 16.2, while profit per unit P−ATC is zero. Marginal and average costs serve different comparisons.

items.stem: A costly brand campaign shifts demand right but also makes demand less elastic. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Output, price, and profit effects depend on both the demand change and campaign cost
Profit must rise
Price must fall
Marginal cost must remain above marginal revenue at every possible quantity after the campaign
items.feedback: Demand and cost effects must be evaluated together.

items.stem: An ad supplies verifiable price and quality information. What possible social benefit follows?
options: Guaranteed allocative efficiency
Lower search costs and better matching between buyers and varieties
Elimination of all selling costs
A perfectly horizontal firm demand curve that prevents sellers from differentiating their products
items.feedback: Information can improve comparison and matching.

items.stem: A firm repeatedly spends heavily on a brand name that would lose value if quality disappoints. The spending may function as:
options: Proof of perfect competition
A per-unit production subsidy
A signal of expected quality
A guarantee that demand is inelastic
items.feedback: A costly, reputation-dependent campaign can signal confidence in repeat business.

items.stem: Which statement distinguishes genuine quality competition from purely persuasive differentiation?
options: Quality competition always lowers fixed cost
Persuasive differentiation always provides measured performance data
They are identical by definition
Quality competition changes the attributes or service buyers receive
items.feedback: A genuine quality change alters delivered value.

items.stem: Why can product variety partly offset the model’s efficiency costs?
options: Consumers may value closer matches to preferences
Variety forces every firm to set price equal to marginal cost at minimum average total cost
Variety eliminates selling costs
Variety guarantees minimum ATC
items.feedback: Variety may create utility even while markup and excess capacity remain.

items.stem: A market has four dominant firms that closely monitor one another’s prices. Why is monopolistic competition a weak model?
options: The products are differentiated, which by itself guarantees monopolistic competition regardless of firm count
Strategic interdependence points toward oligopoly
Firms advertise
Demand slopes downward
items.feedback: Few-firm strategic interaction is outside the monopolistic-competition model.

items.stem: A city has hundreds of differentiated restaurants but zoning makes new locations nearly impossible. Which assumption is weakened most?
options: Product differentiation is weakened because zoning changes the physical attributes of restaurant meals
Downward-sloping demand
Relatively easy entry and exit
Nonprice competition
items.feedback: Severe entry barriers undermine the standard long-run adjustment.

items.stem: A fixed advertising campaign raises ATC above demand at the previous output but leaves MR and MC unchanged. What happens first?
options: Output falls because MR changes
Price rises because the fixed advertising expense shifts demand outward at every possible price
AVC rises by the same amount
The short-run output remains the same, but profit falls
items.feedback: A pure fixed-cost increase does not alter MR=MC output.

items.stem: A per-unit delivery promise raises MC and also shifts demand right. Which outcome is certain?
options: No direction for output or profit is certain without magnitudes
Output must rise because a rightward demand shift always dominates any increase in marginal cost
Profit must rise
Price must fall
items.feedback: Demand and marginal-cost changes push decisions in potentially opposing directions.

items.stem: Why does a markup not prove that a monopolistically competitive firm in long-run equilibrium earns economic profit?
options: Markup equals fixed cost
Price can exceed MC while equaling ATC
MR can exceed demand
Entry forces price below average variable cost even though the firm remains in long-run equilibrium
items.feedback: Long-run zero profit coexists with P>MC.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Using the chosen output, price, and ATC, which statement correctly describes the firm’s economic result?
options: It earns zero economic profit because MR equals MC
It incurs a $200 economic loss
It earns $700 because price exceeds MC by $14
It earns positive economic profit of $200
items.feedback: The firm earns ($37 − $33) × 50 = $200 in economic profit.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What are total revenue and total cost at Q = 50?
options: $1,650 revenue and $1,850 cost
$1,850 revenue and $1,650 cost
$1,150 revenue and $1,650 cost
$1,850 revenue and $1,150 cost

items.stem: Calculate revenue at the profit-maximizing output. Does it cover all economic costs, including the owner’s normal return?
options: $972; revenue covers all explicit and implicit economic costs, including normal return.
$864; revenue covers all explicit and implicit economic costs, including normal return.
$972; zero economic profit means the owner receives no return and implicit costs are uncovered.
$864; zero economic profit means the owner receives no return and implicit costs are uncovered.
items.feedback: At Q = 36, price and ATC both equal $27. Revenue and total economic cost are 36 × 27 = $972. Zero economic profit includes coverage of opportunity costs and the normal return required to remain.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At the chosen output, compare price with marginal cost. What does the gap imply?
options: The firm is allocatively efficient because economic profit is zero
The firm has a positive markup even though economic profit is zero
The firm must be earning $12 of profit per unit
The firm should raise output until price equals ATC again
items.feedback: Zero economic profit does not eliminate markup; P still exceeds MC by $12.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. How does the monopolistically competitive firm’s price compare with marginal cost, and how would this differ for a perfectly competitive firm in long-run equilibrium?
options: The markup is $8; the competitive firm also prices above marginal cost.
The markup is $12; the competitive firm also prices above marginal cost.
The markup is $12; the competitive firm’s price equals marginal cost.
The markup is $8; the competitive firm’s price equals marginal cost.
items.feedback: At Q = 36, P = ATC = 27 and MC = 15, leaving a 12 markup. In monopolistic competition downward-sloping firm demand permits this markup at zero profit, unlike the standard competitive long-run equality P = MC = min ATC.

items.stem: What output maximizes this firm’s profit? Why would expanding to the minimum-ATC output reduce profit?
options: 30 units; beyond that output MC exceeds MR, so expanding merely to lower ATC reduces profit.
36 units; lower ATC always guarantees higher profit even when MC exceeds MR.
30 units; lower ATC always guarantees higher profit even when MC exceeds MR.
36 units; beyond that output MC exceeds MR, so expanding merely to lower ATC reduces profit.
items.feedback: MR crosses MC at Q = 36, while minimum ATC is at Q = 50. Between them, added units cost more than their added revenue. Minimizing ATC is not the firm’s profit-maximizing output rule.

items.stem: How much excess capacity does the firm have? Does producing below minimum-ATC output mean that it earns an economic loss?
options: 14 units; the firm earns zero economic profit because price equals ATC at its chosen output.
10 units; the firm earns zero economic profit because price equals ATC at its chosen output.
14 units; unused efficient scale necessarily means the firm is making an economic loss.
10 units; unused efficient scale necessarily means the firm is making an economic loss.
items.feedback: The firm produces 36 where MR = MC and P = ATC = 27. Minimum ATC occurs at 50, leaving 14 units of excess capacity. Producing below efficient scale is productive inefficiency, but it does not contradict zero profit.

items.stem: At the profit-maximizing output, how much does price exceed marginal cost? What does this imply about allocative efficiency?
options: $7.5; marginal willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost, so the allocation is not marginally efficient.
$11.5; marginal willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost, so the allocation is not marginally efficient.
$11.5; any profit-maximizing output must be allocatively efficient even when price exceeds MC.
$7.5; any profit-maximizing output must be allocatively efficient even when price exceeds MC.
items.feedback: At Q = 36, price is $27 and MC $15.5, giving markup $11.5. Allocative efficiency compares marginal willingness to pay on demand with MC. The private rule MR = MC does not make P = MC.

items.stem: Firm A sells a differentiated snack with many close substitutes. Firm B holds an exclusive patent on a drug with no close substitute. Which comparison is most plausible?
options: Firm A faces more elastic demand than Firm B
Firm A faces less elastic demand than Firm B
Both firms face perfectly elastic demand
Both firms must face the same elasticity because each has a downward-sloping demand curve
items.feedback: Close substitutes make buyers more responsive to Firm A’s price, while the patent shields Firm B from close substitution.

items.stem: A boutique raises its price by 4 percent and loses 7 percent of its customers, but many buyers remain because they prefer its style. What does this pattern most strongly indicate?
options: The firm is a price taker with perfectly elastic demand
The firm has monopoly power protected by an entry barrier
The market must contain only a few strategically interdependent firms
The firm has limited market power, not complete control of demand
items.feedback: Differentiation can give a firm some control over price while close substitutes still constrain it.

items.stem: A market has many sellers and easy entry. Each seller faces a downward-sloping demand curve for its own product. Which additional fact is most consistent with monopolistic competition?
options: A single legal franchise blocks all new rivals
A few firms closely track each rival’s strategic moves
Products are differentiated but remain close substitutes
Products are identical and firms accept one market price
items.feedback: Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry.

items.stem: Food-delivery technology makes customers almost indifferent to which neighborhood a restaurant occupies. Other features are unchanged. What happens to location as a source of differentiation?
options: It turns the market into a natural monopoly
It becomes weaker because distance matters less to customers
It becomes stronger because delivery creates a new legal barrier
It guarantees each restaurant a perfectly inelastic demand curve
items.feedback: When location matters less to buyers, location creates less product differentiation and less insulation from rivals.

items.stem: Two campaigns cost the same fixed amount. Campaign A shifts demand right but leaves elasticity unchanged. Campaign B leaves demand quantity unchanged but makes demand less elastic. Why can the profit effects differ?
options: Fixed advertising cost always changes MC by the same amount
Only Campaign A can affect marginal revenue
Only Campaign B can affect the price the firm charges
The campaigns alter the firm’s revenue conditions in different ways even though both add the same fixed cost
items.feedback: A demand shift and an elasticity change can alter MR and optimal price/output differently, while the fixed cost enters profit separately.

items.stem: A firm can spend on product quality that shifts demand right but also raises MC. Which conclusion is economically sound before seeing the magnitudes?
options: Profit must fall because marginal cost increases
Optimal output cannot change because price was not directly altered
Profit may rise or fall because both revenue and marginal cost conditions change
Profit must rise because buyers value the improvement
items.feedback: The net effect depends on how much the improvement changes willingness to pay relative to the increase in marginal cost.

items.stem: Suppose a regulator could force every differentiated firm to price at marginal cost, but doing so would reduce firms’ ability to cover fixed product-development costs and some varieties would disappear. What is the best conclusion?
options: Marginal-cost pricing must raise welfare because P=MC is always sufficient
Variety loss is irrelevant because all firms initially earned zero economic profit
The policy must lower welfare because regulation can never improve allocation
The welfare effect depends on the gain from lower markups relative to the loss of valued variety
items.feedback: The standard markup is inefficient, but differentiated products may create variety benefits and require fixed costs. Both sides matter.

items.stem: Atlas Coffee publishes verified wait times and prices. Which welfare test should be applied to the Atlas Coffee action?
options: Count additional seller revenue as the entire social benefit
Count all advertising expenditure as a loss without benefits
Compare consumer benefits, resource costs, and market-power effects
Infer full efficiency from the eventual zero-profit condition
items.feedback: A balanced welfare test includes value, resources, and pricing effects.

options: Count additional seller revenue as the entire social benefit
Compare consumer benefits, resource costs, and market-power effects
Count all advertising expenditure as a loss without benefits
Infer full efficiency from the eventual zero-profit condition
items.feedback: A balanced welfare test includes value, resources, and pricing effects.

options: Compare consumer benefits, resource costs, and market-power effects
Count additional seller revenue as the entire social benefit
Count all advertising expenditure as a loss without benefits
Infer full efficiency from the eventual zero-profit condition
items.feedback: A balanced welfare test includes value, resources, and pricing effects.

Infer full efficiency from the eventual zero-profit condition
items.feedback: A balanced welfare test includes value, resources, and pricing effects.

options: Count additional seller revenue as the entire social benefit

Count all advertising expenditure as a loss without benefits
Infer full efficiency from the eventual zero-profit condition
items.feedback: A balanced welfare test includes value, resources, and pricing effects.

options: Compare consumer benefits, resource costs, and market-power effects
Count additional seller revenue as the entire social benefit
Count all advertising expenditure as a loss without benefits
Infer full efficiency from the eventual zero-profit condition
items.feedback: A balanced welfare test includes value, resources, and pricing effects.

Infer full efficiency from the eventual zero-profit condition
items.feedback: A balanced welfare test includes value, resources, and pricing effects.

items.stem: Atlas Coffee publishes verified wait times and prices. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Atlas Coffee action?
options: Economic profit must become permanent
Search costs fall and demand responsiveness may change
Price must equal marginal cost
All rival firms must exit
items.feedback: Publishing verified prices and wait times makes comparison less costly. It can alter demand and responsiveness, but does not establish a particular markup or permanent profit.

items.stem: Bloom Cosmetics links the brand to prestige without measurable performance claims. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Bloom Cosmetics action?
options: Demand may rise or become less elastic without a quality change.
Higher sales guarantee lasting profit despite free entry.
Differentiation makes the firm accept a fixed market price.
Greater customer loyalty eliminates the possibility of entry.
items.feedback: Prestige-based branding may change willingness to pay or loyalty even without a measured quality improvement. Its effect is on demand, not a guarantee that entry disappears.

items.stem: Crown Dental offers a costly long warranty tied to its reputation. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Crown Dental action?
options: Higher sales guarantee lasting profit despite free entry.
Differentiation makes the firm accept a fixed market price.
Greater customer loyalty eliminates the possibility of entry.
Demand may rise or become less elastic without a quality change.
items.feedback: A credible warranty can change beliefs about reliability and reduce perceived risk. Buyers may become more willing to buy or less willing to switch without a measured change in the physical service itself.

items.stem: Dahlia Delivery buys an annual sponsorship unrelated to order volume. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Dahlia Delivery action?
options: Economic profit must become permanent
Price must equal marginal cost
ATC rises, but the initial MR=MC output is unchanged
All rival firms must exit
items.feedback: The order-independent sponsorship adds a fixed expense. Its cost effect raises ATC without changing MC; holding demand fixed isolates why the original MR=MC output is unchanged.

items.stem: Ember Meals pays a platform fee on every order. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Ember Meals action?
options: Economic profit must become permanent
MC, AVC, and ATC rise, so output may fall
Price must equal marginal cost
All rival firms must exit
items.feedback: A fee on each order adds to the cost of the marginal order and to average variable and total cost. With demand fixed, higher MC can reduce the profit-maximizing output.

items.stem: Flint Apparel uses more durable fabric and better construction. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Flint Apparel action?
options: Higher customer value may raise demand, but added costs matter.
Higher sales guarantee lasting profit despite free entry.
Differentiation makes the firm accept a fixed market price.
Greater customer loyalty eliminates the possibility of entry.
items.feedback: Better fabric and construction can raise willingness to pay, but the added materials and workmanship also use resources. A demand gain alone does not establish the net profit effect.

items.stem: Glade Fitness offers benefits that members keep by staying with the gym and lose if they switch, making them less responsive to its price. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Glade Fitness action?
options: Higher sales guarantee lasting profit despite free entry.
Differentiation makes the firm accept a fixed market price.
Greater customer loyalty eliminates the possibility of entry.
Demand becomes less elastic, allowing a larger markup.
items.feedback: Benefits from staying with the gym make buyers less responsive to price, giving the firm scope for a larger markup. They do not guarantee that the resulting economic profit survives entry.

items.stem: Haven Hotels offers accommodation for guests who prefer less noise, light, and other sensory stimulation. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Haven Hotels action?
options: Higher sales guarantee lasting profit despite free entry.
Differentiation makes the firm accept a fixed market price.
Higher customer value may raise demand, but added costs matter.
Greater customer loyalty eliminates the possibility of entry.
items.feedback: Reducing noise, light, and other sensory stimulation can increase value for its target customers and shift demand outward. The resources used to provide the feature must also enter the profit comparison.

items.stem: Ivory Retail supports a tool that makes rival prices easy to compare. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Ivory Retail action?
options: Economic profit must become permanent
Search costs fall and demand responsiveness may change
Price must equal marginal cost
All rival firms must exit
items.feedback: The comparison tool reduces the time and effort needed to find rival prices. That can change demand responsiveness; it does not force all prices to equal marginal cost.

items.stem: Jasper Learning develops a genuinely improved tutoring format. What is the most defensible immediate implication of the Jasper Learning action?
options: Higher customer value may raise demand, but added costs matter.
Higher sales guarantee lasting profit despite free entry.
Differentiation makes the firm accept a fixed market price.
Greater customer loyalty eliminates the possibility of entry.
items.feedback: A better tutoring format can increase customers’ willingness to pay, while development and delivery impose costs. Both demand and resource cost matter to its economic benefit.

items.stem: Calculate the markup at Q1. How can the firm charge more than marginal cost and still earn zero economic profit?
options: $17.60; price equals ATC but lies above MC.
$13.60; price equals ATC but lies above MC.
$17.60; price above MC necessarily equals profit per unit.
$13.60; price above MC necessarily equals profit per unit.

items.stem: The graph shows the long-run outcome after short-run profit attracted entry. What price does the firm charge now? How did entry change its demand and economic profit?
options: $23; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
$27; entry eliminated profit by making each firm choose minimum ATC regardless of demand and MR.
$23; entry eliminated profit by making each firm choose minimum ATC regardless of demand and MR.
$27; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
items.feedback: The plotted profit-maximizing quantity is 36, where demand is tangent to ATC at $27. Entry reduces incumbent demand until economic profit is zero. The firm still chooses output using MR = MC, and the tangency lies below the minimum-ATC output.

items.stem: The graph shows the long-run outcome after short-run profit attracted entry. What price does the firm now charge, and how did entry change its demand?
options: $23; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
$27; entry eliminated profit by making each firm choose minimum ATC regardless of demand and MR.
$23; entry eliminated profit by making each firm choose minimum ATC regardless of demand and MR.
$27; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
items.feedback: The plotted profit-maximizing quantity is 36, where demand is tangent to ATC at $27. Entry reduces incumbent demand until economic profit is zero. The firm still chooses output using MR = MC, and the tangency lies below the minimum-ATC output.

items.stem: The firm considers expanding from Q1 to the minimum-ATC output Q2. What is Q1, and how would producing the additional units affect profit?
options: 24 units; MC exceeds MR beyond that point, so lowering ATC by expansion does not maximize profit.
20 units; falling ATC guarantees higher profit even when MC exceeds MR.
20 units; MC exceeds MR beyond that point, so lowering ATC by expansion does not maximize profit.
24 units; falling ATC guarantees higher profit even when MC exceeds MR.
items.feedback: Q1 = 20 is the MR–MC crossing, while Q2 = 34.64 minimizes ATC. Between them, MC exceeds MR, so extra units reduce profit despite lowering average cost.

items.stem: Calculate the markup at Q1. Why can the firm earn zero economic profit while still being allocatively inefficient?
options: $16.20; price exceeds marginal cost, so P = ATC does not establish marginal efficiency.
$12.20; price exceeds marginal cost, so P = ATC does not establish marginal efficiency.
$16.20; price equaling ATC automatically establishes marginal efficiency despite P exceeding MC.
$12.20; price equaling ATC automatically establishes marginal efficiency despite P exceeding MC.
items.feedback: At Q1 = 18, price and ATC are $64 and MC is $47.80. The markup is $16.20. P = ATC means zero profit; allocative efficiency requires price, a marginal willingness to pay, to equal MC.

items.stem: Calculate the firm’s current economic profit. If this profit attracts entry, how will incumbent demand adjust in the long run?
options: $150; entry reduces incumbent demand until it is tangent to ATC at the new MR = MC output.
$200; entry leaves incumbent demand fixed and makes the firm choose minimum ATC regardless of MR.
$200; entry reduces incumbent demand until it is tangent to ATC at the new MR = MC output.
$150; entry leaves incumbent demand fixed and makes the firm choose minimum ATC regardless of MR.

options: 36 units; beyond that output MC exceeds MR, so expanding merely to lower ATC reduces profit.
30 units; beyond that output MC exceeds MR, so expanding merely to lower ATC reduces profit.
36 units; lower ATC always guarantees higher profit even when MC exceeds MR.
30 units; lower ATC always guarantees higher profit even when MC exceeds MR.
items.feedback: MR crosses MC at Q = 36, while minimum ATC is at Q = 50. Between them, added units cost more than their added revenue. Minimizing ATC is not the firm’s profit-maximizing output rule.

items.stem: Calculate the firm’s current economic profit. If entry eliminates that profit, where will demand meet ATC relative to the new MR = MC output?
options: $200; entry reduces incumbent demand until it is tangent to ATC at the new MR = MC output.
$150; entry reduces incumbent demand until it is tangent to ATC at the new MR = MC output.
$200; entry leaves incumbent demand fixed and makes the firm choose minimum ATC regardless of MR.
$150; entry leaves incumbent demand fixed and makes the firm choose minimum ATC regardless of MR.
items.feedback: At Q = 50, price is $37 and ATC $33, so economic profit is (37−33) × 50 = $200. Entry adds substitutes and reduces each incumbent’s demand until the profit-maximizing output has P = ATC.

items.stem: A student says zero economic profit makes the firm both allocatively and productively efficient. Calculate its markup over marginal cost and compare its output with the minimum-ATC output. Does the graph support the claim?
options: $12; zero profit proves neither P = MC nor production at minimum ATC.
$8; zero profit proves neither P = MC nor production at minimum ATC.
$12; zero profit is sufficient to prove both forms of efficiency despite the markup.
$8; zero profit is sufficient to prove both forms of efficiency despite the markup.
items.feedback: At Q = 36, P = ATC = $27 but MC = $15, so the markup is $12. ATC continues falling to the right of this output. Zero profit establishes cost recovery, not marginal efficiency or minimum average cost.

items.stem: Suppose the firm must charge marginal cost at its current output, with output and costs held fixed. Calculate its economic loss. What does this reveal about recovering total costs through marginal-cost pricing?
options: $306; marginal-cost pricing at that quantity fails to cover total economic costs.
$414; price equaling marginal cost necessarily covers total economic costs.
$414; marginal-cost pricing at that quantity fails to cover total economic costs.
$306; price equaling marginal cost necessarily covers total economic costs.
items.feedback: At Q = 36, MC is $15.50 and ATC is $27. With output held fixed, charging MC gives profit (15.50−27) × 36 = −$414. This price does not cover total economic cost. It does not establish an efficient quantity: the demand curve still shows marginal willingness to pay above MC at this fixed output. A full policy analysis must allow quantity to respond.

items.stem: The graph shows the outcome after entry eliminated short-run profit. What price does the firm now charge? Explain how entry changed demand and profit, and whether it also eliminated excess capacity.
options: $23; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output, which remains below minimum-ATC output.
$27; price equals ATC after entry, so the firm is productively efficient even though its output remains below minimum-ATC output.
$27; entry ends when P equals AVC, leaving no reason to cover the remaining fixed costs in the long run.
$27; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output, which remains below minimum-ATC output.
items.feedback: At Q = 36, P = ATC = $27 and output is below the minimum-ATC quantity of 50. Entry has removed economic profit, not excess capacity. Productive efficiency requires minimum ATC; covering AVC alone is insufficient for long-run survival.

items.stem: For quantities 0 through 5, a firm has prices in dollars [0, 30, 28, 26, 24, 22] and total costs [80, 98, 120, 145, 175, 212]. Which output maximizes profit?
options: 2 units
1 unit
3 units
28 units
items.feedback: For quantities 0 through 5, profit (P × Q − TC) is $-80, $-68, $-64, $-67, $-79, $-102. The largest value occurs at Q = 2; this minimizes the loss.

33 units

options: 1 unit

2 units
30 units
items.feedback: For quantities 0 through 5, profit (P × Q − TC) is $-72, $-60, $-55, $-62, $-82, $-115. The largest value occurs at Q = 2; this minimizes the loss.

items.feedback: For quantities 0 through 5, profit (P × Q − TC) is $-84, $-71, $-68, $-76, $-97, $-132. The largest value occurs at Q = 2; this minimizes the loss.

items.stem: At its chosen output, a firm sells 21.15 units at $67.70 and has ATC $30.21. What is economic profit? Use the displayed values and round to the nearest cent.
items.feedback: Total profit is the absolute price–ATC gap times output: |67.7 - 30.21| × 21.15 = $792.91. The keyed amount uses only the displayed data.

items.stem: At its chosen output, a firm sells 23.33 units at $62.67 and has ATC $30.10. What is economic profit?
items.feedback: Total profit is the absolute price–ATC gap times output: |62.67 - 30.1| × 23.33 = $759.86. The keyed amount uses only the displayed data.

items.stem: At its chosen output, a firm sells 19.43 units at $76.42 and has ATC $35.21. What is economic profit?
items.feedback: Total profit is the absolute price–ATC gap times output: |76.42 - 35.21| × 19.43 = $800.71. The keyed amount uses only the displayed data.

items.stem: At its chosen output, a firm sells 23.77 units at $60.35 and has ATC $26.50. What is economic profit? Use the displayed values and round to the nearest cent.
items.feedback: Total profit is the absolute price–ATC gap times output: |60.35 - 26.5| × 23.77 = $804.61. The keyed amount uses only the displayed data.

items.stem: A firm produces 18.14 units at price $61.72 with ATC $61.31. What is its economic profit? Use the displayed values and round to the nearest cent.
items.feedback: Total profit is the absolute price–ATC gap times output: |61.72 - 61.31| × 18.14 = $7.44. The keyed amount uses only the displayed data.

items.stem: A firm produces 17.68 units at price $69.09 with ATC $70.07. What is its economic loss? Use the displayed values and round to the nearest cent.
items.feedback: Total loss is the absolute price–ATC gap times output: |69.09 - 70.07| × 17.68 = $17.33. The keyed amount uses only the displayed data.

items.stem: A firm produces 19.47 units at price $58.89 with ATC $55.27. What is its economic profit? Use the displayed values and round to the nearest cent.
items.feedback: Total profit is the absolute price–ATC gap times output: |58.89 - 55.27| × 19.47 = $70.48. The keyed amount uses only the displayed data.

items.stem: At the MR=MC output of 18 units, price is $42, AVC is $48, and ATC is $62. What should the firm do in the short run?
options: Produce 18 units because price covers ATC
Produce 18 units because MR=MC overrides AVC
Exit immediately and eliminate all fixed cost
Shut down and incur fixed cost
items.feedback: Price is below AVC, so operating adds to the loss.

items.stem: At the MR=MC output of 24 units, price is $50, AVC is $55, and ATC is $66. What should the firm do in the short run?
options: Shut down and incur fixed cost
Produce 24 units because price covers ATC
Produce 24 units because MR=MC overrides AVC
Exit immediately and eliminate all fixed cost
items.feedback: Price is below AVC, so operating adds to the loss.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm in long-run equilibrium produces 20 units at price $70, with ATC = $70. What is total economic profit?
items.feedback: When P=ATC, economic profit is zero.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm in long-run equilibrium produces 24 units at price $76, with ATC = $76. What is total economic profit?
items.feedback: When P=ATC, economic profit is zero.

items.stem: Long-run equilibrium has price $64 and MC $47.80. Calculate the markup.
items.feedback: Markup is P−MC.

items.stem: Long-run output is 28 and minimum-ATC output is 43. Calculate excess capacity.
options: 28 units
43 units
15 units
items.feedback: Excess capacity is QminATC−Q.

items.stem: Long-run equilibrium has price $68 and MC $50.40. Calculate the markup.
items.feedback: Markup is P−MC.

items.stem: A firm’s annual revenue would be $80,000 without a proposed campaign and $102,000 with it. Production-related variable cost would rise from $35,000 to $41,500. The campaign costs $12,000, and an unavoidable $8,000 lease payment is the same under either plan. What is the campaign’s incremental contribution to profit?
items.feedback: Incremental revenue = $22,000; incremental variable cost = $6,500. Subtract the $12,000 campaign: $22,000 − $6,500 − $12,000 = $3,500. The unchanged lease payment cancels.

items.stem: A delivery guarantee is offered on 5,000 orders, but 1,000 customers collect their orders and incur no guarantee charge. The guarantee costs $2 for handling plus $1 for insurance on each delivered order. A separate annual advertising fee is $6,000, and product manufacturing costs are unchanged. What additional variable selling cost does the guarantee create?
items.feedback: Delivered orders = 5,000 − 1,000 = 4,000. Variable guarantee cost = ($2 + $1) × 4,000 = $12,000. Exclude the fixed advertising fee and unchanged manufacturing costs.

items.stem: Amber Café, a monopolistically competitive firm, faces P=108−2Q. At its MR=MC output of about 20.93 units, what price does it charge?
items.feedback: Read price from demand after choosing quantity.

items.stem: Grove Coffee publishes verified prices and wait times in its advertisements. Which type of advertising is this?
options: Perfectly competitive price taking
Oligopoly collusion
Informational advertising
A natural-monopoly cost condition
items.feedback: Publishing verifiable information reduces customers’ search costs.

items.stem: Grove Coffee publishes verified prices and wait times in its advertisements. How can customers benefit directly?
options: Price must equal MC
Economic profit must become permanent
Entry must become impossible
Lower search costs can improve matching
items.feedback: Verified prices and wait times help customers find an offer that better fits their needs, reducing search costs.

items.stem: Grove Coffee publishes verified prices and wait times in its advertisements. How should its net benefit to society be assessed?
options: Weigh customer benefits against resource costs and effects of market power.
Count differentiated products as waste, regardless of what customers value.
Count every advertisement as a net benefit, regardless of its cost.
Treat zero economic profit as proof that the market is efficient.
items.feedback: Consider any value or useful information customers gain, the resources used, and any effects of market power. The stated facts alone do not establish the net benefit. Differentiation, advertising, or zero economic profit does not settle that comparison.

items.stem: Halo Cosmetics advertises its brand as a status symbol without providing new performance information. Which type of advertising is this?
options: Perfectly competitive price taking
Persuasive advertising
Oligopoly collusion
A natural-monopoly cost condition
items.feedback: The campaign aims to change perceptions rather than communicate new product facts.

items.stem: Halo Cosmetics advertises its brand as a status symbol without providing new performance information. What is a likely direct effect?
options: Price must equal MC
Economic profit must become permanent
Demand may shift through changed perception
Entry must become impossible
items.feedback: Changed perceptions may raise willingness to pay and shift demand; they do not prevent entry or guarantee lasting profit.

items.stem: Halo Cosmetics advertises its brand as a status symbol without providing new performance information. How should its net benefit to society be assessed?

items.stem: Indigo Dental advertises a costly long-term warranty that would be expensive to honor if its work were poor. What economic role can this warranty play?
options: Advertising as a quality signal
Perfectly competitive price taking
Oligopoly collusion
A natural-monopoly cost condition
items.feedback: A warranty is a credible quality signal when poor-quality providers would face higher costs of honoring it.

items.stem: Indigo Dental advertises a costly long-term warranty that would be expensive to honor if its work were poor. What can the warranty communicate to potential customers?

The campaign can signal confidence in consistently high quality
Economic profit must become permanent

items.feedback: The warranty can signal confidence in consistent quality because poor results would create costly claims.

items.stem: Indigo Dental advertises a long-term warranty that would be costly to honor if its work were poor. How should its net benefit to society be assessed?

Weigh customer benefits against resource costs and effects of market power.

options: Perfectly competitive price taking
Oligopoly collusion
A natural-monopoly cost condition
A fixed selling cost
items.feedback: The fee is fixed with respect to output.

items.stem: Jade Delivery adds an annual sponsorship fee that is the same at every output level. Holding output and all other costs constant, what happens to its cost curves?
options: ATC rises while MC is unchanged
Price must equal MC
Economic profit must become permanent
Entry must become impossible
items.feedback: The fixed fee raises total cost and ATC at any positive output, but does not change the cost of an additional delivery, so MC is unchanged.

items.stem: Jade Delivery pays the same annual sponsorship fee regardless of its delivery volume. How should its net benefit to society be assessed?
options: Count differentiated products as waste, regardless of what customers value.
Weigh customer benefits against resource costs and effects of market power.
