The demand curve shifts right by the tax amount
The tax creates a price ceiling
items.feedback: Legal remittance does not determine economic burden. Prices adjust based on supply and demand elasticities.

items.stem: A tax is placed on buyers instead of sellers. In a standard supply-demand model, why is the final outcome similar to an equal seller tax?
options: Both taxes create the same buyer–seller price wedge.
Only buyer taxes reduce quantity
Only seller taxes raise prices
The tax disappears if buyers legally pay it
items.feedback: A buyer tax or seller tax of the same size creates the same wedge and reduces quantity similarly.

items.stem: A seller tax and a buyer tax of the same size create the same wedge in the same market. What does this imply about the market outcome?
options: The market outcome is equivalent even if the legal payer differs
The seller tax always hurts sellers more
The buyer tax always hurts buyers more
Only the tax on sellers reduces quantity
items.feedback: Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome.

items.stem: A $5 tax is legally placed on sellers. After the tax, buyers pay $3 more than before and sellers receive $2 less than before. What does this show?
options: The legal side pays the government, but buyers and sellers share the economic burden
The legal side bears the full burden because sellers are the ones sending in the tax
The buyer side avoids the burden because the law places the payment on sellers
The seller side avoids the burden because buyers now pay a higher market price
items.feedback: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden. Buyers and sellers share the tax through changes in prices.

items.stem: A $5 tax is placed on buyers instead of sellers. Supply and demand conditions are unchanged. What should happen compared with an equal tax on sellers?
options: The same wedge, quantity reduction, and burden split occur
Buyers bear all of the tax because they legally pay it
Sellers bear all of the tax because they receive less
The tax disappears because sellers are not legally charged
items.feedback: A tax on buyers and an equal tax on sellers create the same wedge and the same economic outcome. The legal side does not control the burden.

items.stem: The tax in the graph is currently collected from sellers. If the same per-unit tax were collected from buyers instead, with demand, supply, and compliance unchanged, which buyer price, net seller price, and quantity would result?
options: Buyer price $18; seller price $12; quantity 80
Buyer price $20; seller price $14; quantity 80
Buyer price $18; seller price $12; quantity 100
Buyer price $20; seller price $14; quantity 100
items.feedback: The graph shows an after-tax buyer price of $18, a net seller price of $12, and 80 units traded. Changing who sends the tax to the government leaves this economic outcome unchanged.

items.stem: A new production method cuts the cost of making solar panels. What happens in the solar panel market?
options: Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Quantity demanded decreases because supply rose
items.feedback: Lower production costs increase supply, which lowers price and raises quantity.

items.stem: A tax on producers raises the cost of selling bottled water. What is the likely market effect?
options: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
Demand increases because taxes fund public services
items.feedback: A tax on producers raises production cost, shifting supply left and reducing quantity.

items.stem: Producers expect the future price of a product to rise sharply, so they hold inventory back today. What happens to current supply?
options: Current supply decreases
Current supply increases
Current demand decreases
Quantity supplied increases because current price changed
items.feedback: If sellers expect higher future prices, they may reduce current supply to sell later.

items.stem: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. Which movement shows an increase in supply with demand fixed at D2?
options: From P3, Q2 to P2, Q3
From P2, Q1 to P1, Q2
From P1, Q2 to P2, Q3
From P2, Q3 to P3, Q2
items.feedback: With demand fixed at D2, moving from S1 to S2 changes equilibrium from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.

items.stem: Workers accept lower wages, but producers also expect the product’s future price to rise and hold inventory for later sale. What can be concluded about current supply?
options: Supply must rise because lower wages dominate the decision to withhold inventory.
Supply must fall because withholding inventory dominates the wage reduction.
The net supply shift is uncertain because lower wages and inventory withholding work in opposite directions.
Supply stays fixed because wages and expected future prices only move firms along supply.
items.feedback: Lower wages reduce production costs and increase supply. Holding inventory for a higher expected future price reduces current supply. Their relative sizes determine the net shift.

items.stem: Use the graph. From A to B, what is the quantity response per $1 price increase, and what economic change does it represent?
options: Quantity supplied rises by 25 thousand units per dollar through movement along the existing supply curve.
Quantity supplied rises by 20 thousand units per dollar through movement along the existing supply curve.
Supply increases by 25 thousand units per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
Supply increases by 20 thousand units per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
items.feedback: Price rises from $6 to $11 and quantity supplied rises from 100 thousand to 225 thousand. The response is 125/5 = 25 thousand units per $1 price increase. Both points lie on the same supply curve, so quantity supplied increases through a movement along supply; supply itself does not shift.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At $9, compare S0 with S1. Which event and quantity change are consistent with that comparison?
options: Lower input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
A fall in the product’s own price; 100 thousand fewer units at the same $9 price.
Higher input costs; 200 thousand fewer units supplied.
Higher input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
items.feedback: At $9, supply falls from 200 thousand on S0 to 100 thousand on S1. Higher input costs can cause this leftward shift. A change in the product’s own price cannot explain different quantities at the same price.

items.stem: Which comparison correctly distinguishes the two changes visible in the taco graph?
options: A to B is an increase in supply; S0 to S1 is movement along supply
A to B is movement along S0; S0 to S1 is an increase in supply
Both A to B and S0 to S1 are movements caused only by price
Both changes are decreases in supply
items.feedback: A and B are points on one curve, so their difference is quantity supplied. Moving from S0 to S1 shifts the entire curve and changes supply.

items.stem: The movie-ticket market moves from A to B after one production cost changes. Which explanation and changes in equilibrium price and quantity match the graph?
options: Higher operating costs reduce supply; price rises $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand
Higher operating costs reduce supply; price rises $4 and quantity falls 50 thousand
Lower operating costs increase supply; price falls $2 and quantity rises 50 thousand
Lower operating costs increase supply; price falls $4 and quantity rises 50 thousand
items.feedback: A is ($10,200 thousand) and B is ($12,150 thousand). The move follows a decrease in supply, consistent with higher operating costs: price rises $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand.

items.stem: Demand rises and the market price increases. Firms respond by producing more with the same technology, input prices, and number of sellers. Which statement is correct?
options: Supply shifts right because firms produce more.
Quantity supplied rises along an unchanged supply curve.
Supply shifts left because the product is now more expensive.
Both supply and quantity supplied must increase.
items.feedback: A change in the good’s own price changes quantity supplied. The supply curve shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.

items.stem: A per-unit input cost falls by $4, but a new per-unit tax raises cost by $6. Holding other determinants fixed, what is the likely supply effect?
options: Supply shifts left because net marginal cost rises by $2 per unit.
Supply shifts right because any input-cost decline dominates a tax.
Supply is unchanged because the two policies offset exactly.
Only quantity supplied falls along the same curve.
items.feedback: The combined change raises marginal cost by $2 per unit, reducing supply at each price.

items.stem: A subsidy lowers marginal cost by $3 per unit, while a regulation raises marginal cost by $3 per unit. What happens to supply if those are the only changes?
options: Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers marginal cost by more than the regulation raises it
Supply shifts left because the regulation raises marginal cost by more than the subsidy lowers it
Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because the product's market price increases
The two per-unit effects offset, so supply is unchanged.
items.feedback: Equal and opposite per-unit cost changes leave marginal cost, and therefore supply, unchanged.

items.stem: Four firms each supply q=2P units at every price. Demand is Qd=120-4P. One firm exits permanently, with the surviving firms’ schedules unchanged. Which statement correctly compares market equilibrium before and after exit?
options: Price rises from $10 to $12; quantity falls from 80 to 72 as remaining firms move along their unchanged individual schedules.
Price stays $10 and quantity becomes 60; unchanged individual schedules prevent equilibrium price adjustment.
Price falls from $10 to $8; exit shifts each surviving firm’s individual supply curve right.
Price rises from $10 to $12 and quantity rises from 80 to 96 because four firms remain in the aggregate schedule.
items.feedback: Before exit supply is 8P, so 120-4P=8P gives P=10, Q=80. Afterward supply is 6P, giving P=12, Q=72. Market supply shifts because a seller exits; survivors respond along unchanged individual supply curves.

items.stem: Technology improves while the expected future selling price rises sharply and firms store current output. What is the strongest conclusion about current supply?
options: Current supply increases because improved technology and storing output for future sale both add to current market supply.
The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
Current supply decreases because the expected future price rises sharply, which establishes that withholding outweighs the technology improvement.
Quantity supplied moves along one curve because both events change the product's current price.
items.feedback: Better technology increases current supply, while withholding output for a higher expected future price reduces current supply. The word “sharply” does not quantify the withholding effect relative to the technology effect, so the net direction remains uncertain. Neither determinant is a change in the product’s current price along a fixed curve.

items.stem: If demand is less elastic than supply, why do buyers bear more of a tax?
options: Buyers are less able to reduce quantity demanded when price rises
Buyers legally pay all taxes
Sellers are less able to adjust quantity supplied
Demand shifts right after the tax
items.feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.

items.stem: If supply is perfectly inelastic and demand is elastic, who bears the tax burden?
options: Sellers bear all of it.
Buyers bear all of it
No one bears it
The government bears it because supply is vertical
items.feedback: With perfectly inelastic supply, quantity supplied cannot respond to the tax. Sellers therefore bear the entire tax burden through a lower net price received.

items.stem: Using the original equilibrium price as the benchmark, how is the per-unit tax burden divided in the graph?
options: Buyers bear $3; sellers bear $3
Buyers bear $2; sellers bear $4
Buyers bear $4; sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $1; sellers bear $5
items.feedback: The original price is $15. Buyers pay $18 after the tax and sellers receive $12, so each side bears $3 of the $6 tax.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What percentage of the $8 tax burden is borne by buyers?
options: 25 percent
75 percent
50 percent
100 percent
items.feedback: The buyer price rises by $6. Buyers therefore bear $6 of the $8 tax, or 75%.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Relative to the original $10 equilibrium price, how is the $4 tax burden divided?
options: Buyers bear all $4; sellers bear none.
Sellers bear all $4; buyers bear none.
Buyers gain $2; sellers bear $6.
Buyers bear $2; sellers bear $2.
items.feedback: Buyer price rises to 12 and seller price falls to 8.

items.stem: A $12 tax causes buyers to pay $7 more and sellers to receive $5 less. Demand is likely less elastic than supply because:
options: Buyers bear more of the tax burden
Sellers bear more of the tax burden
The legal tax must have been placed on buyers
The tax increased quantity sold
items.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. Buyers bear $7, so demand is likely less elastic.

items.stem: A tax is imposed on a good with elastic demand and highly inelastic supply. Which result is most likely?
options: Sellers bear most of the burden
Buyers bear most of the burden
Demand increases because the tax is high
The legal assignment alone determines burden
items.feedback: The less elastic side bears more. If supply is highly inelastic, sellers bear most of the tax.

items.stem: A student says, 'The price rose after the tax, so buyers paid the entire tax.' What is the flaw?
options: Buyers bear only the increase above the old equilibrium price.
Any price increase means buyers pay everything
Sellers cannot bear taxes if buyers pay more
Tax incidence is unrelated to prices
items.feedback: Buyers bear the part of the tax reflected in the higher price they pay; sellers bear the part reflected in the lower price they receive.

items.stem: Before tax, price is $20. After tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. Which statement correctly splits the burden?
options: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
Buyers bear $6 and sellers bear $0
Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18
items.feedback: Buyers pay $4 more than before, while sellers receive $2 less than before.

items.stem: Before a tax, buyers pay $30 and sellers receive $30. After a tax, buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Who bears more of the burden?
options: Buyers
Sellers
They split it equally
No one bears any burden
items.feedback: Buyers pay $4 more, while sellers receive $3 less. Buyers bear more of the burden.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the buyers’ tax burden on the units still traded, excluding surplus lost on missing trades?
items.feedback: The per-unit buyer burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. On the units still sold after the tax, what is the sellers’ total loss from receiving a lower price? Exclude surplus lost on sales that no longer occur.
items.feedback: The per-unit seller burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. On the units still traded, what is the combined tax burden on buyers and sellers, equal to government tax revenue?
items.feedback: The $6 wedge applies to 80 continuing trades, so the rectangle is $480. This is the combined per-unit incidence times taxed quantity. Lost gains from the missing trades are additional welfare loss and are not government revenue.

items.stem: For the units still purchased after the tax, what is the buyers’ total additional payment compared with paying the original price for those same units? Exclude the welfare effect of purchases forgone.
options: $200: $2.50 extra on each of 80 units
$300: $3 extra on each of 100 units
$240: $3 extra on each of 80 units
$250: $2.50 extra on each of 100 units
items.feedback: The graph shows the buyer price rising from $15 to $18 and after-tax quantity falling to 80. The extra payment on purchases still made is ($18-$15)*80=$240. Lost gains on the 20 forgone purchases are excluded.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. A seller group divides the fall in total sales revenue after paying the tax by the 80 units still sold and calls the result its tax burden per unit still sold. Why is that calculation misleading?
options: The $540 decline in sales revenue includes fewer units sold; the tax burden per unit still sold is $3.
The $540 decline in sales revenue is entirely a price effect; the burden on each continuing unit is $6.75.
The $240 decline in sales revenue includes fewer units sold; the tax burden per unit still sold is $6.
The $300 decline in sales revenue is entirely a quantity effect; the tax burden per unit still sold is $0.
items.feedback: Receipts fall from $15 x 100 = $1,500 to $12 x 80 = $960, a $540 decline. This combines $300 from 20 fewer units valued at the old price and $240 from receiving $3 less on each of 80 continuing sales. The per-unit seller tax burden is $15 - $12 = $3; gross receipts are not a measure of producer surplus.

items.stem: A $6 tax is imposed. Before the tax, buyers paid $20. After the tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. How much of the tax burden falls on buyers and sellers?
options: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
Buyers bear all $6 and sellers bear $0
Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18
items.feedback: Buyers now pay $4 more than before. Sellers receive $2 less than before. The $6 tax burden is split $4 on buyers and $2 on sellers.

items.stem: Demand is much less elastic than supply. A tax is imposed on the good. Who bears more of the tax burden, and why?
options: Buyers bear more because they are less able to reduce quantity demanded
Sellers bear more because supply is more elastic
Buyers and sellers must split the burden equally
Sellers bear more because buyers pay the tax through the market price
items.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax because it is less able to change behavior in response to the tax.

items.stem: Supply is much less elastic than demand. A tax is imposed. What is the likely result?
options: Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive
Buyers bear more of the burden because demand is more elastic
The burden must be equal because the tax wedge is fixed
The side required to remit the tax bears more because statutory payment determines the economic burden
items.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic than demand, sellers bear more of the burden.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the tax wedge and what happens to quantity sold?
options: The wedge is $6 and quantity falls from 100 to 80
The wedge is $3 and quantity falls from 100 to 80
The wedge is $6 and quantity rises from 80 to 100
The wedge is $30 and quantity stays at 100
items.feedback: The wedge is $18 - $12 = $6, and quantity falls from 100 before the tax to 80 after the tax.

items.stem: What is the full per-unit tax in the graph, and why is the increase in buyer price alone insufficient to measure it?
options: $6; buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less than before.
$8; buyers pay $4 more and sellers receive $4 less than before.
$6; only the buyer-price increase is part of the tax, and the seller-receipt decline should be excluded.
$8; only the buyer-price increase is part of the tax, and the seller-receipt decline should be excluded.
items.feedback: The original price is 15; taxed buyers pay 18 and sellers receive 12. The wedge is 18−12 = 6, combining each side’s 3 burden. A tax wedge uses both prices, not just the change faced by buyers.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. After the tax is imposed, how much tax revenue is collected?
items.feedback: Read the $4 per-movie wedge and the 100-thousand post-tax quantity from the graph. Revenue is $4 × 100,000 = $400,000.

items.stem: What revenue and quantity change are shown?
options: Revenue is 800,000 dollars; trips rise by 50 thousand
Revenue is 600,000 dollars; trips do not change
Revenue is 600,000 dollars; trips fall by 50 thousand
Revenue is 400,000 dollars; trips fall by 150 thousand
items.feedback: Four dollars times 150 thousand is 600,000; quantity falls by 50 thousand.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. How much daily tax revenue is generated?
options: 400,000 dollars
1,000,000 dollars
1,200,000 dollars
800,000 dollars
items.feedback: The 4 dollar wedge applies to 200 thousand trips.

items.stem: What daily tax revenue is shown?
options: 400,000 dollars
800,000 dollars
1.2 million dollars
1.6 million dollars
items.feedback: The 8 dollar wedge applies to 150 thousand trips.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. For the buyer-side tax, what are the wedge and revenue?
options: A 6 dollar wedge and 900,000
An 8 dollar wedge and 1.2 million dollars
An 8 dollar wedge and 1.6 million
A 2 dollar wedge and 300,000
items.feedback: Buyers pay 16, sellers receive 8, and 150 thousand tickets are taxed.

items.stem: A market begins in equilibrium. A tax is imposed, and quantity falls from 1,000 to 850. Buyers pay $4 more and sellers receive $6 less. What is the tax revenue?
items.feedback: The tax is $4 + $6 = $10 per unit. Revenue is $10 × 850 = $8,500.

items.stem: A market starts at price $40. After a tax, buyers pay $46 and sellers receive $34. Quantity sold falls from 500 to 420. What is total tax revenue?
items.feedback: The tax is $46 - $34 = $12. Tax revenue is $12 × 420 = $5,040.

items.stem: Calculate the changes in the buyer’s price, the seller’s receipt and quantity traded after the tax. What separates the two prices?
options: Buyer price rises $2, seller receipt falls $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand; a tax separates buyer and seller prices.
Buyer price rises $3, seller receipt falls $3 and quantity falls 75 thousand; a tax separates buyer and seller prices.
Buyer price rises $2, seller receipt falls $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand; both sides still face the same price after tax.
Buyer price rises $3, seller receipt falls $3 and quantity falls 75 thousand; both sides still face the same price after tax.
items.feedback: The untaxed point is P = 12, Q = 250 thousand. After tax buyers pay 14, sellers receive 10 and Q = 200 thousand. The wedge changes both prices and reduces the amount traded.

items.stem: A clerk multiplies only the buyer-price increase by the original quantity and reports $300 of revenue. Calculate the correct revenue and identify both errors.
options: $6 on 80 units gives $480; use both sides of the wedge and the post-tax quantity.
$8 on 70 units gives $560; use both sides of the wedge and the post-tax quantity.
$6 on 80 units gives $480; the buyer-price increase alone and the untaxed quantity are the correct definitions.
$8 on 70 units gives $560; the buyer-price increase alone and the untaxed quantity are the correct definitions.
items.feedback: The graph has Pb 18, Ps 12 and taxed Q 80. Full tax 6 times 80 gives 480, which is 180 above the report. Using only the buyer increase 3 misses the seller burden; using 100 wrongly includes trades that no longer occur.

items.stem: Before a tax, price is $20 and quantity is 1,000. Afterwards buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18 and 850 units trade. An analyst says the buyer burden is the entire tax and calculates revenue using the original quantity. Which correction is right?
options: The wedge is $6, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $2; revenue is $5,100.
The wedge is $4, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $0; revenue is $3,400.
The wedge is $6, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $2; revenue is $6,000.
The wedge is $6, buyers bear $6 per unit and sellers $0; revenue is $5,100.
items.feedback: The wedge is $24−$18=$6, split into the $4 buyer-price increase and $2 seller-receipt decrease. Only 850 units are taxed, so revenue is $6×850=$5,100.

items.stem: A tax produces a $6 wedge and 850 sales, down from 1,000 without tax. A proposed increase would produce an $8 wedge and 600 sales. Which comparison correctly evaluates revenue and lost trades?
options: Revenue falls from $5,100 to $4,800 while lost trades increase from 150 to 400.
Revenue rises from $5,100 to $6,800 while lost trades remain 150.
Revenue falls from $6,000 to $4,800 while lost trades decrease from 400 to 150.
Revenue rises from $5,100 to $6,000 while lost trades increase from 150 to 400.
items.feedback: Revenue uses the quantity remaining under each tax: $6×850=$5,100 versus $8×600=$4,800. Relative to 1,000 untaxed trades, losses are 150 and 400. A higher rate does not guarantee more revenue.

items.stem: An unregulated market trades 100 units. A binding ceiling makes sellers offer 60 units while buyers want 140; a tax instead produces 70 trades with buyers paying $12 and sellers receiving $9. Assume no evasion or government purchases. Which policy comparison follows?
options: The ceiling limits trades to 60 and leaves a shortage of 80; the tax permits 70 trades and raises $210.
The ceiling permits 140 trades and leaves a shortage of 80; the tax permits 70 trades and raises $210.
The ceiling limits trades to 60 and leaves a shortage of 40; the tax permits 70 trades and raises $300.
The ceiling limits trades to 100 and leaves a shortage of 40; the tax permits 70 trades and raises $210.
items.feedback: Ceiling trades are limited by the 60 units supplied, and shortage is 140−60=80. Under the tax, the $3 wedge on 70 actual trades yields $210. The two policies reduce trades by different mechanisms.

items.stem: An economy has 180 million employed, 12 million unemployed, and 68 million not in the labor force. What are the unemployment rate and labor force participation rate?
options: 6.25% unemployment and 73.85% participation
6.67% unemployment and 69.23% participation
4.62% unemployment and 73.85% participation
6.25% unemployment and 69.23% participation
items.feedback: Labor force = 192M; unemployment = 12/192 = 6.25%; adult population = 260M; participation = 192/260 = 73.85%.

items.stem: An economy has 95 employed, 5 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. Ten people who were not in the labor force begin looking for work but do not find jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?
items.feedback: Unemployed rises to 15 and labor force rises to 110, so unemployment = 15/110 = 13.6%.

items.stem: An economy has 100 employed and 20 unemployed. Five unemployed workers find jobs, while five others stop looking. What happens to the unemployment rate?
options: It falls because unemployment decreases and the labor force shrinks
It rises because employment rises
It stays unchanged because ten workers changed status
It becomes zero
items.feedback: Unemployed falls to 10 and labor force falls to 115, so the unemployment rate falls from 16.7% to about 8.7%.

items.stem: If the unemployment rate falls because many jobless workers stop searching, what is the best interpretation?
options: Discouraged workers can lower the rate without employment gains.
Employment must have increased strongly
Structural unemployment disappeared
GDP must have increased
items.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if discouraged workers leave the labor force.

items.stem: A person has no job, wants work, is available, but has not searched in six weeks because they think no jobs exist. How is this person classified and why does it matter?
options: Outside the labor force; this can understate labor-market weakness
Unemployed; all jobless people are counted
Employed; wanting work is enough
Structurally employed; skills do not matter
items.feedback: Without active search, discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed, which can understate weakness.

items.stem: A laid-off engineer searches actively for work in the same field. A retired teacher does not want work. A discouraged factory worker wants work but stopped searching. Who is counted as unemployed?
options: Only the laid-off engineer
The engineer and retired teacher
The engineer and discouraged factory worker
All three
items.feedback: Only jobless people actively searching are counted as unemployed.

items.stem: An economy has 155 million employed, 9 million unemployed, and 96 million not in the labor force. What are the unemployment rate and labor force participation rate?
options: 5.49% unemployment and 63.08% participation
5.81% unemployment and 59.62% participation
3.46% unemployment and 63.08% participation
5.49% unemployment and 59.62% participation
items.feedback: Labor force = 164M; unemployment = 9/164 = 5.49%; adult population = 260M; participation = 164/260 = 63.08%.

items.stem: An economy has 120 employed, 8 unemployed, and 72 not in the labor force. Four unemployed workers find jobs, and six people outside the labor force begin searching but do not find work. What is the new unemployment rate?
items.feedback: New employed = 124, unemployed = 10, labor force = 134. Unemployment = 10/134 = 7.46%.

items.stem: Adult population is 300 million. Labor force participation is 62%. The unemployment rate is 5%. How many people are unemployed?
options: 9.3 million
15 million
114 million
186 million
items.feedback: Labor force = 0.62 x 300 = 186M. Unemployed = 0.05 x 186 = 9.3M.

items.stem: The unemployment rate falls from 6% to 5%, but employment also falls. What likely happened?
options: Some unemployed workers left the labor force
Labor demand must have increased
Every discouraged worker found a job
The adult population became zero
items.feedback: The unemployment rate can fall even when employment falls if enough jobless workers stop searching.

items.stem: An economy has 200 adults. 130 are employed and 10 are unemployed. If 10 employed workers retire and stop looking for work, what happens to labor force participation?
options: It falls from 70% to 65%
It rises from 65% to 70%
It stays at 70%
It falls from 65% to 60%
items.feedback: Initial labor force = 140, participation = 70%. New labor force = 130, participation = 65%.

items.stem: A recession causes job loss, and some unemployed workers become discouraged. Why might the unemployment rate understate the recession's damage?
options: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop searching
Discouraged workers are counted twice
All discouraged workers are counted as employed
The unemployment rate includes only retired people
items.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, which can hide labor market weakness.

items.stem: An economy has 90 employed, 10 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. Five employed workers lose jobs and search; five unemployed workers stop searching. What happens to unemployment rate?
options: It rises slightly to 10.5%
It rises to 15%
It falls to 5%
It becomes 0%
items.feedback: Employed falls to 85. Five newly unemployed workers replace five workers who stop searching, so unemployed remains 10 and the labor force falls to 95. The rate is 10/95 = 10.53%.

items.stem: A jobless worker applied to three jobs last week. Another jobless worker wants work but last searched two months ago. A third works 3 hours per week but wants full-time work. How are they classified?
options: Unemployed; not in labor force; employed
Unemployed; unemployed; unemployed
Employed; unemployed; not in labor force
Not in labor force; unemployed; employed
items.feedback: Recent active search means unemployed; no recent search means not in labor force; any paid work means employed.

items.stem: If measured unemployment falls because 1M unemployed workers become discouraged, while employment is unchanged, what happens to labor force participation?
options: It falls
It rises
It stays unchanged
It becomes equal to unemployment
items.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, so labor force participation falls.

items.stem: Adult population is 250 million, labor force participation is 64%, and unemployment is 8 million. How many people are employed?
options: 152 million
160 million
242 million
168 million
items.feedback: Labor force = 0.64 x 250 = 160 million. Employed = 160 - 8 = 152 million.

items.stem: An economy has 170 employed and 17 unemployed adults. Two separate policy evaluations observe the same fall in unemployed people. In A, they find jobs; in B, they stop searching. With adult population fixed, which extra indicator distinguishes the cases?
options: Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed
Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
Employment is unchanged and participation falls in A; employment rises with unchanged participation in B
Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls
items.feedback: Job finding moves people within the labor force from unemployed to employed. Discouragement moves people out of unemployment and the labor force without raising employment. The same unemployment change can conceal different labor outcomes.

items.stem: Of 180 employed workers, ten full-time workers lose half their hours but retain paid jobs. No one enters or leaves the labor force. Which observation would reveal the deterioration that the official unemployment rate misses?
options: Hours fall; employment, unemployment and participation remain unchanged.
Employment falls by five; two half-time jobs equal one employed person.
Unemployment rises by ten; each loss of full-time hours counts as joblessness.
Participation falls by ten; paid part-time workers leave the labor force.
items.feedback: A paid part-time worker is employed. Head-count employment, UR and LFPR can stay constant while hours and underemployment worsen; hours-based evidence supplies the missing margin.

items.stem: Initially 190 adults are employed and 19 unemployed. A recession causes 9 employed workers to lose jobs and actively search, while an equal number of previously unemployed people stop searching. Which joint result can occur?
options: Employment falls but participation is fixed; unemployment head count doubles
Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed
Employment falls and unemployment head count falls; the unemployment rate necessarily falls
Employment and labor-force participation fall; unemployment head count stays fixed and its rate rises
items.feedback: Layoffs move employed people to unemployment; discouraged exits remove an equal number from unemployment. U is unchanged, E and the labor force fall, so U/LF rises. Equal flows do not cancel employment or participation effects.

items.stem: A survey records 126 employed adults, 14 available jobless adults actively searching, and 60 adults outside the labor force. Which participation calculation is correct, and how does it differ from unemployment?
options: 70% participation; unemployment uses 14 divided by 140
63% participation; unemployment uses 14 divided by 200
90% participation; unemployment uses 14 divided by 126
7% participation; unemployment and participation are the same ratio
items.feedback: Participation is (126 + 14)/(126 + 14 + 60) = 70%. Unemployment instead divides the 14 unemployed by the labor force of 140, yielding 10%. The denominators answer different questions.

items.stem: Of 400 adults, 200 are employed and 20 are unemployed and actively looking for work. A survey also finds 20 people who want work but have stopped searching. What are the unemployment rate and labor-force participation rate?
options: Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%
Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%
Include discouraged workers only in the labor force; UR is about 8.3% and LFPR is 60%
items.feedback: The labor force is 200+20 = 220. The discouraged are not active searchers. UR = 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9.1%; LFPR = 1.1/2 = 55%.

items.stem: Employment is 210 and unemployment is 21. Then 10 previously inactive adults begin actively searching; nobody finds or loses a job. Which interpretation reconciles the rate change with employment?
options: Employment is unchanged while unemployment and participation rise; the rate increase does not show job destruction
Employment falls while unemployment rises; every new searcher must have left a job
Employment rises and unemployment falls; entering the labor force counts as finding work
Employment is unchanged and both rates are unchanged; inactive adults cannot affect the denominator
items.feedback: Active searchers without jobs enter both unemployment and the labor force. Employment is unchanged; unemployment rises relative to the larger labor force, and participation rises. A higher unemployment rate need not mean jobs were lost.

items.stem: A jobless adult who had stopped searching accepts a paid part-time job but still wants full-time work. With other adults unchanged, which immediate changes follow?
options: Employment and the labor force rise; involuntary part-time work can remain
Unemployment rises because the worker still wants a full-time job
Employment rises but the labor force stays fixed because the job is part time
Participation falls because part-time employment is outside the labor force
items.feedback: The worker moves from outside the labor force to employed. Both employment and the labor force rise, while wanting more hours does not change the official employed classification. The hours shortfall remains relevant to labor-market well-being.

items.stem: An economy has 220 employed and 22 unemployed adults. Two separate policy evaluations observe the same fall in unemployed people. In A, they find jobs; in B, they stop searching. With adult population fixed, which extra indicator distinguishes the cases?
options: Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls
Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed
Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
Employment is unchanged and participation falls in A; employment rises with unchanged participation in B
items.feedback: Job finding moves people within the labor force from unemployed to employed. Discouragement moves people out of unemployment and the labor force without raising employment. The same unemployment change can conceal different labor outcomes.

items.stem: An economy has 120 employed, 12 unemployed, and 68 not in the labor force. Four unemployed workers find jobs, and four employed workers move to part-time work but keep paid jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?
items.feedback: New employed = 124, unemployed = 8, labor force = 132. Unemployment = 8/132 = 6.1%. Part-time workers remain employed.

items.stem: An economy has 200 adults, 120 employed, 10 unemployed, and 70 not in the labor force. Then 10 unemployed workers become discouraged. What are the new unemployment rate and participation rate?
options: 0% unemployment and 60% participation
5% unemployment and 65% participation
0% unemployment and 65% participation
10% unemployment and 60% participation
items.feedback: Unemployed becomes 0 and labor force becomes 120. Unemployment = 0%; participation = 120/200 = 60%.

items.stem: Consider three labor-market observations: a worker is counted as employed even though they want full-time work, another worker is not counted as unemployed because they stopped searching, and actual unemployment is above the natural rate. What do these observations tell us about labor-market conditions?
options: Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural proves only structural unemployment
Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
Part-time employment counts as unemployment, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits remain unemployed, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
items.feedback: This pulls together underemployment, discouraged workers, and cyclical unemployment.

items.stem: Of 500 adults, 250 are employed and 25 are unemployed and actively looking for work. A survey also finds 25 people who want work but have stopped searching. What are the unemployment rate and labor-force participation rate?
options: Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%
Include discouraged workers only in the labor force; UR is about 8.3% and LFPR is 60%
Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%
items.feedback: The labor force is 250+25 = 275. The discouraged are not active searchers. UR = 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9.1%; LFPR = 1.1/2 = 55%.

items.stem: Employment is 260 and unemployment is 26. Then 13 previously inactive adults begin actively searching; nobody finds or loses a job. Which interpretation reconciles the rate change with employment?
options: Employment rises and unemployment falls; entering the labor force counts as finding work
Employment is unchanged and both rates are unchanged; inactive adults cannot affect the denominator
Employment is unchanged while unemployment and participation rise; the rate increase does not show job destruction
Employment falls while unemployment rises; every new searcher must have left a job
items.feedback: Active searchers without jobs enter both unemployment and the labor force. Employment is unchanged; unemployment rises relative to the larger labor force, and participation rises. A higher unemployment rate need not mean jobs were lost.

items.stem: An economy has 270 employed and 27 unemployed adults. Two separate policy evaluations observe the same fall in unemployed people. In A, they find jobs; in B, they stop searching. With adult population fixed, which extra indicator distinguishes the cases?
options: Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed
Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
Employment is unchanged and participation falls in A; employment rises with unchanged participation in B
Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls
items.feedback: Job finding moves people within the labor force from unemployed to employed. Discouragement moves people out of unemployment and the labor force without raising employment. The same unemployment change can conceal different labor outcomes.

items.stem: Employment rises by 100,000, unemployment rises by 50,000, and labor-force participation rises. What likely happened?
options: The labor force must have shrunk
The labor force grew faster than employment
The unemployment rate must be zero
Everyone who entered the labor force became employed
items.feedback: Unemployment can rise when more people enter the labor force and some are still searching.

items.stem: Of 200 adults, 100 are employed and 10 are unemployed and actively looking for work. A survey also finds 10 people who want work but have stopped searching. What are the unemployment rate and labor-force participation rate?
options: Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%
Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%
Include discouraged workers only in the labor force; UR is about 8.3% and LFPR is 60%
items.feedback: The labor force is 100+10 = 110. The discouraged are not active searchers. UR = 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9.1%; LFPR = 1.1/2 = 55%.

items.stem: Employment is 110 and unemployment is 11. Then 5 previously inactive adults begin actively searching; nobody finds or loses a job. Which interpretation reconciles the rate change with employment?
options: Employment is unchanged while unemployment and participation rise; the rate increase does not show job destruction
Employment falls while unemployment rises; every new searcher must have left a job
Employment rises and unemployment falls; entering the labor force counts as finding work
Employment is unchanged and both rates are unchanged; inactive adults cannot affect the denominator
items.feedback: Active searchers without jobs enter both unemployment and the labor force. Employment is unchanged; unemployment rises relative to the larger labor force, and participation rises. A higher unemployment rate need not mean jobs were lost.

items.stem: A worker is laid off when a recession cuts sales. By the time demand recovers, the firm has automated the old job and the worker lacks the new required skills. What best describes the worker’s unemployment now?
options: It began as cyclical but is now primarily structural
It remains purely cyclical because the original layoff occurred in a recession
It is frictional because every unemployed worker is searching
It is no longer unemployment once the original recession ends
items.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

items.stem: A worker is laid off because a recession reduces sales. Six months later, the worker's old industry adopts technology that permanently eliminates the job type. How should the unemployment diagnosis change?
options: Cyclical at first; structural if the job type disappears
It is always frictional
It is never unemployment
It must be natural unemployment only
items.feedback: Weak demand causes cyclical unemployment, but permanent skill/job mismatch is structural.

items.stem: A regional downturn eliminates jobs at several firms. One year later overall demand has recovered, but many displaced workers remain unemployed because growing industries require different credentials. Which diagnosis is most accurate?
options: Cyclical unemployment fell, while structural unemployment remains
The remaining unemployment must still be entirely cyclical
The recovery eliminates both structural and frictional unemployment
The remaining unemployment is frictional simply because workers are looking for jobs
items.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

items.stem: With a fixed labor force, unemployment initially consists of 2 percentage points from normal job search, 3 from persistent skill mismatch and 4 from recession layoffs. Recovery removes the recession component, while improved matching reduces normal search to 1 point. What happens to the natural rate and the final actual unemployment rate?
options: The natural rate falls from 5% to 4%, and final actual unemployment is 4%
The natural rate stays at 5%, and final actual unemployment is 4%
The natural rate falls from 9% to 4%, and final actual unemployment is 4%
The natural rate falls from 5% to 1%, and final actual unemployment is 1%
items.feedback: Normal search is frictional and persistent mismatch is structural, so the initial natural rate is 2+3=5%. Better matching makes it 1+3=4%. Recovery removes cyclical unemployment; final actual unemployment therefore equals that 4% natural rate.

items.stem: A regional study follows 150 jobless workers after national demand recovers. Former miners still lack skills for local health-care vacancies, while new graduates are interviewing for matching jobs. Which diagnosis and response pair is appropriate?
options: Miners face structural mismatch suited to retraining; graduates face frictional search suited to matching assistance
Miners face cyclical unemployment suited only to demand stimulus; graduates face structural unemployment suited to changing industries
Both groups face cyclical unemployment because neither is currently employed
Both groups face structural unemployment because job search always requires new skills
items.feedback: The persistence of a skill mismatch after demand recovers identifies a structural problem. Graduates searching for suitable existing matches illustrate frictional unemployment. Each remedy should address its actual mechanism.

items.stem: Demand has recovered, yet displaced factory workers remain unemployed while hospitals advertise vacancies requiring different credentials. Which observation changes the diagnosis and policy emphasis?
options: Recovered demand proves the remaining unemployment is cyclical and requires only more spending
Vacancies prove the workers are already employed, so no labor-market issue remains
Different credentials show purely frictional search that cannot be helped by training
Unfilled jobs with incompatible skills point to structural mismatch and retraining, beyond demand support
items.feedback: Recovery removes the original demand explanation as a sufficient account. Simultaneous vacancies and missing credentials identify a mismatch that demand stimulus alone need not solve.

items.stem: Job vacancies and active job seekers both remain high in a region with 170 displaced workers, even after aggregate sales return to normal. Which added evidence best distinguishes persistent mismatch from ordinary search?
options: Whether every unemployed worker has zero current earnings
Whether the statistical agency counts the employed in the labor force
Whether the workers' skills and locations fit the available vacancies
Whether job seekers want higher real incomes than before
items.feedback: Vacancies alongside unemployment can reflect search or mismatch. Evidence about skill/location fit addresses that distinction; the other facts do not identify its source.

items.stem: A skills survey finds qualified applicants but slow vacancy matching. A separate industry has vacancies requiring qualifications its displaced workers lack. Which allocation addresses both frictions directly?
options: Classify both groups as outside the labor force; neither can affect unemployment.
Improve matching for qualified applicants; retrain workers facing the qualification gap.
Retrain all qualified applicants; improve matching alone for the qualification gap.
Expand aggregate demand for both groups; matching and skills are already adequate.
items.feedback: Slow matching of otherwise qualified workers is frictional. A mismatch between workers' skills and vacancies is structural. Matching assistance and retraining address different barriers rather than substituting automatically for one another.

items.stem: A worker is first laid off because recession reduces sales. Sales later recover, but the old job has been permanently automated and available vacancies require skills the worker lacks. Why might restoring aggregate demand alone no longer remove this worker’s unemployment?
options: An initially structural loss has become cyclical, so demand recovery is irrelevant to the original layoff
Both stages are frictional search, so training cannot affect access to the new vacancies
Both stages are necessarily cyclical, so recovered sales guarantee a job regardless of required skills
An initially cyclical loss has become a structural mismatch, so the remaining barrier requires skills or matching adjustment
items.feedback: Weak aggregate demand explains the initial cyclical layoff. Once sales recover but skill mismatch blocks reemployment, the remaining unemployment is structural. Demand restoration does not by itself supply the newly required skills.

items.stem: Unemployment rises from its estimated natural rate of 5% to 8% during a recession. After demand recovers, it returns to 5%, with skills and labor-market institutions unchanged. What portion of the recession unemployment rate was cyclical, and what does the remaining 5% imply for policy?
options: About 5 percentage points were cyclical; the remaining 3 points show that demand has not recovered.
All 8 percentage points were cyclical; a return to normal demand should therefore eliminate unemployment.
About 3 percentage points were cyclical; eliminating the rest requires addressing search or structural factors rather than repeating demand stimulus.
About 3 percentage points were structural; the remaining 5 points must disappear with another demand expansion.
items.feedback: The recession gap above the natural rate is 8−5=3 points. Returning to the natural rate removes that cyclical component. Frictional and structural unemployment can remain at normal demand, so the remaining rate is not evidence of an equal demand shortfall.

items.stem: A matching platform shortens job searches, but a recession simultaneously reduces vacancies. Which prediction distinguishes the affected components without assuming their sizes?
options: Frictional falls, cyclical rises; the net change needs relative sizes.
Frictional falls, cyclical falls; improved matching offsets the recession's lost vacancies.
Frictional rises, cyclical rises; recession makes faster searches less effective by definition.
Frictional is unchanged, cyclical rises; faster searches affect participation alone.
items.feedback: Faster matching reduces normal search duration, while weaker demand creates cyclical joblessness. The net change cannot be signed without magnitudes.

items.stem: Job vacancies and active job seekers both remain high in a region with 220 displaced workers, even after aggregate sales return to normal. Which added evidence best distinguishes persistent mismatch from ordinary search?
options: Whether job seekers want higher real incomes than before
Whether every unemployed worker has zero current earnings
Whether the statistical agency counts the employed in the labor force
Whether the workers' skills and locations fit the available vacancies
items.feedback: Vacancies alongside unemployment can reflect search or mismatch. Evidence about skill/location fit addresses that distinction; the other facts do not identify its source.

items.stem: A job-search platform improves matching, but firms simultaneously require a new certification that many applicants lack. The unemployment rate is unchanged. Does that result prove the platform failed?
options: Yes; unchanged total unemployment proves every component remained unchanged.
No; certification changes cyclical unemployment while matching changes only participation.
Yes; improved matching should immediately supply every missing certification.
No; a frictional reduction can be offset by a new structural barrier.
items.feedback: An unchanged total can conceal offsetting component changes. Faster matching may lower frictional unemployment while the new qualification barrier raises structural unemployment. The aggregate outcome does not isolate the platform's effect.

items.stem: A retraining program reduces unemployment caused by persistent skill mismatch by 2 percentage points. At the same time a recession raises unemployment from weak sales by 2 points. Frictional unemployment and the labor force are unchanged. A report says the unchanged total proves retraining did not lower the natural rate. Which conclusion follows?
options: The natural rate falls 2 points, while rising cyclical unemployment offsets that improvement in the measured total
The natural rate is unchanged because equal changes in structural and cyclical unemployment cancel within it
The natural rate rises 2 points because recession unemployment is its only changing component
The natural rate falls 4 points because both changes reduce persistent skill mismatch
items.feedback: Retraining reduces structural unemployment, a component of the natural rate. Cyclical unemployment is outside that benchmark. Its increase offsets the structural fall in actual unemployment, not in the natural rate.

items.stem: Vacancies increase in a region, yet long-term unemployment remains high. Qualified applicants are hired quickly, but most long-term job seekers fail employers’ skill requirements. What evidence supports retraining rather than a general job-information campaign?
options: Existing information produces quick matches for qualified applicants; the persistent unemployed lack the skills needed for the vacancies.
The rise in vacancies proves aggregate demand is too low; retraining works mainly by reducing spending.
Quick hiring of qualified applicants proves all remaining unemployment is voluntary search for better offers.
The coexistence of vacancies and unemployment proves workers need more vacancy listings regardless of their qualifications.
items.feedback: Fast matches among qualified applicants indicate that missing vacancy information is not the main obstacle for this group. The evidence identifies a skills mismatch among the long-term unemployed, which retraining can address.

items.stem: Job vacancies and active job seekers both remain high in a region with 270 displaced workers, even after aggregate sales return to normal. Which added evidence best distinguishes persistent mismatch from ordinary search?
options: Whether the statistical agency counts the employed in the labor force
Whether the workers' skills and locations fit the available vacancies
Whether job seekers want higher real incomes than before
Whether every unemployed worker has zero current earnings
items.feedback: Vacancies alongside unemployment can reflect search or mismatch. Evidence about skill/location fit addresses that distinction; the other facts do not identify its source.

items.stem: A recession ends and firms restore spending, but displaced workers still lack the qualifications for available jobs. Which inference limits the claim that demand recovery eliminates the remaining unemployment?
options: Recovery can remove cyclical weakness; the qualification mismatch can remain structural.
Recovery removes structural mismatch; remaining joblessness must be entirely cyclical.
Recovery turns qualified job seekers into nonparticipants; unemployment therefore disappears.
Recovery eliminates frictional search; remaining vacancies prove no skill mismatch exists.
items.feedback: Demand recovery can restore jobs lost through weak spending. It does not by itself change workers' qualifications, so a structural mismatch can remain after the cyclical component shrinks.

items.stem: Group A lost jobs because economy-wide sales fell; their skills still match the jobs firms would offer at normal sales. Group B is searching between jobs even at normal sales. If the economy returns to potential output with matching conditions unchanged, which forecast follows?
options: A’s structural unemployment must remain; B’s frictional search must disappear
A’s frictional unemployment should recede; B’s cyclical unemployment can remain
Both groups must remain unemployed because returning to potential never affects hiring
A’s cyclical unemployment should recede; B’s frictional search can remain
items.feedback: Restoring normal demand removes the stated cyclical reason for A’s layoff. Potential output is compatible with ongoing frictional job search, so it does not imply zero unemployment for B.

items.stem: Automation removes routine jobs while creating technical vacancies. Aggregate spending and total vacancies remain strong, but displaced workers lack the required certification. A wage subsidy for the old jobs ends after six months; a training program leads to recognized certification. Which policy addresses the persistent unemployment mechanism, and why might the subsidy’s effect fade?
options: The subsidy addresses cyclical unemployment permanently; training cannot affect employability while vacancies remain strong.
Training only speeds frictional search; the subsidy permanently restores the old demand for routine tasks.
Training addresses the skill mismatch; the temporary subsidy may postpone displacement without qualifying workers for the new vacancies.
Both policies permanently remove the mismatch because any temporary employment creates the required certification.
items.feedback: The obstacle is the changed demand for skills, not weak aggregate spending. Certification targets that structural mismatch. A temporary subsidy may support employment while it operates without changing workers’ qualifications for the new jobs.

items.stem: A recession idles workers in otherwise viable firms. A separate group loses jobs permanently to automation and lacks the skills sought by expanding firms. Which policy comparison recognizes the two causes?
options: Demand recovery helps both groups; automation creates only a spending shortfall.
Demand recovery helps recession layoffs; retraining helps the automation mismatch.
Retraining helps both groups; recession layoffs indicate only a skills mismatch.
Neither helps either group; retaining no job places both outside the labor force.
items.feedback: Weak aggregate demand creates cyclical unemployment; a changed pattern of skill demand creates structural unemployment. Recovery need not reverse a permanent mismatch.

items.stem: Job vacancies and active job seekers both remain high in a region with 120 displaced workers, even after aggregate sales return to normal. Which added evidence best distinguishes persistent mismatch from ordinary search?
options: Whether the workers' skills and locations fit the available vacancies
Whether job seekers want higher real incomes than before
Whether every unemployed worker has zero current earnings
Whether the statistical agency counts the employed in the labor force
items.feedback: Vacancies alongside unemployment can reflect search or mismatch. Evidence about skill/location fit addresses that distinction; the other facts do not identify its source.
